## Abhidhamma Piṭaka
## Pañcapakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā
## Dhātukathā-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
The Great Hero, the conqueror of the five Māras, who clearly revealed the various elements, having taught the Vibhaṅga in eighteen divisions, taught this Dhātukathā immediately following that Vibhaṅga.

I shall now clarify the meaning of that Dhātukathā; listen to that explanation with concentrated minds.

## 1. Mātikāvaṇṇanā
## 1. Nayamātikāvaṇṇanā
It is stated in the Atthasālinī that this Dhātukathā is divided into fourteen methods by virtue of terms such as "Inclusion and Non-inclusion" (saṅgaho asaṅgaho). The entirety of this Dhātukathā consists of two parts: the Summary (uddesa) and the Exposition (niddesa). Among them, the Matrix (mātikā) is called the Summary. That Matrix is of five kinds: the Matrix of Methods (nayamātikā), the Internal Matrix (abbhantaramātikā), the Matrix of the Doors of Methods (nayamukhamātikā), the Matrix of Characteristics (lakkhaṇamātikā), and the External Matrix (bāhiramātikā).

Among those five, this Matrix set forth with fourteen terms, starting from "Inclusion, Non-inclusion..." to "Inclusion and Non-inclusion by that which is dissociated" (vippayuttena saṅgahitaṃ asaṅgahitaṃ), is called the Nayamātikā. It is called Nayamātikā because it is established to show the analysis of the dhammas in the Dhātukathā through these methods such as inclusion. Since it is the foundation of these terms, it is also appropriate to call it the Root Matrix (mūlamātikā).
2:
## 2. Abbhantaramātikāvaṇṇanā
This Matrix, established with 125 terms starting from the five aggregates (khandha) up to attention (manasikāra), is called the Internal Matrix (abbhantaramātikā). Indeed, this Matrix is called Abbhantaramātikā because, instead of stating "the entire Dhammasaṅgaṇī is the matrix of the Dhātukathā," it specifically shows the dhammas such as the aggregates that are to be analyzed in detail through methods like inclusion, and places them within the Dhātukathā itself. Since these terms like the aggregates are not included in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Matrix, it is also appropriate to call it the Miscellaneous Matrix (pakiṇṇakamātikā).

## 3. Nayamukhamātikāvaṇṇanā
This Matrix, established with these four terms: "Inclusion by three," "Non-inclusion by three," "Association with four," and "Dissociation from four," is called the Nayamukhamātikā. Indeed, in this Matrix, for all the dhammas of the Matrix such as the five aggregates as well as the triads starting with the Wholesome (kusala-tika), inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) should be applied only through the three terms: aggregate, base, and element. Likewise, association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga) should be applied through the four mental aggregates. These are called Nayamukhamātikā because they are established to show the "doors" (mukha) or entry points for these methods of inclusion, non-inclusion, and so on.

## 4. Lakkhaṇamātikāvaṇṇanā
This Matrix, established with these two terms: "Homogeneous" (sabhāga) and "Heterogeneous" (visabhāga), is called the Lakkhaṇamātikā. Indeed, this is called Lakkhaṇamātikā because it is established to show the characteristics of inclusion and so on, by virtue of homogeneous and heterogeneous characteristics, such as the method of inclusion through dhammas having homogeneous characteristics, the method of non-inclusion through dhammas having heterogeneous characteristics, and likewise the methods of association and dissociation.

## 5. Bāhiramātikāvaṇṇanā
This Matrix, which states "the entire Dhammasaṅgaṇī is the matrix of the Dhātukathā," is called the External Matrix (bāhiramātikā) because it is established by summarizing the 66 triad terms and the 200 dyad terms. Indeed, it is called Bāhiramātikā because, instead of being stated within the Dhātukathā as "the five aggregates... attention," it is placed outside the Dhātukathā matrices as "the entire Dhammasaṅgaṇī."
3:
Having thus understood the existence of the Matrix in its fivefold division, now, in the texts starting with "Inclusion and Non-inclusion," inclusion (saṅgaha) is first of all fourfold: inclusion by class (jātisaṅgaha), inclusion by origin (sañjātisaṅgaha), inclusion by action (kiriyāsaṅgaha), and inclusion by counting (gaṇanāsaṅgaha).

Among those four, the inclusion expressed as, "Let all those of the Khattiya caste come, all those of the Brāhmaṇa caste, all those of the Vessa caste, all those of the Sudda caste come," or as, "Friend Visākha, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these dhammas are included in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha)," is called Jātisaṅgaha. This is because, just as in the statement "Let those of the same class come," here too all dhammas reach a single inclusion by way of their class.

The inclusion expressed as, "Let all those from the Kosala country come, all those from Magadha, all those from the village of Bhārukaccha come," or as, "Friend Visākha, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these dhammas are included in the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha)," is called Sañjātisaṅgaha. This is because, just as in the statement "Let those born and raised in the same place come," here too all dhammas reach a single inclusion by way of their place of birth or place of residence.

The inclusion expressed as, "Let all elephant-riders come, all horse-riders, all chariot-riders come," or as, "Friend Visākha, right view and right thought—these dhammas are included in the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha)," is called Kiriyāsaṅgaha. All these people and dhammas reach a single inclusion by way of performing their respective functions.

As in the question and answer, "In which aggregate is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) counted? It is counted in the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha)," if the eye-base is counted in the form-aggregate, because of that counting, it should certainly be said, "The eye-base is included in the form-aggregate." This is called Gaṇanāsaṅgaha. In this text, only this Gaṇanāsaṅgaha is intended. Non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) should be understood as the opposite of that inclusion. Through various classifications of that inclusion and non-inclusion, the methods such as "Inclusion with non-inclusion" (saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ) arise.

Association (sampayoga) occurs by way of having the same arising, the same cessation, the same physical base, and the same object. Dissociation (vippayoga) occurs as the opposite of that association. Through various classifications of that association and dissociation, the methods such as "Associated with dissociation" (sampayuttena vippayuttaṃ) arise. Through the combined classification of both inclusion-non-inclusion and association-dissociation, the methods such as "Included with association and dissociation" (saṅgahitena sampayuttaṃ vippayuttaṃ) arise.

Terms such as the five aggregates should be understood according to the methods taught in the Vibhaṅga and other texts. However, terms such as contact (phassa) in this Internal Matrix are taught because they are common to all consciousness-arisings associated with the nature of decision (adhimokkha).

## The Commentary on the Matrix is finished.

## 2. Niddesavaṇṇanā

## 1. Paṭhamanayo Saṅgahāsaṅgahapadavaṇṇanā

## 1. Khandhapadavaṇṇanā

Now, in order to show the matrix (mātikā) laid down by way of the five aggregates and so forth, in conjunction with the method matrix terms (nayamātikapada) such as 'inclusion' (saṅgaha) and 'non-inclusion' (asaṅgaha), the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra) is commenced with the method: "By how many aggregates is the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) [included]?" In this Niddesavāra, because the Method-Head Matrix (Nayamukhamātikā) is established for the Method Matrix (Nayamātikā) of 'inclusion, non-inclusion,' etc., as 'inclusion by three (aggregates, bases, elements), non-inclusion by three,' only the three terms—aggregates, bases, and elements—are extracted to show the inclusion (saṅgaha) of the form aggregate and so forth, as "By how many aggregates, by how many bases, by how many elements [is it included]?" Not even one of the terms such as 'the four truths' is dealt with.

Because the Characteristic Matrix (Lakkhaṇamātikā) is established as 'homogeneous' (sabhāga) and 'heterogeneous' (visabhāga), it is stated in the answer to this question: "The form aggregate is [included] by one aggregate," and so forth. This is because these aggregates and so forth are homogeneous (sabhāga) to that form aggregate. In that answer, 'by one aggregate' means by the form aggregate alone. Whatever form there is, because it is of the same nature as the form aggregate, it is included and counted only as the form aggregate; therefore, it is counted only by the form aggregate, and that form is delimited only by the form aggregate. 'By eleven bases' means by the eleven bases excluding the mind base (manāyatana). Indeed, the entire form aggregate consists of the ten gross (oḷārika) bases and a portion of the mental-object base (dhammāyatana); therefore, it is counted and delimited by eleven bases. 'By eleven elements' means by the eleven elements excluding the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu). This is because there is no such thing as form that is not included within these eleven elements.

In the exposition of the method of non-inclusion (asaṅgahanaya niddesa), the question is asked only in brief: "By how many is it not included?" In the answer to that question, however, because the things that are heterogeneous (visabhāga) to the form aggregate are the four mental aggregates, the one mind base, and the seven consciousness elements, it is stated: "By four aggregates," and so forth. In this way, inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) should be understood in all terms.

In this Exposition of Aggregates (Khandhaniddesa), in the single-root (ekamūlaka) inclusion method starting with "By how many aggregates is the form aggregate [included]?", the five questions and five answers are shown in their specific forms. In the non-inclusion method, the five questions and five answers are shown in brief. By this means, the questions and answers in the double-root (dukamūlaka) and so forth should also be understood. Here, only the dyads (duka), triads (tika), and tetrads (catukka) based on the form aggregate are shown. But in the pentad (pañcaka)...
5:
"The aggregate of form... and... the aggregate of consciousness," thus by way of classification, and "How many aggregates are the five aggregates?" thus by way of non-classification, two types of questions and answers were made. In this way, the method of the Pali text should be understood.

## 2. Commentary on the Bases (Āyatana), etc.

In the exposition of the bases (āyatana-pada-niddesa) and so forth, first, in the exposition of the bases, it should be understood that the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) is included by only one aggregate, namely the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha); by only one base, namely the eye-base; and by only one element, namely the eye-element (cakkhudhātu). In the ear-base (sotāyatana) and so forth, inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) should be understood in this same way.

Regarding the phrase "excluding the unconditioned from the aggregates" (asaṅkhataṃ khandhato ṭhapetvā), because Nibbāna, which is called the unconditioned mind-object base (asaṅkhata-dhammāyatana), does not fall under the inclusion of aggregates, it is said "excluding from the aggregates."

"By four aggregates" (catūhi khandhehi) means by the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations. The mind-object base (dhammāyatana), excluding Nibbāna, is included by these aggregates. However, excluding the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), the mind-object base and the mind-object element (dhammadhātu) are not included in the remaining bases and elements. Therefore, it is said: "It is not included by one aggregate, eleven bases, and seventeen elements."

Just as the methods based on the aggregate of form were shown below, here too, the methods based on the eye-base should be understood. In the Pali text, showing only the dyads (duka), the question and answer were made without classification as "twelve bases" (dvādasāyatanāni). In the exposition of elements (dhātu-niddesa) as well, the method is the same.

In the exposition of truths (sacca-niddesa), all dyads, triads (tika), and tetrads (catukka) are shown in the Pali text. Since the answer for the path truth (magga-sacca) is similar to the origin truth (samudaya-sacca) in the dyads and triads, the path truth is mentioned immediately after the origin truth.

In the exposition of faculties (indriya-niddesa), when the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is included by two aggregates, the physical life-faculty is included by the aggregate of form, and the mental life-faculty is included by the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). The rest should be understood according to the method already mentioned. The structure of the Pali text here is identical to the exposition of bases and elements.

## 6. Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda)

In the exposition of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda-niddesa), without starting with the question "By how many aggregates is ignorance (avijjā)...?", only the answer "Ignorance is by one aggregate..." is shown. There, in the Pali "with mental formations as condition, consciousness" (saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ), all resultant consciousness (vipāka-viññāṇa) occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and during the course of existence (pavatti) should be taken.
6:
Therefore, the Buddha said: "It is included by seventeen elements." Nāmarūpa (name-and-form) should also be understood by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence. For that reason, in this exposition of Nāmarūpa, the sound-base (saddāyatana) is also included, and the inclusion by eleven bases is shown. In terms such as contact (phassa), the distinction of aggregates should be understood. Indeed, contact is included by one aggregate other than the feeling-aggregate (i.e., the formations-aggregate); feeling is included by the other, the feeling-aggregate; while craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), and kamma-existence (kammabhava) are included only by the formations-aggregate. In this exposition of dependent origination, the term 'existence' (bhava) is analyzed into eleven types by way of kamma-existence and so on. Among those eleven types of existence, kamma-existence is shown together with terms such as contact because it has the same answer as contact and the rest. Rebirth-existence (upapattibhava), sensual-existence (kāmabhava), perception-existence (saññābhava), and five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava) are shown together because they have the same answer as each other. Since these, such as rebirth-existence, are only clung-to states (upādinnaka-dhamma), it is said: "by eleven bases and seventeen elements." Indeed, the sound-base is not a clung-to form; therefore, it is not taken here in rebirth-existence and the rest.

In the exposition of fine-material existence (rūpabhava): "by five bases" refers to the eye, ear, mind, visible-form, and mental-object bases. "By eight elements" refers to the eye-element, ear-element, eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, visible-form element, mental-object element, mind-element, and mind-consciousness element. The three types of existence such as immaterial existence (arūpabhava) are also shown together because they have the same answer. Similarly, non-percipient existence (asaññābhava) and one-constituent existence (ekavokārabhava) are shown together. In that exposition of non-percipient existence, "by two bases" refers to the visible-form base and the mental-object base. The same method applies to the elements. Indeed, because the Brahmas other than the non-percipient beings who live on the same level have the eye, and because it is the object of that eye, the visible-form base is extracted and shown in that exposition of non-percipient existence.

"Birth (jāti) is by two aggregates" means the birth of form is included by the form-aggregate, and the birth of name is included by the formations-aggregate. The same method applies to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa). In sorrow (soka) and the rest, "by one aggregate" means sorrow, pain (dukkha), and grief (domanassa) are included by the feeling-aggregate; lamentation (parideva) by the form-aggregate; and despair (upāyāsa) and the rest by the formations-aggregate. Thus, the distinction of aggregates should be understood.

"The bases of power (iddhipāda) are by two" means they are included by the formations-aggregate and the consciousness-aggregate; by the mind-base and the mental-object base; and by the mental-object element and the mind-consciousness element. "Absorption (jhāna) is by two" means it is included by the feeling-aggregate and the formations-aggregate. The immeasurables (appamaññā) and the rest are shown together because they have the same answer. As for the mind (citta), although it is placed immediately after volition (cetanā), it is taken later because it does not have the same answer. In those immeasurables and the rest, "by one aggregate" means feeling is included by the feeling-aggregate, perception (saññā) by the perception-aggregate, and the remaining states by the formations-aggregate. Thus, the distinction of aggregates should be understood.

## 7. Commentary on the Triad Terms (Tika-pada-vaṇṇanā)
Having thus shown the inclusion in the internal matrix (abbhantara-mātikā), the Buddha now began the words "Wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā) and so on to show the inclusion in the external matrix (bāhira-mātikā). Among those (wholesome states, etc.), in the feeling triad (vedanā-ttika), "by three elements" means they are included by the body-consciousness element, the mind-consciousness element, and the mental-object element. "By seven elements" means they are included by the eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness elements, as well as the mind-element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. In the resultant triad (vipāka-ttika), "by eight elements" means they are included by those same seven elements together with the body-consciousness element. As for the states that have resultants (vipākadhamma-dhamma), they are taken together with the defiled and conducive to defilement states (saṅkiliṭṭha-saṅkilesika) because they have the same answer. Just as these are taken, so in all the triad and dyad terms, whichever term has the same answer as another term, that term is taken and answered together with it, even if it is not in the order of the matrix. In this regard, the method of inclusion and non-inclusion (saṅgaha-asaṅgaha) should be understood by following the method already stated.

## Commentary on the Terms of Inclusion and Non-inclusion (Saṅgaha-asaṅgaha-pada-vaṇṇanā)

## 2. The Second Method: Commentary on the Terms 'Included and Not Included' (Saṅgahita-asaṅgahita-pada-vaṇṇanā)
Now, to analyze the terms 'included and not included' in detail, the Buddha began the words "By the eye-base" (cakkhāyatanena) and so on. In this regard, the characteristic to be noted is as follows: In this section (of the second method), whatever state is included by the aggregate-term but not included by the base-term and element-term, or is included by the aggregate-term and base-term but not included by the element-term—the non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) of that state by aggregates and so on is questioned and the answer is given. However, that answer is not appropriate for states such as the form-aggregate. This is because by the form-aggregate, only the form-aggregate itself is included. And that form-aggregate is not such that it is not included by the eleven (gross bases, mental-object base, gross elements, and mental-object element). By the feeling-aggregate, only the feeling-aggregate itself is included. And that feeling-aggregate is not such that it is not included by the mental-object base and the mental-object element. Thus, because there is no state of non-inclusion, these terms such as the form-aggregate and feeling-aggregate, along with other terms of such nature like the mind-base and mental-object base, are not taken in this section (of the second method). However, terms that can show a portion of form not mixed with mental states, and a portion of consciousness not mixed with other states, are taken in this section. And at the end—
8:
"Ten bases, seventeen elements,
seven faculties, unconscious existence, one-constituent existence,
lamentation, visible and impingent,
invisible and impingent, and again visible, impingent, and derived."

Thus it has been shown by this summary verse (uddāna-gāthā). Therefore, inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) should be understood only by way of these terms. Indeed, in this second method of exposition (niddesavāra), eight questions have been formulated by grouping twenty states that have similar answers by way of the bases and elements. One question was made by grouping the seven consciousness elements; one by grouping the seven faculties; one by grouping the two types of existence; one by lamentation and visible-impingent states; one by invisible-impingent states; one by visible states; and one by impingent and derived states. Thus, eight questions were made.

In these eight questions, the distinction of aggregates and so on should be understood in the following manner. To wit—in the first question, 'by four aggregates' means by the four immaterial aggregates (being non-included). 'By two bases' means by one of the gross bases (oḷārikāyatana) such as the eye base, together with the mind base (being non-included). 'By eight elements' means by one of the gross elements such as the eye element, together with the seven consciousness elements (being non-included).

In those questions, this is the method for conveying the meaning. Indeed, when the eye base is categorized by aggregate, the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is included. In that included form aggregate, when categorized by base, only the eye base is included. The remaining ten bases are not included. Even when categorized by element, only the eye element is included by that eye base. The remaining ten elements are not included. Thus, there are ten bases that are not included by that eye base. Those ten bases are not included by the two bases, namely the eye base and the mind base. There are also ten elements that are not included by that eye base. Those ten elements are not included by the eye element and the seven consciousness elements. This same method applies to the visible base and so on.

In the second question—since there is no such thing as the aggregate of consciousness, which is included by any consciousness element, not being included by the mind base, it is therefore said to be 'included by the inclusion of bases.' In this second question, 'by four aggregates' means by the four aggregates such as the form aggregate (being non-included). 'By eleven bases' means by the bases excluding the mind base (being non-included). 'By twelve elements' means by the remaining twelve elements after removing the six consciousness elements as appropriate (being non-included). Indeed, the eye-consciousness element includes only the eye-consciousness element; the other six consciousness elements are not included. This same method applies to the ear-consciousness element and so on.
9:
In the third question, the answer for the eye faculty and so on is exactly the same as for the eye base and so on. Specifically, for the feminine faculty (itthindriya) and masculine faculty (purisindriya), two bases (the mind base and the mental-object base) and eight elements (the mental-object element and the seven consciousness elements) should be understood.

In the fourth question, 'by three bases' means by the visible base, the mental-object base, and the mind base. In those existences, only two bases are included by way of the visible base and the mental-object base. The remaining nine gross bases are said to be not included by those three bases, namely those two (visible and mental-object) and the mind base. 'By nine elements' means by the seven consciousness elements together with the form element and the mental-object element.

In the fifth question, 'by two bases' is meant with reference to the first term, by the sound base and the mind base. With reference to the second term, it is by the visible base and the mind base. Regarding the elements, they should be understood as the seven consciousness elements together with each of those respective elements.

In the sixth question, 'by ten bases' means by the bases excluding the visible base and the mental-object base. 'By sixteen elements' means by the elements excluding the form element and the mental-object element. How? States that are invisible and impingent (anidassanasappaṭigha) are the nine gross bases. When those states are included by aggregate, they are included in the form aggregate. When included by base, those same nine bases are included. The visible base and the mental-object base are not included. Even when included by element, those same nine elements are included. The form element and the mental-object element are not included. Thus, the two bases not included by those states are not included by the ten bases, namely the nine gross bases excluding the visible base, and the mind base. The two elements not included by those states should be understood as not included by the sixteen elements, namely the nine gross elements excluding the form element, and the seven consciousness elements.

In the seventh question, 'by two bases' means by the visible base and the mind base. 'By eight elements' means by the seven consciousness elements together with the form element.

In the eighth question, 'by eleven bases' means, with reference to impingent states (sappaṭigha), by the bases excluding the mental-object base; and with reference to derived states (upādā), by the bases excluding the tangible-object base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana). The same method applies to the elements. The application of the meaning should be understood only by the method already mentioned below.

## Saṅgahitenāsaṅgahitapadavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the section on what is included and what is not included).
10:
## 3. Commentary on the Third Method: Inclusion by the Excluded

Now, in order to analyze the term 'Inclusion by the Excluded' (asaṅgahitena-saṅgahita), the Blessed One began the discourse with the words 'vedanākkhandhena' (by the aggregate of feeling), and so forth. In this method of inclusion by the excluded, the following is the characteristic to be noted: Indeed, in this third section (vāra), whatever phenomenon is not included (not counted) by a certain aggregate term but is included (counted) by sense-base (āyatana) and element (dhātu) terms, the Blessed One has asked about the inclusion of that phenomenon by aggregates and so forth, and has provided the answer.

That answer is not applicable to phenomena such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), and so forth. Indeed, the aggregate of form does not include the four (mental) aggregates within the inclusion of aggregates. Among those non-included phenomena, there is not even a single phenomenon that is said to be included by sense-base or element through that aggregate of form. If it is argued, 'Are not phenomena such as feeling included by the mind-object base (dhammāyatana)?', they are indeed included. However, the aggregate of form as a whole is not the mind-object base, because only the subtle form (sukhumarūpa) from within the aggregate of form belongs to the mind-object base. Therefore, whatever phenomena are included by the mind-object base, those phenomena are not said to be included by the aggregate of form.

By the aggregate of consciousness also, the remaining four aggregates are not included. Among those four aggregates, there is not even one aggregate that is said to be included by sense-base or element through that aggregate of consciousness. Because of this absence of inclusion by sense-base and element, these aggregates of form and consciousness, as well as other terms of such nature like the eye-base and so forth, are not taken in this third section. However, those terms which can indicate a portion of the mind-object base that is unmixed with consciousness or gross form (oḷārikarūpa) are taken here. The summary (uddāna) of those terms taken is as follows:

'The three aggregates of mental factors, and likewise the three truths,
And the sixteen faculties,
Fourteen terms in the section on dependent origination, and fourteen terms above.
There are thirty terms in the ten groups (gocchaka),
Two in the minor intermediate dyads (cūḷantara-duka), and eight in the major intermediate dyads (mahantara-duka).'

Among these ninety terms, the Blessed One taught all twelve problems (questions) by grouping together the terms that have similar answers. In those problems, the distinction of aggregates should be understood in the following way. Regarding sense-bases and elements, however, there is no distinction. Therein, first, in the first problem, 'by three aggregates' means they are included by the aggregate of form, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations. Sense-bases and elements should be understood by way of the mind-object base (dhammāyatana) and the mind-object element (dhammadhātu).

In those problems, this is the method for understanding the meaning: Indeed, by the aggregate of feeling, Nibbāna, subtle form, perception, and mental formations are not included (asaṅgahita) in the inclusion of aggregates, but are included in the inclusion of sense-bases and elements. Among those phenomena, Nibbāna does not come into the state of being included by aggregates; the remaining subtle form, perception, and mental formations come into inclusion by the aggregate of form, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations. As for inclusion by sense-base and element, Nibbāna also certainly reaches it. Therefore...
11:
The Blessed One has taught: 'Excluding the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) from the aggregates, they are included by three aggregates, one sense-base, and one element.' In this first problem, in the portion of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), excluding perception and including feeling, the three aggregates should be understood. In phenomena such as mental formations (saṅkhāra), excluding the aggregate of mental formations, the three aggregates should be understood by way of form, feeling, and perception.

In the second problem, 'by four aggregates' refers to the four aggregates excluding consciousness. This is because those aggregates, together with the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca), are not included by aggregate-inclusion but are included by sense-base and element inclusion.

In the third problem, 'by two' refers to the aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception. This is because, together with the physical life-faculty and mental life-faculty, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness are not included by aggregate-inclusion. Among those phenomena, only feeling and perception are included by sense-base and element inclusion. Therefore, it was taught: 'by the aggregates of feeling and perception.' By this method, the distinction of aggregates should be understood in all problems. Hereafter, I shall mention only the names of the aggregates.

In the fourth problem, 'by three aggregates' means: in the femininity faculty and masculinity faculty, they are included by feeling, perception, and mental formations; in the fivefold feeling, by form, perception, and mental formations; and in the phenomena beginning with the faith faculty and ending with contact, they are included by the aggregates of form, feeling, and perception. Regarding feeling in the context of dependent origination, the decision is the same as for the aggregate of feeling. Regarding craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), and kammic-existence (kammabhava), the decision is the same as for the aggregate of mental formations.

In the fifth problem, regarding birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), the decision is the same as for the life-faculty. Specifically, together with Jhana, Nibbāna, subtle form, and perception are not included by aggregate-inclusion but are included by sense-base and element inclusion. Therefore, with reference to that subtle form and perception, the two aggregates should be understood by way of the aggregate of form and the aggregate of perception.

In the sixth problem, regarding the three phenomena such as sorrow (soka), there is a decision similar to that of feeling. In phenomena such as despair (upāyāsa), there is a decision similar to that of mental formations. Again, regarding feeling included in the group of seven beginning with contact (phassa-sattaka), the decision is similar to the aggregate of feeling; regarding perception, similar to the aggregate of perception; and regarding phenomena such as volition (cetanā), similar to the aggregate of mental formations. By this method, inclusion and non-inclusion should also be understood in the seventh problem and so forth.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on Inclusion by the Excluded.
12:
## 4. Fourth Method: Explanation of the Term 'Included by the Included' (Saṅgahitena-saṅgahita-pada-vaṇṇanā)

Now, the words beginning with "By the truth of origin" (samudayasaccena) are commenced in order to analyze the term 'included by the included'. In this term 'included by the included', such as the truth of origin, that phenomenon which is included by way of aggregates and so on is included by the power of aggregates and so on; then, the inclusion of that very phenomenon by way of aggregates and so on is questioned and answered. That answer is not appropriate for terms that stand by taking the entirety of any one group among the aggregates, bases, and elements. This is because there is no other phenomenon included by way of aggregates etc. which, having included the phenomenon that includes itself by a term such as 'aggregate' that expresses the whole, could again reach the state of being included by the power of those very aggregates and so on. Therefore, terms of such nature are not taken in this fourth exposition (niddesavāra).

Only those terms which can show a portion of formations (saṅkhāra), or a portion of feeling (vedanā), or subtle matter (sukhumarūpa), or a portion of sound (sadda), without mixing with other phenomena, are taken in this section. The summary (uddāna) of those terms is as follows:

"Two truths, fifteen faculties,
Eleven links of dependent origination,
Again eleven above,
The group-terms (gocchaka) here are of thirty kinds."

In this fourth method, there are only two types of questions (problems). Among those two, regarding the very term such as the truth of origin that is extracted in the question, those phenomena such as the forty-nine formations are included by the power of aggregates and so on; with reference to those phenomena such as the forty-nine formations, it is stated in all terms as "by one aggregate" and so on. Herein, this is the method (naya): by the truth of origin, the remaining formations excluding craving are included by way of aggregates and so on. Again, those formations include craving itself. That craving is again included by those very formations by way of aggregates and so on. This very method applies to all terms.

In this fourth method, among the questions on mental phenomena, either the formation aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha) or the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha) is called 'one aggregate'. In the questions on material phenomena, the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is called 'one aggregate'. In the question on the term 'lamentation' (parideva), the sound base (saddāyatana) is called 'one base'. The sound element (saddadhātu) is called 'one element'. In the remaining places, the meaning should be understood only by way of the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) and the mental-object element (dhammadhātu).

## Explanation of the Term 'Included by the Included'.

## 5. Fifth Method: Explanation of the Term 'Unincluded by the Unincluded' (Asaṅgahitena-asaṅgahita-pada-vaṇṇanā)

Now, the words beginning with "By the form aggregate" (rūpakkhandhena) are commenced in order to analyze the term 'unincluded by the unincluded'. In this term 'unincluded by the unincluded', that phenomenon which is not included by way of aggregates and so on is not included by the power of aggregates and so on; then, the non-inclusion of that very phenomenon by way of aggregates and so on is questioned and answered. That answer, for those terms that can take all five aggregates...
13:
In terms such as the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), and in terms such as 'non-apparent and non-impinging' (anidassana-appaṭigha) which can take subtle matter along with consciousness, [this method] is not appropriate. This is because, by such a term, Nibbāna cannot reach even the mere counting of inclusion by way of aggregate. Apart from Nibbāna, there are no phenomena that are not included by way of aggregates and so on. Therefore, terms of such nature are not taken in this section. Those terms which cannot show the five aggregates, or consciousness together with subtle matter as a single whole, are taken here. The summary (uddāna) of those terms is:

"All aggregates, likewise bases and elements, three truths,
All faculties, and twenty-three from dependent origination.
Sixteen terms thereafter, forty-three in the triads,
Seventy-two in the groups (gocchaka), seven in the lesser intermediate (cūḷantara).
Eighteen terms are said in the greater intermediate (mahantara), thereafter
Only eighteen should be known; the rest are not spoken of here."

In this section, when terms with similar answers are combined and counted, there are thirty-four in total. Therein, regarding the very term extracted in the question, those which are not included by way of aggregates and so on, with reference to those phenomena, it is stated as "by one aggregate" and so on.

Herein, the method is as follows: the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is not included in the four [mental] aggregates and Nibbāna by way of aggregate-inclusion. However, by way of base and element inclusion, excluding consciousness, the remaining phenomena are included. Therefore, only consciousness is said to be 'unincluded' by all three: aggregate, base, and element. Again, the four aggregates together with that consciousness and Nibbāna are not included by way of inclusions such as aggregate. All those phenomena are again not included by consciousness itself by way of inclusions such as aggregate. Therefore, it is said that they are not included by one aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha), one base (manāyatana), and seven elements (7 viññāṇadhātu).

Alternatively, another method: the form aggregate is not included by the three inclusions only in that consciousness; those consciousness-phenomena are also not included by the three inclusions only in those form-phenomena. Again, those form-phenomena are not included by the three inclusions by consciousness itself. Consciousness, by way of aggregate, is one consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha); by way of base, one mind base (manāyatana); and by way of element, seven consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu). Therefore, it is stated as "by one aggregate" and so on. By this means, in all terms, regarding the very term extracted in the question, those phenomena by which it is not included by way of aggregates and so on, the aggregates etc. should be known by the power of those phenomena.

Therein, in the second question, aggregates and so on should be known by way of gross matter (oḷārikarūpa) and consciousness (viññāṇa). This is because feeling and so on are not included by way of aggregates etc. even by gross matter and consciousness. Those matter and consciousness are 2 aggregates, 11 bases, and 17 elements. In the third question, because consciousness is not included by the four aggregates such as the form aggregate, aggregates etc. should be known by way of those four aggregates. In the fourth question, because the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) is not included by the four aggregates such as feeling, aggregates etc. should be known in this manner in all problems.
14: ...should be understood by way of [their respective nature]. For feelings and so forth are not included in the inclusion of aggregates and so forth by gross matter and consciousness themselves. Those two—gross matter and consciousness—constitute two aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements. In the third question: 'Consciousness is not included by the four [aggregates] such as matter,' thus aggregates and so forth should be understood by way of those [four]. In the fourth question: 'The eye-base is (not included) by the four aggregates such as feeling,' in this manner, aggregates and so forth should be understood in all problems. At the conclusion: 'Matter and the mind-object base (dhammāyatana),' the very things shown in the summary verse (uddāna-gāthā) are shown in brief by another method. ## Explanation of the terms 'Unincluded by the Unincluded' (Asangahitena-asangahita). ## 6. Sixth Method: Explanation of the terms 'Association and Dissociation' (Sampayoga-Vippayoga). Now, to analyze the terms of association and dissociation, the text beginning with 'The matter aggregate' (rūpakkhandho) is commenced. Therein, all that is obtainable and not obtainable regarding association and dissociation is taken in the question. In the answer, however, what is not obtainable is rejected as 'does not exist.' Because of the word: 'associated with four, dissociated from four, similar (sabhāga), dissimilar (visabhāga),' association is obtained only among mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) that are similar, arising at the same moment in a single continuum. There is no such thing as association of material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) with matter or with Nibbāna, nor of Nibbāna with matter. Likewise, there is no association of matter and Nibbāna with mental aggregates, because those [matter and Nibbāna] are dissimilar (visabhāga) to mental aggregates. Just as there is no association of mental aggregates with matter and Nibbāna, so too there is no association with mental phenomena of different continua or occurring at different moments. For they too are dissimilar due to the dissimilarity of continuum and moment. This dissimilarity, however, does not exist in the method of inclusion (sangaha-naya) because it would contradict the meaning of inclusion. For the meaning of inclusion is merely coming into the count. But in the method of association (sampayoga-naya), it [dissimilarity] does exist, because the meaning of association is the characteristic of arising together (ekuppādatā) and so forth. Thus, here, even though a phenomenon that does not fit the characteristic of association with even a single other phenomenon is included in the question, it is rejected in the answer as 'does not exist.' The dissociation of a phenomenon that fits the characteristic of dissociation is shown. However, those terms which indicate phenomena mixed with matter or Nibbāna, which are not dissociated from even a single consciousness among the seven consciousness elements, do not fit here in any way and thus are not taken. The summary (uddāna) for them is as follows:
15: 'The mind-object base, the mind-object element, the truth of suffering, and the life faculty; the sixfold base, mentality-materiality, and the four great existences; birth, aging, and death; nineteen in the triads, fifty in the clusters, eight terms in the small intermediate sets, fifteen in the great intermediate sets, and eighteen in the subsequent end-couplets—these one hundred and twenty-three terms are not obtainable in the method of association (and dissociation).' The mind-object base, being mixed with matter and Nibbāna, cannot be said to be associated even with consciousness that is not included in that mind-object base. However, since feelings and so forth in this mind-object base are associated with consciousness, it cannot be said to be dissociated either. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. Thus, because these terms are unsuitable in every way, they are not taken here (in the sixth method). Since the remaining terms such as aggregates are suitable, they are taken, and the explanation of questions is made both individually and by combination. Among those questions, in the first question: 'by one base' means by the mind-base (manāyatana). 'With certain phenomena' means with feeling, perception, and mental formations included in the mind-object base and mind-object element. In the second question: 'by three' means by the remaining three aggregates, excluding the one being questioned. 'Is associated with certain phenomena' means the feeling aggregate is associated with perception and mental formations. The other aggregates also, excluding themselves, are associated with the others. 'Is dissociated from certain phenomena' means dissociation from matter and Nibbāna. Thus, in all questions, in the case of dissociation of matter, mental phenomena in the mind-object base and mind-object element should be understood; in the case of dissociation of mental phenomena, matter should be understood. The third question has a clear meaning. In the fourth question, without saying 'by how many aggregates' and so forth, it is said 'there is no association.' That absence should be understood by way of aggregates and so forth. In subsequent similar questions, the method is the same. For in the first question, it is shown in detail (sarūpato), and thereafter the Pali text is abbreviated. In this way, the application of meaning should be understood in all questions. Where the meaning is not very clear, we shall proceed only after making it clear. In saying 'by sixteen elements,' the eye-consciousness element is first dissociated from the six consciousness elements (excluding itself) and the ten material elements. In the remaining elements, the method is the same.
16:
"By three aggregates" (tīhi khandhehīti) means association with the remaining three aggregates, excluding the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). "By one element" (ekāya dhātuyāti) means association with the single mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). This is because the Truth of Origin (samudayasacca) and the Truth of the Path (maggasacca) have no association with any element other than the mind-consciousness element. "By one aggregate" (ekena khandhenāti) means association with the single aggregate of mental formations; "by one base" (ekena āyatanenāti) means association with the single mental-base (dhammāyatana); "by one element" (ekāya dhātuyāti) means association with the single mental-element (dhammadhātu). Indeed, these two Truths are associated with certain states among these: the aggregate of mental formations, the mental-base, and the mental-element.

In the questions concerning the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya), etc., "by three" (tīhīti) means association with the three aggregates: perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa). "By one element" (ekāya dhātuyāti) means association with the body-consciousness element (kāyaviññāṇadhātu) and the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). "By six elements" (chahi dhātūhīti) means association with the six consciousness elements, excluding the body-consciousness element.

In the question of form-existence (rūpabhava), it is stated that they are "not dissociated from anything" because all mental aggregates and mental bases are present. However, it is stated that they are "dissociated from three elements" because the nose-consciousness element (ghānaviññāṇadhātu), tongue-consciousness element (jivhāviññāṇadhātu), and body-consciousness element (kāyaviññāṇadhātu) are absent.

In the question of decision (adhimokkha), "by two elements" (dvīhi dhātūhīti) means association with the two: mind element (manodhātu) and mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). "By fifteen" (pannarasahīti) means dissociation from the remaining ten material elements and the five consciousness elements such as eye-consciousness, etc.

In the question of wholesome (kusala) states, since all four mental aggregates are already included by the wholesome states, association (sampayoga) is rejected.

In the question of the triad of feeling (vedanāttika), "by one aggregate" (ekena khandhenāti) means association only with the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). "By fifteen" (pannarasahīti) means dissociation from the four consciousness elements (eye, ear, nose, tongue), the one mind element, and the ten material elements. "By eleven" (ekādasahīti) means dissociation from the ten material elements together with the body-consciousness element.

In the question of states that are neither resultants nor resultant-yielding (nevavipākanavipākadhammadhamma), "by five" (pañcahīti) means dissociation from the five [consciousness elements] such as eye-consciousness, etc.

In the question of states that are not acquired by clinging and not subject to clinging (anupādinnānupādāniya), "by six" (chahīti) means dissociation from the six consciousness elements, excluding the mind-consciousness element.

In the question of states with initial and sustained application (savitakkasavicāra), "by fifteen" (pannarasahīti) means dissociation from the ten material elements together with the five consciousnesses.

In the question of states without initial application but with sustained application only (avitakkavicāramatta), the phrase "by one aggregate," etc., should be understood only by way of the aggregate of mental formations. Excluding the sustained application (vicāra) present in the second jhāna, the remaining states are called "without initial application but with sustained application only." Excluding zest (pīti), the remaining states are called "accompanied by zest." Among those, since sustained application is not associated with sustained application, and zest is not associated with zest, they are said to be associated with certain states among the aggregate of mental formations, the mental-base, and the mental-element. "By sixteen" (soḷasahīti) means dissociation from the remaining sixteen elements, excluding the mental-element and the mind-consciousness element.
17:
In the question of states without initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra), "by one element" means dissociation from the mind element (manodhātu). States accompanied by pleasure and states accompanied by equanimity are the same as explained in the triad of feeling. States to be abandoned by vision (dassanenapahātabba), etc., are similar to the wholesome states.

States with limited objects (parittārammaṇa) are similar to resultant (vipāka) states. "By one element" means dissociation from the mental-element (dhammadhātu). "By some" (kehicīti) means dissociation from those states which are not "with limited objects" within that [mental-base and mental-element]. However, since the mental-element, as mental factors, is already included within the four mental aggregates by way of the six consciousness-arisings having limited objects, it falls under the first rejection: "there is no association." States with great objects (mahaggatārammaṇa), etc., are similar to the wholesome states.

In the case of unarisen states (anuppanna), "by five elements" means dissociation from the five elements such as eye-consciousness, etc. Although those [five consciousnesses] are definitely of the nature of states that will arise (uppādidhamma), they also fall into the category of the arisen (uppanna). States with present objects (paccuppannārammaṇa), etc., are similar to states with limited objects. Roots (hetu), etc., are similar to the Truth of Origin. States that have roots but are not themselves roots (sahetukā ceva na ca hetū) are similar to states accompanied by zest. Likewise, states associated with misapprehension (parāmāsasampayutta). Unacquired states (anupādinna) are similar to unarisen states. In all questions, the remaining group of terms has an obvious meaning.

## Explanation of the Terms Association and Dissociation

## 7. The Seventh Method: Explanation of the Terms 'Dissociated from the Associated'

Now, in order to analyze the terms 'dissociated from the associated', [the Buddha] began with "by the aggregate of feeling" (vedanākkhandhena), etc. Herein, this is the characteristic: In this section of the exposition of the seventh method, the question asks about the dissociation from aggregates, etc., of those states which are themselves dissociated from the states that are associated with the term raised in the question. However, that [explanation] is not appropriate for the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), etc. For there is no such thing as a state associated with the aggregate of matter. Therefore, the aggregate of matter and other such terms are not taken in this method. Those terms which can show the states associated with the mental-element, and the consciousness unmixed with other non-associated states, are taken here in this exposition of the seventh method. The summary verse (uddāna) for those terms is as follows:
18:
The four mental aggregates, one mind-base (manāyatana), two faculties (indriya) (the mind-faculty and the equanimity-faculty), seven consciousness elements (viññāṇa-dhātu), three factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) (consciousness, contact, and feeling), the dyad of the heptad of contact (phassa-sattaka-duka), three terms in the triads (tika) (neither-painful-nor-pleasant, with initial and sustained thought, and accompanied by equanimity), seven terms in the Mahantara-duka, one 'with initial thought' (savitakka), one 'with sustained thought' (savicāra), and one 'associated with equanimity' (the 'accompanied by equanimity' from the Piṭṭhi-duka).

At the end, this same meaning is also encompassed by the words beginning with "khandhā caturo" (the four aggregates). In this exposition of the seventh method, terms with identical answers are grouped together, not in their original order, to form seven problems starting with the feeling aggregate (vedanā-khandha). In these problems, the classification of aggregates and so on should be understood as follows: In the problem of the feeling aggregate, "ekena" means by the one mind-base (manāyatana). "Sattahi" means by the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇa-dhātu). "Kehi-ci" means by feeling and others included in the mind-object base (dhammāyatana).

In the problem of the consciousness elements, in the phrase "those states are not (dissociated) from any states," "those states" refers to the six consciousness elements, materiality (rūpa), and Nibbāna, excluding the consciousness element mentioned in the question. Since these states encompass all aggregates and bases, they are not dissociated from any aggregates or bases. "Ekāya dhātuyā" means by whichever single element is mentioned in the question.

In the problem of the equanimity-faculty, "pañcahi" means by the five elements such as the eye-consciousness element associated with equanimity. In this manner, the meaning in all problems should be understood by way of the states that are dissociated from the term mentioned in the question.

## Explanation of the section on 'Dissociated from the Associated'.

## 8. The Eighth Method: Explanation of the section on 'Associated with the Dissociated'

Now, to analyze the section on 'Associated with the Dissociated,' the text beginning with "rūpakkhandhena" (by the materiality aggregate) is commenced. In this exposition of 'Associated with the Dissociated,' all questions are void questions (mogha-pucchā) that lack a positive answer. This is because the states dissociated from the materiality aggregate are the four mental aggregates, and there is no association (sampayoga) of those mental aggregates with any other states. The states dissociated from the feeling aggregate are materiality and Nibbāna, and there is no association of that materiality and Nibbāna with any state. Thus, it should be understood for all terms. The absence of association for dissociated states should be recognized. Thus, because the questions are void, in all answers it is stated only as "natthi natthi" (there are none, there are none).

## Explanation of the section on 'Associated with the Dissociated'.
19:
## 9. The Ninth Method: Explanation of the section on 'Associated with the Associated'

Now, to analyze the section on 'Associated with the Associated,' the text beginning with "vedanākkhandhena" (by the feeling aggregate) is commenced. In this exposition of 'Associated with the Associated,' the states associated with a certain aggregate and so on are asked again regarding their association (sampayoga) with those same aggregates and so on, and then answered. That meaning is not appropriate with materiality, or with states mixed with materiality, or with terms that encompass all materiality aggregates. This is because there is no association (sampayoga) of other states with materiality or with states mixed with materiality. Since all aggregates and so on that are capable of association have already been taken by the terms encompassing all materiality aggregates, there are no other states left to be associated with them. Therefore, terms of such nature are not included here. Only terms that represent a portion of mental phenomena without being mixed with materiality are included here. The summary verse (uddāna-gāthā) for these terms is as follows:

"The four mental aggregates, the mind-base (manāyatana),
the seven consciousness elements, the two truths, the fourteen faculties,
twelve terms in dependent origination (paccaya), sixteen terms above that,
eight in the triads (tika), forty-three in the groups (gocchaka),
seven in the Mahantara-duka, and six in the Piṭṭhi-duka;
these terms are included in the exposition of the ninth section, Associated with the Associated."

In all problems, the classification of aggregates and so on should be understood by way of the companion states with which the states mentioned in the question are associated. The other three aggregates are associated with the feeling aggregate; in turn, the feeling aggregate is associated with those three aggregates. That feeling aggregate is associated with the three aggregates such as perception (saññā), with the one mind-base (manāyatana), with the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇa-dhātu), and only with certain perceptions and mental formations (saṅkhāra) included in the mind-object base (dhammāyatana) and the mind-object element (dhamma-dhātu). This method applies in all cases.

## Explanation of the section on 'Associated with the Associated'.

## 10. The Tenth Method: Explanation of the section on 'Dissociated from the Dissociated'

Now, to analyze the section on 'Dissociated from the Dissociated,' the text beginning with "rūpakkhandhena" (by the materiality aggregate) is commenced. In this exposition, the same states such as the materiality aggregate that were mentioned in the exposition of 'Association and Dissociation' (sampayoga-vippayoga) are mentioned in all questions. However, terms with identical answers are grouped together...
20:
Because terms with identical answers are grouped together, the terms appear in an order different from the sequence in the sixth method (chaṭṭha-naya). In that (tenth method), the term extracted in the question is not associated with certain states; the classification into aggregates and so forth should be understood by way of those non-associated states. The aggregate of form and states such as feeling are not associated, and the aggregate of form is also not associated with those states such as feeling. Nibbāna, however, follows the same nature as subtle form (sukhumatūpa). That aggregate of form is not associated with the four (mental) aggregates, the one mind-base (manāyatana), the seven consciousness-elements (viññāṇadhātu), and only with certain states such as feeling included within the mind-object base and mind-object element. In all problems, the method should be understood in this same way.

## Commentary on the Term "Non-associated with the Non-associated" (Vippayuttena-vippayutta-pada)

## 11. The Eleventh Method: Commentary on the Term "Associated and Non-associated with the Included" (Saṅgahitena-sampayutta-vippayutta-pada)

Now, in order to analyze the term "associated and non-associated with the included," [the Buddha] began with "By the origin truth" (samudaya-saccena) and so forth. In that (exposition of the eleventh method), the same states such as the origin truth that were extracted in the exposition of the fourth method (saṅgahitena-saṅgahita-pada-niddesa) are extracted in all questions. However, because terms with identical answers are grouped together, the terms appear in an order different from the sequence in the fourth method. In that (eleventh method), certain states are included by the term extracted in the question within the group of aggregates and so forth; the association or non-association of other states with those included states occurs, and the classification into aggregates and so forth should be understood by way of those states.

Herein, this is the method: First, by the origin truth, the states (the 49 states excluding craving) included in the aggregate of mental formations are included within the group of aggregates and so forth. Those states are said to be "associated with some" because they are associated with the remaining three (mental) aggregates, the one mind-base, the seven consciousness-elements, and the remaining states within the aggregate of mental formations, the mind-object base, and the mind-object element, excluding craving. However, they are not associated with the one aggregate of form, the ten sense-bases of form (rūpāyatana), and the ten elements of form (rūpadhātu); they are said to be "non-associated with some" because they are not associated with the subtle form and Nibbāna included within the one mind-object base and the mind-object element. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all problems.

## End of the Commentary on the Term "Associated and Non-associated with the Included."
21: ## 12. Description of the Twelfth Method: Classification of Inclusion and Non-inclusion by way of Association. Now, in order to analyze the term 'Inclusion and Non-inclusion by way of Association,' the Blessed One began with 'By the aggregate of feeling' (vedanākkhandhena) and so forth. In this exposition of the Twelfth Method, those states such as the aggregate of feeling, which were extracted in the Ninth Method (Association by way of Association), are extracted in all the questions. In this Twelfth Method, one should understand the distinction of aggregates and so forth by way of those states which are associated with the term extracted in the question, and whether those associated states are included or not included by other states. The method therein is as follows: The aggregate of feeling is associated with perception and so forth. Those states such as perception are included in three aggregates such as the aggregate of perception, in two bases—namely, the mind base (manāyatana) and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana)—and in eight elements—namely, the mental-object element (dhamma-dhātu) and the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇa-dhātu). They are not included in the remaining aggregates, bases, and elements. In this way, the entire meaning should be understood. ## Description of the Twelfth Method: Classification of Inclusion and Non-inclusion by way of Association. ## 13. Description of the Thirteenth Method: Association and Dissociation by way of Non-inclusion. Now, in order to analyze the term 'Association and Dissociation by way of Non-inclusion,' the Blessed One began with 'By the aggregate of matter' (rūpakkhandhena) and so forth. In this exposition of the Thirteenth Method, only those states like the mental-object base and mental-object element which have questions similar to the aggregate of matter in the Fifth Method (Non-inclusion by way of Non-inclusion), and those states similar to the formless existence (arūpa-bhava) such as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), are extracted. The remaining states are not extracted because they do not fit the answer. For instance, by way of aggregates and so forth, gross matter and consciousness are not included with the aggregate of feeling. And there is no such thing as association (sampayoga) between that gross matter and consciousness. Therefore, only those terms such as the aggregate of matter that fit the answer are extracted, combined with terms having similar answers. In this Thirteenth Method, those states such as the aggregate of consciousness are not included by way of aggregates and so forth with the states such as the aggregate of matter extracted in the question. One should understand the detailed analysis of aggregates and so forth by way of those states (like the aggregate of consciousness) which are associated with states like the aggregate of feeling and dissociated from states like the aggregate of matter. The method therein is as follows: Firstly, the aggregate of matter does not include consciousness by way of the three types of inclusion. That consciousness is associated with the three aggregates such as feeling, and with those same states like feeling included in the mental-object base and mental-object element. It is dissociated from the one aggregate of matter, the ten gross bases of matter (oḷārikāyatana), and the ten gross elements of matter (oḷārika-dhātu)...
22:
In the case of the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu), there is dissociation (vippayutta) from the phenomena of form (rūpa) and Nibbāna. With reference to that [consciousness], it is said: "Those states are [dissociated] from three aggregates," and so forth. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

## Explanation of the Terms Associated and Dissociated with the Unincluded

## 14. The Fourteenth Method: Explanation of the Terms Included and Unincluded by the Dissociated

Now, in order to analyze the terms included and unincluded by the dissociated, the text begins with "By the aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandhena) and so forth. In that exposition, those terms for which dissociation is not applicable (not possible) are not taken in this section. Which are those terms? They are the terms such as the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana). Indeed, for the base of mental objects, dissociation from even a single state among the aggregates and so forth is not applicable. The same method applies to the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu) and others. The summary (uddāna) of those [terms not taken] is as follows:

"The base of mental objects, the element of mental objects, and likewise the life-faculty,

The term 'mind-and-form' (nāmarūpa), and the term 'sixfold base' (saḷāyatana),

The group of three beginning with birth (jāti) as one, one in the twentieth triplet (tika),

One at the end of the triplets, and seven terms in the minor intermediate (cūḷantara) section,

There are only ten in the groups (gocchaka), and fourteen in the great intermediate (mahantara) section,

Six terms above that; in brief, all

Forty-seven terms are not obtained (in this section)."

At the conclusion [of the Pali text], the verse beginning with "Dhammāyatanaṃ dhammadhātu" was also spoken to clarify this very meaning. Setting aside these forty-seven terms, all remaining terms are obtained. The classification of aggregates and so forth in those terms should be understood exactly according to the method already stated.

## Explanation of the Terms Included and Unincluded by the Dissociated

## Concluding Remarks

By this much—

The Buddha, who is skilled in the classification of elements, taught this Dhatukatha;

The clarification of the various methods and aspects of that [Dhatukatha] is now completed.

By this clarification of the various methods, though spoken as a brief discourse,

It is capable of making all methods known.

If I were to speak of the details of each individual term,

The words would be excessively numerous, but the meaning would not be different.

Thus, this text which I have composed according to the scriptures is less than two recitations (bhāṇavāra) in length;

May the merit (puñña) gained from such composition be for the happiness of the world.

## The Commentary on the Dhatukatha is finished.

## Abhidhamma Piṭaka
## Commentary on the Designation of Individuals (Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakatha)
## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One

After the Teacher, the master of gods and men, taught the text named Dhatukatha, which has subtle meaning and clarifies the classification of elements, in the abode of the gods (Tāvatiṃsa),

Immediately after that, the Conqueror, the supreme individual in the world, taught the Puggalapaññatti, which clarifies the various designations.

Since the opportunity to provide a commentary on that Puggalapaññatti has now arrived,

I shall therefore explain it; listen to that explanation with concentrated minds.

## 1. Explanation of the Matrix (Mātikā)

"Six designations: the designation of aggregates... etc... the designation of individuals"—this statement is the table of contents (uddesa) of the Puggalapaññatti. Therein, "six" (cha) is a numerical delimitation. By that term "six," the Buddha shows the delimitation of designations in brief by way of number for the states he wishes to designate in this text. "Designations" (paññattiyo) refers to the pointing out of the delimited states. In that term "paññattiyo," in contexts such as "he tells, teaches, designates, establishes," designation (paññatti) means making known, showing, and manifesting. In contexts such as "the couch and stool are well-designated (well-placed)," designation (paññatti) means setting down and placing. Here, both meanings are appropriate. For in the phrase "six designations," both "six ways of making known, showing, and manifesting" and "six ways of setting down and placing" are intended. Indeed, the designation of names (nāmapaññatti) both shows those respective states and establishes them in their respective groups.

Phrases such as "designation of aggregates" (khandhapaññatti) show the nature of those designations in brief. Therein, making known, showing, manifesting, setting down, and placing the aggregates as "aggregates" is called the designation of aggregates (khandhapaññatti). Making known, showing, manifesting, setting down, and placing the bases as "bases," the elements as "elements," the truths as "truths," the faculties as "faculties," and individuals as "individuals" is called the designation of individuals (puggalapaññatti).
26:
According to the Commentarial method, which is independent of the Pāḷi Canon, there are another six types of designations: designation of the existent, designation of the non-existent, designation of the non-existent by means of the existent, designation of the existent by means of the non-existent, designation of the existent by means of the existent, and designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. Among these six designations, the designation of a state that is manifest and arisen in the sense of ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭhaparamattha), such as wholesome and unwholesome states, is called 'designation of the existent' (vijjamānapaññatti). Similarly, the designation of things like 'woman' or 'man', which do not exist in the ultimate sense but are established merely by worldly parlance, is called 'designation of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti). The designation of things that are absolutely unattainable in any way and are merely objects of speech, such as a 'fifth truth', or the concepts of 'atom' (aṇu), 'primordial nature' (pakati), and 'soul' (purisa) of the sectarians, is also 'designation of the non-existent'. However, since such designations do not fall within the Dispensation (sāsana), they are not included here. Thus, the remaining designations should be understood by way of various combinations of these existent and non-existent meanings.

Indeed, in terms such as "tevijjo" (one with triple knowledge) and "chaḷabhiñño" (one with six direct knowledges), the three knowledges and six direct knowledges are existent, while the 'person' is non-existent. Therefore, because a non-existent person is designated by means of an existent state—as in "he has three knowledges, thus he is tevijjo" or "he has six direct knowledges, thus he is chaḷabhiñño"—such a designation is called 'designation of the non-existent by means of the existent' (vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti). In terms such as "itthirūpaṃ" (female form) and "purisarūpaṃ" (male form), however, 'woman' and 'man' are non-existent, while 'form' (rūpa) is existent. Therefore, because an existent form is designated by means of a non-existent woman or man—as in "the form of a woman, thus itthirūpaṃ" or "the form of a man, thus purisarūpaṃ"—such a designation is called 'designation of the existent by means of the non-existent' (avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti). In terms such as "cakkhusamphasso" (eye-contact) and "sotasamphasso" (ear-contact), both the eye, ear, etc., and contact are existent. Therefore, because an existent state is designated by means of an existent state—as in "contact in the eye," "contact born of the eye," or "contact which is the result of the eye, thus cakkhusamphasso"—such a designation is called 'designation of the existent by means of the existent' (vijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti). In terms such as "khattiyaputto" (son of a Khattiya), "brāhmaṇaputto" (son of a Brahmin), and "seṭṭhiputto" (son of a merchant), both the Khattiya, etc., and the son are non-existent. Therefore, because a non-existent thing is designated by means of a non-existent thing—as in "the son of a Khattiya, thus khattiyaputto"—such a designation is called 'designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent' (avijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti).

Among these six designations, only the first three are found in this treatise. In the section "designation of the aggregates... designation of the faculties," the 'designation of the existent' is found because only existent things are designated. In the term "designation of individuals" (puggalapaññatti), the 'designation of the non-existent' is found. Later, in terms such as "tevijjo" and "chaḷabhiñño," the 'designation of the non-existent by means of the existent' is found.

According to the method of the Teachers, which is independent of the Commentaries, there are another six designations: derivative designation (upādāpaññatti), relative designation (upanidhāpaññatti), collective designation (samodhānapaññatti), additive designation (upanikkhittapaññatti), appropriate designation (tajjāpaññatti), ...
27:
...and continuity designation (santatipaññatti). Among these, although a 'being' (satta) does not exist as a nature attainable in the sense of ultimate reality like the aggregates of form, feeling, etc., whether as identical to or different from them, the designation 'being' is established depending on or based on the various aggregates such as form and feeling. Similarly, the designations 'chariot', 'house', 'fist', and 'tripod' are based on their respective parts; 'pot' and 'cloth' are based on form, etc.; 'time' and 'direction' are based on the revolution of the moon and sun, etc.; and the 'learning sign' (uggahanimitta) and 'counterpart sign' (paṭibhāganimitta), which appear in various modes, are established depending on or based on the respective signs of the elements and the benefits of meditation. Such a designation is called 'derivative designation' (upādāpaññatti). This is called a designation (paññatti) in the sense of 'that which is made known' (atthapaññatti), not in the sense of 'that which makes known' (nāmapaññatti). The name that makes that meaning known is simply a 'designation of the non-existent'.

The designation that makes something known by comparing it to the first, second, etc., as 'second', 'third', etc., or by mutual comparison as 'long', 'short', 'far', 'near', etc., is called 'relative designation' (upanidhāpaññatti). Furthermore, this relative designation is of many kinds, such as: relative to something else (tadaññāpekkhūpanidhā), relative to what is in the hand (hatthagatūpanidhā), relative to what is associated (sampayuttūpanidhā), relative to what is placed upon (samāropitūpanidhā), relative to what is nearby (avidūragatūpanidhā), relative to a counterpart (paṭibhāgūpanidhā), relative to abundance (tabbahulūpanidhā), and relative to a distinction (tabbisiṭṭhūpanidhā).

Among these, 'second', 'third', etc., are called 'relative to something else' because they are spoken of in relation to the first, etc. 'One with an umbrella in hand', 'one with a weapon in hand', etc., are called 'relative to what is in the hand' because they are spoken of in relation to an object held in the hand. 'One with earrings', 'one with a crest', 'one with a crown', etc., are called 'relative to what is associated' because they are spoken of in relation to an associated object. 'Grain-cart', 'ghee-pot', etc., are called 'relative to what is placed upon' because they are spoken of in relation to an object placed within or upon. 'Indasāla cave', 'Piyangu cave', 'Serīsaka mansion', etc., are called 'relative to what is nearby' because they are spoken of in relation to something located nearby. 'One with a golden complexion', 'one who walks like a bull', etc., are called 'relative to a counterpart' because they are spoken of in relation to a similar object. 'Lotus pond', 'Brahmin village', etc., are called 'relative to abundance' because they are spoken of in relation to the abundance of those lotuses or Brahmins. 'Ruby bracelet', 'diamond bracelet', etc., are called 'relative to a distinction' because they are spoken of in relation to being distinguished by those rubies or diamonds.

The designation that makes something known by considering the collection of various things, such as 'three sticks', 'eight-squared board', 'heap of grain', and 'heap of flowers', is called 'collective designation' (samodhānapaññatti). The designation that makes something known by placing a preceding thing nearby, such as 'two', 'three', 'four', etc., is...
28:
This is called upanikkhittapaññatti. Designation as earth, fire, hardness, heat, and so on, in consideration of the respective nature of things (dhamma-sabhāva), is called tajjāpaññatti. Designation as one who is eighty years old, ninety years old, and so on, in consideration of the non-interruption of the continuity of the aggregates of mind and matter, is called santatipaññatti. Among these, tajjāpaññatti is only vijjamanapaññatti (designation of what is truly existent). The remaining designations belong to the category of the non-existent (avijjamanapakkha), or they associate with the category of the non-existent through what is non-existent.

According to the method of the teachers, which is not directly mentioned in the Commentaries, there are six other types of designation: kiccapaññatti, saṇṭhānapaññatti, lingapaññatti, bhūmipaññatti, paccattapaññatti, and asaṅkhatapaññatti.
