Among these six, designation by way of function, such as 'reciter' or 'dhamma-preacher', is called kiccapaññatti. Designation by way of shape, such as 'thin person', 'fat person', 'round', or 'square', is called saṇṭhānapaññatti. Designation by way of gender or mark, such as 'woman' or 'man', is called lingapaññatti. Designation by way of plane or locality, such as 'one of the sense sphere', 'one of the fine-material sphere', 'one of the immaterial sphere', 'a person from Kosala', or 'a person from Madhurā', is called bhūmipaññatti. Designation by way of merely giving a personal name, such as 'Tissa', 'Nāga', or 'Sumana', is called paccattapaññatti. Designation of the unconditioned state, such as 'cessation' or 'Nibbāna', is called asaṅkhatapaññatti. Among these six, some bhūmipaññatti and asaṅkhatapaññatti are only vijjamanapaññatti. Kiccapaññatti associates with the category of the non-existent through what is existent. The remaining designations are called avijjamanapaññatti.

Now, the essence of those designations has been shown briefly in the uddesavāra (summary section). To show them by way of analyzing the aggregates and so forth, which are the bases of those designations, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Kittāvatā" (By how much?). In that question, the meaning should be understood thus: By how much extent of designation does the making known, the showing, and the establishing of the aggregates as "aggregates" in the continuity of beings occur? This is a question asked with the desire to teach. The same method applies to the subsequent questions such as "Kittāvatā āyatanānaṃ" (By how much for the sense bases?). In the answer as well, the meaning should be understood thus: By as much designation as there is briefly as "five aggregates", or by way of division as "materiality aggregate ... consciousness aggregate", and even therein, "the materiality aggregate is of the sense sphere, and the remaining four mental aggregates belong to the four planes"—such a designation occurs. By this much extent of designation, the designation of the aggregates as "aggregates" occurs.

Likewise, by as much designation as there is briefly as "twelve sense bases", or by way of division as "eye base ... mind-object base", and even among those twelve sense bases, ten sense bases...
29:
...ten sense bases are of the sense sphere, and two sense bases belong to the four planes—such a designation occurs. By this much designation, the designation of the sense bases as 'sense bases' occurs.

By as much designation as there is briefly as 'eighteen elements', or by way of division as 'eye element ... mind-consciousness element', and even among those elements, sixteen elements are of the sense sphere, and two elements belong to the four planes—such a designation occurs. By this much designation, the designation of the elements as 'elements' occurs.

By as much designation as there is briefly as 'four truths', or by way of division as 'truth of suffering ... truth of cessation', and even among those truths, two truths are mundane and two truths are supramundane—such a designation occurs. By this much designation, the designation of the truths as 'truths' occurs.

By as much designation as there is briefly as 'twenty-two faculties', or by way of division as 'eye faculty ... faculty of one who has known', and even among those faculties, ten faculties are of the sense sphere, nine faculties are mixed, and three faculties are supramundane—such a designation occurs. By this much designation, the designation of the faculties as 'faculties' occurs. By this much extent, the five designations have been shown by way of briefly analyzing the subject matter.

Now, to show the designation of individuals (puggalapaññatti) by way of detailed analysis of the subject matter, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'samayavimutto asamayavimutto'. Indeed, just as one might scatter sesame seeds or shred hemp fibers, the Blessed One has already taught the aggregates and so forth, which are the basis of these five designations, without remainder in the preceding Vibhaṅga treatise; therefore, he teaches those things here only in part. However, the sixth designation, the designation of individuals, was not taught below [in the Vibhaṅga]. Even in this text, it was taught only in part in the uddesavāra. Therefore, wishing to teach that designation of individuals in detail, he set forth the mātikā (matrix) from the groups of one (ekaka) up to the groups of ten (dasaka), beginning with 'samayavimutto asamayavimutto'.

## Commentary on the Matrix
30:
## 2. Commentary on the Designations
## 1. Commentary on the Designation of Individuals by One

Now, in order to show the analysis of the established matrix (mātikā) from the beginning, he said: "What kind of person is temporarily liberated (samayavimutta)?" and so forth. In that statement, "idha" means in this world of beings. "Ekacco puggalo" means a certain individual. In the phrase "kālena kālaṃ," the meaning should be understood by the power of the locative case; it means from time to time or occasionally. "Samayena samayaṃ" is merely a synonym for the preceding phrase. "Aṭṭha vimokkhe" refers to the eight attainments (samāpatti) of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. They are called "liberations" (vimokkha) because they liberate from opposing states. "Kāyena" means with the mental body (nāmakāya) that is co-nascent with liberation. "Phusitvā viharati" means dwelling having attained (those liberations).

However, at what time does this person dwell having attained the liberations? For a person who wishes to enter an attainment, there is an appropriate time (kāla) and an inappropriate time (akāla). Among these two, the time for early morning bodily care and the time for performing duties are called inappropriate times (akāla) for entering attainment. For a person who, after caring for the body and performing duties, enters his dwelling place and sits down, the interval before the time for going for alms arrives is called the appropriate time (kāla) for entering attainment.

For one who has noted the time for going for alms and set out, the time for paying homage to the shrine, the time for standing in the reflection hall surrounded by the community of monks, the time for going for alms, the time for wandering in the village, the time for drinking gruel in the refectory, and the time for performing duties are also called inappropriate times (akāla) for entering attainment. If there is a secluded place in the refectory, the interval before the mealtime arrives is also called the appropriate time (kāla) for entering attainment. The time for eating the meal, the time for returning to the monastery, the time for putting away the bowl and robes, the time for performing daytime duties, and the time for teaching and questioning are also called inappropriate times (akāla) for entering attainment. Whatever is an inappropriate time (akāla) is indeed an inappropriate occasion (asamaya). Excluding all those inappropriate times, the person who dwells attaining the aforementioned eight liberations with the co-nascent mental body at every remaining appropriate time and occasion is said to be: "Here, a certain individual... dwells."
31:
Furthermore, this temporarily liberated person indeed touches the co-nascent states with the co-nascent mental states including contact; figuratively, he indeed touches absorption (appanā). He indeed touches a subsequent absorption with a preceding absorption. For whatever states are co-nascent with another, those are said to be attained by it. They are also said to be touched by contact (phassa). Access (upacāra) is also a cause for the attainment of absorption; likewise, a preceding absorption is a cause for a subsequent absorption. In this context, the touching of co-nascent states by co-nascent states should be understood thus: the first jhāna has five factors such as initial application (vitakka) and so on. In that first jhāna, excluding those jhāna factors, the remaining fifty or more states are called the four mental aggregates. With that mental body (nāmakāya), he dwells having touched and attained the liberation of the first jhāna attainment. The second jhāna has three factors: rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (citt'ekaggatā). The third jhāna has two factors: happiness and one-pointedness of mind. The fourth jhāna has two factors: equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind. Likewise, from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are two factors each. In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, excluding those jhāna factors, the remaining fifty or more states are called the four mental aggregates. With that mental body, he dwells having touched and attained the liberation of the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"Having seen with wisdom" means having seen conditioned states with insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and the four noble truths with path wisdom (magga-paññā). "Some taints are destroyed" means the partial destruction of taints that are to be abandoned by the first path and so on. This person is called "temporarily liberated" (samayavimutta). In this context, although it could be said that a worldling (puthujjana) who has attained the eight attainments dwells touching with that mental body, he is not included because the Pāḷi text states "some taints are destroyed," and there are no destroyed taints in a worldling. Although it could also be said that an Arahant (khīṇāsava) who has attained the eight attainments dwells touching with that mental body, he is also not included because there are no undestroyed taints in that Arahant. It should be understood that the name "temporarily liberated" (samayavimutta) belongs only to the three: the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi), and the Non-returner (Anāgāmi).

In the designation of the "liberated regardless of time" (asamayavimutta), it should be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. In this context, "asamayavimutta" is the name for the dry-insight Arahant (sukkhavipassaka-khīṇāsava). Dry-insight Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners, as well as Arahants with the eight attainments and worldlings, are not found in this dyad of samayavimutta and asamayavimutta.
32:
There are persons who are released from the dyad. Therefore, the Teacher, due to his state of being a well-enlightened Buddha, wishing to present in the Pali text those persons mentioned below as well as those not mentioned, together with those remaining behind (piṭṭhivaṭṭaka), said: "All noble persons (sabbepi ariyapuggala)," and so forth. In that Pali, "noble liberations (ariye vimokkhe)" refers to the supramundane liberations which are called "noble" because they are far from the defilements. The intended meaning is this: for a person who attains the eight attainments (samāpatti) that are outside the supramundane, there is a proper time to attain them and an improper time. However, in the liberation from defilements through the Path (magga-vimokkha), there is no such thing as a proper time or an improper time. If a person has strong faith and has undertaken insight (vipassanā), there is no such thing as being unable to penetrate the Path and Fruit while walking, standing, sitting, lying down, chewing, or eating. Thus, the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, presented this Piṭṭhivaṭṭaka Pali text, encompassing both the persons already mentioned and those not yet mentioned, stating that in liberation through the Path, there is neither a proper time nor an improper time. A worldling (puthujjana) who has attained the meditative attainments is not included in this Pali text. However, if such a person is brought into the fold, they may be considered a person liberated by time (samaya-vimutta) by virtue of the defilements being suppressed by the attainments.

In the explanation of those subject to falling away (kuppadhamma) and those not subject to falling away (akuppadhamma): a person whose attained meditative state falls away or disappears is called a kuppadhamma person. "Accompanied by form (rūpasahagatānaṃ)" refers to the attainments that occur together with form, known as the material signs (rūpa-nimitta). This means the four fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara jhāna) which occur with that form and cannot exist without the material object. "Accompanied by the formless (arūpasahagatānaṃ)" refers to that which is other than form; because it is not form, it is called formless. This means the four immaterial sphere jhānas (arūpāvacara jhāna) which occur with that formless and cannot exist without the immaterial object. "Not obtaining at will (na nikāmalābhī)" means not being able to obtain the attainment in the desired manner because one has not practiced the five kinds of mastery (vasībhāva), such as mastery in adverting. It means one whose attainment is not thoroughly mastered. "Not obtaining without difficulty (na akicchalābhī)" means one who obtains with difficulty or with suffering. A person who, at the beginning of practicing meditation, suppresses defilements, reaches access concentration (upacāra), reaches absorption concentration (appanā), and attains the concentration that is like a casket of the mind only through suffering, difficulty, and strenuous effort, is called one who does not obtain without difficulty. "Not obtaining without trouble (na akasiralābhī)" means one who does not obtain abundantly. Even after reaching the attainment, they cannot sustain it for a long duration. It means that after the mind occurs for only one or two moments, they immediately emerge from it. "Yatthicchakaṃ" refers to the place where one wishes to sit after reaching the attainment. "Yadicchakaṃ" refers to whichever attainment one wishes, whether it be a kasina jhāna, an ānāpāna jhāna, or a brahmavihāra jhāna...
33:
...or an asubha jhāna, and so forth, whichever attainment one wishes to sit in after reaching it. "Yāvatiicchakaṃ" refers to the duration of time, for as long as one wishes. The meaning is this: even if one wishes to enter or emerge from a particular attainment in a particular place for a particular duration, one is unable to enter or emerge from that attainment for that duration in that place. For example, if one enters jhāna after determining, "I will emerge when this moon or this sun reaches such a position," but is unable to emerge according to that determination and emerges in the interval, it is because the attainment has not been thoroughly mastered.

"Due to negligence (pamādamāgamma)" means on account of negligence. "This person is called" refers to a person of this nature who is called one subject to falling away (kuppadhamma). This is a designation for three types of persons: the worldling (puthujjana), the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and the once-returner (sakadāgāmi) who have attained the eight attainments. For these persons, the states that obstruct concentration and the states that obstruct insight have not been well-suppressed or well-shaken off; therefore, their attainments disappear or decline. Such decline is not due to a breach of virtue (sīla) or the commission of an offense (āpatti). However, this attainment is like the delicate nature of city-dwellers; it can disappear even due to a minor duty or a mere failure in performing a duty (vatta).

Regarding the disappearance of attainment due to failure in duty, there is this story: It is said that an Elder used to enjoy his attainments. While that Elder had entered the village for alms, some children played in the monastery compound and then left. When the Elder returned, he thought, "The compound should be swept," but without sweeping it, he entered the monastery and sat down, thinking, "I will enter an attainment." Being unable to enter it, he reflected on his virtue, asking, "What is the hindrance?" but did not see even a minor transgression. When he looked to see if there was a failure in duty, he realized the compound had not been swept. After sweeping it, he entered the monastery and sat down, and he immediately entered the attainment.

The explanation of those not subject to falling away (akuppadhamma) should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said for kuppadhamma. The name "akuppadhamma" is a designation for two types of persons: the non-returner (anāgāmi) and the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) who have attained the eight attainments. For them, the states that obstruct concentration and the states that obstruct insight have been well-suppressed and well-shaken off; therefore, even if they spend time with negligence suitable to themselves, such as delighting in talk or delighting in company, their attainment does not fall away or disappear. However, the dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka) stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and Arahant are not included in this dyad.
34:
They are not found in the pairs; there are individuals who are free from the pairs. Therefore, the Teacher, because of his state as a true Buddha and a true knower, having gathered those individuals already mentioned below and those not yet mentioned, and wishing to establish the teaching in this pair along with the followers, said: "All noble persons also," and so forth. For the eight attainments (samāpatti), there might be corruption or disappearance; however, for the supramundane Dhamma once realized, there is no such thing as corruption or disappearance. This statement was made with reference to that non-disappearance. The descriptions of 'one liable to fall away' (parihāna-dhamma) and 'one not liable to fall away' (aparihāna-dhamma) should also be understood by way of the descriptions of 'one of shakable nature' (kuppa-dhamma) and 'one of unshakable nature' (akuppa-dhamma). Specifically, here, the falling away or non-falling away of states is taken based on the person's negligence; this is merely a difference in the figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā). In all other respects, it is the same as those (shakable and unshakable natures).

In the description of 'one capable through volition' (cetanābhabba): 'capable through volition' means one who is capable of reaching the state of not falling away (from attainment) because of volition. "If he repeatedly intends" means if he enters into (the attainment). For one who enters into an attainment is said to "repeatedly intend." He does not fall away; the other falls away.

In the description of 'one capable through guarding' (anurakkhaṇābhabba): 'capable through guarding' means one who is capable of reaching the state of not falling away because of guarding. "If he guards" means if he enters into (the attainment) while abandoning unhelpful states and cultivating helpful states. One who practices in this way is said to "guard." He does not fall away; the other falls away.

Both of these individuals are capable of making the attainment stable and firm. However, the one capable through guarding is stronger than the one capable through volition. For the one capable through volition does not know helpful and unhelpful states. Because he does not know, he removes helpful states and cultivates unhelpful states. By cultivating them, he falls away from the attainment. The one capable through guarding knows helpful and unhelpful states. Because he knows, he removes unhelpful states and cultivates helpful states. By cultivating them, he does not fall away from the attainment.

For example: Just as there are two field guards, one is sick with jaundice and cannot endure cold, etc., while the other is healthy and can endure cold, etc. The sick one does not go down from the field hut and abandons the night watch and day watch. In his field, during the day, parrots, peacocks, etc., descend and eat the heads of the rice; at night, deer, wild boars, etc., enter and...
35:
...cut through it as if leveling the threshing floor and go. Because of his negligence, he does not even get the seeds again. The other does not abandon the night watch and day watch. Because of his diligence, he gets four or even eight carts of grain from a field of one karīsa.

In this analogy, the one capable through volition should be understood like the sick field guard. The one capable through guarding should be understood like the healthy field guard. Just as the sick person, through his negligence, does not even get the seeds again, the falling away from attainment of the one capable through volition should be understood—who, not knowing helpful and unhelpful states, abandons the helpful and cultivates the unhelpful. Just as the other healthy person, through his diligence, can take out four or eight carts of grain from a field of one karīsa, the non-falling away from attainment of the one capable through guarding should be understood—who, knowing helpful and unhelpful states, abandons the unhelpful and cultivates the helpful. Thus, it should be understood that the one capable through guarding is stronger than the one capable through volition in making the attainment stable.

## Description of the Worldling (Puthujjana-niddesa)
"The three fetters" are the fetter of wrong view, the fetter of attachment to rites and rituals, and the fetter of doubt. These fetters are said to be abandoned at the moment of Fruition (phala). This shows that this worldling does not exist even at the moment of Fruition. "Of those states" means for the sake of (abandoning) those fetter-states. At the moment of the Path (magga), one is said to be practicing for the sake of abandoning those fetters. This worldling does not exist even at the moment of the Path. By this much, it should be understood that only the foolish worldling (bāla-puthujjana) with thick defilements, who has abandoned the meditation subject, is spoken of here.

## Description of the Change-of-lineage (Gotrabhū-niddesa)
"Of which states" means (immediately after) those more than fifty wholesome states that arise together with the change-of-lineage knowledge. "Of the noble Dhamma" means of the supramundane Path. "There is a descent" means there is an entry, an arising, a manifestation. "This person is called (a change-of-lineage person)" means this person, through the knowledge that has Nibbāna as its object, transcends all names of "worldling," the lineage of "worldling," the circle of "worldling," and the designation of "worldling," and enters the name of "noble," the lineage of "noble," the circle of "noble," and the designation of "noble"; therefore, he is called a change-of-lineage person.

## Description of One Refraining through Fear (Bhayūparata-niddesa)
"One who refrains through fear" is called Bhayūparata. The seven types of learners (sekha) and worldlings refrain from evil because they fear the danger; they do not [commit] evil...
36: ...they perform. Among those individuals, worldlings (puthujjanas) fear four types of fear: the fear of woeful states (duggati-bhaya), the fear of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-bhaya), the fear of defilements (kilesa-bhaya), and the fear of reproach (upavāda-bhaya). Among these, 'duggati-bhaya' means the woeful states (the four lower realms) themselves, because they are to be feared. The same method applies to the remaining fears. Among those four fears, a worldling does not commit evil because he fears the woeful states, thinking: 'If you commit evil, the four lower realms are like hungry pythons waiting with open mouths; how will it be when you experience suffering in those realms?' The beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) itself is called 'vaṭṭa-bhaya'. All unwholesome states are called 'kilesa-bhaya'. The blame of others is called 'upavāda-bhaya'. Fearing these as well, the worldling does not commit evil. However, the three types of noble learners (sekkhas)—Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners—do not commit evil because they fear the remaining three fears, having already transcended the woeful states. Learners standing on the Path (maggaṭṭha-sekkhas) are called 'those who abstain through fear' (bhayūparata), either because they are facing the Path or because they have not yet completely eradicated fear. An Arahant does not fear even one of these four fears. Since he has completely eradicated all fear, he is called 'one who does not abstain through fear' (abhayūparata). If it is asked, 'Does he not even fear reproach (upavāda)?', the answer is: He does not fear it. However, it should be said that he guards against reproach, like the Arahant Elder in the village of Doṇuppalavāpi. In the Exposition on those Incapable of Attaining (Abhabbāgamana-niddesa): One is called an 'incapable person' (abhabbāgamana) because he is incapable of reaching the Certainty of Rightness (sammatta-niyāma). 'By the obstruction of kamma' (kammāvaraṇa) refers to the five heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma). 'By the obstruction of defilement' (kilesāvaraṇa) refers to fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). 'By the obstruction of result' (vipākāvaraṇa) refers to rebirth with rootless (ahetuka) or double-rooted (duhetuka) consciousness. 'Faithless' (assaddha) refers to those who lack faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. 'Lacking desire' (acchandika) refers to those who lack the wholesome desire to act (kattukamyatā-kusala-chanda). Excluding Jambudīpa, those living in the other three continents should be understood as such. Indeed, the humans in those three continents have entered a state of lacking wholesome desire. 'Unwise' (duppañña) refers to those who lack bhavanga-wisdom (bhavanga-paññā). 'Incapable' (abhabba) refers to those who have not attained the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit. 'Certainty' (niyāma) refers to the Certainty of the Path (magga-niyāma), the Certainty of Rightness (sammatta-niyāma). 'To enter' (okkhamituṃ) means they are incapable of entering, penetrating, or becoming established in that Certainty known as 'Rightness' among wholesome states. The Exposition on those Capable of Attaining (Bhabbāgamana-niddesa) should be understood by the opposite of the method already stated. Thus, in this dyad, those individuals who have committed the five heinous crimes, those who hold fixed wrong views, those who have taken rootless or double-rooted rebirth, those who do not have faith in the Buddha and so forth, those who lack the desire to act wholesomely, those who are not endowed with bhavanga-wisdom, and those who lack the supporting condition for the Path and Fruit—all these are said to be incapable of entering the Certainty of Rightness. Those who are the opposite are said to be capable.
37:
In the Description of the Certain and the Uncertain (Niyata-aniyata-niddesa):—

'Those with immediate results' (ānantarika) refers to those possessed of the heinous crimes with immediate results (ānantarika-kamma). 'Those with wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhika) refers to those possessed of fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). All these persons are called 'certain' (niyata) because they are certain to go to hell. The eight noble persons (ariya-puggala) are also called 'certain' (niyata) because they are fixed in the right state for the sake of the higher paths and fruits, and for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna).

The remaining persons, however, have an uncertain destination (gati). Just as a stick thrown into the air, when falling to the ground, it is unknown whether it will fall on its tip, its middle, or its base; even so, because there is no certainty that 'they will be reborn in such and such a destination,' they should be known as 'uncertain' (aniyata).

As for the statement that the inhabitants of Uttarakuru have a certain destination, that is not by the power of the 'fixed law' (niyata-dhamma). Indeed, only those fixed in wrongness (micchatta-niyata) and those fixed in rightness (sammatta-niyata) are called 'certain.' It is by the power of these factors that this certainty of persons (puggala-niyama) is spoken of.

In the Description of those on the Path (Paṭipannaka-niddesa):—

'Those possessed of the path' (maggasamaṅgī) refers to the eight persons standing on the path. They are called 'practitioners' (paṭipannaka) because they are practicing for the sake of the fruit. 'Those possessed of the fruit' (phalasamaṅgī) are so called because they are possessed of the attainment of the fruit. From the moment they attain the fruit, even if they are not currently in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), they are still considered as 'established in the fruit.'

In the Description of the Equal-Headed (Samasīsī-niddesa):—

'Not before, not after' (apubbaṃ acarimaṃ) means not earlier and not later, but simultaneously. 'Exhaustion' (pariyādāna) means the end. This person is called 'equal-headed' (samasīsī). That person is of three kinds: the posture equal-headed (iriyāpatha-samasīsī), the disease equal-headed (roga-samasīsī), and the life equal-headed (jīvita-samasīsī).

Among them, the person who, while walking, develops insight, reaches Arahatship, and attains Parinibbāna while still walking—like the Elder Paduma; or who, while standing, develops insight, reaches Arahatship, and attains Parinibbāna while still standing—like the Elder Tissa who resided at Koṭapabbata Vihāra; or who, while sitting, develops insight, reaches Arahatship, and attains Parinibbāna while still sitting; or who, while lying down, develops insight, reaches Arahatship, and attains Parinibbāna while still lying down—this person is called 'posture equal-headed' (iriyāpatha-samasīsī).

The person who, having contracted a certain disease, develops insight within that very disease, reaches Arahatship, and attains Parinibbāna through that same disease—this person is called 'disease equal-headed' (roga-samasīsī).
38:
## Who is the person called a jīvitasamasīsī?
There are thirteen heads (sīsa). They are: craving (taṇhā), which is the head of obstacles that block the path to Nibbāna; conceit (māna), which is the head of fetters in saṃsāra; wrong view (diṭṭhi), which is the head of misapprehension; restlessness (uddhacca), which is the head of distraction; ignorance (avijjā), which is the head of defilement and suffering; faith (saddhā), which is the head of resolution; energy (viriya), which is the head of exertion; mindfulness (sati), which is the head of establishment on the object; concentration (samādhi), which is the head of non-distraction; wisdom (paññā), which is the head of vision; the life faculty (jīvitindriya), which is the head of the occurring rounds of existence; liberation (vimokkha, i.e., Nibbāna), which is the head of the object; and cessation (nirodha), which is the head of the end of formations (saṅkhāra).

Among these thirteen, the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) completely exhausts ignorance (avijjā), the head of defilements. The death consciousness (cuticitta) exhausts the life faculty (jīvitindriya), the head of occurrence. The consciousness that exhausts ignorance (the Path of Arahantship) is not able to exhaust the life faculty. The consciousness that exhausts the life faculty (the death consciousness) is not able to exhaust ignorance. The consciousness that exhausts ignorance is of one kind, and the consciousness that exhausts the life faculty is of another kind. For the person in whom these two heads reach exhaustion simultaneously, that person is called a jīvitasamasīsī (one who equals the heads of life).

How does this equality occur? It occurs because of the equality of the vāra (mental turns). In the turn where the emergence from the Path occurs, one stays in nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa)—five in the Path of Stream-entry, five in the Path of Once-returning, five in the Path of Non-returning, and four in the Path of Arahantship—and then, descending into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), one attains final Nibbāna (parinibbāna). Because of this equality of mental turns, the exhaustion of these two heads is said to be equal. Therefore, this person is called a jīvitasamasīsī. And it is this very person who is intended here in this definition (samasīsīniddesa).

## Ṭhitakappīniddesa
One is called a ṭhitakappī because of having a sustained aeon (kappa). It means one who is capable of making the aeon stay. For such a person, even if it is the time for the aeon to be consumed by fire, as long as this person who is endowed with the Path has not yet realized the Fruit of Stream-entry, the aeon cannot yet burn. Even if it is already burning, it would remain without burning further. The destruction of an aeon is a great transformation and a great event, the destruction of a great world-system through the burning of a hundred thousand crores of universes. It is said that even such a great destruction would remain suspended. However, while the Dispensation (sāsana) remains, there is no such thing as the destruction of the aeon. When the aeon is destroyed, the Dispensation no longer exists. The destruction of the aeon occurs only when the time has reached its final limit. Even so, the Teacher brought forth this reason to demonstrate the absence of obstacles: "Even if this destruction of the aeon were to occur, it could not create an obstacle for the attainment of the Fruit by one endowed with the Path." If this person were to make the aeon stay, for how long a time could he make it stay?
39:
When the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) which is the Path occurs, the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) that turns the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises. After that, for such a duration, there may be three moments of conformity (anuloma), one moment of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), one moment of Path-consciousness (magga-citta), two moments of Fruition-consciousness (phala-citta), and five instances of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). This meaning is also illustrated by an external analogy from outside the Dispensation: If a solid rock of one yojana were tied with a triple-strand rope and suspended over the head of one possessed of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), if one strand breaks, it would be held by two; if two break, it would be held by one; even if that one strand breaks, it would remain in the sky like a cloud, and it could not cause any obstacle to the Fruition (phala) immediately following the Path (magga) of that person. This illustration is small; the previous one (regarding the destruction of the world) is grand. It is not only the person standing in the Path of Stream-entry who can stay for an aeon; others possessed of the Path can also stay. Therefore, the Blessed One, encompassing all those mentioned below and those not yet mentioned, together with those remaining on the back-circle, presented this teaching: "All persons possessed of the Path are aeon-stayers (ṭhitakappī)."

## In the Description of the Noble Ones (Ariya-niddesa) -
They are called Noble Ones (ariya) because they are far from defilements. They are called Noble Ones because they are worthy of being approached by the world including the devas. Since the meaning of 'ariya' is 'purity,' they are called Noble Ones because they are pure. Others are called ignoble (anariya) because they are not pure.

## In the Description of the Learners (Sekha-niddesa) -
Those possessed of the Path at the moment of the Path, and those possessed of Fruition at the moment of Fruition, are called Learners (sekha) because they are still training in the three trainings, such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). An Arahant has already completed the three trainings at the moment of the Fruition of Arahantship, and since there is no further task of training for that person, he is called a Non-learner (asekha). Thus, the seven types of Noble Ones are called Learners because they are still training. Arahants are called 'trained non-learners' (sikkhita-asekha) because they have completed the training in virtue, etc., under others. Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas are called 'self-become non-learners' (asikkhita-asekha) because they are self-enlightened. Other persons are called 'neither-learners-nor-non-learners' (neva-sekha-nāsekha) because they are neither training nor have they completed the training.

## In the Description of those with Threefold Knowledge (Tevijja-niddesa) -
One who first attains the knowledge of recollection of past lives and the divine eye, and later reaches the Fruition of Arahantship, as well as one who first reaches the Fruition of Arahantship and later attains the knowledge of recollection of past lives and the divine eye, is called one with threefold knowledge (tevijja). Since Suttanta discourse is figurative (pariyāya-desanā) and Abhidhamma discourse is non-figurative (nippariyāya-desanā), in this context, the original source is primary. Therefore, one who first attains the two knowledges and later reaches the Fruition of Arahantship is intended here. The same method applies to those with six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiñña).
40:
## In the Description of the Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha-niddesa) -
'In things not heard before' means in the final life, at the time of penetrating the Four Noble Truths, regarding dhammas not heard before in the presence of any other person. However, in lives prior to that final life, the omniscient Bodhisattas, having gone forth in the Buddha's Dispensation and learned the three Pitakas, practiced meditation associated with the duties of coming and going (gatapaccāgatavatta), and were able to reach and maintain the stages up to conformity (anuloma) and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). Therefore, this was said with reference to the state of having no teacher only in the final life. Indeed, at that time, the Tathāgata, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), personally penetrates the Four Noble Truths with his own direct knowledge in the conditioned (sankhata) and unconditioned (asankhata) dhammas not heard before in the presence of another teacher, realizing: "This is suffering... this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."

'In that also' means in that Path of Arahantship, which is called the knowledge that penetrates the Four Truths. 'Attains omniscience and mastery over the powers' means he attains omniscient knowledge and the state of practiced mastery over the ten powers. For the Buddhas, from the moment of attaining omniscient knowledge and the ten powers of knowledge, there is no other task to be done. Just as a prince of noble birth from both parents, from the moment of receiving his consecration, it cannot be said that "such and such royal power has not yet arrived," for all has already arrived; similarly, for the Buddhas, from the moment of reaching the Path of Arahantship, it cannot be said that "such and such a quality has not yet arrived, has not been penetrated, or has not been realized," for all omniscient qualities have already arrived, been penetrated, and been realized. 'This person is described' means the person who has penetrated all omniscient qualities through the Noble Path by the power of the completion of the perfections is called a Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha).

In the Description of the Silent Buddha (Paccekabuddha-niddesa) also, the meaning of the phrase 'in things not heard before' should be understood in the same way as mentioned before. For the Silent Buddha also, in the final life, penetrates the Truths only through his own self-attained knowledge without a teacher. However, he does not attain omniscient knowledge or mastery over the powers.

## In the Description of the One Liberated in Both Ways (Ubhatobhāgavimutta-niddesa) -
'Dwells having touched the eight deliverances with the body' means he dwells having attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) through the co-nascent mental body (nāma-kāya). 'And having seen with wisdom' means because of seeing the conditioned states of mind and matter through insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and the Four Noble Truths through Path-wisdom (magga-paññā), the four taints (āsavas) are exhausted. This...
41:
...such a person is called one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta). This person is called "liberated in both ways" because he is liberated from the defilements twice through two parts. In explaining this "liberated in both ways," the following are the views of the Elders (Theras):

Firstly, the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga stated: "He is liberated twice through two parts because he is liberated by the liberation of suppression (vikkhambhana-vimokkha) through the attainments, and by the liberation of eradication (samuccheda-vimokkha) through the Path."

However, the Elder Tipitaka Mahādhammarakkhita said, "This person is one who is dependent on the mental (nāma)," and citing the Sutta:
"Just as a flame tossed by the force of the wind goes out and does not reach a designation, so the sage, liberated from the mental body (nāmakāya), goes out and does not reach a designation (in terms of name, lineage, etc.)." (Sutta Nipāta 1080).
Having cited this, he stated: "He is called liberated in both ways because he is well-liberated from both the mental body and the material body (rūpakāya)."

The Elder Tipitaka Cūḷābhaya, however, stated: "He is called liberated in both ways because he is liberated once by the liberation of suppression through the attainments, and once by the liberation of eradication through the Path."

All three of these Elders were wise; since the reasoning in the views of all three is evident, all three views have been established as the tradition of the Commentaries. In brief, however, he is liberated from the material body by the formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) and liberated from the mental body by the Path; thus, being liberated from both parts, he is called "liberated in both ways."

That person is of five types: the four who reach the fruit of Arahatship after emerging from each of the four formless attainments, and the Non-returner (anāgāmī) who reaches the fruit of Arahatship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Among these five, the first four are called "liberated in both ways" in a figurative sense (pariyāya) because they cannot enter the attainment of cessation, which is the peak of attainments. The Non-returner who possesses the eight attainments, enters that attainment of cessation, emerges from it, develops insight, and reaches the fruit of Arahatship, is called the "foremost liberated in both ways" in the literal sense (nippariyāya).

If it is asked: "Is it not the case that since the formless sphere jhana has two factors due to equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, and the fourth jhana of the fine-material sphere is the same, therefore a person who reaches Arahatship based on that fourth fine-material jhana should also be one liberated in both ways?"

The answer is: He should not be. Why? Because he is not yet liberated from the material body. That fourth fine-material jhana is liberated only from the body of defilements, not from the material body. Therefore, a person who reaches Arahatship after emerging from that jhana is not called one liberated in both ways...
42:
Since the formless jhana is liberated from both the mental body (nāmakāya) and the material body (rūpakāya), a person who reaches the fruit of Arahantship based on that formless jhana should be known as 'one liberated in both ways' (ubhatobhāgavimutta).

In the description of 'one liberated by wisdom' (paññāvimutta): One who is liberated from defilements through the wisdom of insight and the wisdom of the path is called 'one liberated by wisdom'. There are five types of such persons: the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and the four types of persons who reach the fruit of Arahantship after emerging from the four fine-material jhanas. Indeed, among these five types of persons, not even one is an attainer of the eight liberations (vimokkha). For this reason, it is said, "without having attained the eight liberations," and so on. However, if one possesses any of the formless jhanas, they are simply called 'one liberated in both ways'.

In the description of the 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī): "Some taints" refers to the taints that are to be abandoned by the three lower paths. A person of such nature is called a 'body-witness'. He is a body-witness because he realizes Nibbāna at the end of the formless jhanas he has attained. He is also called a body-witness because he first touches the contact of jhana and later realizes Nibbāna, which is the cessation of conditioned things. There are six types of body-witnesses, starting from the one established in the fruit of stream-entry up to the one established in the path of Arahantship.

In the description of 'one attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta): "This is suffering" means this mundane state (tebhūmaka) excluding craving is suffering; suffering is only this much; there is no suffering beyond this mundane state. The same method applies to the terms "origin of suffering" and so on. "Knows as it really is" means, setting aside craving, one knows the five aggregates of clinging as the 'truth of suffering' (dukkha-sacca) according to their actual nature. Craving produces suffering, brings it into existence, and originates it; because of that craving, that suffering arises well. Therefore, one knows that craving as the 'truth of the origin of suffering' (dukkha-samudaya-sacca) as it really is. Since this suffering and its origin cease, become tranquil, and reach non-occurrence upon reaching Nibbāna, one knows that Nibbāna as the 'truth of the cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha-sacca) as it really is. The noble Eightfold Path leads to that Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. Therefore, one knows that path as the 'practice leading to the cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā) as it really is. By this much, the definition of the four truths at different moments is shown. Now, to show the realization of the truths at a single moment, the words "proclaimed by the Tathāgata" (tathāgatapappavedita) and so on are spoken. In that context, "proclaimed by the Tathāgata" refers to the truths penetrated, known, and made manifest by the Blessed One while sitting at the terrace of the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa). "Dhamma" refers to the four noble truths. "Voditṭhā" means they are well seen. "Vocariitā" means they are well explored by wisdom. It means that in these four truths, this person has well exercised his wisdom. A person of such nature is called 'one attained to vision'. This is because he has reached the end of the path of stream-entry, which sees the truths. The knowledge that "conditioned things are suffering, Nibbāna is bliss"...
43:
...is seen, known, realized, and touched by wisdom; therefore, he is called 'one attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta). This person also has six varieties, just like the body-witness. In the description of 'one liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta): In the phrase "not like the one attained to vision," it means that the taints of the one liberated by faith are not exhausted in the same way as the taints of the one attained to vision are exhausted. If asked, "Is there a difference in their abandoning of defilements?", the answer is "No." If there is no difference, why does the one liberated by faith not reach the state of one attained to vision? The answer is: because of the difference in the practice (paṭipadā) that leads to the path. Indeed, at the moment the path arises, the one attained to vision is able to separate from defilements without suffering, without difficulty, and without exhaustion. The one liberated by faith, however, is able to separate from defilements only with suffering, difficulty, and exhaustion; therefore, he cannot reach the state of one attained to vision. Furthermore, there is also a difference in their wisdom. For the one attained to vision, insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in the three higher paths proceeds being sharp, courageous, and clear. For the one liberated by faith, insight knowledge does not proceed being sharp, courageous, and clear; for this reason also, he cannot reach the state of one attained to vision.

For example, it is like two young men performing a feat of skill, where one has a sharp sword in his hand and the other has a blunt sword. When a banana tree is cut with a sharp sword, it makes no sound. But when cut with a blunt sword, it makes a "kat-kat" sound. In this analogy, the sharp, courageous, and clear nature of the insight knowledge in the three higher paths of the one attained to vision should be understood like the cutting of the banana tree with a sharp sword without making a sound. The non-sharp, non-courageous, and non-clear nature of the insight knowledge in the three higher paths of the one liberated by faith should be understood like the cutting of the banana tree with a blunt sword while making a sound. Having rejected this method [of wisdom difference] with the word "No," the conclusion is made that the one liberated by faith does not reach the state of one attained to vision only because of the difference in the practice that leads to the path.

In the Āgama commentaries, however, it is stated: "Among these persons, for the one liberated by faith, the destruction of defilements (the path of Arahantship) occurs at the moment of the preceding path as if believing, as if entering with knowledge, and as if resolving firmly. For the one attained to vision, at the moment of the preceding path, the wisdom that cuts defilements proceeds without hesitation, being sharp and courageous. Therefore, for example, just as the cut surface of a banana tree cut by a person with a non-sharp sword is not smooth, and the sword does not move quickly but a sound is heard and a greater effort must be made, such a nature should be understood to exist in the preceding path-development (magga-bhāvanā) of the one liberated by faith."
44:
The development of the path preceding [the fruition] for a person liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) has such a nature. Furthermore, just as for one who cuts a banana tree with a well-sharpened sword, the place of cutting is smooth, the sword moves swiftly, no sound is heard, and there is no need for powerful effort; in the same way, the development of the path preceding [the fruition] for a person who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta) should be understood. "This person is spoken of" means that a person of such nature is called a saddhāvimutta. This person is called a saddhāvimutta because he is liberated while having faith. This person also, like the body-witness (kāyasakkhī), is of six types.

## Dhammānusārī-niddesa

By the words "for one who practices," the person established in the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) is shown. "Adhimatta" means powerful (balava). He is called a paññāvāhī because he leads wisdom towards Nibbāna. It is also said he is a paññāvāhī because wisdom leads this person to Nibbāna. "Having wisdom as the precursor" means [developing the path] by making wisdom the precursor. "This person is spoken of" means that a person of such nature is called a dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī). He is called a dhammānusārī because he follows or follows along with the Dhamma known as wisdom. This is the name for one established in the path of stream-entry. However, upon reaching the fruition, he is called one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta).

## In the Saddhānusārī-niddesa also

He is called a saddhāvāhī because he leads faith towards Nibbāna. It is also said he is a saddhāvāhī because faith leads this person to Nibbāna. "Having faith as the precursor" means [developing the path] by making faith the precursor. "This person is spoken of" means that a person of such nature is called a faith-follower (saddhānusārī). He is called a saddhānusārī because he follows by means of faith. This is the name for one established in the path of stream-entry. However, upon reaching the fruition, he is called one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta).

For those who bring about the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), there are two burdens (dhura), two inclinations (abhinivesa), and two summits (sīsa). Among them, the two burdens are the burden of faith (saddhā-dhura) and the burden of wisdom (paññā-dhura). One monk enters by firmly inclining towards serenity (samatha), and another enters by firmly inclining towards insight (vipassanā); these are the two inclinations. When a monk reaches the summit which is the fruition of Arahantship, one is liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) and another is liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta); these are the two summits. Whoever brings about the supramundane states, they all make these two qualities of faith and wisdom the predominant factors, incline firmly towards these two states of serenity and insight, and are liberated from the defilements through these two modes of being liberated in both ways and being liberated by wisdom. Among those persons, whichever monk, having attained the eight attainments (samāpatti), makes wisdom the predominant factor, inclines firmly by the power of serenity, and having made one of the immaterial attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) the proximate cause, develops insight and reaches the fruition of Arahantship—that monk is called a dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the path of stream-entry. Thereafter, in the six stages [the three higher paths and three lower fruitions], he is called a body-witness (kāyasakkhī). Upon reaching the fruition of Arahantship, he is called one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
45:
Another person, making wisdom the predominant factor, enters through the power of insight and, by contemplating either pure formations (suddha-saṅkhāra) or one of the fine-material jhanas (rūpāvacara-jhāna), reaches the fruition of Arahantship. This person also is called a dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the path of stream-entry. After obtaining the path of stream-entry, in the six stages, he is called one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatta). Upon reaching the fruition of Arahantship, he is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta). In this case of the inclination towards insight with wisdom as the predominant factor, these two names [diṭṭhippatta and paññāvimutta] are new. Together with the previous names, they become five.

Another person who has attained the eight attainments, making faith the predominant factor, enters through the power of concentration (samādhi) and, having made one of the immaterial attainments the proximate cause, strives in insight and reaches the fruition of Arahantship. This person is called a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the path of stream-entry. After obtaining the path of stream-entry, in the six stages, he is called only a body-witness (kāyasakkhī). Upon reaching the fruition of Arahantship, he is called only one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta). In this case of the inclination towards serenity with faith as the predominant factor, only one name [saddhānusārī] is new. Together with that name, the previous five names become six.

Another person, making faith the predominant factor, enters through the power of insight and, by contemplating either pure formations or one of the fine-material jhanas, reaches the fruition of Arahantship. This person also is called a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the path of stream-entry. After obtaining the path of stream-entry, in the six stages, he is called one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta). Upon reaching the fruition of Arahantship, he is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta). In this case of the inclination towards insight with faith as the predominant factor also, only one name [saddhāvimutta] is new. Together with that name, the previous six names become seven. These seven persons are called the highest worthy of offerings (aggadakkhiṇeyya) in the world.

## In the explanation of the Sattakkhattuparama-niddesa:

"Sattakkhattu" means up to seven times. For that stream-enterer, there is the reaching of births or the taking up of existence with a maximum limit of seven times; because he does not take up an eighth existence beyond those seven births, he is called a "sattakkhattuparama" (one with seven births at most). In the text "sotāpanno hoti," "sota" (the stream) is the Noble Path; the person endowed with that Noble Path is called a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). How is it taught?

"Sāriputta, 'the stream, the stream' it is said. What, Sāriputta, is the stream?" When asked thus, [Sāriputta] replied: "Venerable sir, this Noble Eightfold Path is the stream; namely, right view ... right concentration." "Sāriputta, 'stream-enterer, stream-enterer' it is said. What, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?" When asked thus, [Sāriputta] replied: "Venerable sir, whoever is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer; that venerable one of such a name and such a clan."
46:
In this way, one is called a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) even at the moment of the Path (magga-kkhaṇa). However, in this context, because the Path gives its name to the Fruit (phala), the Stream-enterer at the moment of the Fruit is intended.

'Avinipātadhamma' refers to one who, by nature, does not go to the planes of misery (apāya) known as 'vinipāta' by way of rebirth. 'Niyata' means one who is fixed by the law of the Path (magga-niyāma). 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa' means one whose ultimate goal is the state of enlightenment. That Stream-enterer is called 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa' because they understand the Four Noble Truths through the Path they have attained. Alternatively, they are called 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa' because they will certainly realize enlightenment through the three higher Paths. 'Among gods and humans' refers to the deva world and the human world. 'Having wandered' means going from one existence to another by way of rebirth. 'Makes an end of suffering' means making a limit or a boundary to the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha). 'This person is called' means a person of such nature is called a 'Sattakkhattuparama' (one who attains enlightenment in seven births at most). It should be understood that this 'Sattakkhattuparama' person is described as having a mixed existence, sometimes in the deva world and sometimes in the human world.

## In the Explanation of Kolaṃkola (Kolaṃkolaniddesa):
One is called 'Kolaṃkola' because they go from family to family (kula to kula). The meaning is that from the moment of realizing the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), there is no rebirth in low-status families; they are born only in families of great wealth. 'Two or three families' means two or three existences in the worlds of gods and humans. Thus, this 'Kolaṃkola' person is also described as having a mixed existence. The phrase 'two or three' is merely a teaching method (desanā-matta). In reality, even one who wanders for up to six existences is still a 'Kolaṃkola'.

## In the Explanation of Ekabījī (Ekabījīniddesa):
The 'seed of the aggregates' (khandha-bīja) is taught here. A Stream-enterer who has only one seed of the aggregates (taking up one more existence) is called an 'Ekabījī'. The phrase 'human existence' here is merely a teaching method. It can also be said that they are reborn in a deva existence. These names are given according to the names adopted by the Blessed One. The Blessed One assigned these names: one who reaches this extent is a 'Sattakkhattuparama', this much is a 'Kolaṃkola', and this much is an 'Ekabījī'. However, there is no fixed rule that 'this specific person' is always a 'Sattakkhattuparama', 'this one' a 'Kolaṃkola', or 'this one' an 'Ekabījī'.
47:
What factor determines this distinction (Sattakkhattuparama, Kolaṃkola, Ekabījī) among those Stream-enterers? Some Elders say, "The past cause (pubba-hetu) determines it." Some say, "The first Path (Sotāpattimagga) determines it." Some say, "The three higher Paths determine it." Others say, "The insight (vipassanā) of the three Paths determines it."

Among these views, in the view that "the past cause determines it," the statement would arise that "a strong dependence-condition (upanissaya) was made for the first Path, but the three higher Paths arose without a strong dependence-condition." In the view that "the first Path determines it," the three higher Paths would become purposeless. In the view that "the three higher Paths determine it," the fault arises that "the three higher Paths have already arisen even before the first Path has arisen." Only the view that "the insight of the three Paths determines it" is appropriate. If the insight of the three higher Paths is powerful, one is an 'Ekabījī'. If the insight is weaker than that, one is a 'Kolaṃkola'. If the insight is even weaker than that, one is a 'Sattakkhattuparama'.

Some Stream-enterers are inclined toward the round of rebirth (vaṭṭajjhāsaya), delighting in the round, and are seen wandering and appearing repeatedly only within the round. Persons such as Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer, Visākhā the laywoman, the young gods Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha, the young god Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka the king of gods, and the young god Nāgadatta are inclined toward the round and delight in it. Starting from the beginning, they will purify the six deva worlds and, staying in the Akaniṭṭha realm, will attain Parinibbāna. These persons are not included here in this classification of Stream-enterers. Not only these, but also those who attain Arahatship after wandering seven times only among humans, or those who attain Arahatship after wandering seven times only among devas, are not included here. It should be understood that in this classification, 'Sattakkhattuparama' and 'Kolaṃkola' are taken only by way of mixed existence (missaka-bhava) between the human and deva worlds, and 'Ekabījī' is taken as one who is reborn in a human existence.

Among those Stream-enterers, each individual reaches four variations by way of the painful practice (dukkhā-paṭipadā), etc. There are twelve types through those who make faith their precursor (saddhā-dhura): four Sattakkhattuparamas, four Kolaṃkolas, and four Ekabījīs. If they are able to produce it through wisdom, thinking "I will produce the supramundane Dhamma," those who reach the state of Sattakkhattuparama etc. by making wisdom their precursor (paññā-dhura) are also twelve by way of practice. Thus, it should be understood that these twenty-four Stream-enterers are taught here by way of those who reside in this sense-sphere and lack jhāna (non-jhāna attainers).

## Explanation of the Once-Returner (Sakadāgāminiddesa)
In the Sakadāgāminiddesa, one is called a 'Once-returner' (Sakadāgāmī) because they come back only once by way of rebirth. 'Sakideva' means only one time. By the phrase 'having come to this world,' only one type of Once-returner is taken, excluding the other four types among the five kinds of Once-returners.
48:
Among the five types of Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), four are excluded and only one is taken here. Indeed, some reach the fruit of Once-returning in this human world and attain Parinibbāna right here; some reach it here and attain Parinibbāna in the deva world; some reach it in the deva world and attain Parinibbāna right there; some reach it in the deva world, are reborn in this human world, and then attain Parinibbāna—none of these four are taken here. It should be understood that only the one who reaches it in this human world, lives in the deva world for the full lifespan, and is then reborn in this human world to attain Parinibbāna is taken here. All other matters to be discussed here have already been stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā in the Lokuttarakusalaniddesa. What is the difference between this Once-returner and the 'One-seeder' (Ekabījī)? The One-seeder has only one more rebirth, while the Once-returner has two rebirths—this is the difference between them.

## In the Exposition on the Non-returner (Anāgāminiddesa):
In the phrase "orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ", "oraṃ" refers to the sensual realm (kāmadhātu). For one in whom these five fetters are not yet abandoned, even if they are reborn in the highest point of existence (the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), they are like a fish that has swallowed a hook or like a crow whose leg is tied with a long string; being pulled by those fetters, they must occur only in the sensual realm. Therefore, the five fetters are called "orambhāgiyā" (belonging to the lower part). "Heṭṭhābhāgiyāni" means those belonging to the lower portion. "Parikkhayā" means by the exhaustion of those fetters. "Opapātiko" means one who has a spontaneous rebirth. By this word, rebirth in a womb (gabbhaseyyā) is excluded. "Tattha parinibbāyī" means one who is habituated to attaining Parinibbāna in that realm of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). "Anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā" means one who, by way of taking rebirth, does not return from that realm to this sensual realm. However, their coming for the sake of seeing the Buddha, seeing the Elders, and hearing the Dhamma is not prohibited. "Ayaṃ vuccati" means such a person is called a "Non-returner" (Anāgāmī) because they do not return again by way of rebirth.

## In the Exposition on the one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (Antarāparinibbāyiniddesa):
"Upapannaṃ vā samanantarā" means immediately after taking rebirth. "Appattaṃ vā vemajjhaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ" means they bring forth the Noble Path without having reached the middle of the lifespan. Due to the alternative function of the word "vā", it should also be understood to mean (bringing forth the Path) having reached the middle. Thus, the three types of those who attain Parinibbāna in the interval are established. "Upariṭṭhimānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ" means of the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojana) or of the eight defilements (kilesa). For the sake of abandoning those (higher fetters or eight defilements), (they bring forth the Path).
49:
(They) bring forth the Path for the sake of abandoning (the higher fetters or the eight defilements). Such a person is called one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī) because they attain the quenching of defilements (Parinibbāna) within the middle of the lifespan.

## Exposition on the one who attains Parinibbāna after more than half the lifespan (Upahaccaparinibbāyiniddesa)
"Having surpassed the middle of the lifespan" means exceeding the midpoint of the life duration. "Having approached death" means having come near to death; it means staying close to the end of the lifespan. Such a person, while having a lifespan of a thousand great aeons in the Aviha realm, surpasses the middle point of five hundred great aeons and stays in the sixth hundredth aeon, or in any of the seventh, eighth, or ninth hundredth aeons, or even in the tenth hundredth aeon, reaches the fruit of Arahantship and attains Parinibbāna through the quenching of defilements; therefore, they are called one who attains Parinibbāna after more than half the lifespan (upahaccaparinibbāyī).

## Exposition on the one who attains Parinibbāna without and with exertion (Asaṅkhāra-sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyiniddesa)
One who has the nature of attaining Parinibbāna through the quenching of defilements without instigating insight knowledge and without making excessive effort is called one who attains Parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). One who has the nature of attaining Parinibbāna through the quenching of defilements only after making excessive effort with difficulty and with the instigation of insight knowledge is called one who attains Parinibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī).

## Exposition on the one who goes upstream (Uddhaṃsotaniddesa)
Because of the state of being carried to higher realms, or because of having the stream of craving or the stream of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) directed upwards, one is called "uddhaṃsota" (one who goes upstream). Alternatively, because of having the stream of the Path, which is to be obtained by going to the higher Akaniṭṭha realm, one is called "uddhaṃsota". In the passages such as "having passed away from the Aviha realm, they go to the Atappa realm", one stays in the Aviha realm for a thousand great aeons, and being unable to reach the fruit of Arahantship, goes to the Atappa realm. There also, staying for two thousand great aeons and being unable to reach the fruit of Arahantship, they go to the Sudassa realm. There also, staying for four thousand great aeons and being unable to reach the fruit of Arahantship, they go to the Sudassī realm. There also, staying for eight thousand great aeons and being unable to reach the fruit of Arahantship, they go to the Akaniṭṭha realm. It means that while staying in that Akaniṭṭha realm, they bring forth the Noble Path.

To understand the divisions of these Non-returners, the tetrad of "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī) should be known. Among those four persons, the Non-returner who, starting from the Aviha realm, purifies the four celestial realms and then goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm to attain Parinibbāna is called "uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī". The person who purifies the three lower celestial realms and stays in the Sudassī celestial realm to attain Parinibbāna is "uddhaṃsota" but not "akaniṭṭhagāmī".
50:
...is called. One who goes directly from this (sensual realm) to the Akaniṭṭha realm and attains Parinibbāna there is called an Akaniṭṭhagāmī who is not an Uddhaṃsoto. One who attains Parinibbāna in any of the four lower Brahma realms is neither an Uddhaṃsoto nor an Akaniṭṭhagāmī. Thus, there are forty-eight types of Non-returners (Anāgāmīs).

How are they [counted]? Firstly, in the Aviha realm, there are three who attain Parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), one who attains Parinibbāna after landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī), and one who is 'upstream-bound' (uddhaṃsoto). These five types of Non-returners become ten, consisting of five who attain Parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī) and five who attain Parinibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). Similarly, in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, there are ten in each, totaling forty. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, there is no Uddhaṃsoto. There are only three who attain Parinibbāna in the interval and one who attains Parinibbāna after landing. These four types become eight, consisting of four who attain Parinibbāna without exertion and four who attain Parinibbāna with exertion. Thus, there are forty-eight in total.

All these Non-returners are illustrated by the simile of sparks (iron chips). Indeed, when the tip of an iron tool such as a needle-eye punch, a small razor, or a small nail-clipper, which has been heated intensely all day, is struck (on an anvil), a spark arises and is extinguished immediately upon arising. A person of such nature should be known as the first type of Antarāparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Parinibbāna through the extinction of defilements immediately after being reborn. When a larger iron tip is struck, a spark leaps up into the sky and is extinguished (while still in the sky). A person of such nature should be known as the second type of Antarāparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Parinibbāna before reaching the middle of their lifespan. When a still larger iron tip is struck, a spark leaps up into the sky and, while falling back, is extinguished before reaching the ground. A person of such nature should be known as the third type of Antarāparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Parinibbāna after reaching the middle of their lifespan but before approaching death. When a still larger iron tip is struck, a spark leaps up into the sky and is extinguished only after falling onto the ground. A person of such nature should be known as an Upahaccaparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Parinibbāna after approaching death and exhausting their lifespan. When a still larger iron tip is struck, a spark falls onto a small heap of grass or wood, burns that small amount of grass or wood, and then is extinguished. A person of such nature should be known as an Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Parinibbāna with little effort and through a swift course of life (or swift knowledge). When a still larger iron tip is struck, a spark falls onto a large heap of grass or wood, burns that large heap of grass or wood, and then is extinguished. A person of such nature should be known as a Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Why? Because with effort...
51:
...they attain Parinibbāna through a course of life or knowledge that is not swift (should be known as a Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). Another spark falls onto a massive heap of grass and wood. While that massive heap of grass and wood is burning, either a glow without flame or a blazing flame leaps up, burns the smith's hut, then burns villages, towns, and kingdoms, and is only extinguished upon reaching the edge of the ocean. A person of such nature should be known as an 'upstream-bound' one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm (Uddhaṃsoto Akaniṭṭhagāmī). Why? Because they attain Parinibbāna only after repeatedly encountering the proliferation of craving, which is the seed of rebirth in many lives, and eliminating it without remainder. Since objects of various sizes, such as the needle-eye punch, are all made of iron, in all sections of the Sutta text, only the term 'iron slab' (ayokapāla) is used.

The manner of teaching is as follows: "Monks, in this teaching, a monk practices thus: 'If [the five past causes] had not been, there would not be my [five present effects]; if [the five present causes] do not come to be, my [five future effects] will not be. What exists, what has come to be, that I abandon.' Reflecting thus, he attains the equanimity of insight knowledge. That monk is not attached to the present life, nor is he attached to a future life. Because of this lack of attachment, he sees the extremely peaceful Nibbāna as it really is with the wisdom of the Path. Although he sees it, he has not yet fully realized that Nibbāna in all its aspects. The underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) has not been entirely abandoned by him, the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) has not been entirely abandoned, and the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) has not been entirely abandoned. Through the destruction of the five lower fetters that lead to the lower sensual realm, he becomes one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (Antarāparinibbāyī). Monks, just as when an iron slab that has been heated intensely all day is struck with a hammer, a spark arises and is then extinguished; even so, monks, when a monk practices in this way... he becomes an Antarāparinibbāyī.

"Monks, in this teaching, a monk practices thus... he becomes an Antarāparinibbāyī. Monks, just as when an iron slab that has been heated intensely all day is struck with a hammer, a spark arises, leaps up, and is then extinguished; even so, monks, when a monk practices in this way... he becomes an Antarāparinibbāyī.

"Monks, in this teaching, a monk practices thus... he becomes an Antarāparinibbāyī. Monks, just as when an iron slab that has been heated intensely all day is struck with a hammer, a spark arises, leaps up, and then..."
52:
Just as a spark might extinguish before reaching the ground; even so, monks, a monk practices in this way: 'If I were not, it would not be mine; if I should not become, it will not become for me; what exists, what has come to be, that I abandon,' and thus he attains equanimity. Such a person is one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī).

Here, monks, a monk practices in this way... and becomes one who attains Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī). Monks, just as when a heated iron ball that has been heated all day is struck with a hammer, a spark is produced and, having flown up, extinguishes upon reaching the ground; even so, monks, a monk practices in this way... and becomes one who attains Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī).

Here, monks, a monk practices in this way... and through the destruction of defilements, becomes one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). Monks, just as when a heated iron ball that has been heated all day is struck with a hammer, a spark is produced and, having flown up, might fall upon a small pile of grass or a small pile of wood. That spark would produce fire and produce smoke in that pile of grass or wood. Having produced fire and smoke, and having consumed that small pile of grass or wood, it would extinguish due to lack of fuel; even so, monks, a monk practices in this way... and through the destruction of defilements, becomes one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī).

Here, monks, a monk practices in this way... and becomes one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). Monks, just as when a heated iron ball that has been heated all day is struck with a hammer, a spark is produced and, having flown up, might fall upon a large pile of grass or a large pile of wood. That spark would produce fire... and having consumed that large pile of grass or wood, it would extinguish due to lack of fuel; even so, monks, a monk practices in this way... and becomes one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī).

Here, monks, a monk practices in this way... and through the destruction of defilements, becomes one who goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī). Monks, just as when a heated iron ball that has been heated all day is struck with a hammer, a spark is produced and, having flown up, might fall upon a vast pile of grass or a vast pile of wood. That spark would produce fire... and having consumed that vast pile of grass or wood, it would burn an ownerless thicket or a forest with an owner. Having burned the thicket and the forest...
53:
Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk practices in this way and goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. Monks, just as that spark, having consumed that vast pile of grass or that pile of wood, would burn an ownerless thicket or a forest with an owner. Having burned the thicket and the forest, and having reached the boundary of green grass, or the boundary of a path, or the boundary of a rocky mountain, or the boundary of water, or a pleasant stretch of ground, it would extinguish due to lack of fuel; even so, monks, a monk practices in this way and becomes one who goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm—thus it was said (in the Purisagati Sutta of the Abyākata Vagga, Sattakanipāta, Aṅguttara Nikāya).

41-44. The descriptions (niddesa) beginning with the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) have clear meanings. Specifically, in the passage "This person is called an Arahant," twelve types of Arahants should be understood. How should they be understood? There are three liberations: the void (suññata), the signless (animitta), and the undirected (appaṇihita). Among these three liberations, an Arahant liberated by the void liberation is of four types according to the mode of practice. Likewise, those liberated by the signless and undirected liberations are also of four types each. Thus, twelve Arahants should be understood. In the same way as these twelve Arahants, there are twelve Sakadāgāmīs, twenty-four Sotāpannas, and forty-eight Anāgāmīs. Persons of such extent, having been released from this Dispensation, do not arise outside; they arise only in this Dispensation of the All-Knowing Buddha.

## Commentary on the Description of the Ones (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā)

## 2. Commentary on the Description of the Twos (Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā)
