'Parapasaṃsanā' is the praise uttered by others in one's presence. 'Paravaṇṇahārikā' is the speech that carries praise initiated by others through successive tradition.

'Cīvaralūkha' is the roughness of the robe due to its poor color and so on. 'Pattalūkha' is the roughness of the bowl in terms of its color, shape, and material. 'Senāsanalūkha' is the roughness of the lodging, bed, and seat due to the lack of decorations. 'Vividha' means having many varieties, such as being an acelaka (naked ascetic). 'Dukkarakārika' refers to practices that cause heat or affliction to the body.

Alternatively, among these four types of persons, one who takes form as the measure and is inspired is called 'rūpappamāṇa'. 'Rūpappasanna' is just another term for the same meaning. One who takes fame as the measure and is inspired is called 'ghosappamāṇa'. One who takes the roughness of robes and bowls as the measure and is inspired is called 'lūkhappamāṇa'. One who takes the Dhamma (virtue, concentration, wisdom) as the measure and is inspired is called 'dhammappamāṇa'. The other terms are merely words expressing their meanings. If all beings are divided into three parts, two parts are rūpappamāṇa and only one part is not. If divided into five parts, four parts are ghosappamāṇa and only one part is not. If divided into ten parts, nine parts are lūkhappamāṇa and only one part is not. However, if divided into a hundred thousand parts, only one part is dhammappamāṇa, and the rest are not. Thus, the world of beings is established in these four measures.

In this world of four measures, those who lack faith in the Buddhas are few, while those with faith are many. For the rūpappamāṇa person, there is no form more inspiring than the physical form of the Buddha. For the ghosappamāṇa person, there is no sound more inspiring than the fame of the Buddhas. For the lūkhappamāṇa person, there is no austerity greater than that of the Buddha, who renounced soft Kāsī cloth, precious golden vessels, and magnificent palaces fully equipped for every season, to rely on rags from the dust-heap (paṃsukūla), a stone bowl, and dwellings at the foot of trees. For the dhammappamāṇa person, there are no other qualities more inspiring than the virtues of the Buddha, such as his peerless virtue (sīla), etc., in the world including the devas. Therefore, the Buddha stands as if holding this world of four measures in the palm of his hand. This concludes the Exposition on the Four Measures (Catuppamāṇa Niddesa).

In terms like attahitāya paṭipanna, 'sīlasampanna' means being endowed with virtue. The same applies to 'samādhisampanna' and so on.
81:
Having abandoned precious golden bowls fit for noble ones, and magnificent palaces endowed with all comforts suitable for the three seasons, the Blessed One habitually resorted to lodgings such as robes made of rags, stone bowls, and the foot of trees. There is no other austerity more inspiring than that of the Blessed One. For a person who measures by the Dhamma (dhammāppamāṇa), there is no other quality of virtue and so forth more inspiring than the unique virtues of the Tathāgata in the world with its devas. Thus, the Blessed One stands as if holding this world of four measures in his fist.

Regarding the terms beginning with attahitāya paṭipanna (one practicing for one's own benefit): Sīlasampanna means being endowed with or possessed of virtue. The same method applies to samādhisampanna and so forth. Here, virtue refers to both mundane and supramundane virtue. Likewise, concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā) are also taught. Vimutti refers only to the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-vimutti). Ñāṇadassana (knowledge and vision) refers to the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). Regarding the terms beginning with no para (not for others): it means that while one undertakes virtue oneself, one does not encourage or make others undertake it by saying, 'You too should be endowed with virtue.' This method applies to all such phrases. Among these four types of persons, the first (one practicing only for one's own benefit) is like the Elder Vakkali. The second (one practicing only for the benefit of others) is like the Sakyan Upananda. The third (one practicing for the benefit of both oneself and others) is like the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The fourth (one practicing for the benefit of neither) is like Devadatta.

Regarding the terms beginning with attantapa: one is called attantapa because one torments or causes suffering to oneself. Attaparitāpanānuyoga means the practice of devotion to self-mortification. Acelaka means one who is clothless, i.e., naked. Muttācāra means one with loose habits. In matters such as defecation and so forth, being devoid of the refined conduct of worldly gentlemen, such a person defecates, urinates, chews, and eats while standing. Hatthāpalekhana means licking one's hands with the tongue when the food in the hand is finished. Alternatively, it indicates that after defecating, one scrapes or wipes with the hand, perceiving the hand itself to be a stick. It is said that they designate a stick as a living being. Therefore, one who fulfills their practice acts in this way. Because one does not come when told, 'Come, venerable,' to receive alms, one is called na-ehibhadantika. Similarly, because one does not stop when told, 'Stop, venerable,' one is called na-tiṭṭhabhadantika. The ascetics do not do both of these, thinking, 'This would mean following his words.' Abhihaṭa refers to alms-food brought forward beforehand. Uddissakata refers to alms-food announced as, 'This has been prepared specifically for you, venerable.' Na nimantana means not delighting in or accepting alms-food invited by saying, 'Please come to such-and-such a family, street, or village.'
82:
Regarding 'from the mouth of a pot' (not accepting alms given from there)—this means not accepting alms that are taken out of a pot and offered. Regarding 'from the mouth of a basket'—'kaḷopီ' means a pot or a basket; alms given from there are also not accepted. Why? Because pots and baskets are subject to being struck by a ladle. Regarding 'from between the thresholds'—this means not accepting alms offered with the threshold in between. Why? Because of the perception: 'This person is using me as a reason to create an obstruction.' The same principle applies to sticks and pestles. Regarding 'from two people' (not accepting alms while they are eating)—this means if one person gets up to offer alms while two are eating, it is not accepted. Why? Because it becomes an obstacle to the [other's] mouthful of food.

In the words beginning with 'from a pregnant woman'—if alms are accepted from a pregnant woman, the child in the womb may suffer. If accepted from a nursing woman, it may interfere with the milk for the child. If accepted from a woman in the company of a man, it is not accepted because it is perceived as an obstacle to their pleasure. Regarding 'food prepared by communal announcement' (saṅkittီ)—this means not accepting food that has been prepared after a public call. It is said that during a famine, disciples of the Acelakas collect rice and so on from various places for the Acelakas and cook food; an eminent Acelaka does not accept that food. Regarding 'where there is a dog'—where a dog is present, waiting with the thought, 'I will get a morsel of food,' the Acelaka does not accept food brought to him without that dog being fed first. Why? Because it becomes an obstacle to the dog's morsel.

'Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinီ' (flies) means those that fly and move about in swarms. If people see an Acelaka and enter the kitchen (fire-house) saying, 'Let us offer alms to this person,' and as they enter, flies resting on the mouth of the basket and so on fly up and move in swarms, he does not accept the food brought from there. Why? Because of the perception: 'Due to me, an obstacle to the flies' search for food has arisen.' 'Thusodaka' (husk-water) is a medicinal liquid called sovီraka made from all kinds of grain. In this context, only drinking intoxicants is blameworthy. However, this Acelaka perceives even this medicinal liquid as blameworthy. One who returns after obtaining alms from only one house is called 'ekāgārika.' One who subsists on only one mouthful of food is called 'ekālopika.' The same principle applies to two houses and so on. Regarding 'with a single bowl'—this means offering with one small bowl. 'Datti' is a small bowl in which the first-portion of alms is placed.

'Eating every other day' (ekāhika) means the practice of having a one-day interval. 'Eating half-monthly' (aḍḍhamāsika) means the practice of having a half-month interval. 'Eating food by turn' (pariyāyabhatta) means eating food according to a rotation. This refers to eating food brought according to a rotation of days, such as a one-day turn, a two-day turn, a seven-day turn, or a half-month turn. A 'leaf-eater' is one who eats fresh leaves. A 'sāmāka-eater' is one who eats sāmāka grain. Regarding 'nီvāra' and so on—'nီvāra' is a type of grain that grows naturally in the forest. 'Daddula' refers to the scraps of hide discarded by tanners after scraping the skin. 'Haṭa' (water-weed)...
83:
Resin, moss, and the sap of trees such as the Kaᅂikāra are called 'sap' (niyyāsa). 'Kaᅂa' means broken rice. 'Ācāma' refers to the burnt rice crust sticking to the rice pot. He takes that rice crust from where it has been discarded and eats it. They also call it 'odanakajiya' (sour rice-gruel). Substances like oil-cake (piāka) and so on are well-known. 'Pavatta-phala-bhojĩ' refers to one who habitually eats fruit that has fallen on its own.

'Sāᅂa' refers to clothes woven from hemp. 'Masāᅂa' refers to clothes woven from a mixture (of hemp and other threads). 'Chavadussa' refers to clothes discarded from a corpse, or clothes made by stringing together Eraka grass and so on. 'Paᅃsukũla' refers to rags discarded on the ground. 'Tirĩᅡa' refers to clothes made from tree bark. 'Ajina' refers to the skin of a black antelope. 'Ajinakkhipa' refers to a garment made from that same skin split down the middle. They also call it 'sakhuraka' (antelope skin with hooves). 'Kusacĩra' refers to a garment made by stringing together Kusha grass. The same method applies to garments made of bark fibers (vākacĩra) and wooden strips (phalakacĩra). 'Kesakambala' refers to a blanket woven from human hair. Regarding that hair-blanket, it was said: "Monks, for example, among all woven garments, the hair-blanket is said to be the worst" (A.N. 3.138). 'Vāᄱakambala' refers to a blanket made from horsehair and the like. 'Ulũkapakkha' refers to a garment made by stringing together owl feathers. 'Ubbhaᅡᅡhaka' refers to one who always remains standing.

'Ukkuᅡikappadhāna-manuyutta' refers to one who repeatedly exerts the effort of squatting. Even when moving, he goes by jumping and leaping while remaining in a squatting position. 'Kaᅂᅡakāpassayika' refers to one who drives iron spikes or natural thorns into the ground, spreads a skin over them, and performs standing or walking meditation there. Even when sleeping, he makes his bed on those thorns. 'Sāyatatiyaka' is so called because the evening is the third time. He lives repeatedly practicing the habit of descending into water, intending: "I will wash away evil three times a day—morning, noon, and evening."

One is called 'Parantapa' because he torments others. He is one who repeatedly practices the conduct that causes distress to others. In terms such as 'Orabbhika'—sheep are called 'urabbha'. One is called 'Orabbhika' because he kills sheep. The same method applies to pig-butchers and so on. 'Ludda' refers to one who is cruel and harsh. 'Macchaghātaka' refers to a fisherman who catches and kills fish. 'Bandhanāgārika' refers to a jailer who guards the prison. 'Kurũrakammanta' refers to those who have cruel occupations.

'Muddhāvasitta' refers to a king who has been anointed on the head through the royal consecration of kings. 'To the east of the city' means in the eastern direction from the city. 'Sandhāgāra' refers to...
84:
Sacrificial hall (*yaññasālā*). 'Having clothed himself in a black antelope skin' (*kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā*) means wearing the skin of a black antelope along with its hooves (or claws). 'With ghee and oil' (*sappitelena*) refers to anointing with both ghee and oil. Excluding ghee, any other oily substance is called 'oil' (*tela*). 'Scratching' (*kaṇḍuvamāno*) means scratching with that (horn) when there is an itch, because the fingernails have been cut. 'On the bare ground' (*anantarahitāya*) means on the ground where no covering has been spread. 'With a calf of similar appearance' (*sarūpavacchāya*) refers to a cow whose calf has the same color as the mother. If the cow is white, the calf is also white; whether it is brindled or red, the calf is likewise; this is called *sarūpavacchā*. 'He spoke thus' (*so evamāha*) means that the king spoke in this manner. 'Young bulls' (*vacchatara*) are those that have passed the stage of being tender calves and have become strong. The same applies to 'heifers' (*vacchatari*). 'For the sake of the sacrificial grass' (*barihisatthāya*) means for the purpose of fencing (the sacrificial hall) and for spreading on the sacrificial ground.

'In this very life' (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this present existence. In the word 'without hunger' (*nicchāto*), craving is called 'hunger' (*chāta*); because that craving is absent, one is called 'without hunger' (*nicchāto*). Because all defilements have been extinguished, one is called 'extinguished' (*nibbuto*). Because one has become cool due to the absence of internal burning defilements, one is called 'become cool' (*sītībhūto*). Because one experiences the happiness of Jhāna, Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, one is called 'experiencing happiness' (*sukhappaṭisaṃvedī*). 'With a self that has become sublime' (*brahmabhūtena attanā*) means living with a mind that has reached a noble state.

To show this person from the time of the Buddha's appearance, the passage beginning with 'Here, a Tathāgata...' (*idha tathāgato*) is stated. Therein, 'Tathāgata' means the Blessed One is called Tathāgata for eight reasons: (1) because He has come in the same way (as previous Buddhas), (2) because He has gone in the same way, (3) because He has arrived at the true characteristics, (4) because He has awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is, (5) because He sees what is true, (6) because He speaks what is true, (7) because He acts truly, and (8) because of the sense of overcoming (all). The terms 'Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One' (*arahaṃ sammāsambuddho*), etc., have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'That Dhamma' (*taṃ dhammaṃ*) refers to the Dhamma endowed with the aforementioned qualities. In the phrase 'A householder or...' (*suṇāti gahapati vā*), why is the householder (*gahapati*) mentioned first? It is because they are free from pride and because they are numerous. Indeed, those who renounce from the warrior-noble class (*khattiya*) tend to be proud based on their birth. Those who renounce from the brahmin class tend to be proud based on the Vedas. Those of low birth cannot remain steady because of their low status. However, the sons of householders, having worked the land until sweat poured from their armpits and salt crystals (efflorescence) appeared on their backs, are free from such pride and arrogance. When they renounce, being without pride or arrogance, to the best of their ability...
85:
...they learn the Buddha's word and, practicing the work of Vipassanā, are able to establish themselves in the Fruition of Arahantship. Those who leave other classes to renounce are not many; only householders are numerous. Thus, because of their lack of pride and their large numbers, the householder is mentioned first.

'Or in some other (family)' (*aññatarasmiṃ vā*) means in any one of the other classes. 'One who is born' (*paccājāto*) refers to a person who has come into existence. 'He gains faith in the Tathāgata' (*tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhati*) means that after hearing the pure Dhamma, he gains the faith of conviction in the Tathāgata, the Lord of Dhamma, thinking, 'The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One.' 'He reflects thus' (*iti paṭisañcikkhati*) means he contemplates in this way. 'Household life is crowded' (*sambādho gharāvāso*) means that even if a couple lives in a house of sixty cubits or even in a place a hundred leagues apart, for them, the household life is indeed crowded in the sense of being full of worldly affairs, ties, and impediments. 'A path of dust' (*rajopatho*) is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā to be the place where the dust of lust and so on arises. It can also be called the path of arrival (for defilements). 'Open air' (*abbhokāso*) means being like the open air in the sense of non-attachment. Even if a monk lives in a gabled house, a jeweled palace, or a celestial mansion with doors and windows well-closed and sheltered, he does not cling, does not get stuck, and is not bound. Therefore, it is said, 'Renunciation is like the open air.'

Furthermore, household life is crowded because there is no opportunity for performing wholesome deeds. It is called a path of dust (*rajopatho*) because it is a gathering place for the dust of defilements, like a place of unrestrained formations. Renunciation is called open air (*abbhokāso*) because there is the possibility of performing wholesome deeds as one pleases. In the phrase 'This is not easy... I should renounce,' the summary is: this holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the threefold training is 'entirely complete' (*ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ*) because it must be practiced without a break for even a single day until the final thought (at death). It is 'entirely pure' (*ekantaparisuddhaṃ*) because it must be kept unstained by the taints of defilements for even a single day until the final thought. It should be practiced like a polished conch shell (*saṅkhalikhitaṃ*), resembling a washed conch. It is not easy for one living in a house, dwelling in the midst of a home, to practice this entirely complete... (holy life). (He reflects:) 'What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron-dyed robes (garments suitable for those practicing the holy life), and leaving the home, renounce into homelessness?' Here, the work of farming, trade, etc., which is beneficial to the home, is called 'household life' (*agāriya*); since that does not exist in renunciation, renunciation should be known as 'homelessness' (*anagāriya*). That is homelessness.
86: "Pabbajeyyaṃ" means "should practice" (paṭipajjeyyaṃ). "Appaṃ vā" (or a small amount) refers to an accumulation of wealth less than a thousand coins, which is called small; from a thousand upwards, it is called great. The circle of relatives is called "ñātiparivaṭṭa" because they are not a bond (in the sense of liberation). This circle of relatives is also called small if it is under twenty people, and great from twenty upwards. "Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno" means having properly attained the training known as the higher virtue (adhisīla) of monks, and the livelihood (sājīva) known as the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed One, in which they live together. "Samāpanno" means fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood, thus having approached both. Regarding "pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya" (having abandoned the taking of life) etc., the detailed explanation of terms like "pāṇātipāta" has already been given below. "Pahāya" means having abandoned the lack of virtue known as the intention to take life. "Paṭivirato hoti" means being one who abstains from that lack of virtue from the moment of abandonment. "Nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho" means one who has laid down the rod and laid down the sword because he does not go about carrying a rod or a weapon to harm others. Here, excluding the rod, all other implements that can destroy living beings should be understood as "weapons" (sattha). Although monks carry a walking stick, a small knife for cutting tooth-sticks, or nail clippers, these are not for harming others. Therefore, they are simply called "those who have laid down the rod and laid down the sword." "Lajjī" means being endowed with shame (lajjā), which has the characteristic of loathing evil. "Dayāpanno" means having reached a state of compassion and loving-kindness. "Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī" means being constantly sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. Because of that compassion, it means having a mind that desires the welfare of all living beings. "Viharati" means he dwells, he protects. "Dinnameva ādiyati" means he takes only what is given, thus he is called "dinnādāyī." Because he desires only what is given even in his mind, he is called "dinnပါဋိကင်္ခီ" (dinnapaṭikaṅkhī). It means he dwells with a pure self because of his non-stealing.
87: "Abrahmacariya" means conduct that is not noble. One is called "brahmacārī" because he practices noble conduct. "Ārācārī" means practicing far away from unchaste conduct. "Methunā" refers to the ignoble practice called "sexual intercourse" (methuna) because it is practiced by those called "couples" (methunaka) due to their similarity through the arousal of passion. "Gāmadhammā" refers to the habits of villagers. "Saccံ vadati" means one who speaks the truth, thus he is called "saccavādī." "Saccasandha" means one who connects truth with truth. It means he does not speak falsely in between. If a person sometimes speaks falsely and sometimes speaks the truth, his truth is interrupted by falsehood and thus truth is not connected with truth; therefore, such a person cannot be called "saccasandha." This person, however, is not like that. Even for the sake of life, he does not speak falsely but connects truth with truth; thus he is "saccasandha." "Theto" means one whose speech is firm. One type of person does not have firm speech, like a cloth dyed with turmeric, like a stump driven into a heap of chaff, or like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back. Another type of person has firm speech, like an inscription on stone or like a city pillar (indakhīla). Even if his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not speak double-tongued words. This person is called "theto." "Paccayiko" means one who is trustworthy. Some persons are not trustworthy. If asked, "Who said this?" and the answer is "So-and-so," it leads to the state where one should say, "Do not believe his words." Some persons are trustworthy. If asked, "Who said this?" and the answer is "So-and-so," it leads to the state where one should say, "If he said it, this itself is the standard; there is no need to investigate further; it is exactly so." This person is called "paccayiko." "Avisaṃvādako lokassa" means not deceiving the world by speaking the truth in that way. "Imesaṃ bhedāya" means for the sake of dividing those from whom he has heard (the report). "Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā" means a reconciler who approaches, one by one, two friends or fellow students of the same preceptor who are divided for some reason, and says, "For people born in such a good family as yours, and who are so learned, this is not proper," and so on. "Anuppadātā" means one who gives support to reconciliation. Seeing two people who are in harmony, [he says], "For people born in such a good family as yours, with such virtues..."
88:
It means one who acts firmly by saying "This is appropriate for those who are endowed with..." and so on. One whose pleasure-ground (ārāma) is harmony is called samaggārāmo. It means that where there are no harmonious people, he does not even wish to stay. There is also a Pali reading "samaggarāmo"; it has the same meaning. Samaggarato means delighting in those who are harmonious. It means he does not even wish to go elsewhere, leaving those harmonious people. One who rejoices upon seeing or hearing harmonious people is called samagganandī. One who habitually speaks words that bring beings into harmony is called samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā. This means he speaks only words that bring beings into harmony and illustrate the virtue of harmony, and not otherwise.

One who speaks after noting the appropriate time for speaking is called kālavādī. One who speaks only what is true, real, and factual is called bhūtavādī. One who speaks only words connected with the welfare of the present life and the future life is called atthavādī. One who speaks words connected with the nine supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) is called dhammavādī. One who speaks words connected with the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya) is called vinayavādī. Nidhāna refers to a place for storage. Speech that has a place for storage is called nidhānavatī. It means one who speaks words worthy of being stored in the heart. Regarding "kālena" (in time): even when speaking such words, he does not speak at the wrong time, thinking "I will speak words worthy of being stored in the heart." It means he speaks only after noting the appropriate time. Sāpadesaṃ means speech with illustrations and reasons. Pariyantavatī means speaking by showing limits. It means speaking in such a way that the limits are clear. Atthasaṃhitaṃ means speaking words full of meaning because they cannot be exhausted even when analyzed by many methods. Or, it means speaking words connected with the benefit (attha) that the atthavādī person speaks. It means not setting aside one thing and speaking another.

Bījagāma-bhūtagāma-samārambhā means one who abstains from destroying by means of cutting, breaking, cooking, etc., the five kinds of seeds known as root-seeds, trunk-seeds, joint-seeds, bud-seeds, and grain-seeds (bīja-bīja), as well as all living plants such as green grass and trees. Ekabhattiko means there are two meals: the morning meal and the evening meal. Among them, the morning meal is defined as being within midday. The other meal is from after midday until dawn. Therefore, within midday...
89:
Even if one eats ten times (within the specified time), he is still one who eats one meal (ekabhattiko). With reference to that, it is said "ekabhattiko". Food eaten at night is called ratti; one who abstains from that is called rattūparato. Food eaten from after midday until sunset is called vikālabhojana (wrong-time meal); because of abstaining from that, one is called virato vikālabhojanā. A spectacle that is like a thorn because it is inconsistent with the Dispensation (Sāsana) is called visūkadassana. Dancing, singing, and music performed by oneself or by causing others to perform, or even spectacles like the dancing of peacocks, which are like thorns, are called naccagīta-vādita-visūkadassana. Indeed, it is not proper for monks or nuns to perform dancing, etc., themselves, to have others perform them, or even to watch them. In the phrase "mālādisu", mālā refers to any kind of flower. Gandha refers to any kind of perfume. Vilepana refers to cosmetics for the skin. Among those, wearing flowers and perfumes is called dhāreti (wearing). Filling in deficient areas is called maṇḍeti (adorning). Enjoying them for the sake of fragrance or for the sake of beautifying the skin is called vibhūseti (beautifying). Ṭhāna refers to the cause. Therefore, it means one who abstains from those acts of wearing garlands, etc., which the general public performs with immoral intention. Uccāsayana refers to a place that exceeds the standard measurements. Mahāsayana refers to unallowable bedding; one who abstains from that is the meaning. Jātarūpa is gold. Rajata refers to things in use such as coins (kahāpaṇa), copper māsaka, lac māsaka, and wooden māsaka. One who abstains from accepting both of these—neither taking it himself, nor having others take it, nor consenting to it being laid down nearby—is the meaning.

Āmakadhañña-paṭiggahaṇā means the acceptance of the seven kinds of raw grain known as sāli rice, paddy, wheat, kangu millet, varaka beans, kudrūsa grain, and samyāka (kauk-lyin). Not only is the acceptance of these grains improper, but even touching them is not proper for monks. In the phrase āmakamaṃsa-paṭiggahaṇā, except for meat specifically allowed, the acceptance of raw meat and raw fish is not proper for monks, but touching them is not (forbidden). In the phrase itthikumārika-paṭiggahaṇā, itthi refers to a woman who has a husband. The other is called kumārikā (a girl). Both the acceptance and the touching of them are improper. In the phrase dāsidāsa-paṭiggahaṇā, the acceptance of them as bondswomen and bondsmen is not proper. However, if one says, "I give a kappiyakāraka (attendant)" or "I give an ārāmika (monastery worker)," it is proper. Regarding goats, sheep, and so on, up to fields and land, the method of what is allowable (kappiya) and unallowable (akappiya) should be examined according to the Vinaya. Among them, a field (khetta) is a place where early crops (pubbaṇṇa) are grown. Land (vatthu) is a place where late crops (aparaṇṇa) are grown. Or where...
90:
In that context, because both [types of crops] can grow there, it is called a field (khetta). The portion of land prepared for that field is called a building site (vatthu). Under the heading of 'fields and building sites,' irrigation channels, tanks, and ponds are also included.

Dūteyya means the work of a messenger. It is the act of taking a letter or a message sent by laypeople and going to various places. Pahīṇagamana means going on minor errands for someone who has sent them to another's house. Anuyoga means performing both of these. Therefore, in this context, the meaning should be understood as repeatedly engaging in being a messenger and running errands. Kayavikkaya means buying and selling. Among tulākūṭa (cheating with scales) and so on—kūṭa means deception (fraud). In that regard, tulākūṭa is of four types: rūpakūṭa, aṅgakūṭa, gahaṇakūṭa, and paṭicchannakūṭa. Therein, rūpakūṭa means making two scales of similar appearance and, when receiving, using the large scale, and when giving, using the small scale. Aṅgakūṭa means pressing the back part of the scale with the hand when receiving, and pressing the front part when giving. Gahaṇakūṭa means holding the base of the string when receiving, and holding the tip when giving. Paṭicchannakūṭa means making the scale hollow and putting iron filings inside; when receiving, making the filings move to the back, and when giving, making them move to the front.

Kaṃsa refers to a gold bowl. Deception with such a gold bowl is called kaṃsakūṭa. How? Having made one genuine gold bowl, they make two or three other bronze bowls to look like gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering the house of a wealthy family, they say, 'Please buy these gold bowls.' When asked the price, they pretend to want to sell them at a very reasonable price. Then, when the buyers ask, 'How can we know if these are real gold?' they say, 'Test them before you buy.' They rub the genuine gold bowl on a stone to demonstrate, then hand over all the bowls and leave.

Mānakūṭa (cheating with measures) is of three types: hadayabheda, sikhābheda, and rajjubheda. Therein, hadayabheda is found when measuring ghee, oil, etc. When receiving those items, using a measure with a hole at the bottom, they say, 'Pour slowly,' and let a large amount leak into their own vessel. When giving, they plug the hole, fill it quickly, and give it. Sikhābheda is found when measuring sesame, rice, etc. When receiving those items, they slowly raise the crest (the heap at the top) and take it. When giving, they fill it with force and cut off the crest. Rajjubheda is found when measuring fields and building sites. When they do not receive a bribe, they measure a field as large even if it is not large.
91:
Among ukkoṭana and so on—ukkoṭana means taking a bribe to make a non-owner the owner. Vañcana means deceiving others by various means. Here is a story—it is said that a hunter caught a large deer and a fawn and was coming along. A trickster said to that hunter, 'Friend, how much for the deer, and how much for the fawn?' When told, 'The deer is two kahāpaṇas and the fawn is one,' he gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, went a little way, and returned, saying, 'Friend, I have no need for the fawn; give me the deer instead.' Then the hunter said, 'In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas.' The trickster said, 'Friend, did I not give you one kahāpaṇa first?' The hunter replied, 'Yes, you did.' 'Take this fawn as well; thus, the one kahāpaṇa already given and this fawn worth one kahāpaṇa, these two together will make two kahāpaṇas.' The hunter, thinking, 'He is speaking with sound reasoning,' took back the fawn and gave him the deer.

Nikati means deception by fraud or by trickery, such as making something that is not an ornament into an ornament, something that is not a gem into a gem, or something that is not gold into gold, and thus deceiving with a counterfeit. Sāciyoga means a crooked scheme. It is simply another name for ukkoṭana and the others. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as ukkoṭana-sāciyoga, vañcana-sāciyoga, and nikati-sāciyoga. Some say that showing one thing and exchanging it for another is sāciyoga. However, that is already included within vañcana (deception).

Among chedana and so on—chedana means the cutting off of hands and feet, etc. Vadha means killing. Bandha means binding with ropes, etc. Viparāmosa (highway robbery) is of two types: hima-viparāmosa and gumba-viparāmosa. When it frosts (or snows), hiding oneself with the frost and robbing travelers is called hima-viparāmosa. Hiding oneself with bushes and the like and robbing is called gumba-viparāmosa. Ālopa means plundering villages, market towns, etc. Sahasākāra means acts of violence. It is entering a house, placing a weapon at people's chests, and taking the desired goods. In this way, that monk is one who abstains from cutting... pe... and acts of violence.

That monk is contented—that monk is endowed with twelvefold contentment regarding the four requisites, being satisfied with whatever requisites he gets. Kāyaparihariika means [robes] just enough to protect the body. Kucchiparihārika means [almsfood] just enough to sustain the stomach. [The monk] takes only the eight requisites of a monk and goes, keeping them always with him.
92:
There is no attachment or binding such as “my monastery, my dwelling, my attendant.” Like an arrow released from a bowstring, or like a great bull elephant that has left the herd, that monk dwells alone and sits alone, making use of whatever lodgings, forest thickets, roots of trees, forest edges, or mountain caves he desires. In all postures, he is alone without a companion.

“One who can go to the four directions, without resentment, content with whatever one gets, enduring dangers, without trembling, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.” In this way, he attains the state of being like the horn of a rhinoceros as praised.

Now, to demonstrate that meaning with a simile, he said “Seyyathāpi” and so forth. There, “pakkhi sakuṇo” means a bird with wings. “Ḍeti” means it flies up. The summary of the meaning here is: a bird, knowing that “in such a place, the tree has ripe fruit,” comes from various directions and eats the fruits of that tree by piercing and shaking them with its claws, wings, and beak. It does not occur to those birds that “this fruit is for today, this fruit will be for tomorrow.” When the fruit is exhausted, they do not keep guard over the tree, nor do they leave behind a feather, a claw, or a beak. Rather, being without longing for that tree, they fly up and go to whatever direction they desire with only the burden of their wings. In the same way, this monk departs without attachment and without longing; therefore, it is said, “he departs taking [only his requisites] with him.” “Ariyena” means blameless (pure). “Ajjhattaṃ” means occurring within one’s own individual existence. “Anavajjasukhaṃ” means blameless happiness.

“Having seen a form with the eye” means that the monk endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having seen a form with eye-consciousness—this is the meaning. In the remaining terms, all that should be said has already been stated below. “Abyāsekasukhaṃ” means happiness unpolluted by defilements. It is also called “avikiṇṇasukhaṃ” (undistracted happiness). Indeed, the happiness of the restraint of the faculties is undistracted because it proceeds by way of “merely seen” etc., regarding the objects seen and so forth.
93:
“In going forward and returning” means that the monk endowed with the restraint of the faculties, the mind being the sixth, is one who acts with clear comprehension by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension in these seven instances such as going forward and returning. The explanation that should be given there has already been stated in the Jhānavibhaṅga.

What is shown by “So iminā ca” and so forth? It shows the endowment of conditions (paccayasampatti) for forest dwelling (araññavāsa). For one who does not have these four conditions, forest dwelling cannot be successful; he falls into the state of having to live and speak with animals or forest-dwellers. Deities residing in the forest make terrifying sounds, thinking, “What is the use of forest dwelling for such an evil monk?” They strike his head with their hands and make him flee. Ill-repute spreads, saying, “Such a monk entered the forest and committed such and such evil deeds.” But for one who has these four conditions, forest dwelling is successful. For that monk, when reflecting on his own virtue and seeing no stain or blemish, joy arises; contemplating that virtue as subject to destruction and vanishing, he enters the noble plane. Deities residing in the forest are delighted and speak words of praise. Thus, his reputation spreads like a drop of oil placed on water. The meanings of terms like “vivittaṃ” are just as stated below. “When the mind is thus concentrated... he knows beings passing away according to their kamma”—all that should be said in this section has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

In the third knowledge, “with the mind thus concentrated” refers to the fourth jhāna mind which is the basis for insight. “For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints” means for the sake of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship. Indeed, the path of Arahatship is called the “destruction of taints” (āsavānaṃ khaya) because it destroys the taints. And this knowledge is so called because it is included in that path. “He directs his mind” means he directs the insight-mind. In the passages such as “He understands: This is suffering,” he understands as it really is through the penetration of the individual characteristic, and he penetrates: “Suffering is only this much, there is no more than this,” thus understanding the entire Truth of Suffering. He understands as it really is and penetrates the craving that produces that suffering as “This is the origin of suffering”; the Nibbāna which is the non-occurrence of those two, the place where they reach and cease, as “This is the cessation of suffering”; and the Noble Path that leads to that Nibbāna as “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,” through the penetration of the individual characteristic—this is how the meaning should be understood.
94:
Having thus shown the Truths in their own nature, he now speaks of 'Ime āsavā' (These are the taints) etc., wishing to show them by way of method through the power of defilements. 'Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato' (For him who thus knows and thus sees) means he is teaching the Path that has reached its peak along with insight for one who thus knows and sees. 'Kāmāsavā' means from the taint of sensual desire. By the word 'Vimuccatī' (is liberated), he shows the moment of the Path (magga-kkhaṇa). By the word 'Vimuttasmiṃ' (in the liberated), he shows the moment of the Fruit (phala-kkhaṇa). For at the moment of the Path, the mind is being liberated; at the moment of the Fruit, it is liberated. By the words 'Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ' (In the liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated'), he shows reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). By the words 'Khīṇā jātī' (Birth is exhausted) etc., he shows the stage (bhūmi) of that Arahant. With that knowledge, that Arahant knows while reviewing, 'Birth is exhausted,' and so on. 'Vusitaṃ' means the practice that should be practiced, has been practiced repeatedly, and has been completed. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' refers to the holy life of the Path. Seven types of noble learners (sekha), along with the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), are still living the holy life. The Arahant, however, is one who has lived the life. Therefore, that Arahant, reviewing his own living of the holy life, knows: 'The holy life has been lived.' 'Kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ' (Done is what had to be done) means that the sixteen-fold task regarding the Four Noble Truths—by way of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā) through the four Paths—has been completed. Virtuous worldlings and others are still performing that task; the Arahant is one who has done what was to be done. Therefore, that Arahant, reviewing his own duty, knows: 'Done is what had to be done.' 'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' (There is no more for this state) means he knows: 'Now, for this kind of state, or for the sake of the sixteen-fold task, or for the exhaustion of defilements, there is no further task of Path-development.'

In the words 'Sarāgādīsu' etc. — 'Appahīno' (not abandoned) refers to one who has not yet abandoned [defilements] by way of abandonment through suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandonment of a limb (tadaṅga-pahāna), or abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna).

In the words 'Lābhī hoti' etc. — 'Lābhī' means one who possesses, one who has attained and remains so. 'Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathassa' means one who has attained the tranquillity of mind (samādhi) that arises in one's own mind, called internal. 'Adhipaññādhamma-vipassanāya' refers to (one who has not attained) insight into the phenomena of the five aggregates, called higher wisdom, which proceeds by way of impermanence etc. 'Rūpasahagatānaṃ' means one who has attained the fine-material sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti) which have material signs as objects. 'Arūpasahagatānaṃ' means one who has attained the immaterial sphere attainments which do not have material signs as objects. Here, the first person is a worldling (puthujjana) who has attained the eight attainments. The second person is a noble disciple who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka). The third person is a noble disciple who has attained the eight attainments. The fourth person should be known as the worldly masses (mahājana).

In the words 'Anusotagāmī' etc. — 'Anusotagāmī' (one who goes with the stream) should be known as a worldling who follows the stream of saṃsāra (vaṭṭa-sota) and is submerged in it. 'Paṭisotagāmī' (one who goes against the stream) is one who goes towards Nibbāna, which is the opposite of the stream of saṃsāra. This is the name for one who does not follow the stream of saṃsāra but goes towards the opposite, Nibbāna.
95:
'Paṭisotagāmī' (one who goes against the stream) is the name of a person who does not follow the stream of saṃsāra but goes towards the opposite (Nibbāna). 'Does not do evil deeds' means not doing them by way of transgressing the prescribed training rules. 'With suffering and with sorrow' means practicing the holy life even with the suffering and sorrow that arise when the obsession of defilements is present. 'Completely' means practicing without deficiency in even one of the three trainings. 'Purely' means practicing so that there are no defilements that cause impurity. 'Brahmacariya' refers to the holy life. By this second section, the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) are taught. If it is asked, 'Do those individuals practice the holy life while weeping?' the answer is 'Yes.' They are said to practice while weeping due to the weeping caused by defilements. A virtuous worldling monk (sīlasampanno puthujjana-bhikkhu) is also included in this category of 'one who goes against the stream.'

'Ṭhitatto' means a person of steady nature. An Anāgāmī (Non-returner) is called a person of steady nature because his mind is unshakable by sensual lust and ill-will, and because he has the nature of not returning from that Brahma world. 'Tiṇṇo' means a person who has crossed over the stream of craving. 'Pāraṅgato' means a person who has reached the far shore, which is Nibbāna. 'Stands on dry land' means standing in the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship, which is like dry land. 'Cetovimutti' refers to the concentration of the Fruit (phala-samādhi). 'Paññāvimutti' refers to the knowledge of the Fruit (phala-ñāṇa). 'This person is called' means this Arahant is called 'a Brahmin who has crossed the stream of craving, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land.' This is because this Arahant is called a Brahmin due to having washed away (bāhita) evil deeds.

In the words 'Appassuta' etc. — 'Having little learning' means having heard and remembered only a very small portion of the Teacher's Dispensation, which has nine factors. 'One who does not know the meaning, does not know the Dhamma, and does not practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma' means one who, though knowing the Commentary and the Pali text, does not practice the preliminary path, which is the Dhamma suitable for the supramundane Dhamma. In this way, the meanings of all should be understood.

In the words 'Samaṇamacala' etc. — 'Samaṇamacala' means 'Samaṇa-acala'; the letter 'ma' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). It means an unwavering recluse, a firm recluse. 'This person is called' means this Stream-enterer is called 'Samaṇamacala' because he is established in the Dispensation with faith that is like a root. The Once-returner, however, is called 'Samaṇapaduma' (Lotus recluse) because the defilement of attachment still exists. For in this fourfold set, the meaning of attachment is the meaning of 'Paduma' (red lotus). The Non-returner is called 'Samaṇapuṇḍarīka' (White lotus recluse) because the defilement of attachment, called sensual lust, does not exist. For in this fourfold set, the meaning of purity is the meaning of 'Puṇḍarīka' (white lotus).
96:
It is said in the ancient commentary: An Arahant is called a 'delicate ascetic' (samaṇasukhumālo) because of the absence of defilements that cause harshness. Also, because of the absence of suffering, that Arahant is indeed a delicate ascetic.

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Fours (Catukkaniddesa-vaṇṇanā).

## 5. Explanation of the Exposition of the Fives (Pañcakaniddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the Exposition of the Fives: 'Therein' (tatra) means among the persons briefly indicated below in the manner beginning with 'He commits [an offense] and becomes remorseful.' 'Yvāyam' is 'yo ayaṃ'. In this term 'ārabhati', the word 'ārambha' occurs in the senses of kamma (action), activity, harming, energy, destruction, and the violation of an offense.

To expand on this: In the passage, 'Whatever suffering arises, all is caused by action (ārambha-paccayā),' it occurs in the sense of kamma. In the passage, 'Great sacrifices, great undertakings (mahārambhā), these are not of great fruit,' it occurs in the sense of activity (kiriya). In the passage, 'They harm (ārabhanti) living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama,' it occurs in the sense of harming (hiṃsana). In the passage, 'Strive (ārabhatatha), go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching,' it occurs in the sense of energy (vīriya). In the passage, 'He is one who abstains from damaging (samārambhā) seeds and plants,' it occurs in the sense of destruction (vikopana). However, in this passage, 'He commits (ārabhati) and becomes remorseful,' it occurs in the sense of violating an offense (āpatti-vītikka-ma). Therefore, the meaning here is that by way of violating an offense, he both commits the offense and, because of that, becomes remorseful (vippaṭisārī).

'Does not know as it really is' (yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti) means he does not know according to the true nature because he has not yet attained [realization]. 'Wherein his' (yatthassa) means having reached which [state], the evil unwholesome states that have arisen in this person cease without remainder. To what state does he reach so that they cease? He reaches the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) and they cease. For one who has reached the Fruit (phala), they are indeed already ceased. Even so, it should be understood that here, by way of the function of the Path, only the Fruit is mentioned. 'Born of violation' (ārambhajā) refers to the taints (āsavas) that arise due to the violation of an offense. 'Born of remorse' (vippaṭisārajā) refers to the taints that arise from remorse. 'They increase' (pavaḍḍhanti) means they grow by arising again and again. 'Sādhu' is a 'sādhu' in the sense of requesting (āyācana).

This is what is meant: 'Venerable sir, it is indeed true that you have committed a great fault; nevertheless, we request of you—by the confession of an offense that should be confessed, by the rehabilitation from an offense from which one should be rehabilitated (vuṭṭhāna), by the making manifest of an offense that should be made manifest (āvikiriyā), by abandoning the taints born of violation...
97:
...and through purity, and by dispelling and removing the taints born of remorse through the reviewing of the state of purity, please develop the mind of insight and the wisdom of insight.' 'By this fifth person' (amunā pañcamena puggalena) means by this fifth person who is an Arahant. 'He will be exactly equal' (samasamော bhavissati) means he will be equal only by way of equality in supramundane qualities (lokuttara-guṇa); thus, it means he should be exhorted by using the Arahant as an example.

'He commits [an offense] but is not remorseful' means he falls into an offense. However, he seeks a person of like views to whom he may confess that offense. Therefore, he does not become remorseful. In the Aṅguttara Commentary, however, it is said, 'He is not remorseful because he has been rehabilitated (vuṭṭhitattā).' 'He does not commit [an offense] but is remorseful' means he does not fall into an offense, but because he is not skilled in the Vinaya regulations, he perceives an offense in what is not an offense and thus becomes remorseful. In the Aṅguttara Commentary, it is said, 'Having once fallen into an offense and then being rehabilitated from it, although he does not fall into it again, he is unable to dispel the remorse.' 'He neither commits [an offense] nor is remorseful' means he neither falls into an offense nor becomes remorseful. If it is asked, 'What kind of person is this?', it is the person with slack energy (ossaṭṭhavīriya). For he thinks, 'What is the use of my attaining Parinibbāna during this Buddha's time? I will attain Parinibbāna in the future during the time of the Metteyya Fully Enlightened Buddha.' Thus, even though he has pure virtue, he does not fulfill the practice. Such a person should also be exhorted: 'Venerable sir, for what purpose do you live negligently? The destiny (gati) of a worldling (puthujjana) is not fixed. You may or may not come face to face with the Metteyya Fully Enlightened Buddha; therefore, develop insight for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship.' Everything else should be understood in the manner already stated.

In the passages beginning with 'Having given, he despises' (datvā avajānāti): A certain bhikkhu is of great merit (mahāpuñña) and a recipient of the four requisites. When he receives robes and so on, he invites another bhikkhu of little merit. That other bhikkhu, even though invited again and again by the one of great merit, simply continues to accept. Then the other [the donor] becomes slightly angry and, wishing to make him feel dejected, says, 'This person does not receive robes and so on by his own nature; he receives them only by depending on us.' Such a person is called one who 'despises after giving.' A certain person, while living with another for two or three years, at first treats that person with respect, but as time goes on, he no longer shows respect, does not rise from his seat, and does not go to attend on him. Such a person is called one who 'despises through living together' (saṃvāsena avajānāti).
98:
'Ādheyyamukha' refers to one who accepts the word spoken at the very beginning. It means one whose mouth (speech) is established only in the first words heard. 'Adhimuccitā hoti' means he is a believer. In this regard, there is this method: A person says of a monk who is accomplished in conduct, "This monk is not accomplished in conduct"; hearing this, the person reaches a conclusion (believes it). Later, even when another similar monk says, "This monk is accomplished in conduct," he does not accept that word, but holds only to the word of the first monk, saying, "Such-and-such a person has already told us, 'This monk has no conduct.'" In another case, if someone says of an immoral person, "He is virtuous," he believes that word; and even when another person later says, "This monk's conduct is not good, it is not proper for you to approach him," he does not accept that word and holds only to the word of the first speaker. If another person speaks of virtues, he accepts it; if they speak of faults, he also accepts it. Such a person is also called 'Ādheyyamukha'. 'Ādhātabbamukha' means that whatever words he hears, his mouth is established only in those words heard.

'Lola' (fickle) means being fickle because faith and other qualities last only for a short time, and thus he is disturbed by lack of faith and so on. 'Ittarasaddha' means one of little faith, one of incomplete faith. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, faith itself is called 'bhatti' (devotion) by virtue of repeated association. 'Pema' (affection) is appropriate as both faith-based affection (saddhā-pema) and household-based affection (gehasita-pema). 'Pasādo' (confidence/clarity) is simply the clarity born of faith. In this way, a person is fickle. Thus, due to the smallness of faith and so on, a person is called fickle (lola). Like a color dyed with turmeric, like a stump driven into a heap of chaff, or like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back, he has an unstable foundation; he becomes confident in a moment, and his confidence is destroyed (he becomes angry) in a moment.

'Mando momũho' means one who is dull (foolish) due to lack of knowledge, and extremely deluded due to lack of clarity. It means one who is greatly confused.

In the warrior (yodhājĩva) similes—'yodhājĩva' refers to those who live by fighting. 'Rajaggaᅃ' refers to the mass of dust (dust cloud) rising from the ground due to the trampling of the feet of elephants, horses, and so on. 'Na santhambhati' means being unable to stand firm. 'Sahati rajaggaᅃ' means being able to endure (withstand) even upon seeing the mass of dust. 'Dhajaggaᅃ' refers to the tips of banners raised either on the backs of elephants, horses, etc., or on chariots. 'Ussāraᅂaᅃ' refers to the high and loud noise of elephants, horses, chariots, etc., and the army. 'Sampahāre' refers to the slight blows (clashes) encountered during battle. 'Hayati' means he becomes exhausted or weary. 'Byāpajjati' means he meets with ruin or abandons his natural state. 'Sahati sampahāraᅃ' means being able to endure even after receiving two or three blows.
99:
He endures. That very battlefield is called the place of the victorious camp. 'Ajjhāvasati' means living and prevailing for about seven days. For what reason? It is to provide medical care for the wounded warriors, to grant promotions upon knowing the special achievements of those who performed their duties, and to enjoy the happiness of sovereignty.

Now, although the Teacher has no need for those who live by fighting, he brought this simile to show five types of persons in this Dispensation who are like those warriors. Therefore, to show those persons, he said 'evamevaṃ' and so on.

In that simile, 'saṃsīdati' means sinking or entering deeply into wrong thoughts (sensual thoughts, etc.). 'Na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ santhāretuṃ' means being unable to protect the practice of the holy life so that it is not interrupted. 'Sikkhādubbalyaṃ āvikatvā' means revealing one's weakness in the training of higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). What is the 'rajagga' (pinnacle of the dust cloud) of that person? It means: being of extraordinary beauty (abhirūpā), worthy of being looked at (dassanīyā), bringing clarity of mind just by being seen (pāsādikā), and being endowed with supreme beauty of body and limbs (paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya).

'Ūhasati' means laughing disparagingly. 'Ullapati' means talking. 'Ujjagghati' means laughing loudly while clapping hands. 'Uppaṇḍeti' means speaking mocking words.

'Abhinisīdati' means sitting nearby or on the same seat in an overpowering manner. The same method applies to the second term (abhinipajjati). 'Ajjhottharati' means overpowering.

'Viniveṭhetvā vinimocetvā' means going where one wishes after disentangling and freeing that woman's hand from where it was held. In this explanation of the warrior simile, the remaining terms have clear meanings.

Among the five types of persons who observe the alms-food eater's practice (piṇḍapātika):
(1) One who, due to being dull and deluded, does not know the undertaking or the benefits, but becomes an alms-food eater only because of his own dullness and delusion.
(2) One who, having evil desires, thinks, 'People will know me as an alms-food eater and will honor me with the four requisites; they will regard me with virtues such as being shameful and having few desires,' and thus, being overwhelmed by that evil desire, becomes an alms-food eater.
(3) One who wanders for alms due to madness or mental derangement is called an alms-food eater due to madness.
(4) One who becomes an alms-food eater thinking, 'This practice of alms-food eating has been praised by the Buddha and his disciples.'
(5) One who observes it thinking, 'By being an alms-food eater in this way, I will have few desires; this practice of mine will be for the sake of fewness of wishes, contentment, and the effacing of defilements.' He is an alms-food eater relying on the thought that 'this practice of alms-food eating is beneficial' or 'I desire only enough to subsist on this alms-food,' and thus subsists on whatever alms-food is received.
100:
He is one who is called an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika). He becomes an alms-food eater by reflecting: "This practice of an alms-food eater is praised and esteemed by the Buddhas and their disciples." Regarding the phrases starting with "depending only on fewness of wishes"—he becomes an alms-food eater by reflecting: "In this way, I shall be one of few wishes; this practice of an alms-food eater will lead to my fewness of wishes"; "In this way, I shall be contented; this practice of an alms-food eater will lead to my contentment"; "In this way, I shall efface the defilements; this practice of an alms-food eater will lead to the effacement of my defilements." He exists depending on the fact that there is benefit in this good practice, or depending on the desire for just this alms-food. It means he exists depending on the fact of being sustained by whatever alms-food is received. Agga means the chief. The remaining terms are just synonyms of that word agga.

"Milk comes from a cow" means that what is called milk does not exist without a cow. The same principle applies to "curds from milk," and so on. Just as among these five products of the cow (pañca gorasā), the cream of ghee (sappimaṇḍa) is the best, even so, among these five types of alms-food eaters, the one who is an alms-food eater depending on fewness of wishes and so forth is the foremost, the best, the principal, the most excellent, and the most distinguished. However, among these five types of alms-food eaters, only two are genuine alms-food eaters; the other three are not genuine alms-food eaters. They should be understood as alms-food eaters by name only. The same principle applies to terms such as khalupacchābhattika (one who refuses later food).

## Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

## 6. Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the Description of the Sixes—tatra means "among those six types of persons." That person should be regarded as a Sammāsambuddha (Omniscient Buddha) because of the omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) produced by himself without a teacher.

In the sentences beginning with "A Paccekasambuddha because of that," that person is a Paccekasambuddha because of that knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekasambodhiñāṇa). Those persons should be regarded as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna because of that knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). Those persons should be regarded as the remaining Arahants because of that making an end of suffering. That person should be regarded as an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) because of that non-returning to this human state. Those persons should be regarded as Sotāpanna (Stream-enterers) and Sakadāgāmī (Once-returners) because of that returning to this human state.

## Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā.
101:
## 7. Description of the Sattaka-niddesa
In the Sattaka-niddesa—"saqiṃ nimuggo" means sunk once. "Ekantakāḷakehi" means [sunk] by means of the fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) known as nihilism (natthika-vāda), the doctrine of non-causality (ahetuka-vāda), and the doctrine of the inefficacy of action (akiriya-vāda), which are absolutely dark. "Evaṃ puggalo" means that because of the reason of being endowed with these dark fixed wrong views, once a person has sunk, he remains sunk. Teachers say that for such a person, there is no such thing as rising again from existence. Like Makkhali Gosāla and others, he becomes merely food for the fires of hell below.

"Sāhu saddhā kusalesu dhammesu" means that faith in wholesome states is a good acquisition (beneficial), and thus he emerges. That person is said to emerge by that much wholesome merit alone. The same method applies to sentences such as "sāhu hirī" (shame is good) and so forth. "Hāyatiyeva" means he only declines, like water poured on a soap-track. "Evaṃ puggalo" means that having emerged once by the power of faith and other such qualities as in "sāhu saddhā," he sinks again due to the decline of those qualities, like Devadatta and others. For Devadatta, although he had attained the eight attainments and the five mundane superknowledges, because he became an adversary and a thorn to the Buddhas, he declined from those virtues. Having committed the deeds of shedding the blood [of a Buddha] and causing a schism in the Saṅgha, after the breaking up of the body, he was reborn in the Avīci hell at the second thought-moment. Kokālika also, because of accusing the two chief disciples, was reborn in the Paduma hell.

"Neva hāyati no vaḍḍhati" means he neither declines when unable nor increases when able. Both this non-decline and non-increase should be shown through the examples of a layperson and a monk. A certain layperson, when unable, commits to providing fortnightly food (pakkhika-bhatta), ticket-food (salāka-bhatta), or rains-residence cloth (vassāvāsika) regularly. Later, even when he is able, he continues to perform only that much of the fortnightly food and so on. A monk also, in the beginning when unable, undertakes the study of the Pali text or an ascetic practice (dhutaṅga). Even when he is endowed with wisdom, strength, and effort and is able, he does not do anything further beyond that. "Evaṃ puggalo" means that because of the stability of these qualities such as faith, the person is said to have emerged and stands still.

"Ummujjitvā vipassati viloketi" means that a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), having emerged [from the water], looks at the path to be traveled or the direction that should be gone.
102:
'He emerges and swims' means that the Once-returner (sakadāgāmi), due to the thinning of defilements, emerges and swims towards the direction to be reached.

'He reaches a firm footing' means that the Non-returner (anāgāmi), having emerged, looks around, swims, and reaches a firm footing in a certain place, stands there, and does not return again.

'Having crossed over and reached the other shore, he stands on dry land' means that having crossed the flood of all defilements and reached the other shore, he stands on the dry land of Nibbāna. These seven persons are illustrated by the simile of water.

It is said: Seven pedestrian merchants on a long journey reached a river full of water. Among those seven merchants, the first man, fearing the water, sank right where he entered and could not emerge again, becoming food for fish and turtles. The second man sank where he entered, emerged once, but sank again and could not emerge, becoming food for fish and turtles. The third man sank and then emerged; he stood in the middle of the river, unable to come back to this shore or go to the other shore. The fourth man emerged and, while standing, looked for the landing place to cross. The fifth man looked for the landing place and swam. The sixth man swam, reached near the other shore, and stood in waist-deep water. The seventh man reached the other shore, bathed with scented powder and so on, put on excellent clothes, anointed himself with fragrant perfumes, wore blue lotuses and so on, and being adorned with various ornaments, entered the great city, ascended a magnificent palace, and enjoyed excellent food.

In that simile, these seven persons should be understood like the seven pedestrian merchants. The round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) should be understood like the river. The sinking of the person with wrong view in the round of rebirths should be understood like the sinking of the first man who feared the water right where he entered. The person who emerges but sinks again due to the decline of faith and other qualities after they have merely arisen should be understood like the man who emerged and then sank again. The person who stands firm due to the stability of faith and other qualities should be understood like the man standing in the middle of the river. The Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) who looks at the path or direction to be reached should be understood like the man looking for the landing place. The Once-returner (sakadāgāmi) who swims due to the thinning of defilements should be understood like the man who is swimming. The Non-returner (anāgāmi) who stands because of the nature of not returning should be understood like the man who swam and stood in waist-deep water. The Arahant-brāhmaṇa who stands on the dry land of Nibbāna having crossed the four floods of defilements should be understood like the man who bathed and reached the other shore to stand on dry land. The Arahant who enters the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object and spends his time should be understood like the man standing on dry land who enters the city, ascends the palace, and enjoys excellent food. Regarding the persons such as the one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)...
103:
...like the man who ascended to the other shore and stands on dry land, the Arahant-brāhmaṇa who has crossed the four floods (ogha) and stands on the dry land of Nibbāna should be understood. Like the man standing on dry land who enters the city, ascends the magnificent palace, and enjoys excellent food, the Arahant who attains the fruition-attainment of Arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object and spends his time should be understood. Persons such as the one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) have already been clearly explained below.

## Explanation of the Sevenfold Section (Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā)

The Eightfold Section (aṭṭhakaniddesa) and the Ninefold Section (navakaniddesa) should also be understood in the same manner as stated below.

## 10. Explanation of the Tenfold Section (Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā)

In the Tenfold Section: "Here" (idha) means in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacarabhūmi). Indeed, for persons such as the "one who is at most a seven-times-returner" (sattakkhattuparama), their completion occurs only in the sense-sphere. It means that the attainment of Arahantship and the attainment of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesanibbāna) occur only in a sense-sphere existence.

"Having left here" (idha vihāya) means the completion of those who, having abandoned this sense-sphere existence, stand in a Pure Abode (suddhāvāsa) existence. For persons such as the "one who attains Nibbāna in the interval" (antarāparinibbāyī), having attained the fruit of non-returning in this sense-sphere existence and passing away from here, they are reborn in the Pure Abodes and, in that existence, attain Arahantship and the element of Nibbāna without remainder. Therefore, it is said: "For these five persons, completion occurs having left here (this sense-sphere existence)."

## Explanation of the Tenfold Section (Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā)

## Concluding Remarks (Nigamanakathā)

By this sequence of words—
The Teacher, who is peerless in the world, taught the text of the Designation of Individuals (Puggalapaññatti) in the abode of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa) in a manner that was not too concise.
Having thoroughly penetrated with knowledge the commentary on that Puggalapaññatti composed in the language of the Island (Sinhalese), as well as the commentaries on the Agamas (Suttas),
104:
Taking from those various commentaries the meanings well-analyzed by the former teachers, without mixing with the doctrines of other sects in various Pali passages, and discarding excessively detailed meanings,
This commentary has been composed in a manner that is neither too concise nor too detailed, without including the decisions already stated in the Visuddhimagga.
By me, who composed this commentary consisting of about seven recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) in the Pali text for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma,
Whatever merit has been acquired, by that merit, may all beings be able to behold the subtle and peaceful True Dhamma (Saddhamma) with the purified eye of Dhamma.

## The Commentary on the Designation of Individuals is finished. (Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.)
105:
## Abhidhamma Piṭaka
## Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
Surrounded by the host of devas and brahmas, seated well upon the Paṇḍukambala stone in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the incomparable Teacher of the world including devas and brahmas.

Skilled in all designations (paññatti), the Supreme Person in the world of beings, having taught the Puggalapaññatti treatise which illustrates various designations.

Because it is the collection of various points of discussion such as the discussion on the person (puggala-kathā), He taught that treatise named Kathāvatthu in brief.

The Matika (matrix) was laid down by the Buddha himself in the abode of the devas, Tāvatiṃsa, by merely establishing the outline, and it was later expanded upon this earth by the Venerable Moggaliputtatissa Thera.

Now, since the time has come for the explanation of the meaning of that Kathāvatthu, I shall expound it. Listen to that explanation with a concentrated mind, O virtuous ones.

## Nidānakathā
At the conclusion of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya), the Blessed One entered the rains retreat in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven on the Paṇḍukambala stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. Having made the Santusita deva, who had been his mother, the chief witness (kāya-sakkhi), he taught the Abhidhamma to the assembly of devas and brahmas. After teaching the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, and Puggalapaññatti, when the turn for the Kathāvatthu discourse arrived, he foresaw: "In the future, my disciple, the great wise elder named Moggaliputtatissa Thera, will arise. When he cleanses the stains of the Sasana and holds the Third Council, he will sit in the midst of the Saṅgha and, combining five hundred suttas of his own school and five hundred suttas of other schools, making a total of one thousand suttas, he will expand this Kathāvatthu treatise." Thus, wishing to provide the opportunity for that Venerable Moggaliputtatissa Thera to expand it, he laid down the Matika in a text not even a full bhāṇavāra in length, beginning with the eight-faced method of argumentation (aṭṭhamukha) based on the two sets of five in the four questions first taught in the Puggalavāda, and continuing through all the sequences of discussion.
106:
Afterwards, having taught the remainder of the Abhidhamma in detail and completed the rains retreat, the Buddha descended from the deva world to the city of Saṅkassa via a jeweled stairway in the middle of golden and silver stairways. Having fulfilled the welfare of beings and lived out his full life span, he attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

Then, the assembly of Arahants led by Venerable Mahākassapa, with King Ajātasattu as their supporter, held the rehearsal (Council) of the Dhamma and Vinaya, the body of the teaching. One hundred years after that, the Vajjiputtaka monks proclaimed (practiced) the ten points. Hearing of those ten points, Venerable Yasa, the son of the brahmin Kākaṇḍaka, with King Kālāsoka, the son of Susunāga, as his supporter, selected seven hundred elders from among one million two hundred thousand monks, suppressed those ten points, and held the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya.

The ten thousand Vajjiputtaka monks who were suppressed by those elders who held the Dhamma rehearsal sought out their own faction. Having found a faction of weak wisdom suitable to themselves, they established a separate school called the Mahāsaṃghika Ācariyakula (Mahāsaṃghika sect). Splitting from that Mahāsaṃghika sect, two other teacher lineages arose: the Gokulika and the Ekabyohārika. Splitting from the Gokulika sect, two other teacher lineages arose: the Paññattivāda and the Bāhulika. The name Bahussutika is also a name for those same Bāhulika teachers. Within those Bāhulika teachers themselves, another teacher-tradition called Cetiyavāda arose. Thus, from the Mahāsaṃghika sect, five teacher lineages arose during the second century. Together with the Mahāsaṃghika, they were six sects.

In that same second century, splitting from the Theravāda sect, two teacher-traditions arose: the Mahīsāsaka and the Vajjiputtaka. Among those two traditions, splitting from the Vajjiputtaka tradition, four other teacher-traditions arose: the Dhammuttariya, the Bhadrayānika, the Channāgārika, and the Samitiya. Again, in that same second century, splitting from the Mahīsāsaka tradition, two teacher-traditions arose: the Sabbatthivāda and the Dhammaguttika. Again, splitting from the Sabbatthivāda lineage, the tradition called Kassapika arose. When the Kassapika tradition split, another tradition called Saṅkantika arose. When the Saṅkantika tradition split, the tradition called Suttavāda arose. Thus, splitting from the Theravāda, these...
107:
Two schools of teachers, namely Mahisāsaka and Vajjiputtaka, arose by splitting from the Theravāda school. From that Vajjiputtaka school, four more schools of teachers arose: Dhammuttariya, Bhadrayānika, Channāgārika, and Samitiya. Again, within that second century, two schools of teachers, Sabbatthivāda and Dhammaguttika, arose by splitting from the Mahisāsaka school. Further, from the lineage of Sabbatthivāda, the schools of teachers known as Kassapika arose. When the Kassapika schools split, the schools of teachers known as Saṅkantika arose. When the Saṅkantika schools split, the schools of teachers known as Suttavāda arose. Thus, eleven schools of teachers arose by splitting from the Theravāda. These eleven schools, together with the Theravāda, make twelve. Thus, these twelve schools and the six schools that split from the Mahāsaṅghika sect make a total of eighteen schools of teachers, all of which arose within the second century of the Sāsana. These are also called the eighteen sects (nikāya) or the eighteen lineages of teachers. Among these eighteen schools, seventeen are considered schismatic (bhinnaka), while the Theravāda alone is to be understood as non-schismatic (abhinnaka).

Regarding this matter, it is stated in the Dīpavaṃsa:

When the wicked Vajjiputtaka monks were expelled by the Elders, those many monks who were proponents of non-Dhamma (adhammavādī) gained another faction.

Ten thousand of them assembled and held a Dhamma council; therefore, this Dhamma council is called the 'Great Council' (Mahāsaṅgīti).

The monks who performed the Great Council acted contrary to the Dispensation; having destroyed the original collection (mūlasaṅgaha), they made another collection.

They placed Suttas collected in one Nikāya into another Nikāya; they destroyed the meaning and the text in the Vinaya and in the five Nikāyas.

Those monks did not know the teachings expressed figuratively (pariyāya) and those expressed directly (nippariyāya), nor did they know the Suttas of explicit meaning (nītattha) and those of implicit meaning (neyyattha).

They assigned a different meaning to words spoken with a specific intention; under the shadow of the letter (byañjana), those monks destroyed much of the meaning.

Discarding portions of the profound Sutta and Vinaya, they composed other counterfeit Suttas and Vinaya.

The Parivāra, the summary of meanings (atthuddhāra), the Abhidhamma, the six books of Abhidhamma, the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the Niddesa, and portions of the Jātaka—

Discarding this much of the Pāḷi Canon, they composed other texts; they also changed the names, grammatical forms, requisites, and the manner of conduct.

Abandoning the original nature, they made those names and other things different; those monks who performed the Great Council were the leaders in schismatic doctrines.
108:
By following the example of those monks who performed the Great Council, many schismatic doctrines arose. After that time, a split occurred within that Mahāsaṅghika sect.

The monks split into two: the Gokulika and the Ekavyohārika. Later, two splits arose from the Gokulika sect.

The monks split into two: the Bahussutika and the Paññatti. Again, the Cetiyavādins, who split from the Mahāsaṅghika sect, further split from the Bahussutika doctrine.

All these five doctrines have the Mahāsaṅghika sect as their root. They destroyed the meaning of the Pāḷi, the Pāḷi text itself, and portions of the Suttas that were compiled in the Council.

Indeed, they discarded portions of the scriptures and composed other scriptures, as well as names, grammatical forms, requisites, and conduct.

Abandoning the original nature, they made those names and other things different. Again, a split occurred within the pure Theravāda.

The monks split into two: the Mahisāsaka and the Vajjiputtaka. Within the Vajjiputtaka doctrine, four splits occurred.

They were the Dhammuttarika, the Bhaddayānika, the Channāgārika, and the Samiti doctrines. Later, two splits arose from the Mahisāsaka sect.

The monks split into two: the Sabbatthivāda and the Dhammagutta. From the Sabbatthivāda, the Kassapika doctrine split, and from the Kassapika doctrine, the Saṅkantika doctrine split.

From the Saṅkantika doctrine, the Suttavāda doctrine split in succession. These eleven doctrines split and emerged from the Theravāda.
