They destroyed the meaning of the Pāḷi, the Pāḷi text itself, and portions of the Suttas that were compiled in the Council. Discarding portions of the scriptures, they composed other scriptures.

Names, grammatical forms, requisites, and conduct—abandoning the original nature, they made those names and other things different.

There are seventeen schismatic doctrines, and the one non-schismatic doctrine is the Theravāda. Together with the schismatic doctrines, all these doctrines are eighteen.
109:
The supreme Theravāda, which is the doctrine of the elders such as the Venerable Mahākassapa, is like a great banyan tree. This doctrine is neither deficient nor excessive; it is purely the teaching of the Conqueror (Jina).

Other doctrines remaining from the Theravāda arose like parasitic plants on a great tree. While there were no divergent doctrines within the first hundred years of the Buddha's Dispensation, seventeen divergent doctrines arose during the second hundred years. (Thus it is said in the Dīpavaṃsa.)

Furthermore, six other teacher-doctrines (ācariyavāda) arose in succession: Hemavatika, Rājagirika, Siddhatthika, Pubbaseliya, Aparaseliya, and Vājiriya. These are not intended to be discussed here. While the Dispensation existed through the eighteen teacher-doctrines that arose earlier, King Asoka the Righteous, having gained faith, spent five hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas] daily: one hundred thousand for the worship of the Buddha, one hundred thousand for the Dhamma, one hundred thousand for the Saṅgha, one hundred thousand for his teacher Nigrodha Thera, and one hundred thousand for medicines at the four city gates, thus bringing about great gain and honor to the Dispensation.

The heretics (titthiyas), whose gain and honor had declined and who could not obtain even mere food and clothing, desired gain and honor. They approached the monks to be ordained as Buddhist monks and presented their own false views, saying, "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's Dispensation." Even those who did not receive ordination cut their own hair, wore saffron robes, and wandered through the monasteries, entering the midst of the Saṅgha during the performance of Uposatha and other acts. Although these pseudo-monks were rebuked by the Saṅgha of monks according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's Dispensation, they did not abide by the practice consistent with the Dhamma and Vinaya, and they caused many dangers, impurities, and thorns to arise in the Dispensation.

Some tended the sacrificial fire, some practiced the fivefold heat-asceticism, some followed the course of the sun, and some promoted their views in various ways, saying, "We will destroy your Dhamma and Vinaya." At that time, the Saṅgha of monks did not perform Uposatha or Pavāraṇā with them. At the Asokārāma monastery, the Uposatha ceremony was interrupted for seven years.

The King tried to have the Uposatha performed by his authority but was unable to do so. Indeed, because a foolish minister with wrong understanding killed many monks, the King felt remorse and was troubled at heart. Desiring to appease his remorse and the dangers that had arisen in the Dispensation, he asked the Saṅgha, "Who is capable in this matter?"
110:
"Who is capable in this matter?" he asked the Saṅgha, and hearing, "Great King, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa is capable," he had the Elder invited from the Ahogaṅgā Mountain according to the Saṅgha's word. Having witnessed a miracle and becoming free from doubt regarding the Elder's power, the King asked about his own moral anxiety (kukkucca) and appeased his remorse. The Elder, residing in the royal garden, taught the King the doctrine (samaya) for seven days.

On the seventh day, the King, having learned the doctrine, assembled the Saṅgha of monks at the Asokārāma monastery. He had a curtain-wall set up and, sitting within the curtain, grouped the monks according to their respective views. Calling each group of monks, he asked, "Venerable sirs, what was the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened Buddha?" Then the Eternalists (Sassatavādī) replied, "He was an Eternalist." The Partial-Eternalists (Ekaccasassatavādī), the Extensionists (Antānantavādī), the Eel-wrigglers (Amarāvikkhepavādī), the Fortuitous-Originists (Adhiccasamuppannavādī), the Believers in Conscious Survival (Saññīvādī), the Believers in Unconscious Survival (Asaññīvādī), the Believers in Neither-Conscious-nor-Unconscious Survival (Nevasaññīnāsaññīvādī), the Annihilationists (Ucchedavādī), and the Proclaimers of Nibbāna in this life (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī) each replied, "He was a Proclaimer of Nibbāna in this life."

Because the King had previously learned the doctrine, he knew, "These are not monks; these are heretics with views outside the Dispensation." He gave them white clothes and expelled them from the monkhood. They numbered sixty thousand in total.

Then he called the other monks and asked, "Venerable sirs, what was the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened Buddha?" They replied, "Great King, He was an Analyst (Vibhajjavādī)." When they said this, the King asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, was the Fully Enlightened Buddha an Analyst?" The Elder replied, "Yes, Great King." Then the King said, "Venerable sirs, the Dispensation is now pure; let the Saṅgha of monks perform the Uposatha." Having provided protection, he entered the city.

The unified Saṅgha assembled and performed the Uposatha. In that assembly, there were six million monks. In that gathering, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, for the purpose of refuting the matters that had arisen then and those that would arise in the future, followed the method given by the Teacher. Analyzing the summary (mātikā) established by the Tathāgata, he brought forth one thousand discourses—five hundred on his own doctrine and five hundred on the doctrines of others—and spoke this Kathāvatthu treatise, which is the crushing of others' false doctrines and a mark for the future.

Thereafter, from among the six million monks, he selected one thousand monks who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka and proficient in the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Just as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa had performed the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya, so too...
111:
(The Elder Moggaliputtatissa), having purified the stains of the Sasana, performed the rehearsal and conducted the Third Council. In that rehearsal, while rehearsing the Abhidhamma, he compiled (collected) this Kathāvatthu treatise exactly as it was spoken (by the Buddha). Therefore, it is said:

"Because it is the basis for discourses such as the Discourse on the Person (Puggalakathā), the Buddha preached the Kathāvatthu treatise in brief.

That treatise, which was established only as a matrix (mātikā) in the celestial realm, was expanded upon on earth by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.

Now, as the sequence for explaining the meaning of that treatise has arrived, I (the commentator) shall explain it; listen to that explanation with a concentrated mind."

## The Introduction (Nidānakathā) is finished.
112:
## 1. Discourse on the Person (Puggalakathā)
## 1. Purely in the Sense of a Real and Ultimate Fact (Suddhasaccikaṭṭha)
## 1. Affirmative and Negative Explanation (Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā)
Among those statements, "Is the person perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?" is the question (pucchā). "Yes (āmantā)" is the affirmation (paṭijānanā). If it is asked, "Whose question is this, and whose affirmation is this?", it should not be said specifically that it is this person's question or that person's affirmation. This is because the Blessed One established the matrix (mātikā) by the power of the Pali text in this Kathāvatthu treatise for the purpose of purifying various doctrines. That matrix was expanded upon by the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa, standing within the method granted by the Teacher, by the power of the Pali text. The Elder did not engage in a contentious debate with as many proponents as there are paths of doctrine shown here. Nevertheless, in order to make the meaning of the various discourses easy to remember, I shall provide the explanation of the meaning only after showing the divisions such as the Proponent's (Sakavādī) question, the Opponent's (Paravādī) question, the Proponent's affirmation, and the Opponent's affirmation.

"Is the person perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?"—this question is the Proponent's (Sakavādī) question. By that question, it is shown that "Those Person-believers (Puggalavādins) who hold the view that 'a person exists' should be questioned in this way." Who are the Person-believers? They are the Vajjiputtakas and the Sammitiyas within the Sasana, and many other sectarians (aññatitthiya) outside the Sasana. In that Pali, "puggala" means the self (atta), a being (satta), or a soul (jīva). "Upalabbhati" means it is perceived or known by approaching with wisdom. In the term "saccikaṭṭhaparamaṭṭhena," "saccikaṭṭha" means the sense of reality, which should not be taken as an unreal form like an illusion or a mirage. "Paramaṭṭha" means the ultimate sense, which should not be taken by way of hearsay and so on. By both these senses, the fifty-seven types of phenomena (dhammas) classified by way of aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and faculties (indriya) are shown later, starting with "The person is perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, and form (rūpa) is also perceived." Just as those fifty-seven phenomena are perceived in the sense of a real nature, the Proponent asks whether your "person" is likewise perceived. The Opponent (Paravādī) affirms, "Yes (āmantā)." Affirmation (paṭijānana) appears in some places as "Āma, bhante" and in some places as "Āma." Here, however, it appears as "Āmantā." In affirming thus, this is the Opponent's intention—that Opponent, based on the Sutta later spoken by the Blessed One, "There is a person who practices for his own benefit"...
113:
...taking that Sutta as a basis, because the Blessed One is a speaker of truth (saccavādī), does not speak with the intention of deceiving, and does not teach the Dhamma merely by way of hearsay, but declares it having personally realized it with higher knowledge (abhiññā) for the world including the devas and Brahmas; therefore, holding the view that what was said by Him, "There is a person who practices for his own benefit," exists in the very sense of a real and ultimate fact, he affirms, "Yes (āmantā)."

Then, not giving an opening to such a sophistical and evasive argument of the Opponent, the Proponent (Sakavādī) said, "That which is a real fact..." and so on. The meaning here is—the fifty-seven types of phenomena such as form (rūpa) and so on, which are clearly shown later as "with cause, without cause, conditioned, unconditioned, with sign, without sign," should not be taken by way of conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) nor by way of hearsay. They are a real fact (saccikaṭṭha) only because of their own actual existence, and they are an ultimate fact (paramaṭṭha) because of their own self-evidence. Referring to those phenomena, he says, "Is that person perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, from that which is a real and ultimate fact?"

The word "tato" (from that) expresses the instrumental sense. Therefore, the meaning here is: "Is that person perceived by that real and ultimate fact?" This is what is meant: Is your person perceived in the same manner as the real and ultimate fact is perceived by way of divisions such as being subject to change (ruppana) or by way of divisions such as having a cause? The Opponent, not desiring such a person, denies it, saying, "It should not be said thus (na hevaṃ vattabbe)." Here, the word-break is "na hi evaṃ vattabbe." It can also be broken as "na hi evaṃ." Both mean "It should not be said thus."

"Acknowledge the refutation (ājānāhi niggahaṃ)" is the statement of the Proponent. Since your latter denial does not follow from your former affirmation, and the former does not agree with the latter, you have reached a refutation. The meaning is: "Accept this fault or failure which is a refutation." Having thus made the refutation known, now, in order to make it clear by way of the proposition (thapanā), and the application (pāpanā) and conclusion (ropanā) through the direct and reverse methods, he said, "If a person..." and so on. In that statement, "If a person is perceived" means if a person could be perceived in the sense of a real and ultimate fact. This is the refutation, application, and conclusion by establishing the Opponent's position...
114:
The Forward Proposition (Anuloma-ṭhapanā) is the characteristic mark (of the refutation, application, and attribution) because it establishes the thesis of the opponent. The phrase beginning with "Tena vata re" is called the Forward Application (Anuloma-pāpanā) because it leads to the refutation (niggaha) in the forward sequence. In that phrase, "tena" is a causal term. "Vata" is a term expressing certainty or determination. "Re" is a term of address. The intended meaning is: "O opponent, for that reason—that a person is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact—it should indeed be said. O fair-faced opponent, for that reason, it should indeed be said."

The phrase beginning with "Yaṃ tattha vadesi" is called the Forward Attribution (Anuloma-ropanā) because it attributes the fault of refutation in the forward sequence. At the end of that statement, before the word "micchā" (false), the words "idaṃ te" (this for you) should be inserted. The meaning here is: "This answer of yours is wrong." This is also directly stated in the later Pali text.

The phrase beginning with "No ce pana vattabbe" is called the Reverse Proposition (Paṭiloma-ṭhapanā), which serves as the characteristic mark of the refutation, application, and attribution in the reverse order, because it establishes the rejected side as "It should not be said thus." The phrase beginning with "No ca vata re" is called the Reverse Application (Paṭiloma-pāpanā) because it leads to refutation in the reverse sequence. Again, the phrase beginning with "Yaṃ tattha vadesi" is called the Reverse Attribution (Paṭiloma-ropanā) because it attributes the fault of refutation in the reverse sequence. Here too, before the final word "micchā", the words "idaṃ te" must be brought in and inserted. This same method applies to similar instances later on.

The summary meaning from the beginning is: If a person is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, then, friend, it should be said that the person is found because of that. But what you said in that problem—"It should be said in the first question that [the person] is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, but it should not be said in the second question that the person is found because of that"—this of yours is wrong. Thus, first, there are the proposition (ṭhapanā), application (pāpanā), and attribution (ropanā) in the forward order.

If it should not be said in the second question that "the person is found because of that," then it should not be said in the first question either. But what you said here—"It should be said in the first question that [the person] is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact, but it should not be said in the second question that the person is found because of that"—this of yours is wrong. Thus, there are the proposition, application, and attribution in the reverse order. In this way, because the fault of refutation (niggaha) and the four applications and attributions in forward and reverse orders are taught, this passage starting with "upalabbhati" is called the Fivefold Forward Sequence (Anuloma-pañcaka). In this Anuloma-pañcaka, although two refutations are made—one by application and attribution in the forward order, and one by application and attribution in the reverse order—this very fault of refutation [referred to in] "Know the refutation"...
115:
In this context, because the first refutation is attributed in two ways based on the first thesis "The person is found," this is indeed a single first refutation.

Now follows the Counter-method (Paccanīka-naya). In that method, the question belongs to the opponent (paravādī). Since that opponent holds the text "There is a person who practices for his own benefit," he does not accept the view "is not found" and asks thus. The proponent (sakavādī) admits "Yes (āmanta)" because the person is not found in the same way that phenomena like form (rūpa) are found. Then the other [the opponent], intending only the saccikaṭṭha (real fact) which is conventional truth as he desires, says "That which is saccikaṭṭha..." etc. Or he says this by combining both conventional truth and ultimate truth. The proponent, however, rejects it saying "It is not thus (na hevaṃ)" because the "person" exists as a derivative designation (upādā-paññatti) and because the question was asked by combining the two truths.

Now, although the proponent first accepted the non-findability by way of ultimate truth, he later rejected it by way of conventional truth or by way of a mixture. The opponent, relying on mere sophistry (chala-vāda) in the words "is not found," says "You have later rejected what you first admitted," as if returning a blow in a quarrel. Seeking to clear his own act of refutation, he says "Know the rejoinder (paṭikamma)." Just as in the Fivefold Forward Sequence the proponent established the thesis and made the refutation clear through application and attribution in forward and reverse orders, now [the opponent], wishing to make the rejoinder clear, says "If the person..." etc. The meaning of that should be understood in the same way as mentioned below.

In this context, "proposition" (ṭhapanā) is merely an establishing of the opponent's side to show "This is your fault"; it does not make the refutation or the rejoinder clear. It is only through application (pāpanā) and attribution (ropanā) that the refutation is made clear. Therefore, because the rejoinder is performed in four ways by means of the four applications and attributions in forward and reverse orders, this should be known as one group of four called the "Fourfold Rejoinder" (Paṭikamma-catukka).

After performing the rejoinder in this way, now wishing to show the bad nature of the refutation made by the proponent in the Fivefold Forward Sequence by relying on that same sophistry, he says "But if you think..." etc. There, "But if you think" means "If you hold the view." The phrase "It should indeed be said" is said in reference to the admission "Yes (āmanta)" in the Counter-method.
116:
The phrase "No ca vattabbe" (It should not be said) is stated with the intention of rejecting [the proposition] by saying "No." For that reason, "Tena tava tattha" means that in the case where you, the Sakavādī, are not found [to be correct], there is the admission "Āmantā" (Yes). "Hevaṃ niggahetabbe" means that the Sakavādī, who again rejects by saying "It is not so," should be refuted in this way. "Atha taṃ niggaṇhāma" means "Since you deserve to be refuted, we refute you." "Suniggahito ca hosi" means "You are well-refuted because you are refuted by your own view." 

Having thus shown the refutability of that Sakavādī, he now says "Hañci" (If) etc., wishing to refute him. In that context, Ṭhapanā (proposition), Pāpanā (leading to the consequence), and Ropanā (attribution) should be understood in the same manner as mentioned below. At the end, "Idaṃ te micchā" means "This statement of yours is wrong." This is called the "Niggaha-catukka" (Fourfold Refutation) because the refutation is performed in four ways through sophistry (chalavāda).

Even after performing the refutation in this way, he now says "Ese ce dunniggahite" (If this is poorly refuted) etc., wishing to show: "If this refutation performed by me according to your view is a wrong refutation, then the refutation you performed against me in the Anuloma-pañcaka (Fivefold Forward Sequence) below is also a wrong refutation." In that context, "Ese ce dunniggahite" means "If this doctrine of yours is poorly refuted by me." Or it means "If this refutation performed by me upon you is a wrong refutation." "Hevamevaṃ tattha dakkha" means "Look at that refutation you performed against me below in the same way (as a wrong refutation)."

Now, having shown the refutation performed by the Sakavādī below with the words "Vattabbe kho" (It should be said) etc., he says "No ca mayaṃ tayā" (And not we by you) etc., wishing to bring that refutation to the state of being a non-refutation. In those words "No ca mayaṃ tayā tattha hetāya patiññāya" etc., the meaning is: Since that refutation you performed against me is a wrong refutation, even though we, who admit in this way with the admission "Āmantā" in that Anuloma-pañcaka, reject it again by saying "It is not so," we should not be refuted by you with the words "Acknowledge the refutation." You refute me who should not be refuted in this way; however, by such a refutation, we are [only] poorly refuted.

Now, to show the refutation regarding which he said "We are poorly refuted," he says "Hañci puggalo... idaṃ te micchā." Thus, this Catukka (fourfold group) is called "Upanayana-catukka" (Fourfold Application) because it brings the refutation performed through the four Pāpanā and Ropanā in forward and reverse order, comparing it with one's own refutation.
117:
Because the refutation (niggaha) made by the fourfold imposition of fault (pāpanāropanā) in forward and reverse order is brought close to one's own refutation, it is called the fourfold application (upanayana-catukka). Now, there is the fourfold conclusion (niggamana-catukka) beginning with "It should not be refuted thus." In that fourfold conclusion, "It should not be refuted thus" means: "In the manner that I have been refuted by you, the Sakavādin, I should not be refuted in that manner." This is because I have established the invalidity of this refutation. "Tena hi" means "for that reason." Because this refutation is an invalid refutation (dunniggaha), therefore, the meaning is: "If a person... [pe]... this is wrong for you," that is, "this refutation of yours is wrong." "Tena hi ye kate niggaha" means: "For the reason that this is wrong, the refutation made by you is badly made (dukkata). Only the rejoinder (paṭikamma) made by me is well made (sukata)." The presentation of the course of speech by way of the fourfold rejoinder, etc., is also well made. Thus, it should be understood that this fivefold forward-negative (anuloma-paccanīka-pañcaka) is pointed out by way of the fivefold forward beginning with "A person is perceived" and the fourfold rejoinder, refutation, application, and conclusion beginning with "is not perceived." By this much of the course of speech, when the Sakavādin presents the opening case, the Paravādin wins by mere similarity of words through sophistry (chalavāda).

## 2. Explanation of the Negative-Forward (Paccanīkānuloma-vaṇṇanā)

Now, to show the arising of the debate and how the Sakavādin achieves a good victory through the Dhamma and truth when the Paravādin presents the opening case, the fivefold negative-forward beginning with "A person is not perceived" is commenced. There, in the negative section, the question belongs to the Paravādin. The affirmation, referring to the real and ultimate sense (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha) consisting of the divisions of form, etc., belongs to the Sakavādin. The further inquiry, "Is that real sense..." referring to either pure conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) or conventional truth mixed with ultimate sense, belongs to the Paravādin. The rejection, "It is not so," belongs to the Sakavādin, because it should not be said that [a person] is not perceived by way of conventional truth, or because the inquiry is confused by way of the mixed truth. The statement "Acknowledge the refutation," etc., based on the mere similarity of words that an affirmation is being rejected, belongs to the Paravādin. Thus, it should be understood that based on the second thesis "This person is not perceived," the second refutation occurs. In this way, the refutation was imposed by him through sophistry.
118:
7-10. Now, in order to demonstrate the victory of one's own doctrine in a righteous and fair manner, in the forward method (anuloma-naya), there is the question of the Sakavādī, and the Paravādī makes an admission based on his own view. The Sakavādī, without giving an opening to the Paravādī's view, cross-examines again by way of ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca); the Paravādī rejects it by way of ultimate truth because a person (puggala) does not exist. After that rejection, for the purpose of showing one's own victory in a righteous and fair manner, the entire statement beginning with "Acknowledge the rejoinder" (ājānāhi paṭikammaṃ) belongs solely to the Sakavādī. In that context, the meaning of the fourfold sets (catukka) of rejoinder (paṭikamma), refutation (niggaha), application (upanayana), and conclusion (niggamana) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Thus, by way of the fivefold reverse method (paccanīka-pañcaka) beginning with "A person is not found" (puggalo nupalabbhati), and by way of the fourfold sets of rejoinder, refutation, application, and conclusion beginning with "is found" (upalabbhati), what is called the fivefold reverse-forward method (paccanīkānuloma-pañcaka) has been explained.

In this way, the two fivefold sets in the first Saccikaṭṭha have been explained. Among those two fivefold sets, in the first forward fivefold set (anuloma-pañcaka), the refutation made by the Sakavādī against the Paravādī is a valid refutation (suniggaha). However, the victory achieved by the Paravādī by making a rejoinder based on sophistry (chala-vāda) is an invalid victory (dujjaya). In the second fivefold set, the refutation made by the Paravādī against the Sakavādī is an invalid refutation (dunniggaha). But the victory achieved by the Sakavādī by making a rejoinder against the Paravādī based on the righteous doctrine is a valid victory (sujaya). This is the first Saccikaṭṭha. Regarding this, it is said:

"In the first fivefold set, the refutation of the Paravādī is pure;
In that same set, the victory of that Paravādī through rejoinder is impure.

In the second fivefold set, the refutation of the Sakavādī is impure;
In that same set, the victory of that Sakavādī through rejoinder is especially pure.

Therefore, in both instances, the victory belongs only to the Sakavādī;
There is only victory through righteousness; how could there be victory through unrighteousness?

Just as in this Saccikaṭṭha, adorned with two fivefold sets,
Victory and defeat are stated by way of righteousness and unrighteousness.

In all other Saccikaṭṭhas following this one,
The wise should understand both victory and defeat in this very same way."
119:
## 2. Okāsa-saccikaṭṭha (Ultimate Sense Regarding Place)
## 1. Description of the Forward and Reverse Methods
Having thus detailed the pure ultimate sense (suddhika-saccikaṭṭha) without mixing it with place (okāsa) and so on, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa now begins the discourse with "A person is found" (puggalo upalabbhati) and so forth, in order to detail that same pure ultimate sense through other methods such as place (okāsa). In that passage beginning with "A person is found," the question (pucchā) is the Sakavādī's question, and the admission (paṭiññā) is the Paravādī's admission. Again, the cross-examination using the term "everywhere" (sabbattha) refers to the body, and this is the Sakavādī's question. Seeing the fault of repeatedly perceiving a self (atta) in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), and the fault of arriving at the view that "the soul is one thing, the body is another" (aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīraṃ), the Paravādī's rejection follows.

The remaining procedure in the forward and reverse fivefold sets (anuloma-paccanīka-pañcaka) of this Okāsa-saccikaṭṭha should be understood in the same way as the pure ultimate sense (suddhika-saccikaṭṭha) mentioned below. However, the Pali text has been summarized by the redactors (saṅgītikāra). In that summarized Pali, because it is stated with reference to the body that "it is not found everywhere," it implies that the person could be found outside the body. Therefore, in the reverse method (paccanīka-naya), the rejection is the Sakavādī's rejection, and the rejoinder (paṭikamma) through sophistry (chala-vāda)—where one first admits and then later denies—is the Paravādī's procedure. The rest is clear.

## 3. Kāla-saccikaṭṭha (Ultimate Sense Regarding Time)
## 1. Description of the Forward and Reverse Methods
In the second method, Kāla-saccikaṭṭha, the cross-examination using the term "always" (sabbadā) refers to the past and future times—the preceding and succeeding births—as well as the present time of existence and the time after Parinibbāna; this is the Sakavādī's question. Seeing the fault of arriving at the meaning such as "that very person who was a brahmin is now a khattiya, and that very person who was a khattiya is now a brahmin," and the fault of there being no distinction between a living person and one who has attained Parinibbāna, the Paravādī's rejection follows. The rest of the procedure is exactly the same as stated in the first method (Okāsa-saccikaṭṭha).

## 4. Avayava-saccikaṭṭha (Ultimate Sense Regarding Parts)
## 1. Description of the Forward and Reverse Methods
In the third method, Avayava-saccikaṭṭha, the cross-examination using the term "in all" (sabbesu) refers to the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and so on; this is the Sakavādī's question. The Paravādī's rejection follows due to the fear of faults such as "there is a self in form" or "there is a self in the eye." The rest of the procedure is just the same as that first method.
120:
## Locus, etc., of the Real and Ultimate Fact
## 2. Explanation of the Negative-Affirmative
In this way, these three (Locus, Time, and Part) are first analyzed in order in the Affirmative-Negative Pentad by the power of the mere affirmative; then, to analyze them in the Negative-Affirmative Pentad by the power of the mere negative, the discourse beginning with "Puggalo nupalabbhati" (The person is not found) is commenced. In that discourse, the meaning should be understood by the method already stated in the Negative section, which comes by abbreviating the Pali of the Affirmative Pentad, and by the method already stated in the Affirmative section, which comes by abbreviating the Pali of the Negative Pentad. By this sequence of words, it should be understood that for each of the four types of real and ultimate facts—namely, the Pure Real and Ultimate Fact and these three (Locus, Time, and Part)—this logical method of debate called the "Eight-faced" (Aṭṭhamukhā) is shown by way of the two pentads: the Affirmative-Negative method and the Negative-Affirmative method. This logical method of debate (vādayuttī) is written in the Pali text as the "Eightfold Refutation" (Aṭṭhakaniggaha) by way of one refutation at each beginning (mukha). In this regard, it is said:

“In this way, in the fourfold type of question, by the division of the two pentads,
This logical method of debate called 'Eight-faced' is clearly revealed.
There are only eight refutations therein; four of them are valid (dhammika),
And four are invalid (adhammika);
In all [pentads], the victory (jaya) belongs to the Proponent (Sakavādī),
And in all [pentads], there is only defeat (parājaya) for the Opponent (Paravādī).”

## The Explanation of the Real and Ultimate Fact is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Pure Comparison
17-27. Now, there is the comparison of the person as a real and ultimate fact with matter (rūpa), etc. In that comparison, the phrase "rūpañca" (and matter) means: just as matter is found in the ultimate sense (paramatthato), is your person also found in the same way? This inquiry, intended as such, is the question of the Proponent (Sakavādī). Taking only the words "the person exists" and admitting it is the admission of the Opponent (Paravādī). If your person exists in the ultimate sense like matter, then just as there is a difference (aññatta) between matter and feeling, etc., does it also arrive at a state of difference for the person? This cross-examination is the inquiry of the Proponent. Seeing the contradiction with the Sutta text of the doctrine and rejecting it is the rejection of the Opponent. The remaining sequence of words is very clear in meaning.
121:
It is very clear in terms of meaning. But in terms of the Pali text, here, by the power of the fifty-seven varieties of the real and ultimate fact (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha), fifty-seven affirmative pentads (anuloma-pañcaka) have been shown in the Affirmative-Negative method based on the Proponent's side. The tetrad of the rejoinder (paṭikammacatukka), etc., are abbreviated. Also in the Negative-Affirmative method based on the Opponent's side, fifty-seven reverse pentads (paṭiloma-pañcaka) have been shown. The tetrad of the rejoinder, etc., are abbreviated.

In that Negative-Affirmative method, by the mere words "It was said by the Blessed One" (Vuttaṃ bhagavatā), the Opponent makes an inquiry to show both the existence of the person and the state of matter being perceivable by wisdom as a real and ultimate fact, in order to make [the Proponent] admit the difference between the two (the person and matter). Because the problem of the identity (ekatta) and difference (nānatta) of conventional truth (sammutisacca) and ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) is one that should be set aside (ṭhapaniya), the Proponent rejects it. The remaining meanings are also clear here.

## Explanation of the Pure Comparison.

## 6. Explanation of the Comparison by Analogy

28-36. Now, there is the comparison of the real and ultimate fact by way of analogy (opamma) with matter, etc., itself. In that comparison by analogy, both the question asking about the difference because matter and feeling are similar in being perceived by wisdom, and the question asking about the similarity of the person and matter in being perceived by wisdom, are the Proponent's questions. Both admissions are the Opponent's admissions. Because of the similarity in perception admitted by the Opponent, the Proponent cross-examines the difference between matter and the person, just like matter and feeling, and the Opponent rejects it. The remaining meaning is also clear here.

But in terms of the Pali text, here, by the power of the cycles (cakka) such as those rooted in matter (rūpa-mūlaka), nine hundred and twenty refutation pentads (niggaha-pañcaka) are shown on the side of the Proponent. How so? Among the aggregates (khandha), there are four in the cycle rooted in matter; also in the cycles rooted in feeling, etc., there are four each, making twenty refutation pentads. Among the bases (āyatana), there are eleven in the cycle rooted in the eye-base (cakkhāyatana-mūlaka); also in the remaining cycles, there are eleven each, making one hundred and thirty-two. Among the elements (dhātu), there are seventeen in the cycle rooted in the eye-element (cakkhudhātu-mūlaka); also in the remaining cycles, there are seventeen each, making three hundred and six. Among the faculties (indriya), there are twenty-one in the cycle rooted in the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya-mūlaka); also in the remaining cycles, there are twenty-one each, making four hundred and sixty-two. Thus, in total, there are nine hundred and twenty refutation pentads.

37-45. Also on the Opponent's side, by the affirmative method itself, "Matter is found," having made [the Proponent] admit the difference of matter, feeling, etc., the Opponent then relies on the Sutta "The person exists" and, by the power of the sixfold discourse (chaḷavāda), posits the person as being similar to matter, etc., in perception, and makes the inquiry regarding the difference.
122:
By the power of the six-fold argument (chaḷavāda), the identity of the person with form and so forth has been presented, and the inquiry into their distinctness has been made. The remaining meaning here is also quite clear. In terms of the Pāḷi text, nine hundred and twenty-plus five-fold rejoinders (paṭikamma-pañcaka) have been shown on the side of the Sakavādī, according to the method already mentioned.

## Comparison of the Real and Ultimate Sense with Form and so forth by way of Simile.

## 7. Commentary on the Comparison by the Four-fold Method

46-52. Now, since the person is found in the real and ultimate sense (sacchikaṭṭha-paramattha), that person must be one of the fifty-seven real and ultimate things such as form, or must exist depending on form and so forth, or must exist apart from form and so forth, or must be the support of form and so forth. Therefore, the comparison of the real and ultimate sense by this four-fold method is begun. In that comparison by the four-fold method (catukkanaya-saṃsandana), the inquiry "Is form the person?" is the questioning of the Sakavādī. The rejection "It should not be said so" due to the fear of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) is the rejection of the Paravādī. The application of the refutation is the act of the Sakavādī.

If it is asked, "Is this application of refutation appropriate? Should not the question 'Is form feeling?' also be rejected?", the answer should be "Yes, it should indeed be rejected." However, that rejection is because the nature of feeling is clearly different from the nature of form, not because of a lack of distinctness. This Paravādī does not desire the distinctness of the person from even a single phenomenon among form and so forth; therefore, the application of the refutation is appropriate. This inquiry is begun with reference to the entire ultimate truth, starting from "Is form the person?" up to "Is the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) the person?"

However, since it is impossible to speak of all ultimate phenomena together according to their individual characteristics, only the characteristic of the mode of inquiry is established according to the order of the Pāḷi text. By this establishment, the wise can clearly understand the meaning. The Sakavādī who wishes to debate should take this characteristic and speak in such a way that the Paravādī finds no opportunity. Thus, because the characteristic of the mode of inquiry is established according to the order of the Pāḷi text, the application of the refutation is indeed appropriate. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all inquiries.

The specific distinction is: in questions such as "Is the person in form?", just as it is appropriate to say that three great elements exist depending on one great element, or that consciousness exists in form depending on the physical base (vatthu-rūpa), so too is the inquiry "Is your person in form?". Furthermore, just as it is appropriate to say that all phenomena such as feeling, or the four immaterial aggregates, or Nibbāna itself, are "found apart from form" because their natures are distinct, so too is the inquiry "Is your person found apart from form?"
123:
Alternatively, just as it is appropriate to say that even the mental phenomenon of Nibbāna is found apart from form, so too in your view, is it appropriate to say that the person is found apart from form? Furthermore, just as it is appropriate to say "Form is in feeling, form is in consciousness" by way of the support of mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), so too in your view, is it appropriate to say that the person is found? In all inquiries, the rejection by the Paravādī is due to the fear of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) and contradiction with their own doctrine. The remaining meaning here in this four-fold comparison is clear.

In terms of the Dhamma, among the fifty-seven real and ultimate things, by applying the four-fold method to each (such as person in form, person in feeling, etc.), five hundred and twenty-eight five-fold refutations (nigga-pañcaka) have been shown by way of refutation. On the side of the Paravādī, the same number of five-fold rejoinders (paṭikamma-pañcaka) have been shown by way of response. In this Paravādī's side, when it is said "The person exists," the Sakavādī's acceptance is an acceptance by way of convention (saṃmuti) as found in the Suttas. The rejection in problems such as "Is form the person?" is the Sakavādī's rejection because the problem of identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is to be set aside. The Paravādī's further clarification is said to be only in connection with the six-fold argument (chaḷavāda).

## The Comparison by the Four-fold Method is finished.

## The Discourse on Comparison is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Logic of Characteristics

Now follows what is called the "Discourse on the Logic of Characteristics" (Lakkhaṇayutti-kathā). In that discourse, setting aside Nibbāna, the remaining real and ultimate things are called "with cause" (sappaccaya) because they are connected to causes such as kamma. They are called "conditioned" (saṅkhata) because they are made by the coming together of causes. They are called "not eternal" (assassata) because they do not exist forever, as they perish after arising. They are called "with a sign" (sanimitta) because they have a sign, which is the cause of their arising. Nibbāna, because it lacks the aforementioned qualities, is "without cause" (appaccaya), "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata), "eternal" (sassata), and "without a sign" (animitta). This is the characteristic of a real and ultimate thing.

Therefore, if the person is also a real and ultimate thing, that person must also be endowed with these characteristics. With this in mind, the eight inquiries such as "Is the person with cause?" are the Sakavādī's questions, and they are rejected by the Paravādī. Here, the words "Understand the refutation" (ājānāhi niggahaṃ) and so forth are shown in brief. Thus, on the side of the Sakavādī, among the positive and negative (anuloma-paccanīka) arguments, eight five-fold sets (pañcaka) should be understood by way of the positive only.

On the side of the Paravādī, among the negative and positive (paccanīka-anuloma) arguments, there are only eight five-fold sets by way of the negative only. There, on the side of the Paravādī, the Paravādī has established conventional truth (saṃmuti-sacca) by way of the Suttas; and for convention...
124:
On the side of the opponent, in the negative-positive (paccanīkānuloma) section, only the eight groups by way of the negative (paccanīka) should be understood. That opponent has established conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) by the power of suttas such as 'There is a person' (Atthi puggalo). In conventional designation (sammuti-paññatti), there is no such nature as being with cause (sappaccaya) and so on. Therefore, because there is no such thing as being with cause in conventional designation, the refutation by the proponent (Sakavādī) is only by way of the actual nature (yāthāvato). All the statements that the opponent should say by way of the six-fold argument (chalavāda), such as 'Acknowledge the rebuttal' (Ājānāhi paṭikammaṃ), are presented here in brief only.

## The Explanation of the Argument from Characteristics is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Purification of Terms

55-59. Now comes the purification of terms (vacanasodhana). In that discussion on the purification of terms, the question 'Is a person perceived? Is that which is perceived a person?' is the question of the proponent (Sakavādī) to purify the statement 'A person is perceived' (Puggalo upalabbhati). The meaning of that question is: Are these two terms, 'person' (puggalo) and 'perceived' (upalabbhati), identical in meaning or different in meaning? If they are different in meaning, it would imply that the person is one thing and being perceived is another, just as matter (rūpa) is distinct from feeling (vedanā). If they are identical in meaning, it would imply that whatever meaning is 'person', that very meaning is 'perceived', just as consciousness (citta) is indeed the mind (mano). Therefore, I say to you, opponent: 'If your person is perceived, then it would imply that whatever is perceived is a person. Do you accept this identity of meaning between person and being perceived?'

Then the personalist (Puggalavādī), while desiring that the person is perceived by wisdom, does not desire that perceived things like matter (rūpa) are the person. Therefore, he says, 'A person is perceived; among perceived things, some are the person and some are not,' and so on. The meaning of that statement is: My person is perceived because of the word of the Teacher, 'There is a person' (Atthi puggalo). However, not everything that is perceived is a person; rather, some things are the person and some are not. In that phrase 'kehici', the word 'ke' is in the sense of 'ko', and the word 'hi' is merely a particle. 'Some is the person, some is not the person' is the meaning here.

This is what is meant: Both the person and things like matter (rūpa) are perceived as some kind of unspecified phenomena. Among those perceived phenomena, only the person is called the person. Among things like matter, not even a single phenomenon is the person. Following that, the proponent says to that opponent: 'Is the person perceived by way of some things and not perceived by way of others?' The meaning of that statement is: If the two terms 'puggalo' and 'upalabbhati' are identical in meaning, then if the phenomenon admitted as 'perceived' is not different from the person, yet if some perception is the person and some perception is not the person...
125:
"Is it the case that some person is perceived by you and some is not perceived? Do you accept this meaning?" When asked thus, the Paravādin rejects it saying "Not so" (na hevaṃ), because he does not desire the non-perception of the person. From here on, everything beginning with "Acknowledge the refutation" is abbreviated. It should be understood in detail. The same method applies to "A person has a real sense" (saccikaṭṭha), etc. All these terms are merely synonyms of "is perceived" (upalabbhati). Furthermore, since the affirmation "A person is perceived in a real and ultimate sense" is the thesis of the Personalist (Puggalavādin), just as he holds the view "A person is perceived," it follows that he also holds the view "A person has a real sense." The Personalist's view "A person exists" (atthi) is just a synonym for the term "existing" (vijjamāna). Therefore, all these words have been cleared.

In that section (of clearing terms), regarding the statement at the end, "A person exists; not every existing thing is a person," etc., this is the intended meaning: The statement made by the Paravādin, "A person exists; for some, there is a person, for some, there is no person," means in essence only this: "A person exists; not every existing thing is a person." Therefore, the Sakavādin, having made him accept that, now cross-examines him thus: "You have taken the view 'A person exists' based on the mere statement 'There is a person who practices for his own benefit.' Just as the Blessed One taught that statement, He also taught 'No person' by the method beginning with 'Mogharāja, always mindful, regard the world as empty' (Sn 1125). Therefore, just as you hold the view 'A person exists; not every existing thing is a person,' it also follows that 'A person does not exist; not every non-existing thing is a person.' Do you accept this meaning?" Then, not wishing to accept it, he rejects it saying "Not so." The rest of the procedure for refutation, etc., should be understood in the same way as already stated.

## The Explanation of the Clearing of Terms (Vacanasodhana-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Inquiry into Designation (Paññattānuyoga-vaṇṇanā)

61-66. Now, there is what is called the inquiry into designation. In the fine-material realm (rūpa-dhātu), the Personalist designates a person as having form (rūpī); likewise, in the immaterial realm (arūpa-dhātu), as being formless (arūpī). To break that view of his, all the questions belong to the Sakavādin, while the affirmation and rejection are the business of the other, the Paravādin.
126:
It is the admission of the other (the opponent/Paravādī). When it is said, "One having form (rūpī)," that opponent admits it both because of the actual existence of the physical body (rūpakāya) and because of the existence of the designation (the name 'rūpī') based on such form. When it is said, "One having sensual desire (kāmī)," he rejects it both because of the existence of Arahants who are free from lust (in the sense-sphere) and because of the non-existence of the designation (the name 'kāmī') based on such sensual desire. Even when it is said, "One without form (arūpī)," he admits it both because of the actual existence of the formless aggregates (arūpakkhandha) and because of the existence of the designation (the name 'arūpī') based on such formless aggregates. In both methods, the term "being" (satta) is used as a synonym for "person" (puggala).

Now, since that opponent desires to hold that in the passage where "one who contemplates the body in the body (kāye kāyānupassī)" occurs, the body is one thing and the person is another, the question of the proponent (Sakavādī) arises as "Is it the body? Is it the physical frame (sarīra)?" and so on, in order to break that view. In that question, "making the body appiya (applied)" means asking by making the body applied to, attached to, brought into a state of unity with, and inseparable from (the physical frame). "Esese" means "Is this (body) that very (physical frame)?" There is also a variant reading "ese ese." It means "Is this that very one?" "Ekaṭṭhe" means "Does it have the same meaning?" "Same samabhāge tajjāte" means "Is it equal? Does it have an equal part? Is it of that nature?" Here, there is a difference only in words. In terms of meaning, however, it asks, "Is this physical frame the body itself?" The opponent, not seeing any difference (between body and physical frame), admits, "Yes (āmantā)." The same method applies to the questions "Is it a person? Is it a soul (jīva)?" and so on. However, when asked, "Is the body something else?" he admits it because he holds such a view due to the teaching on the contemplation of the body. But when asked, "Is the soul something else?" he denies it, being unable to reject the Sutta directly spoken (by the Buddha). After that, the phrases such as "Acknowledge the refutation (niggaha)" are quite clear in meaning.

On the side of the opponent, when asked, "Is the body one thing and the person another?" the proponent (Sakavādī) rejects it because it is an undeclared question (ṭhapanīyapañhā) that should be set aside. The opponent then performs a cross-examination through sophistry (chala). That point is also clear in meaning.

## The Explanation of the Application of Designations is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Application of Destinations (Gati)

69-72. Now, there is the examination of death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi) by way of the change in destinations (gati). In that application of destinations, because the Personalist (Puggalavādī) holds the view that "the person wanders" based on Suttas such as "That person, having wandered and transmigrated for seven times at most...", the question "Does one wander?" and so on is the question of the proponent (Sakavādī) to break that view. Therein, "wanders (sandhāvati)" means transmigrates or performs the act of going and coming in saṃsāra. The admission based on his own view is the admission of the opponent. The examinations such as "That person..." are also the questions of the proponent, and the rejection is that of the other (the opponent).
127:
The opponent speaks thus. Therefore, to break the view of that opponent, the question beginning with "sandhāvati" is the question of the proponent (Sakavādī). In that question, "sandhāvati" means going continuously from one existence to another, or performing the act of going and coming. The admission based on his own view is the admission of the opponent. The examinations such as "That person (so puggala)" are also the questions of the proponent, while the rejection is the rejection by the other, the opponent. In that context, "so" means "that very person." The opponent, when thus questioned, rejects it out of fear of falling into the view of Eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). When asked, "Is it another?" he rejects it out of fear of Annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi). When asked, "Is it both that person and another?" he rejects it out of fear of Partial Eternalism (ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi). When asked, "Is it neither that person nor another?" he rejects it out of fear of the view of Eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhi). Furthermore, when all four questions are asked together, he rejects them out of fear of all four views; then, wishing to show the Suttas upon which his view is based, he says, "Therefore, the person wanders (tena hi puggalo sandhāvati)," and so on.

Again, when the proponent asks with the intention, "This one who wanders according to your view, is he the very same one in this world and the next?" and fixes it as "that very one (sveva)," the opponent rejects it out of fear of Eternalism. When asked again firmly in the same manner, he admits it because that person is indeed himself and not any other nature, and also because there is a Sutta stating, "He, having passed away from there, was reborn here," and so on. When asked, "Is he that very same human?" he rejects it because a human cannot (remain) a human when becoming a deva.

When asked again, he admits it by the power of the Sutta such as, "At that time, I was the teacher named Sunetta." Then, the proponent, wanting to reveal that the opponent's statement is false because of the difference between the rebirths of devas and humans, says, "Having been a human (manusso hutvā)," and so on.

In that passage, "hevaṃ maraṇaṃ na hehiti" means "if it were so, death would no longer exist." From this point onwards, the variation in the examination according to the difference in individual existence (attabhāva) such as "yakkha, peta," and so on should be understood.

The terms such as "khattiya" (warrior-noble) are spoken by way of caste (jāti) as well as by way of physical defects and so on.
128:
When the Paravādī asks, "Should it not be said that 'that very person transmigrates'?", the Sakavādī gives the first admission because a person stationed in this world cannot go to the next world by way of rebirth-linking. The second admission is also that of the Sakavādī, because a Sotāpanna does not abandon the state of a Sotāpanna even in another life. The statement beginning with "Hañci" belongs to the Paravādī.

The Sakavādī again investigates by questioning, showing that one born in the deva world no longer possesses the state of a human.

Following that, in the phrase "not another, not distinct," "not another" means being identical in every aspect. "Not distinct" means not being distinct even by a single aspect. Because one born in the deva world no longer has the state of a human, it is said, "It should not be said so."

When questioned firmly again, he admits according to his own view that "that very person transmigrates." The words beginning with "one with severed hands" are spoken to destroy the view that "one transmigrates without being distinct" by showing the loss of physical aspects. In that context, "one with severed hands" refers to one whose thumbs or big toes are severed. "One with severed tendons" refers to one whose major tendons are severed.

In the problems beginning with "together with form," in the first question, he rejects it referring to the fact that there is no going along with this physical body (rūpakāya). In the second question, he admits it referring to the person in the intermediate state (antarābhava). According to that opponent's view, that person in the intermediate state goes with the same form and enters the mother's womb. Thereafter, that form breaks up. When asking, "Is that soul the same as that body?", since he goes together with the body called form, the question is whether that form itself is the soul, or that soul itself is the body. The Paravādī rejects this because the body is discarded in this life and because it contradicts the Suttas.

In the problems beginning with "together with feeling," he rejects it referring to birth in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), and admits it referring to birth in other realms. When asking, "Is that soul the same as that body?", since he goes together with the body called feeling and so on, the question is whether that feeling itself is the soul, or that soul itself is the body. In this view, all five aggregates are intended as the "body" (sarīra). The Paravādī rejects this because it contradicts the Suttas.

In the problems beginning with "formless," in the first question, he rejects it referring to the intermediate state. In the second question, he admits it referring to one being born from the formless realm into a realm with form. As for "another soul"...
129:
He asks: "Having abandoned that body known as form, one transmigrates formless; in that case, is your body one thing and the life-principle (jīva) another?" The other (the opponent) rejects it because it contradicts the Suttas.

In the problems beginning with "without feeling" (avedana), he rejects it with reference to the realm of perception (saññībhava), and admits it with reference to rebirth in the non-percipient realm (asaññasatta) and the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). He asks: "Having abandoned that body known as feeling and so on, one transmigrates without feeling and without consciousness; in that case, is your body one thing and the life-principle another?" The other rejects it because it contradicts the Suttas.

In the problems beginning with "form transmigrates," a person is designated depending on the aggregates such as form; he asks: "When that person transmigrates, does that form also transmigrate?" The opponent rejects it because the Suttas state only that "beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving transmigrate and wander on," thus speaking only of the transmigration of a being. When asked again, he admits it with the notion that since there is no person apart from the phenomena of form and so on, if that person transmigrates, that form must also transmigrate. The same method applies to feeling and so on.

In the problems beginning with "form does not transmigrate," since according to your view form is not the person and only that person transmigrates, the question is: "Does your form not transmigrate?" The other rejects it with the notion that when a person transmigrates, the form which is the object of clinging (upādāna) cannot transmigrate. When asked again, he admits it because of the statement that only beings transmigrate. The remaining explanations here are clear.

The meaning of the verses (gāthā) is as follows: According to the venerable one's view, just as a shadow exists depending on a tree, and just as fire exists depending on fuel, a person exists depending on the aggregates. If, while there is no transmigration of form and so on, that person of yours perishes when those phenomena of the aggregates break up, then you would fall into the view of annihilation (ucchedadiṭṭhi), which is an unwholesome view avoided by the Blessed One. He shows: "We do not mean the annihilation spoken of figuratively as 'The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist.'" Furthermore, if that person does not perish even when those phenomena of the aggregates break up, then the person would be an eternal person (sassata-puggalā). Consequently, that person would be exactly equal to Nibbāna. Just as Nibbāna is neither produced nor destroyed, so too your person would be exactly equal to Nibbāna.
130:
(Because of the permanence of the person, that person would be extremely similar to Nibbāna.) "Samasamo" means extremely similar, or similar by way of equality, or similar only by way of equality. Just as Nibbāna does not arise and does not break up, so too your (the Paravādin's) person would be extremely similar to that Nibbāna.

## The investigation of death and rebirth by way of the change of destination (gati) is finished.

## Explanation of the Investigation (Anuyoga-vaṇṇanā).

## 12. Explanation of the Investigation of Designation by Attachment (Upādā-paññatta-anuyoga-vaṇṇanā)

Now is the investigation of designation by attachment. In that investigation, the question is by the Sakavādin, and the acceptance and rejection are the answers of the Paravādin. That Paravādin desires the designation, the making known, the understanding of a person based on form (rūpa) etc., just as a shadow depends on a tree, or fire depends on fuel. Therefore, when asked "Based on form (is the person designated)?", he accepts. Again, just as a shadow based on a tree has the nature of impermanence etc. like the tree, and fire based on fuel has the nature of impermanence like the fuel, so too, when asked this meaning: "Is the person based on form etc. impermanent like form etc.?", he stands by his own view and rejects it.

In the problems such as "A blue person based on blue form", he rejects it because he does not desire the identity of the person with the blue form, nor the plurality of the person by way of the many blue forms in a single body.

In the problem "Wholesome feeling" (kusala-vedanā), he also rejects it because he does not desire the identity of the person with the feeling, nor the plurality of the person by way of the many wholesome feelings in a single continuity. In the second method, because of the existence of expressions such as "a person skilled in the path", he accepts it referring to the sense of being skilled (cheka). When asked problems such as "a person with fruit", he rejects it because such a conventional expression does not exist.

On the unwholesome side, he accepts it referring to the sense of being unskilled (acheka).

On the indeterminate side, he accepts it referring to the indeterminate state by way of permanence (sassata) etc. The remaining meaning here should be understood in the same way as mentioned below.
131:
In the problems such as "Based on the eye" (cakkhuṃ upādāya), he accepts because of the clear existence of conventional expressions such as "Just as a person with eyes avoids uneven objects... so should one avoid evil deeds" (Udāna 43). He rejects it because he does not desire the cessation of the person through the cessation of the eye-faculty etc.

In the phrase "Based on form, based on feeling", other dyads, triads, and tetrads rooted in form apart from feeling should also be understood. Since the person is designated based on the aggregates (khandhas), he accepts the designation based on two, three, four, or five aggregates. However, he rejects it because two or five (aggregates) cannot exist simultaneously in a single continuity. The same method applies to the sense bases (āyatanas) etc.

Now, to show that just as a designated object (shadow, fire) is impermanent and distinct because the object it depends on (tree, fuel) is impermanent, so it follows for that person, (the Sakavādin) says "Just as a tree" (yathā rukkhaṃ) etc. There, "upādāya" means depending on, having come to, not excluding that (form etc.). The Paravādin, not desiring that (impermanence and distinctness of the person), stands by his view and rejects it.

"Nigala" means an iron shackle. "Negalika" means a person bound by that iron shackle. In the Pali "To whom there is form, he is one having form"—just as the shackle is not the person having the shackle, and the shackle is distinct from the shackled person, so too form is not the one having form, and form is distinct from the one having form.

In the problems such as "In mind, in mind" (citte citte), he accepts by way of the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā), referring to the state of having lust etc. by way of the different minds having lust etc. When asked by the method "It arises" (jāyati) etc., he rejects it because he does not desire the momentary (khaṇika) nature of the person arising and passing away at every moment. When asked "Is it the same person?" or "Is it another?", he rejects it out of fear of the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) and the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). Again, when asked "Should one say 'a young boy' or 'a young girl'?", he accepts that "it should be said" out of fear that worldly convention (loka-vohāra) would be destroyed. The remaining meanings here are clear.

Now, the Paravādin, wishing to establish his view in another way, says "It should not be said that a person is found" etc. There, "It should not be said" means: "What is the use of this extensive investigation of designation by attachment to you (Sakavādin)? First answer this question: Should it not be said that 'a person is found in the sense of a real and ultimate fact'?" When the Sakavādin answers "Yes (āmantā)" to that question, the Paravādin says again "He who sees" etc. There, "He (yo)" refers to the person.
132:
"The person" refers to the individual. "The object" refers to the visible form. "By which means" refers to the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). "That person" refers to the individual. "That object" refers to the visible form. "By that means" refers to the eye-sensitivity. This statement means: "Does not the person who sees a certain form with a certain eye-sensitivity become the person who sees that form with that eye-sensitivity?" Even if the Sakavādī (the proponent of the orthodox view) truly holds that only the eye-sensitivity, which serves as the physical basis for eye-consciousness, sees the form—and likewise, only the ear-sensitivity hears the sound, only the nose-sensitivity smells the odor, only the tongue-sensitivity tastes the flavor, only the body-sensitivity feels the touch, and only the mind-consciousness cognizes the mental object—he nevertheless admits "Yes" (āmantā) by way of conventional designation (sammuti-paññatti), such as in the expression: "The Arahant has an eye; the Arahant sees the form with the eye."

After this admission, the Paravādī (the opponent), having established the validity of speaking about a person based on the sixfold discourse, turns that very doctrine around and asserts, "A person is found," and so forth. In that statement, "one who does not see" refers to the blind, the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), those born in the formless realm (arūpabhūmi), and those who have entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Even for one who is not blind, they are said to "not see" at times other than when they are actually seeing. The same method applies to the remaining sections. The rest of the sequence of words should be understood according to the Pali text in terms of its meaning.

In the problem of "Comparison with the Suttas" (Sutta-saṃsandana), it is said that "one sees the form" because the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) has the visible form as its domain. In the second section, it is said that "one sees the person" because of the teaching, "I see beings." In the third section, it is said that "one sees both" because of the view that "having seen the form, one discerns the person." Since among the fourfold collection of the seen (diṭṭha), the heard (suta), the sensed (muta), and the cognized (viññāta), only the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is included as the object to be seen, the Sakavādī investigates by asking: "Is the form the person? Is the person the form? Are both the form?" The meaning of this inquiry is quite clear.

## Description of the Inquiry into Derived Designation (Upādā-paññatta-anuyoga-vaṇṇanā)

## 13. Description of the Inquiry into Human Agency (Purisakāra-anuyoga-vaṇṇanā)

Now follows the inquiry into human agency. Therein, the question asked with the view that "if there is an action (kamma), there must necessarily be a doer (kāraka) of that action" is the question of the Paravādī. The admission that such actions exist is the admission of the Sakavādī. Again, the question "Is there a doer (kattā) and an instigator (kāretā)?" is the question of the Paravādī. Therein, "doer" refers to the one who performs those actions himself. "Instigator" refers to the one who causes the action to be done through means such as commanding or teaching. Now...
133:
Because the Paravādī asks "Is there a doer (kattā)?" by referring to a person and not merely to the act of doing, the Sakavādī rejects it. 124. In the phrase "Is there a doer or an instigator of that person?", the meaning is: if a certain (wholesome or unwholesome) kamma is found, and a person who performs that kamma is also found, then is another person found who is the doer and instigator of that person as well? The Paravādī, not desiring such an infinite regress, rejects this due to the fear of falling into the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord (issara-nimmāna-vāda). 125. When questioned again, he admits it by referring to this sense: because parents bring a person into being, give them a name, and nurture them, the parents are called the "doers" (kattā) for that person. And those spiritual friends (kalyāṇa-mitta) or teachers who train him in various branches of knowledge and arts are called the "instigators" (kāretā). (In reality), only past kamma should be considered both the doer and the instigator of that person.

By the phrase "of that one, and of that one alone," he asks this: if there is a doer of the doer of actions, and a doer of that one, and a doer of that one, then the preceding person must necessarily be made by the succeeding person. Thus, according to your view, this person who performs the kamma would be made by another person in the future, and that one by another; consequently, there would be no making an end of suffering, no cutting off of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and no Nibbāna without conditions (appaccaya-parinibbāna). That Nibbāna which was taught (by the Buddha) as the absence of suffering—which is bound to causes—due to the absence of causes (kamma), would not exist according to your view. Alternatively, "of that one, and of that one alone" means: if kamma is not merely kamma, but there is a person who is the doer of that kamma, and a doer of him, and a doer of him, thus creating a lineage of persons, then the making an end of suffering by preventing the occurrence of the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa), as taught (by the Buddha), would not be possible. The Paravādī, not desiring this consequence, rejects it. In other general inquiries about the "doer" where the term "is found" is used, the terms "doer" and "instigator" are stated with reference only to a person, not to a cause (paccaya). It is not that causes do not exist for the great earth and so forth (they certainly do exist).

135. The question "Is the doer of wholesome and unwholesome kammas another?" is rejected due to the fear of the wrong view (diṭṭhi) such as "the self possesses formations (saṅkhāra)." 136. The passage beginning with "A result (vipāka) is found" was spoken (by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa) to refute the view of the Paravādī who wishes to demonstrate the existence of a person by way of an experiencer of results (vipāka-paṭisaṃvedī). Therein, the inquiry "Is there an experiencer of results?" is the opponent's investigation. The Sakavādī rejects it because there is no experiencer other than the occurrence of the result itself. 137. The further questioning is by the Sakavādī, and the admission is by the Paravādī. "An experiencer of that one" refers to one who experiences the person who experiences the result. This is because that which is experienced is indeed the result (vipāka).
134: The Sakavādin rejects the proposition because there is no experiencer other than the arising of the result. The Sakavādin asks again, and the other, the Paravādin, concedes. 'Tassa paṭisaṃvedī' means the one who experiences that result. In reality, that which is to be experienced is only the result (vipāka), and a person (puggala) is not the result. Therefore, the Paravādin rejects it. When asked again, because one stands in the result of merit, the person experiencing the result kisses and embraces a son, a husband, a mother, or a wife. Therefore, referring to such experience, the Paravādin concedes. 'Tassa tasseva' means: if the result were not merely the result but there were a person who experiences that result, then there would be a succession of persons—an experiencer of that one, and an experiencer of that one, and so on. If this were so, the teaching on the ending of suffering through the non-occurrence of the round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa) would be impossible. From here on, in the questions regarding the experiencer (paṭisaṃvedī) by way of similarity to the word 'upalabbhati' (is found), the meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated below. The question 'Is another the experiencer of the results of good and bad deeds?' is rejected due to the fear of the wrong view such as 'the self possesses feeling' (vedanavantam attānaṃ). The passage beginning with 'Dibbaṃ sukhaṃ' (divine happiness) is started by way of classifying the results of good and bad deeds. All of that should be understood in the same manner as stated below. Here, it should be understood that the Sakavādin's rejection of the experiencer is only by way of the person (puggala), not by way of the feeling (vedanā) that experiences. Indeed, the arising of feelings that experience by making the great earth etc. an object is not prohibited. The passage beginning with 'The doer, the one who causes to do, the experiencer of the result' is started by way of the mixed method (vōmissakanaya). There, 'he does' means: regarding the person whom you, the Paravādin, call the doer and the experiencer, does that same person act, and does that same person experience? This is the Sakavādin's inquiry, which the Paravādin rejects for fear of contradicting the Suttas.
135: When asked again by way of the Sutta beginning with 'Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices' (Dhammapada 18), the Paravādin concedes that it is the same person. Then, the Sakavādin, wishing to block the Paravādin's opportunity for speech, says: 'Is pleasure and pain self-created (sayaṃkata)?' In that context, the statement 'another does it' is said by way of inquiring into the difference between the doer and the experiencer. Thereafter, the Paravādin rejects it for fear of contradicting the Suttas, but when asked again, thinking 'having acted as a human, one experiences as a deity,' he concedes. To the Paravādin who speaks thus, it follows that 'pleasure and pain are created by another (paraṃkata)'; when asked by way of that, he rejects it again. The statement 'he and another' is said by way of inquiring into the identity and difference of the doer and the experiencer. Thereafter, the Paravādin rejects it for fear of contradicting the Suttas, but when asked again, he concedes by combining both previous methods. To the Paravādin who speaks thus, it follows that 'pleasure and pain are both self-created and created by another'; when asked by way of that, he rejects it again. The statement 'neither does he do it' is said by way of rejecting both the identity and difference of the doer and the experiencer. Thereafter, the Paravādin rejects it for fear of contradicting the Suttas, but when asked again, thinking 'a human, having performed a deed for rebirth in the deva world, does not experience it as a human, nor does another than the doer experience it; therefore, the experiencer is neither that doer nor another,' he concedes. Is this not merely a wrong view? To the Paravādin who speaks thus, it follows that 'pleasure and pain are not self-created, nor created by another, but arise fortuitously (adhiccasamuppanna)'; when asked by way of that, he rejects it again. Furthermore, in this mixed method (vōmissakanaya), from the beginning, the meaning should be understood in this way: because this Puggalavādin desires both a doer and an experiencer of deeds, he faces this dilemma: 'Should the one who is the doer be the same as the experiencer, or should it be another, or should it be both, or should it be neither?' The Sakavādin, inquiring into this very dilemma, states all four alternatives beginning with 'he does.' The rest is as already explained. At the conclusion, all four questions are asked together. There, the rejection, the concession, and the falling into faults such as 'self-created' should be understood according to the previous method.
136:
Following this problem, without mentioning the words "kalyāṇapāpakāni," the methods already stated below have been shown through the alternative (vikappa) such as "kammaṃ atthi" (kamma exists). The meaning of those problems should also be understood by the same method stated below.

## Purisakarānuyogavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Inquiry into Human Effort)
## The name Kalyāṇavagga is also the name of this very Purisakarānuyoga.
## 14. Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Inquiry into Higher Knowledge)
Following this Purisakarānuyoga, the accomplishment of the fruit of Arahantship occurs by means of the inquiry into higher knowledge (abhiññā) and so forth. In that Abhiññānuyoga, when the Sakavādī (proponent) has accepted with "Āmantā" (Yes), the Paravādī (opponent), thinking that "There is no attainment of the distinction of psychic powers (iddhividha) and so forth in external, non-sentient matter (anindriyabaddha-rūpa); it exists only in internal, sentient matter (indriyabaddha-rūpa); therefore, there must be a person who brings about such powers," says the statement beginning with "Is it not that some person can perform psychic transformations?" All those statements have an obvious meaning.

## Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā
## 15-18. Ñātakānuyogādivaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Inquiry into Relatives, etc.)
Now is the section for inquiring into relatives (ñātaka) beginning with "mātā" (mother). The section for inquiring into caste (jāti) beginning with "khattiyo" (warrior-noble). The section for inquiring into practice (paṭipatti) as "gahatṭho pabbajito" (householder or renunciant). The section for inquiring into rebirth (upapatti) as "devo manusso" (deva or human). The section for inquiring into penetration (paṭivedha) beginning with "sotāpanno" (stream-enterer) is also called "Ariyānuyoga" (Inquiry into the Noble Ones). All those inquiries have an obvious meaning. However, the problem "Having been an Arahant, is one not an Arahant?" is not stated here because it is a futile question (moghapañhā).

The passage beginning with "cattāro purisayugā" (four pairs of men) is the inquiry into the Saṅgha (Saṅghānuyoga). That Saṅghānuyoga also has an obvious meaning.

The passage beginning with "saṅkhato" (conditioned) is the inquiry into the nature of the ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭhasabhāvānuyoga). In that inquiry, the question "tatiyā koṭī" (the third point) is the question of the Sakavādī. Because such an ultimate reality does not exist, the Paravādī rejects it. When asked again, the acceptance with reference to a person is the acceptance of that very Paravādī.
137:
211. In the problem "Is the person other (than the aggregates)?", the Paravādī himself rejects it because he does not desire the person to be something different from the conditioned aggregates.

212. The passage beginning with "The aggregates are conditioned" was spoken (by Elder Moggaliputtatissa) for the purpose of asking about the distinctness of the person by showing the conditioned and the unconditioned in their true nature.
