213. The passage beginning with "Matter is conditioned" was spoken for the purpose of asking about the distinctness of the person by showing the aggregates through their divisions.

214. The question "Is there the arising of a person?" is the question of the Sakavādī, and the Paravādī accepts it by the power of the Sutta passage beginning with "Beings are of the nature to be reborn, of the nature to grow old, and also of the nature to die." However, the Paravādī does not desire the conditioned status of that person; therefore, he rejects it.

215. Again, when asked by the method beginning with "The arising is not perceived," the Paravādī accepts that the arising and so forth of a person are not appropriate because of the scriptural words beginning with "Only suffering arises, suffering stands, and passes away."

216. In the word "atthatthami," "attha" refers to Nibbāna. The Sakavādī asks whether (the person) exists in that Nibbāna. Because of the existence of that person in Nibbāna, the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) would follow; because of non-existence, the view of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) would follow. The Paravādī, not desiring either of those two views, subsequently rejects it.

## 19. Paṭivedhānuyogādivaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Inquiry into Penetration, etc.)

217. In the problem "depending on existence (bhava)," "bhava" refers to rebirth-process existence (upapattibhava).

218. In the problem "while experiencing feeling (vedanā)," only the practitioner (yogāvacara) who has discerned feeling through insight-knowledge knows when feeling is experienced; the foolish worldling (bālaputhujjana) does not know.

224. The problems such as the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā) and so forth have an obvious meaning.
138:
In the verse from the Pārāyana section, "Look upon the world as empty" means look upon the world of aggregates by way of emptiness of a being. The question "Does the person look?" is the question of the Sakavādī. This is because the Paravādī holds the view that whoever looks in the verse "Look upon the world as empty" is a person; therefore, the Sakavādī asks him thus. "Together with form" means together with the physical body (rūpakāya). It means looking without having emerged from that form. Having accepted this by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra), when asked again "Is that the soul (jīva)?", he rejects it for fear of contradicting the Suttas. "Without form" means having accepted this by way of the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra), when asked again "Is it another soul?", he rejects it for the same fear of contradicting the Suttas. The terms "having entered within" and "having gone outside" are descriptive terms for what was stated below as "together with form" and "without form." Therein, "having entered within" means having gone inside the form, remaining within the limits of form without emerging from this side or that side. "Having gone out" means having transcended the limits of form, looking without depending on form.

"Anattā" (non-self) means being devoid of a self, a soul, or a person. It means that even in a single phenomenon (dhamma), there is no person. Thus, the meaning of all Suttas should be understood according to the method stated in the Agamatthakathās (Commentaries). Here, however, I shall state only the meaning intended (sandhāyabhāsita).

The passage "ghee-pot" (sappikumbha) and so forth spoken by the Blessed One is brought forward to show that "The meaning of all teachings should not be taken solely by the power of the literal words as they are heard." For example, just as a pot made of gold, being a modification of gold, is called a "gold-pot" (suvaṇṇakumbha), there is no such thing as a "ghee-pot" which is a modification of ghee made by taking ghee. But the pot in which ghee is placed is called a "ghee-pot"; this is the meaning here. The same method applies to oil-pots and so forth. And just as Nibbāna is permanent and stable, there is no such permanent meal (bhatta) or gruel (yāgu). However, without making a time limit, by way of the designation of a duty established as "We shall give day after day," it is called "permanent meal" (niccabhatta) or "constant gruel" (dhuvayāgu); this is the meaning here. In the passages such as "There is a person who practices for his own benefit," just as phenomena like form exist by way of their individual characteristics (paccattalakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), it is not so...
139:
Regarding 'person' (puggala): when form and so forth exist, the usage 'such a name, such a clan' occurs. Thus, by means of this worldly usage, worldly convention (sammuti), and worldly language (nirutti), the meaning 'a person exists' is intended here. In this regard, the Blessed One also said: 'Citta, these are worldly names, worldly languages, worldly usages, and worldly designations.' However, phenomena such as form and so forth are said to 'exist' because they are made known through their specific characteristics (paccatta-lakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa), without depending on worldly convention.

The Buddhas have two types of discourse (kathā): conventional discourse (sammuti-kathā) and ultimate discourse (paramattha-kathā). Therein, conventional discourse refers to the teaching of 'being', 'person', 'deity', 'brahma', and so forth. Ultimate discourse refers to the teaching of 'impermanence', 'suffering', 'non-self', 'aggregates', 'elements', 'bases', 'foundations of mindfulness', 'right efforts', and so forth.

Among these two types of discourse, if a person is able to understand the meaning, penetrate the Four Noble Truths, escape from the round of rebirths, and seize the banner of Arahantship when taught through conventional teaching as 'being'... 'brahma', the Blessed One teaches him from the beginning using terms like 'being', 'person', 'man', 'deity', or 'brahma'. If a person is able to understand, penetrate, escape, and seize the banner of Arahantship upon hearing any one of the ultimate teachings such as 'impermanence' or 'suffering', He teaches him one of those ultimate teachings like 'impermanence'. Likewise, for a being who would understand through conventional discourse, He does not first teach ultimate discourse; rather, after making him understand through conventional discourse, He later teaches ultimate discourse. For a being who would understand through ultimate discourse, He does not first teach conventional discourse; rather, after making him understand through ultimate discourse, He later teaches conventional discourse. By nature, if He were to teach ultimate discourse first, the teaching would appear harsh (lūkha). Therefore, the Buddhas first teach conventional discourse and later teach ultimate discourse. Even when they teach conventional discourse, they speak only the truth, the actual nature, and not falsehood. Even when they teach ultimate discourse, they speak only the truth, the actual nature, and not falsehood. For it is said:

'The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.'

(The Blessed One, the most excellent among speakers, taught two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth; a third truth cannot be found.)

Among these two truths, worldly convention is true because it is the cause of non-deviation (in meaning), and thus the symbolic language recognized by the world is true. Ultimate speech is also true because it makes known the actual characteristics of ultimate realities. Alternatively, the Blessed One's teaching is twofold: ultimate teaching by way of aggregates and so forth, and conventional teaching by way of 'a pot of ghee' and so forth. Indeed, the Blessed One does not override common designation (samaññā). Therefore, one should not form a dogmatic adherence (abhinivesa) merely from the words 'a person exists'. In truth, the Teacher has shown the ultimate truth without overstepping designation. Therefore, another wise person, when making known the ultimate truth, should not override common designation. It should be understood that the meaning of the remaining words is clear in all the Pali texts.
140:
Among these two truths, symbolic speech (saṅketa-vacana), which expresses the meaning recognized in the world, is true because worldly convention is the cause of non-deviation. Ultimate speech (paramattha-vacana), which expresses the ultimate, is also true because it is the mark of knowing the actual nature of phenomena.

Alternatively, the Blessed One's teaching is twofold: ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā) by way of aggregates and so forth, and conventional teaching (sammuti-desanā) by way of 'a pot of ghee' and so forth. The Blessed One does not override the common designation recognized equally by all people. Therefore, one should not form a dogmatic adherence merely from the words 'a person exists'. For the Blessed One has taught:

'Without overstepping designation, the ultimate truth is made known.
Therefore, another wise person should not override common designation;
When making known the ultimate truth, one should not override common designation.'

The meanings of all the remaining terms are clear in all places.

## The Discussion on the Person (Puggalakathā) is concluded.
141:
## 2. Parihānikathā
## 1. Vādayuttiparihāni-vaṇṇanā

Now follows the Discussion on Falling Away (Parihānikathā). Regarding the nature of falling away and the nature of not falling away, based on Suttas such as: "Monks, these two things lead to the falling away of a monk who is a trainee (sekha)" and "Monks, these five things lead to the falling away of a monk who is temporarily liberated (samayavimutta)," the Sammitiya, Vajjiputtaka, and Sabbatthivāda schools, as well as some members of the Mahāsaṅghika school, hold the view that even an Arahant can fall away (from the fruit of Arahantship). Therefore, to refute the views of these schools or others who hold such an opinion, the Sakavādin asks: "Does an Arahant fall away from Arahantship?"

In that question, "falling away" (parihāna) is of two kinds: falling away from what has been attained (patta-parihāni) and falling away from what has not yet been attained (appatta-parihāni).

Among these two, the statement: "Venerable Godhika fell away from that temporary liberation of mind (jhāna-samāpatti) for the second time," is called falling away from what has been attained (patta-parihāni). The statement: "May the benefit of recluseship of the virtuous not fall away from you who desire the benefit of recluseship," is called falling away from what has not yet been attained (appatta-parihāni). Among these two, falling away from what has been attained (patta-parihāni) is intended here. With this intention, the Paravādin affirms, "Yes (Āmantā)."

In our own school (Sakasamaya), this falling away from what has been attained is accepted only regarding mundane attainments (lokiya-samāpatti), and not regarding the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) such as Arahantship. In the opponent's school (Parasamaya), they do not accept that falling away in all fruits of recluseship, in all planes of existence, at all times, or for all persons. Since that is merely their own view, the teaching was expanded using the method starting with "Everywhere? (Sabbattha)" and so on, in order to break the entire web of their views.

In that context, because the Paravādin does not accept the falling away of an Arahant who has gradually fallen away and stands in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), but only accepts it for an Arahant standing in the higher fruits; and because they do not accept the falling away of an Arahant standing in the fine-material (rūpa) and immaterial (arūpa) planes, but only accept it for an Arahant standing in the sense-sphere plane (kāma-bhava) due to the presence of things leading to decline such as delight in work (kammārāmatā), they reject the question when asked, "Everywhere?"

When asked again firmly, they affirm it with reference to the sense-sphere plane. This is because in the entire sense-sphere plane, there are sensual pleasures that cause falling away; therefore, it is the Paravādin's view that one can fall away in that sense-sphere plane.

In the third question, the term "falling away" is used to ask about the causes that lead to falling away. In that question, the causes of falling away are things like delight in work (kammārāmatā), or specifically, sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (byāpāda). Since these things do not exist in the fine-material and immaterial planes, the Paravādin rejects it, saying, "It should not be said thus."

The question "Always? (Sabbadā)" asks about the time of falling away. Among those questions, in the first problem, the Paravādin rejects it because there is no falling away during the time of wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). In the second problem, they affirm it because during unwise reflection (ayoniso manasikāra), one can fall away at all times, whether by night or by day. In the third problem, when there is a conjunction with the causes of falling away, falling away occurs only for a moment. Therefore, considering that there is no falling away for an Arahant who has not yet fallen away before that conjunction, or for one who has already fallen away, the Paravādin rejects it... of the Arahant.
142:
In the third question, "Does an Arahant fall away everywhere?", the term "falling away" is used (by the Sakavādin) to ask about the causes that lead to falling away. In that question, because the causes of falling away are things like delight in work (kammārāmatā) and so on, or specifically, only sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (byāpāda), and since these things do not exist in the fine-material and immaterial planes, the Paravādin rejects it, saying, "It should not be said thus."

The question "Always?" (Sabbadā) is a question about the time of falling away. Among those questions of time, in the first problem, the Paravādin rejects it because there is no falling away from the fruit of Arahantship during the time of wise reflection. In the second problem, the Paravādin affirms it because an Arahant who practices unwise reflection can fall away at all times, whether by night or by day. In the third problem, when there is a conjunction with the causes of falling away, falling away occurs only for a moment. Thinking that there is no such thing as falling away for an Arahant who has not yet fallen away before such conjunction, nor for an Arahant who has already fallen away, the Paravādin rejects it.

Among the problems "Is it all Arahants?", in the first problem, the Paravādin rejects it with reference to Arahants with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya). In the second problem, they affirm it with reference to Arahants with dull faculties (mudindriya). In the third problem, only those with sharp faculties are intended. This is because it is the view of that Paravādin that falling away does not occur for all those with sharp faculties.

In the section illustrating with the example of a banker (seṭṭhi), the first question is the Paravādin's question, and the second is the Sakavādin's question. The meaning in those questions is as follows: "When an Arahant falls away from the fruit of Arahantship, does he fall away from all four fruits?"—this is what you Sakavādins ask me, the Paravādin. In that matter, I ask you in return: "When a banker who has achieved the status of a banker with four hundred thousand falls away from one hundred thousand, has he fallen away from the status of a banker?"—this is the Paravādin's counter-question.

Then, when the Sakavādin says "Yes" with reference to a partial falling away, the Paravādin asks again, "Has he fallen away from all his wealth?" Since he has not fallen away from all his wealth, the Sakavādin says, "It is not so." After that, the Sakavādin asks the Paravādin, who holds the view that "Just like this example, an Arahant can fall away from the fruit of Arahantship but not from all four fruits," the second possible problem.

The Paravādin, not seeing the fixed rule that there is no falling away from the status of a banker, affirms it (that one can fall away from being a banker). Then, when asked if an Arahant can fall away from all four fruits, the Paravādin takes the meaning of the scriptural statement "Niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo" (Assured, bound for enlightenment) in an improper way and, standing by his own view, rejects it (the falling away from all four fruits) with the intention that there can be no falling away from the fruit of Stream-entry. However, it should be noted that this view is merely the view of that Paravādin.

## Thus ends the Logic of the Argument (Vādayutti).
143:
## 2. Exposition on the Falling Away by Comparison of Noble Persons

Now, the comparison of Noble Persons (ariyapuggala-saṃsandanā) is begun. In this examination, some desire the falling away from the fruit of Arahantship for the Arahant only; some for the Non-returner (anāgāmī) as well; and some for the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) as well. However, regarding the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), all schools do not desire the possibility of falling away. Those who desire the falling away of those who, having fallen from the fruit of Arahantship, remain in the state of a Non-returner or a Once-returner, do not desire the falling away of other ordinary Non-returners or Once-returners. Since even they do not desire the falling away of a Stream-enterer in any way, the question is posed by way of ellipsis (peyyāla). In that question, the affirmation (paṭiññā) and denial (paṭikkhepa) should be understood according to their respective views. In the problem, "Does a Non-returner fall away from the fruit of Non-returning?", the denial is according to those who do not desire the falling away of a Non-returner. The affirmation is according to those who desire the falling away of either a natural Non-returner or a Non-returner who remains after falling from the fruit of Arahantship; this is the opening method (nayamukha) here. Following this method, all ellipses should be understood according to their meaning.

As for the statement made here, "Immediately after the fruit of Stream-entry, does one realize the fruit of Arahantship?", this is said with reference to the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship by one who, having fallen from it, strives again. The other [the opponent] denies it because there is no immediate attainment of the fruit of Arahantship following the fruit of Stream-entry.

Thereafter, in order to investigate sequentially by way of "Would this so-called falling away be due to the weakness of the abandonment of defilements, or due to the lack of intensity in the development of the path (magga-bhāvanā) etc., or due to the non-seeing of the truths?", it is said, "In whom are more defilements abandoned?" and so forth. All these words have an obvious meaning. The meaning of the Sutta texts, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Agama Commentaries (āgama-aṭṭhakathā).

In the statement, "The samayavimutta Arahant falls away from the fruit of Arahantship," their view is that one with dull faculties (mudindriya) is called 'samayavimutta' (temporarily liberated), and one with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya) is called 'asamayavimutta' (irreversibly liberated). But in our own view (saka-vāda), a Jhana-attainer who has not yet reached mastery (vasībhāva) is called 'samayavimutta', while a Jhana-attainer who has reached mastery and all Noble Persons are called 'asamayavimutta' in regard to Noble Liberation (ariya-vimokkha). That opponent, taking his own view, says, "The samayavimutta Arahant can fall away from the fruit of Arahantship; the asamayavimutta Arahant, other than the samayavimutta, cannot fall away." The remaining words in this Ariyapuggala-saṃsandana-parihāni-kathā are clear.

The Exposition on the Falling Away by Comparison of Noble Persons is finished.

## 3. Exposition on Falling Away Proven by Suttas
265. Now, after having set forth the Ariyapuggala-saṃsandana-parihāni-kathā, there will be the discourse on proving by Suttas (sutta-sādhana). In that Sutta-sādhana-kathā, "uccāvacā" means high and low, by way of the distinction between noble practice and base practice...
144:
"The samayavimutta Arahant can fall away from the fruit of Arahantship; the other, the asamayavimutta, cannot fall away," he says. The remaining words here have an obvious meaning.

## Exposition on the Falling Away by Comparison of Noble Persons.

## 3. Exposition on Falling Away Proven by Suttas.

Now is the discourse on proving by Suttas (sutta-sādhana). In that Sutta-sādhana-kathā, "uccāvacā" refers to practices that are both high and low, by way of the distinction between noble and base practices. "Paṭipādā" means practices. "Samaṇena pakāsitā" means revealed by the Buddha, the Ascetic who has stilled all defilements. Indeed, the practice that is pleasant (sukha-paṭipadā) and of quick intuition (khippābhiññā) is high. The practice that is painful (dukkha-paṭipadā) and of slow intuition (dandhābhiññā) is low. The remaining two practices are high in one factor and low in another. Alternatively, only the practice mentioned first is high, and the other three are low. By that practice, whether high or low, they do not go to the further shore—Nibbāna—twice; the meaning is that they do not go to Nibbāna twice by a single path. Why? Because the defilements that have been abandoned by a certain path do not need to be abandoned again by that same path. By this, the absence of things that lead to falling away is shown. "Nayidaṃ ekaguṇaṃ mutaṃ" means that the further shore, Nibbāna, is not fit to be touched only once. Why? Because all defilements cannot be abandoned by a single path. By this, it is shown that the fruit of Arahantship cannot occur by a single path alone.

"Atthi chinnassa chediyaṃ" means, "Is there anything further to be cut in the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa) that has already been cut?" Thus he asks. The other, the opponent, denies it with reference to an Arahant with sharp faculties, and when asked again, affirms it with reference to an Arahant with dull faculties. The proponent (sakavādī), citing a Sutta, shows the non-existence of such a thing. In that Sutta, "oghapāsa" means the flood of defilements and the snare of defilements.

"Katassa paṭicayo" means the repeated development of a path already developed. Here too, the denials and affirmations should be understood according to the previous method.

"Parihānāya saṃvattanti" means that in the Sutta cited by the opponent, the five things lead to falling away from states not yet attained and from mundane attainments (lokiya-samāpatti). But that opponent perceives it as falling away from the attained fruit of Arahantship. Because of that very misconception, he says, "The Arahant has delight in activity (kammārāmatā)." The other opponent also...
145:
The opponent (paravādī) denies with reference to the asamayavimutta Arahant and admits with reference to the other, the samayavimutta Arahant. Or, he denies that Arahant who exists by the power of sensual lust (kāmarāga) and admits that Arahant who exists in another way. However, when asked about the existence of lust and so forth, the opponent is no longer able to admit it.

In the term "pariyuṭṭhita", it means: by what state is one completely obsessed, pursued, or overwhelmed (and thus falls away)? In the question regarding underlying tendencies (anusaya), the denial and admission should be understood only by the power of those with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya) and dull faculties (mudindriya). Or, he admits by merely using the word "good underlying tendency" (kalyāṇānusaya) due to the similarity of the term "anusaya". The statement "lust increases" is made by the proponent (sakavādī) with reference to the lust that has been abandoned by the development (bhāvanā) of the higher path. The same method applies to the subsequent mentions of hatred and delusion. However, since personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so forth have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) which first realizes the Four Noble Truths, their further increase is not desired. In all sections, the remaining words have clear meanings.

## Parihānikathā niṭṭhitā.
146:
## 3. Brahmacariyakathā
## 1. Suddhabrahmacariyakathāvaṇṇanā
Now follows the Discussion on the Holy Life (Brahmacariyakathā). In this discussion, there are two types of living the holy life (brahmacariyavāsa): the cultivation of the Path (maggabhāvanā) and renunciation (pabbajjā). Renunciation does not exist among any of the devas. As for the cultivation of the Path, it is not prohibited among the remaining devas, excluding the unconscious beings (asaññasatta).

In this discussion, the question "It does not exist among devas" is the question of the Sakavādin, referring to the Paravādins such as the Sammitiyas who do not accept even the cultivation of the Path among the devas higher than the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. Relying on this Sutta: "Monks, in three respects the people of Jambudīpa excel those of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa devas. What are the three? They are courageous, they are mindful, and the holy life is lived here [in Jambudīpa]," the admission that "Both types of living the holy life do not exist among devas" is the admission of the Paravādin based on their arisen view.

Furthermore, the question "Are all devas deaf and dumb?" solely due to the nature of states that obstruct both types of the holy life is the question of the Sakavādin. In that question, "hatthasaṃvācika" refers to those who speak with hand gestures like mutes. Thereafter, the question "It exists among devas" is the question of the Paravādin, and the admission referring to the cultivation of the Path is the admission of the Sakavādin. The further inquiry by way of renunciation, without noting the meaning of the admission, is the question of the Paravādin.

In the problem "Where renunciation does not exist," the rejection referring to the attainment of the Path by laypeople and some devas is the rejection of that Paravādin. Again, when questioned, the admission referring to the people of the border regions and the unconscious beings is the admission of that Paravādin. In questions such as "One who renounces," etc., the method should be understood in this same way. Furthermore, in the problem "It exists among devas," the admission of the Sakavādin refers only to the cultivation of the Path; when it is said "Among all devas?", the rejection referring to the unconscious beings is the rejection of that Sakavādin.

In the two problems "Among humans?", the admission referring to the people of Jambudīpa and the rejection referring to the people of the border regions should be understood. "It exists where it exists" means those devas exist, or that place exists, where it exists; thus, the explanation starting with the classification of beings and regions is the explanation of the Sakavādin. In this way, all intermediate questions should be understood.
147:
In investigating the arising of the fruit (phaluppatti) through the Sutta, the question "Where does the fruit arise?" is the proponent's question as to where the arising of the fruit of Arahantship occurs for that Non-returner (anāgāmī). "In that very place" means in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).

"Handa hi" is a particle used in the sense of a reason. This is what is meant: Since the Non-returner realizes the fruit in those Pure Abodes by the path developed in this world, and does not further develop another path in that realm, therefore, there is no living of the holy life among the devas.

## 2. Saṃsandanabrahmacariyavaṇṇanā

Now, to show that if the realization of the fruit in another realm is possible by the path developed in a different realm, it should also be possible for Stream-enterers and others, the proponent asks the comparative question starting with "Anāgāmī". In that question, the opponent's view is to admit the realization of the fruit for the Non-returner and to deny the realization of the fruit for the remaining persons. For the Non-returner who has developed the path here is called "one who has finished by leaving this realm" (idhavihāyaniṭṭho). Having developed the path of non-returning here, based on the statement "He is of spontaneous birth and attains Nibbāna there," the opponent holds the view that "he realizes the fruit of Arahantship by the power of rebirth alone, without further development of the path." However, since Stream-enterers and Once-returners develop the path in that realm and are those who are reborn there, they do not return here. Thus, when asked about the Non-returner's realization of the fruit, the opponent admits it, but denies it for the others.

In the problem "The Non-returner by the path developed in that realm...", he denies it because of the view that "for the Non-returner, there is no more development of the path in that realm." The question "The path is developed, yet the defilements are not yet abandoned" is the proponent's question, and the other (opponent) admits it with reference to the path of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacaramagga). For by the fine-material sphere path, that person has become "one who has finished by leaving this realm".

In the problem "Has the Non-returner done what was to be done?", he admits it with reference to the Non-returner's completion of tasks through rebirth itself, based on the statement "He is of spontaneous birth and attains Nibbāna there." In the problem "Is he an Arahant?", he denies it with reference to the Arahant who attains Nibbāna here. When asked again, he admits it with reference to the one who attains Nibbāna there.

In the problems such as "Does the Arahant have further rebirth?", the meaning should be understood only with reference to those who attain Nibbāna there and those who attain Nibbāna here. When asked, "Does he attain Nibbāna there without having penetrated the fruit of Arahantship?"...
148:
If asked, desiring the penetration of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) of that Non-returner (Anāgāmī) through the Path (Magga) developed only in this sensual realm (kāmabhūmi), the opponent (Paravādī) denies it.

The first example, "like a beast," is the opponent's example, and the second example is the proponent's (Sakavādī). The remaining words have clear meanings in all places.

## The Discussion on the Holy Life (Brahmacariyakathā) is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discussion on "In Parts" (Odhisokathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now comes the Odhisokathā. Therein, for those like the current Sammitiya sect who desire the abandonment of defilements (kilesa) in parts (odhiso)—by way of various realizations (abhisamaya) of the Four Truths such as the seeing of suffering (dukkha) by Stream-winners (Sotāpanna) and so on—the question "In parts?" is asked by the proponent to refute that doctrine, and the opponent's answer is an affirmation. Again, the further investigation is the proponent's question, and the opponent's denial is because the state of being a Stream-winner and so on does not exist in parts. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections (vāra).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on "In Parts" is finished.

## 4. Discussion on "Abandoning" (Jahatikathā)

## 1. Explanation of the Discussion on the Citation of Suttas

Now comes the Jahatikathā. Therein, for those like the current Sammitiya sect who hold the view: "A worldling (puthujjana) who has attained jhāna becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) simultaneously with the penetration of the Truths; for that person, sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (byāpāda) have already been abandoned even during the stage of a worldling," the question "Does a worldling abandon?" is asked by the proponent to refute that doctrine. The opponent's affirmation is because they do not see the arising of those defilements that have been suppressed (vikkhambhita) by jhāna. Because those defilements suppressed by jhāna [are abandoned] only by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimagga)...
149:
...there is final abandonment. Therefore, the proponent further investigates with "Finally?" and so on. Since there is no such abandonment [at that stage], the opponent denies it. The question "Does he suppress?" is asked by the proponent referring only to final suppression (vikkhambhana). After that, there is a comparison between the one standing on the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimaggaṭṭha) and a worldling. That meaning is clear.

Thereafter, when asked "Does he stand in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala)?", the opponent affirms, referring to the state of a Non-returner through jhāna. When asked "Does he stand in the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala)?", he denies it because there is no abandonment of the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) by the Path of Seeing (dassanamagga).

When asked "Does he develop the three paths simultaneously (without before or after)?", he denies it because there is no such development (bhāvanā). When asked again, he affirms, referring to the completion of the function (kicca) of the three paths (the abandonment of defilements). The same method applies to the questions on the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). When asked "By which path?", he says "By the Path of Non-returning," referring to the state of a Non-returner through jhāna. Again, when asked about the abandonment of fetters (saṃyojana), he denies it because those three defilements (sakkāyadiṭṭhi, etc.) should not be abandoned by the Path of Non-returning. When asked a second time, he affirms, referring to the first path (Sotāpattimagga) being the path of a Non-returner through jhāna. The remaining meanings here are clear.

## Discussion on "Abandoning" (Jahatikathā).

## 5. Discussion on "Everything Exists" (Sabbamatthītikathā)

## 1. Explanation of the Logical Arguments (Vādayutti-vaṇṇanā)

Now comes the Sabbamatthītikathā. Therein, for those like the current Sarvāstivādins (Sabbamatthivādī) who hold the view: "Because of the word, 'Whatever form (rūpa) is past, future, or present... this is called the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha),' all things with distinctions such as past and so on do not abandon their nature as aggregates; therefore, everything truly exists," the proponent asks "Does everything exist?" to purify their doctrine. Standing on the aforementioned view, the opponent affirms. "In every way" (sabbathā) asks if everything exists in the entire body. "At all times" (sabbadā) asks if everything exists at all times. "Entirely in every respect" (sabbena sabbaṃ) asks if everything exists in every mode. "In all things" (sabbesu) asks if everything exists in all phenomena.
150:
Ayoga means unsuitability (impropriety). Indeed, union (yoga) can only occur between things of different natures, not of a single nature. Thus, in this problem, the proponent asks "Does everything exist?" by making form (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā) identical in characteristic, without distinction. By the question "Does that which does not exist also exist?", he asks if something like a sixth aggregate or a rabbit's horn, which is clearly non-existent, also exists in the opponent's doctrine. He asks if it exists in your system in this way: "Is the view 'Everything exists' a wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) because it is untrue, and is our view a right view (sammādiṭṭhi) because it is true?" The other (the opponent) denies it because existence in the manner described does not exist in all these methods. In all these methods, the entire course of the discussion should be understood in detail starting from "Acknowledge the refutation" (ājānāhi niggahaṃ). This is the logical argument (vādayutti) for investigating the suitability of the doctrine in this Sabbamatthītikathā.

## 2. Explanation of the Comparison of Times (Kālasaṃsandana-vaṇṇanā)

283-284. Now comes the comparison of times (kālasaṃsandana) stating "The past exists." In that comparison of times, "The past exists" and so on is the pure comparison (suddhika-saṃsandana) without involving aggregates. "Past form exists" and so on is the comparison of times by way of aggregates (khandha-vasena).

"Having applied the present form" means setting aside the past and future form and making only the present form undivided and unified. In the question "Does it abandon the nature of form?", he denies it because even the ceased form is included in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). In the inverse question "It does not abandon the nature of form," he affirms because it is indeed grasped by the aggregate of form. In this context of "Having applied the white cloth," although not all cloth is white, when the proponent said "Having applied the white cloth" instead of just "cloth," the opponent accepted the identity of meaning. In the question "Does it abandon the white nature?", the proponent affirms, referring to the disappearance of the color. In the question "Does it abandon the nature of cloth?", however, he denies it because the designation (paññatti) of cloth has not disappeared. The same method applies to the inverse question.

When asked "Does the past not abandon its past-ness?", he affirms, thinking "If it were to abandon it, it would become future or present." But when asked "Does the future not abandon its future-ness?", [he thinks] "If it does not abandon it..."
151:
If the future state were to abandon its nature as future, it would remain only as future; it would not be able to reach the state of the present—thinking thus, he rejects it. In the problem of the present as well, he rejects it, thinking that there would be the fault of not reaching the state of the past. In the conformable problems (anuloma-pañha) as well, the meaning should be understood in this very way.

Having thus stated the method of pure comparison of time, the Buddha spoke of 'past matter' (atītaṃ rūpaṃ) and so forth to show it again by way of the aggregates (khandha). All of that can be known only according to the sequence of the Pali text.

## Vacanasodhana-vaṇṇanā

Now, there is the purification of words (vacanasodhana) such as 'the past does not exist.' In that purification of words, 'the past does not exist' means: if the past state does not exist. The statement 'the past exists' is false; the statement that it is both past and currently existing is indeed false. When asked whether that very future state is the present, he rejects it due to the difference in time, intending that its state as present does not exist at the very moment it is future.

When asked a second time, he acknowledges it because it is present at the time it has arisen, which was future before its arising. In the phrase 'having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes' (hutvā hoti, hutvā hoti), by the power of your view which says 'having been future, it becomes present,' it is said 'having been either future or present, it becomes.' Does that state also, according to your wish, 'having been, become'? The other (the opponent/Paravādī) rejects it, saying 'It is not so,' because a state that has already been does not become again.

When asked a second time, since that future state, in becoming present, comes to be designated as 'having been, it becomes,' he acknowledges it. Then the Sakavādī asks the question 'not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become' with the intention: 'If, according to your wish, that future state, in becoming present, comes to be designated as "having been, it becomes" and then becomes again; if there were a rabbit's horn which, not being future and not becoming present, comes to be designated as "not having been, it does not become," does that rabbit's horn also, for you, again not having been, not become?' The other (the opponent) rejects it, thinking: 'Let that which does not exist, because of its very non-existence, be called "not having been, it does not become" in the sense that not having been future, it does not become present; but how could there be for that rabbit's horn the state of "again not having been, not becoming"?' In the problem of whether that very present state is the past, he also rejects it due to the difference in time, intending that its state as past does not exist at the very moment it is present.
152:
When asked in the second problem, the opponent acknowledges it because that very state which was present before reaching the state of the past has indeed become past. Regarding 'having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes,' you, the opponent, who say 'having been present, it becomes past,' mean by the power of the view 'that very state is present, that very state is past' that 'having been either present or past, it becomes.' Does that state also, according to your wish, 'having been, become'? (The Sakavādī asks). Another opponent rejects it, saying 'It is not so,' because a state that has already been does not occur again.

In the second problem, since that state, in being present and becoming past, comes to be designated as 'having been, it becomes,' he acknowledges it. Then the Sakavādī asks the question 'not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become' with the intention: 'If, according to your wish, that very state, in being present and becoming past, comes to be designated as "having been, it becomes" and then becomes again; if there were a rabbit's horn which, not being present and not becoming past, comes to be designated as "not having been, it does not become," does that rabbit's horn also, for you, again not having been, not become?' Another opponent rejects it, thinking: 'Let it be that a non-existent thing, because of its very non-existence, is called "not having been, it does not become" in the sense that not being present, it does not become past; however, how could the state of "again not having been, not becoming" exist for that rabbit's horn?' In the third problem, where both (present and past) are brought together, the application of the meaning of terms should be made in this very way.

Another method: If that very state is future and that very state is present, then the state of 'hoti' (is/becomes) as stated in the present would apply to the future state, and the state of 'hutvā' (having been) as stated in the future would apply to the present state. If this were so, the future would also be called 'having been, it becomes.' The present would also be called 'having been, it becomes.' Therefore, we ask you: 'According to your wish, does either one of these, the future or the present, "having been, become; having been, become"?' The other opponent rejects it by the same method used in the problem 'that very state is future, that very state is present,' and when asked again, he acknowledges it by the same method used in the second problem. Then the Sakavādī, in connection with the problem 'that very state is future, that very state is present,' reverses the previously rejected question and asks the opponent who acknowledges each of those future and present states as 'having been, it becomes,' by asking 'not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become?' The meaning of that question is: 'When it was said by you "that very state is future, that very state is present," did you not, in rejecting the first problem, reject the state of "hoti" (is/becomes) for the future and the state of "hutvā" (having been) for the present? Therefore, the future state is called "does not become" (na hoti), and the present state is called "not having been" (na hutvā).'
153:
In the second problem also, it has been admitted that that very future phenomenon is that very present phenomenon. If this is so, the future phenomenon is also called 'not having been, it does not become.' The present phenomenon is also called 'not having been, it does not become.' Therefore, I ask you, Paravādī— "According to your view, is each of these future and present phenomena called 'not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become'?" The Paravādī, like one enveloped in darkness on all sides, not seeing the state of 'not having been, it does not become' of those phenomena, denies it, saying "It is not so."

In the second round also, if that very present phenomenon were that very past phenomenon, the 'state of becoming' (hoti-bhāva) said of the present in the past, and the 'state of having been' (hutvā-bhāva) said of the past in the present, would occur. If this is so, the present phenomenon is also called 'having been, it becomes,' and the past phenomenon is also called 'having been, it becomes.' Therefore, I ask you, Paravādī— "According to your view, is each of these present and past phenomena called 'having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes'?" Another Paravādī, having denied it by the same method used in the problem "that very present is that very past," when asked again, admits it by the same method admitted in the second problem. Then the Sakavādī, wishing to ask by reversing the previously denied problem to the Paravādī who is admitting that each of those phenomena is 'having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes' by the power of the problem "that very present is that very past," asks, "Not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become?"

The meaning of that question is— "When you said 'that very present is that very past,' by denying the first problem, was not the 'state of becoming' of the present and the 'state of having been' of the past denied? Therefore, the present is called 'does not become,' and the past is called 'has not been.'"

In the second problem also, you have admitted that 'that very present is that very past.' If this is so, the present is also called 'not having been, it does not become,' and the past is also called 'not having been, it does not become.' Therefore, I ask you, Paravādī— 'According to your view, is each of these phenomena called "not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become"?' The Paravādī, like one enveloped in darkness on all sides, not seeing the state of 'not having been, it does not become' of those phenomena, denies it, saying 'It is not so.'

In the third round also, if that very future were that very present and that very past, the 'state of becoming' said of the future and present in the present and past, and the 'state of having been' said of the present and past in the future and present, would occur. If this is so, the future is also called 'having been, it becomes.' Both the present and the past are also called 'having been, it becomes.' Therefore, I ask you, Paravādī— 'According to your view, is each of these three phenomena called "having been, it becomes..."'
154:
"...having been, it becomes"? Another person (Paravādī), having denied it by the same method used in the problem "that very future is that very present, that very present is that very past," when asked again, admits it by the same method admitted in the second problem. Then the Sakavādī, wishing to ask by reversing the previously denied problem to that person who is admitting each of those phenomena as "having been, it becomes; having been, it becomes" by the power of the problem "that very future is that very present, that very present is that very past," asks, "Not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become?" The meaning of that problem is— "When it is said 'that very future is that very present, that very present is that very past,' you who deny the first problem, have you not denied the state of becoming of the future and present, and the state of having been of the present and past? Therefore, the future and present are called 'do not become.' The present and past are also called 'have not been.'" In the second problem also, you have admitted that "that very future is that very present, that very present is that very past." If this is so, the future is also called 'not having been, it does not become,' and both the present and the past are also called 'not having been, it does not become.' Therefore, I ask you— "Is each of these phenomena called 'not having been, it does not become; not having been, it does not become'?" The Paravādī, like one enveloped in darkness on all sides, not seeing the state of 'not having been, it does not become' of those phenomena, denies it, saying "It is not so." In this explanation of the purification of terms, the refutations (niggaha) and so forth should be applied in the same manner as stated below.

## The Commentary on the Purification of Terms (Vacanasodhana-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Past Eye, Forms, etc. (Atītacakkhurūpādikathāvaṇṇanā)

In the problems such as "The past eye exists," he admits the state of existence because of not abandoning the nature of the eye and so forth. But when asked problems such as "Does it see?", he denies it because of the absence of the function of seeing and so forth of that eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) and so forth.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Past Knowledge, etc. (Atītañāṇādikathāvaṇṇanā)

In the problem "Does one perform the function of knowledge with that knowledge?", he denies it because he does not see the existence of the function of that knowledge, as that knowledge has ceased (niruddha). When asked again, the present knowledge which has a past object, because of knowing past phenomena, [is called] past...
155:
Knowledge, in a metaphorical sense, refers to present knowledge being designated as "past knowledge," and because that knowledge performs the function of knowledge, it is affirmed. At that time, the Sakavādī, without giving the Paravādī an opportunity for metaphorical expression, says, "Does one fully understand suffering with that knowledge?" and so forth. The other Paravādī rejects this because the four functions, such as fully understanding the truth of suffering, do not exist in that present knowledge which has a past object. The same method applies to the questions regarding the future. The questions concerning the present and those involving comparison are of clear meaning.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Arahants, etc.

In the questions such as "Does an Arahant have past lust?", the opponent affirms (with "Āmantā") because the state of lust and so forth [as past events] is not discarded. In questions such as "Is an Arahant possessed of lust?", the opponent rejects it out of fear of contradicting the Suttas and fear of contradicting logic.

## Commentary on the Purification of Terms

Having understood all the Pali according to the sequence of the text, the meaning of the passage "It exists; it may be past, it may be not past" should be understood thus: That which is only past is called "past." That which is present or future exists, but it is not called "past." Therefore, "the past is not the past, and the not-past is the past" means that for that reason, what is called past is [in another sense] not past, and what is not called past is [in another sense] past. The same method applies to the questions regarding the future and the present.

## Commentary on Establishing by Sutta

In the statement establishing by Sutta that "It should not be said that the past exists or the future exists," the question is that of the Paravādī, and the affirmation is that of the Sakavādī. Again, relying on his own doctrine, the inquiry "Bhikkhus, whatever form..." and so forth is the questioning of the Paravādī alone. In the second method, the question is that of the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is that of the other Paravādī. Thus, the question and affirmation should be understood in all places. As for the statement presented by the Paravādī to establish the existence of the future, "Bhikkhus, if there is [lust] for edible food..." at the end of the Sutta, "there is the production of renewed existence in the future," and so forth, that does not [prove] the future's...
156: This statement is not a proof that establishes the manifest existence of future phenomena. This is because it was taught in that Sutta with reference to the fact that the result will definitely arise because the causes have been completed. This is the intended meaning of the Sutta. The remaining words have clear meanings in all places. ## The Commentary on the Discourse 'Everything Exists' (Sabbamatthītikathā) is finished. ## 6. Atītakkhandhādikathā ## 1. Commentary on the Discourse without Sutta Evidence (Nasuttasādhana) Now, the discourse beginning with 'The past is an aggregate' (Atītaṃ khandhā) occurs. Therein, the question of the Paravādī, who desires the existence of the past and future because they do not abandon the state of being aggregates and so on, is 'Is the past an aggregate?'. The affirmation 'Yes' is the response of the Sakavādī, because the past is included within the aggregates. Again, the question 'Does the past not exist?' is the question of the Paravādī. The rejection of this is the response of the Sakavādī, because the manifest existence of that past is prohibited by the Niruttipathasutta. In the questions regarding the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), in the problems concerning the future, in the problems that come by way of direct and reverse order (anuloma-paṭiloma) in comparison with the present, and in the problems beginning with 'Is the past matter (rūpa)?', the meaning should be understood in this very same way. ## 2. Commentary on the Sutta Evidence (Suttasādhana) In the section on Sutta evidence, the question 'Should it not be said?' is the question of the Sakavādī. Therein, in the phrase 'nathi cetete', the meaning is 'these phenomena also do not exist'. The affirmation 'Yes' is the response of the Paravādī, who does not desire non-existence while the state of being aggregates and so on exists. Then, the citing of the Sutta to prove the non-existence of those phenomena is the work of the Sakavādī. The second question is also the question of the Paravādī, the affirmation is the response of the Sakavādī, and the citing of the Sutta is the work of the Paravādī. However, that Sutta only proves for them the state of being aggregates and so on, but does not prove manifest existence; therefore, even though it is cited, it is as if it were not presented. ## The Commentary on the Discourse beginning with 'The past is an aggregate' is finished.
157:
## 7. Ekaccaṃatthītikathā
## 1. Atītādi-ekaccakathāvaṇṇanā

Now follows the discourse on "Some Exist" (Ekaccaṃatthītikathā). In this discourse, for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of the opponents such as the Kassapikas, who hold the view that "some past [phenomena] exist," the Proponent (Saka-vādī) asks the question, "Does the past exist?" and the Opponent (Para-vādī) answers, "Some exist."

The intended meaning is: Kamma that has not yet produced its result (unripened) exists; kamma that has already produced its result (ripened) does not exist. The Proponent further inquires, "Have some ceased?" The meaning of this question is: If, according to your wish, some past phenomena exist and some do not, then it follows as a logical consequence that some past phenomena have ceased while others have not ceased and remain as they are. The same method applies to terms such as "vanished" (vigata) and so on.

The statement "Some phenomena whose results have not yet ripened exist" is spoken by the Opponent to challenge the Proponent, because they desire the existence of those phenomena whose results have not yet ripened, and those phenomena are also indeed past. The statement "phenomena whose results have ripened" is spoken to challenge based on those phenomena which the Opponent desires to be non-existent. The statement "phenomena without results" (avippāka) is spoken to challenge based on indeterminate (abyākata) phenomena. Thus, by means of these three groups, the affirmation and negation in all direct and reverse questions should be understood.

"Past phenomena are partly those whose results have ripened and partly those whose results have not yet ripened" refers to phenomena whose results are in progress (vippakatavipāka). Indeed, the kamma that has produced rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) also has life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and death (cuti) as its results. Therefore, from rebirth-linking until death, that kamma is called "result in progress" (vippakatavipāka). This statement is made with reference to phenomena of such nature.

Thinking that "they will produce results," the Proponent asks, "Do those phenomena exist?" Just as a person who is a "bearer of the Dhamma" (dhammadhara) is said to "have" many teachings even while sleeping, the Opponent affirms the existence with reference to worldly usage. Thinking that "they will produce results," in the second question "Are they present?", the Opponent affirms by standing on the view that "there is a certain formation (saṅkhāra) called the accumulation of kamma (kammūpacaya), which is described as the non-destruction of kammas."

In problems such as "the future exists," the Proponent speaks of phenomena that will definitely occur. In all problems, the remaining text has a clear meaning according to the method already stated above.

The explanation of the discourse on "Some Exist" (Ekaccaṃatthītikathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.
158:
## 2. Anāgatādi-ekaccakathāvaṇṇanā

Regarding problems such as "the future exists" (anāgataṃ atthi), the Proponent speaks of "some exist" (ekaccaṃ atthi) with reference to phenomena that will definitely arise. In all problems, the remaining meaning is very clear as it follows the method already stated below.

## Ekaccaṃatthītikathāvaṇṇanā.

## 8. Satipaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Now follows the discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānakathā). In that discourse, following the method taught in the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta: "Monks, I will teach the origin and the cessation of the four foundations of mindfulness," the view that "all phenomena are foundations of mindfulness," taking the objects of mindfulness such as the body and so on, is the view of the Andhakas at present. The Andhaka schools—namely, the Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, Rājagiriyas, and Siddhatthikas—are schools that arose after the Third Council. For the purpose of setting aside and examining their view, there are the Proponent's questions and the Opponent's affirmations.

In the term "satipaṭṭhāna": "Mindfulness is established in these [objects], therefore they are foundations (paṭṭhāna). What is established? Mindfulness. The foundations of mindfulness are satipaṭṭhāna." By this meaning, the objects of mindfulness are also called satipaṭṭhāna. "They are established in the objects, therefore they are the phenomena that establish (paṭṭhāna). What are established? Mindfulnesses. Mindfulnesses themselves are the establishing phenomena, therefore they are satipaṭṭhāna." By this meaning, mindfulnesses themselves are called satipaṭṭhāna. Therefore, both views are suitable in a figurative sense (pariyāyena).

However, those Opponents who, setting aside that figurative sense, say that "all phenomena are absolutely foundations of mindfulness," are the ones to whom the Proponent's questions are directed, and the Opponent affirms based on the sense of the object. When examined with the question "Are all phenomena mindfulness?", the Opponent himself must reject it because the nature of mindfulness does not exist in all phenomena.

In that context, terms such as "leading to destruction" (khayagāmī) and so on are attributes of the Path. Indeed, the Ariyan Path, which is the "sole way" (ekāyanamagga), is called "leading to destruction" because it goes to Nibbāna, which is the destruction of defilements. It is called "leading to enlightenment" (bodhagāmī) because it goes while realizing the Four Noble Truths. It is called "leading to undoing" (apacayagāmī) because it goes while undoing the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Thus, with these terms, the Proponent asks, "According to your wish, do all phenomena have such a nature? Is your sole way the Path?" Terms such as "taintless" (anāsavā) and "not conducive to fetters" (asaṃyojaniyā) are spoken for the purpose of inquiring about the supramundane state. Terms such as "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānussati) are spoken by way of inquiring into the distinction between mundane and supramundane foundations of mindfulness.
159:
The problem beginning with "Is the eye-base a foundation of mindfulness?" is stated by way of inquiry into the distinctions of all phenomena. In that problem as well, there is a rejection by way of mindfulness and an acceptance by way of the object. The meaning in all such problems should be understood in this manner. Since it is established by the Sutta, the meaning is quite clear.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Discourse on "Is it Thus?" (Hevatthikathā)

Now is the time for the Hevatthikathā. In this Hevatthikathā, referring to those who hold the view—such as the various sects of the Andhakas at present—that "All phenomena with distinctions such as the past, etc., exist by way of form, etc.; the past does not exist by way of the future and present, and the future and present do not exist by way of the past, etc.; therefore, all this exists in this way [as form, etc.] and does not exist in that way [as past, etc.]"—the Proponent (Sakavādī) asks, "Does the past exist?" The answer "It exists thus, it does not exist thus" is the reply of the Opponent (Paravādī). In that statement, "heva" means "thus" (eva၁).

Then the Proponent, wishing to ask the Opponent, "If it is your view that a past phenomenon such as form exists thus as form, etc., but does not exist thus as past, etc., then in that case, does that very thing exist, and does that very thing not exist?", says, "It exists thus, it does not exist thus." The Opponent rejects it, referring to its existence by its own nature and its non-existence by that same nature. When asked a second time, he accepts it, referring to its existence by its own nature (as form, etc.) and its non-existence by another nature (as past, etc.). Beyond that, he continues to ask, "Is the sense of existence the sense of non-existence?" or "Is the nature of existence called the nature of non-existence?" The meaning should be understood in all sections (vāra) by this method. At the conclusion, having said, "Therefore, the past exists thus, and does not exist thus," and "Therefore, form exists thus, and does not exist thus," etc., although the Opponent establishes his own view, because it is established through improper reasoning (ayoniso), that view is indeed unestablished.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on "Is it Thus?" is finished.

## The Great Group (Mahāvagga) is finished.
