## 2. The Second Group (Dutiya Vagga)
## 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Assistance by Others (Parũpahārava၁၁anā)

Now the Parũpahārakathā (Discourse on the bringing [of impurity] by others) arises. In that Parũpahārakathā, just like the Pubbaseliya and Aparaseliya sects of the present time, those who see the emission of semen in persons who claim to be Arahants—either those who are over-estimative (adhimānika) thinking they have attained what they have not, or those who are deceitful (kuhaka) claiming Arahantship—think: "Deities belonging to Māra's host bring impure semen and apply it to the body of an Arahant." With reference to them, the question "Does an Arahant have [emission]?" is the Proponent's inquiry, and the acceptance "It exists" is the Opponent's answer. Now, since what is called seminal emission arises from lust (rāga), the inquiry (anuyoga) "Does an Arahant have lust?" is begun. All that text is quite clear in meaning.

In the question "Do deities belonging to Māra's host [bring] their own [semen]?" etc., he [the Opponent] rejects it, saying "Not so," because those deities do not have seminal emission, nor can they take the semen of others and bring it, and furthermore, there is no semen at all in an Arahant.

In the question "Not their own?", he accepts it based on the view that they create it and bring it. In the question "Through the pores?", he rejects it, seeing that there is no bringing through the pores as in the case of ghee or oil.

"Handa hi" is a particle in the sense of determination (vyavasāya). The meaning is that they bring it having made a determination: "We will cause him to have doubt, thinking 'Am I an Arahant or not?'" When asked, "Does an Arahant have doubt?", he [the Opponent] rejects it with reference to the eightfold doubt (vicikicchā). When asked a second time, he accepts it with reference to the lack of certainty regarding the names and clans of men and women.

"Does he have an abode (āsaya)?" asks whether there is a place for that semen to stay, like the place for excrement and urine.

"Sadhamma-kusalassa" refers to an Arahant liberated by wisdom (paā-vimutta) who is skilled only in his own state of Arahantship. "Paradhamma-kusalassa" means [skilled] in something other than his own Dhamma...
161: The term 'skilled in the phenomena of others' (paradhammakusala) is said with reference to an Arahant liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) who is also proficient in the eight mundane attainments other than his own fruition of Arahantship. In this Parūpahārakathā, the remaining meanings of the Pali should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text itself. ## Commentary on the Discourse on Gifts Given by Others (Parūpahārakathā). ## 2-3-4. Commentary on the Discourse on Ignorance, etc. Now, there are three discourses called the Discourse on Ignorance (Aññāṇa), the Discourse on Doubt (Kaṅkhā), and the Discourse on Being Guided by Others (Paravitaraṇa). Therein, those such as the current Pubbaseliyas hold the following views: 'Because Arahants lack the occurrence of knowledge regarding the names and clans of women, men, etc., there is ignorance (aññāṇa); because they cannot reach a conclusion in those very names and clans, there is doubt (kaṅkhā). And because others guide, declare, and inform them of those matters, there is being guided by others (paravitaraṇa) for them.' To break those views of theirs, the question in all three discourses is by the Sakavādī, and the affirmation and rejection are by the other (Paravādī). Therein, in all questions and answers, the meaning should be understood by following the sequence of the Pali text. ## Commentary on the Discourse on Ignorance, etc. ## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Breaking of Speech Now, there is the discourse called the Discourse on the Breaking of Speech (Vacībhedakathā). Therein, those such as the current Pubbaseliyas hold the view: 'For one who has attained the first jhāna at the moment of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), the word "suffering" (dukkha) breaks forth (is uttered).' With reference to them, the question 'Is there breaking of speech for one who has attained?' is asked by the Sakavādī, and the Paravādī affirms it, standing by his view. Again, when asked 'Does it occur in all [existences]?' with reference to the three planes of existence, he rejects it with reference to the formless (arūpa) existence. When asked 'Does it occur at all times?' by way of time, he rejects it with reference to all times of attainment other than the attainment of the first jhāna at the moment of the first path. When asked 'Does it occur to all who have attained?' he rejects it with reference to those who have attained mundane attainments. When asked 'Does it occur in all attainments?' he rejects it with reference to the supramundane jhānas starting from the second jhāna and all mundane attainments.
162:
Kāyabheda (bodily expression) refers to bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) that occurs by way of moving forward and so on. "Those very minds which originate vocal intimation also originate bodily intimation. If that is so, why does bodily expression (kāyabheda) not also occur?" This question is asked for the purpose of objection. The other (the Paravādī) both denies and affirms according to his own view. Now, if that person utters the word "Dukkha" at the moment of the path, should he not also utter words such as "Samudaya" (origin)? Or, if he does not utter that word "Dukkha," should he not also refrain from uttering other words? For the purpose of such objection, the questions beginning with "knowing it as Dukkha" are stated. The other, however, both affirms and denies only according to his own view. Indeed, his view is that one who has attained the supramundane first jhāna contemplates specifically as "Dukkha, Dukkha."

"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to the supramundane knowledge of the Four Truths. "Ear" (sota) means the ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa) by which one hears that sound. "Of the two contacts" refers to ear-contact (sotasamphassa) and mind-contact (manosamphassa).

"Indeed, O friends, it should not be said" means that if there is no vocal expression (vacībheda) for one who has entered any attainment without distinction, then it should not be said without distinction that "there is vocal expression for one who has entered an attainment." The rest of the words in this Vacībhedakathā, along with the establishment by Sutta, have a clear meaning. The opponent cites the Sutta ending with "Ananda, of the Blessed One Sikhī..."; in that Sutta, the very attainment-mind that originates that vocal expression also originates bodily expression. Moreover, that mind is not the supramundane first jhāna mind; therefore, it is said that it does not serve as a valid proof.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Vocal Expression (Vacībhedakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on Uttering 'Dukkha' (Dukkhāhārakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now, it is the Discourse on Uttering 'Dukkha' (Dukkhāhārakathā). In this discourse, those such as the present-day Pubbaseliyas hold the view: "One who utters the words 'Dukkha, Dukkha' brings forth knowledge regarding suffering; that is called the 'bringer of Dukkha' (dukkhāhāra). And that knowledge is a factor of the path included within the Eightfold Path." With reference to them, the question "Is it a bringer of Dukkha?" is the Sakavādī's question, and the affirmation is the Paravādī's answer. In the first question, "Whoever..." and so on, he denies it with reference to those who do not practice insight (vipassanā).
163: In the second question, he affirms with reference to a practitioner of insight (vipassaka), but that statement is merely his own view. Therefore, to break the doctrine that 'all of them develop the path', the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'foolish worldlings' (bālaputhujjanā). The meaning of that statement is clear. ## Commentary on the Discourse on the Bringing of Suffering (Dukkhāhārakathā). ## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Duration of Consciousness (Cittaṭṭhitikathā) Now, there is the discourse called the Discourse on the Duration of Consciousness. Therein, those such as the various types of Andhakas mentioned below, seeing the attainment-consciousness and the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga) occurring in succession, hold the view: 'A single consciousness lasts for a long time.' To clear that view of theirs, the question 'Does a single consciousness last for a whole day?' is the question of the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is the response of the Paravādī. In this context, 'Is half a day the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa)?', without touching upon the moment of presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa), the question was made by way of arising and vanishing (vaya) according to the method of the teaching: 'Impermanent indeed are formations, they have the nature of arising and vanishing.' When asked 'Are those phenomena as quickly changing as consciousness?', he rejects it because he does not see phenomena that change more quickly than consciousness. When asked a second time, he affirms with reference to that consciousness whose long duration he desires. In the question 'Does it last as long as life?', by the power of the words beginning with 'Those deities who remain for eighty-four thousand aeons (kappas)', he rejects it in places other than the formless realm (āruppa) and affirms it in the formless realm. In the question 'Does it arise moment by moment?', the Paravādī affirms it for fear of contradicting Suttas such as 'they have the nature of arising and vanishing'. However, he desires its duration by the power of his own view. The remaining words here have clear meanings. ## Commentary on the Discourse on the Duration of Consciousness. ## 8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Hot Ashes (Kukkuḷakathā) Now, there is the discourse called the Discourse on the Hot Ashes. Therein, those who, by improper means, [interpret] Suttas such as 'All, O monks, is burning' and 'All formations are suffering'...
164:
"O Bhikkhus, all things are burning; all formations are suffering," taking such suttas inappropriately, the view that "all formations are, in the direct sense and not figuratively, like hot ashes mixed with embers without flames, similar to the Hell of Hot Ashes (Kukkula Niraya)" is held, as is the case with the Gokulikas at present. To dispel that view by showing various types of happiness, the Sakavādī asks the question, and the Paravādī concedes. In that question, "without making a limit" (anodhiṃ katvā) means without making a boundary or portion, meaning all without distinction. All the rest should be understood according to the method of the Pali text along with the scriptural evidence.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Hot Ashes (Kukkulakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 9. Commentary on the Discourse on Gradual Realization (Anupubbābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discourse on Gradual Realization. In that discourse, taking suttas such as: 
"Gradually, little by little, moment by moment, the wise man should blow away his own impurities, just as a smith blows away the impurities of silver" (Dhp. 239) inappropriately, the view of various realizations arises as follows: "One practicing for the realization of the Fruit of Stream-entry abandons some defilements by seeing the Truth of Suffering, some by seeing the Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path; likewise in the remaining Paths; thus, having abandoned defilements gradually through sixteen portions, the attainment of Arhatship occurs." This is the view held at present by the Andhakas, Sabbatthikas, Sammitiyas, and Bhadrayānikas. To dispel their view, the Sakavādī asks, "Is there a gradual realization?" and the other concedes. When asked, "Is the Path of Stream-entry [developed] gradually?", he rejects it for fear of the consequence that a single Path would become many. When asked a second time, he concedes by way of seeing the Truth of Suffering and so on. Or, he concedes that those four knowledges are just the single Path of Stream-entry, but since he desires only a single Fruit, he rejects it. The same method applies to the Path of Once-returning and so on.

In the problem "Does one who has seen the Path stand in the Fruit?", because the act of seeing is not completed by seeing the Truth of Suffering etc., but is completed only by seeing the Truth of the Path, at that time he is said to be "standing in the Fruit"; therefore, he concedes.
165:
To the question, "When the Truth of Suffering is seen, are all four Truths seen?", the Paravādī asks, and the Sakavādī concedes by way of a single realization (ekābhisamaya). Again, in the inquiry, "Is the Truth of Suffering the four Truths?", the Sakavādī himself rejects it because the four Truths are different from one another by nature.

To the question, "Is the aggregate of form seen as impermanent?", the Sakavādī asks, and the Paravādī concedes with the view that "Just as by knowing the taste of a single drop of water from the ocean, the remaining water is known, so when one thing is realized as impermanent and so on, all things are realized."

"By four knowledges" means by the knowledges of the Truth of Suffering and so on [realizing the Fruit of Stream-entry]. "By eight knowledges" means by the four Truth-knowledges common to disciples and the four knowledges of analytical insight (paṭisambhidā). "By twelve knowledges" means by the knowledges of the twelve factors of Dependent Origination. "By forty-four knowledges" means by the knowledges stated in the Nidānavagga such as "knowledge of aging and death, knowledge of the origin of aging and death." "By seventy-seven knowledges" means by the knowledges stated in that same Nidānavagga as: "Bhikkhus, aging and death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of the nature of wasting, of the nature of vanishing, of the nature of fading away, of the nature of cessation." The remaining meaning in this Discourse on Gradual Realization should be understood according to the method of the Pali text along with the scriptural evidence.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Gradual Realization (Anupubbābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on Conventional Speech (Vohārakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discourse on Conventional Speech. In that discourse, there is a view held by the Andhakas of the present time that "The Blessed Buddha speaks only with supramundane (lokuttara) speech." Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks, and the Paravādī concedes according to his view. The phrases such as "Does it strike the supramundane ear?" are spoken to show the Paravādī's inappropriate view. The meaning here is: "According to you, is only the sound-base (saddāyatana) supramundane, or are the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda) and so on also supramundane?"

In the phrase, "If the speech (voice) of the Blessed Buddha strikes the mundane ear...", one should not take the meaning as "If it strikes the supramundane ear, it would be supramundane speech." Rather, the meaning to be taken here is that there is no such thing as being supramundane for a sound that is struck upon a mundane ear. Also, in the phrase "Is it not known by mundane consciousness?"...
166:
It means "they know only by mundane consciousness." Otherwise (without the word 'eva'), it would be indefinite. This is because supramundane states are also known by mundane knowledge. Thus, everything should be understood accordingly. In the questions "Do all those people develop the Path?", the rejection is made with reference to those who have not yet attained the Path. The affirmation is made with reference to those who have attained the Path.

"Sovaṇṇamayāya" means "made of gold" (referring to a staff). This is an example used by the Paravādī (the opponent).

"Eḷaṇḍiyāya" means "made of a castor-oil stalk." This is an example used by the Sakavādī (the proponent). The view that the voice of the Blessed One, when speaking of mundane things, is mundane, is also a certain doctrine. This is currently the view of some members of the Andhaka school. The remaining words in this Vohārakathā have clear meanings.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Common Usage (Vohārakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathā). In this discourse, for those who hold the view that both "cessation not through deliberation" (appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) and "cessation through deliberation" (paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) together constitute the "Truth of Cessation" (nirodha-sacca)—such as the Mahīsāsakas and Andhakas of the present time—the question "Are there two cessations?" is asked by the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is the Paravādī's response. In the questions "Are there two cessations of suffering?", the Paravādī rejects it because they do not accept two Truths of Suffering. They affirm it because they accept that suffering ceases in two ways (appaṭisaṅkhā and paṭisaṅkhā). In the questions "Are there two Truths of Cessation?", they reject it because they do not accept it in terms of the cessation of two Truths of Suffering. They affirm it because suffering ceases in two ways. The same method applies to the questions "Are there two refuges (tāṇa)?" and so on.

In the questions "Are there two Nirvāṇas?" and so on, they reject it because they do not see any superiority or inferiority in Nirvāṇa.

"Appaṭisaṅkhā-niruddha" refers to those conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras) which are said to be "ceased" (niruddha) not because they have been ceased by supramundane knowledge through deliberation, but because of their pure nature or because they do not occur due to the power of study and inquiry, etc. "Paṭisaṅkhā nirodhenti" means they cause cessation through supramundane knowledge; they bring about the state of non-arising. The question "Are not the saṅkhāras ceased without deliberation?"...
167:
...is the question of the Paravādī. In that problem, the Sakavādī affirms the state of being absolutely broken (destroyed), either because the defilements that have been broken are not broken again, or because the saṅkhāras, which are said to have ceased without deliberation, cease in that manner when the Noble Path arises. The remaining meanings here are clear.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā)

## Second Group (Dutiya Vagga)

## 3. Third Group (Tatiya Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Powers (Balakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discourse on Powers (Balakathā). In this discourse, some, such as the Andhakas of the present time, wrongly grasp the ten discourses in the Anuruddha Saṃyutta, such as: "Friends, it is because I have developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness that I understand, as it really is, what is a cause as a cause and what is not a cause as not a cause" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.913). They hold the view that "The power of the Tathāgata is shared with the disciples." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question, and the Paravādī, standing by their view, gives the affirmation.

What is called the power of the Tathāgata is sometimes shared with the disciples, sometimes unshared, and sometimes both shared and unshared. Among these three, the knowledge of the destruction of taints (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) is a shared power. The knowledge of the maturity of the faculties of others (indriyaparopariyatti-ñāṇa) is an unshared power. The remaining knowledges are both shared and unshared. For the disciples know causes and non-causes, etc., partially, while the Tathāgatas know them completely (without remainder). Thus, those knowledges are shared in terms of their brief description (uddesa), but not in terms of their detailed explanation (niddesa). However, this Paravādī says that everything is shared without distinction.

To distinguish the Paravādī from that view, the cross-examination "Is the power of the Tathāgata the power of the disciple?" is begun. In that matter, in the first question, the Sakavādī rejects it with reference to the scope of all aspects in detail. In the second question, they affirm it in terms of knowing just the cause and non-cause, etc., in brief.

In the problems "Are they the same powers?", etc., they reject it because there is no lack of distinction or equality in every aspect. "Former effort" (pubbayoga) and "former conduct" (pubbacariyā) are the same in meaning. Likewise, "expounding the Dhamma" (dhammakkhāna) and "teaching the Dhamma" (dhammadesanā) are the same.

In the problem concerning the maturity of the faculties (indriyaparopariyatti), they affirm it in the domain of the disciples with reference to it being shared in one part.
168:
Now, because a disciple knows the possible and the impossible (ṭhāna and aṭṭhāna) and so forth in brief, the questions of the opponent (paravādī) arise to demonstrate such knowledge of the disciple and to establish that these powers are common (sādhāraṇa) to disciples by virtue of the similarity in merely knowing them, such as "A disciple knows the possible and the impossible."

In those questions, the knowledge of the maturity of faculties (indriyaparopariyatti-ñāṇa) is not included as being common, because it is one of the six unshared knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa). In the phrase "by the destruction of taints, the destruction of taints," there is no distinction to be made regarding the disciple's destruction of taints in relation to the Buddha's destruction of taints. In the phrase "by liberation, liberation," the same method applies. The remaining text here has an obvious meaning.

Now, the questions of the opponent, such as "In the destruction of taints," arise again to ask about the commonality of the remaining knowledges by comparing them with the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), which the Sakavādī has admitted to be common. In the answers to those questions, the Sakavādī admits that knowledge to be common because there is no distinction in the destruction of taints. However, regarding the other knowledges, commonality is rejected because there is a distinction. Again, the question concerning unshared nature (asādhāraṇa), comparing the possible and the impossible and so forth with the destruction of taints, is the opponent's question alone. In that case, the rejection regarding the knowledge of the destruction of taints and the admission regarding the remaining knowledges is the Sakavādī's answer. After that, the question concerning unshared nature, comparing with the knowledge of the maturity of faculties, is the opponent's question. It is shown in brief. Even though shown in brief, the admission regarding the knowledge of the maturity of faculties and the rejection regarding the remaining knowledges is the Sakavādī's answer. After that, the question concerning the commonality of the knowledge of the maturity of faculties, comparing it with the possible and the impossible and so forth, is the opponent's question. That too is shown only in brief. In that case, the rejection regarding the knowledge of the maturity of faculties and the admission regarding the remaining knowledges is the Sakavādī's answer.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Powers (Balakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of "Noble" (Ariyantikathāvaṇṇanā)

Now, there is the discussion called "Ariyanti." In this regard, for those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas at present—that "Not only is the knowledge of the destruction of taints noble (ariya), but indeed the preceding nine powers are also noble," the question "Is it noble?" is the Sakavādī's question, and the admission is the other's (opponent's) answer. Again, the question "If that knowledge is noble, should it be included as one of the factors such as the Path (magga)?" is the Sakavādī's question, and the rejection is the other's answer.
169:
The question asked in terms of the Path and so forth, "Should it be one of those?", is the Sakavādī's question, and the rejection is the other's (opponent's) answer.

Again, the question asked in terms of having emptiness (suññatā) as an object is the Sakavādī's question. In that emptiness, there are two kinds: emptiness of a being (satta-suññatā) and emptiness of conditioned things (saṅkhāra-suññatā). Emptiness of a being refers to the five aggregates being empty of a "being" as imagined by wrong view. Emptiness of conditioned things refers to Nibbāna, which is empty of, secluded from, and escaped from all conditioned things. Among those two types of emptiness, the opponent rejects it with reference to having Nibbāna as an object, but admits it with reference to having conditioned things as an object. Even when asked, "Does one attend to it?", they reject it with reference to Nibbāna and admit it with reference to conditioned things. Thereafter, the Sakavādī, taking this principle that "Attention to the possible and the impossible and so forth has conditioned things as an object, while attention to emptiness has Nibbāna as an object," asks, "Is there a conjunction of two contacts and two consciousnesses?" Finding no opening for an excuse, the opponent rejects it. This same method applies to the signless (animitta) and the desireless (appaṇihita). Indeed, the aggregates are signless because they lack the sign of a being. Nibbāna is signless because it lacks the sign of conditioned things. Even in a single phenomenon, the aggregates are desireless (appaṇihita) by way of the desire for a being (satta-paṇidhi), which is called 'paṇihita' in the sense of being established and aimed at by projecting a being onto them. Nibbāna is desireless by way of the desire of craving (taṇhā-paṇidhi) or by way of the desire for all conditioned things which are the objects of craving. Therefore, here too, the rejection and admission should be understood according to the previous method.

Thereafter, the forward and backward (anuloma-paṭiloma) questions arise: "Just as the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are noble and have emptiness and so forth as their objects, is the knowledge of the possible and the impossible like that?" In those questions, all admissions and all rejections belong to the opponent alone. By this means, the questions and answers regarding the remaining knowledges should be understood. In the Pali text, however, the remaining knowledges are abbreviated, and only the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa) is analyzed in detail at the end. After that, even in one's own tradition (Sakasamaya), questions arise in forward and backward order regarding whether the remaining knowledges are noble, by comparing them with the knowledge of the destruction of taints, which is established as "noble." All those are the opponent's questions, and the admission and rejection are the Sakavādī's answers. Their meanings are indeed obvious. In this Pali of the Ariyantikathā, only the first and the ninth knowledges are shown, while the seven knowledges in the middle are abbreviated.

## Commentary on the Discussion of "Noble" (Ariyantikathāvaṇṇanā)

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation (Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā)
Now is the Discussion of Liberation. Therein, for those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas at present—that "There is no such thing as the benefit of liberation for minds free from lust. However, just as a soiled cloth is freed from dirt when being washed, so a mind with lust is freed from lust," the Sakavādin asks "sarāgaṃ" (Is the mind with lust liberated?) and the other [the Paravādin] gives his assent. Thereafter, when questioned by the method beginning with "rāgasahagataṃ" (associated with lust), he [the Paravādin] rejects it, saying that at the moment of the Path (magga-kkhaṇa), the mind is said to be "being liberated," and at that moment, such a mind [associated with lust] does not exist.

Even when questioned by the method beginning with "saphassaṃ" (with contact), he rejects it because he does not see the liberation of lust itself, just as both contact and mind are freed from lust. In the problems concerning "with hatred" (sadosa) and so on, the meaning should be understood in this very same way.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation.

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of 'Being Liberated' (Vimuccamānakathāvaṇṇanā)
Now is the Discussion of 'Being Liberated.' Therein, for those who hold the view that "A mind liberated by the liberation of suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti) through jhāna is 'being liberated' (vimuccamāna) by the liberation of cutting off (samuccheda-vimutti) at the moment of the Path," the Sakavādin asks "vimuttaṃ vimuccamānaṃ" (Is that which is liberated "being liberated"?) and the other gives his assent.

Again, the Sakavādin asks "ekadesaṃ" (partially). Therein, the word "ekadesaṃ" is a neuter noun used adverbially. He asks, "Just as a liberated mind is not yet liberated either partially or in a certain part, is it thus partially liberated and partially not liberated?" Why does he ask this? Because it was stated as an incomplete state, "the liberated [mind] is being liberated." Indeed, just as mats and so on that are being made are partially finished and partially unfinished because they are incomplete, so this mind would also be partially liberated and partially not liberated. Therefore, the Paravādin rejects this in the first problem because the mind does not have parts like mats and so on, but in the second problem, he gives his assent because of the unfinished liberation of the mind that is "being liberated." Alternatively, he rejects it with reference to the moment of mundane (lokiya) jhāna. Indeed, at that moment of mundane jhāna, it is not "being liberated" by the liberation of cutting off. He gives his assent with reference to the moment of supramundane (lokuttara) jhāna. Indeed, at that time, his view is that it is "being liberated" by a part of the liberation through the liberation of cutting off. Thereafter, the Sakavādin says, "If your..."
171:
...single mind is partially liberated and partially not liberated, then if it were so, a person who becomes a Sotāpanna with a single mind would also, according to your view, result in being partially a Sotāpanna and partially not a Sotāpanna." To make this objection, he said "partially a Sotāpanna" and so on. The other [the Paravādin], not seeing such a provision, rejects it. In the remaining sections (vāra) as well, this is the same method.

In the problem concerning the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa), if a single mind is both liberated and being liberated, it would result in being liberated at one moment and being liberated at the [same] moment. The meaning is: "According to your view, does such a mind exist?"

In proving by means of the Suttas, the first Sutta belongs to the Paravādin. Therein, his intention is: the word "is being liberated" (vimuccati) is an incomplete designation. Therefore, the mind of that practitioner who thus knows and thus sees "is being liberated" from these taints (āsava); that [mind] is called "being liberated" (vimuccamāna). The second Sutta belongs to the Sakavādin. Therein, his intention is: "If, according to your view, the liberated [mind] is 'being liberated' because of the statement 'is being liberated,' then in this [second Sutta], because of the absence of the statement 'is being liberated,' it should only be 'liberated,' not 'being liberated.'"

Now, to make the objection, "If, according to your view, it is 'being liberated' because of incomplete liberation, then are there also such things as 'being lustful' (rajjamāna) and so on because of incomplete lust and so on?", he again began with "Does the mind exist?" and so on. The Paravādin, not seeing such a mind, rejects everything. Then the Sakavādin, wishing to make him understand that "There are only two categories, there is no third," said "the lustful mind and the non-lustful mind" and so on. The meaning is: "Is it not, my good man, that there are only two categories—the mind associated with lust is 'lustful' (ratta) and the mind dissociated from lust is 'not lustful' (aratta)—and there is no third category called 'being lustful' (rajjamāna)?" In the problems concerning "being hateful" (dussamāna) and so on, this is the same method. Then the Paravādin stands having assented, saying "Yes." To show that there are only two categories on the side of liberation as well, he said "If the lustful mind..." and so on. The meaning is: "If you accept these two categories, then also accept these two: the non-liberated mind and the liberated mind. Indeed, the mind associated with defilements is called 'non-liberated' (avimutta), and the mind dissociated from them is 'liberated' (vimutta). In the ultimate sense (paramatthato), there is no third category called 'being liberated' (vimuccamāna)."

## Commentary on the Discussion of 'Being Liberated'.

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighth Person

Now is the Discussion of the Eighth Person (Aṭṭhamakakathā). In this discussion, the Sakavādin questions a certain Paravādin, such as the Andhakas and Sammitiyas of the present time, who hold the view that the two obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) have already been abandoned by the eighth person, the one standing on the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimaggaṭṭha), because there is no occurrence of defilements during the moments of conformity (anuloma), change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and the path (magga). The Paravādin admits this, referring to the non-arising of wrong view (diṭṭhi) from the moment of the path onwards. Following this, the Sakavādin cross-examines, "Is the eighth person a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna)?" because this wrong view is only abandoned by one standing in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphalaṭṭha), not by one standing on the path (maggaṭṭha). The same method applies to the question of doubt (vicikicchā). In the question of underlying tendencies (anusaya), since they hold the view that the underlying tendency is different from the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), the Sakavādin rejects it with "Na hevaṃ" (Not so).

In the question of adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa), the Paravādin rejects it because they do not find the term 'obsession of adherence to rites and rituals' (sīlabbataparāmāsapariyuṭṭhāna). They hold the view that only the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) has been abandoned for that person. In the question "Has the path been developed?", they reject it because at that moment the path is still being developed and has not yet been fully developed. In the cross-examination beginning with "Does one abandon by what is not the path?", the Paravādin rejects it, intending that abandonment occurs only by the first path, the path of Stream-entry. This is because if abandonment occurred by what is not the path, it would lead to the fault that abandonment has also occurred in the person of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and so on. The question "Will it arise?" is the Paravādin's question, and the answer is the Sakavādin's answer. All remaining meanings are clear.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighth Person is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person

Now is the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person (Aṭṭhamakassa Indriyakathā). Therein, referring to the Andhakas of the present time who hold the view that "the eighth person is in the process of acquiring the faculties at the path-moment, but has not yet acquired them," the Sakavādin asks, "Is there no faith-faculty (saddhindriya)?" and the Paravādin admits it. However, when asked, "Is there no faith (saddhā)?", the Paravādin rejects it, considering the difference between the faith-faculty and faith. The same method applies to the remaining faculties. Just as for one who has a mind (mano), there is also the mind-faculty (manindriya), so too...
173:
To show the meaning that for one who has faith and so on, there are also the faculties of faith and so on, the Sakavādin begins the questioning with "There is mind, there is the mind-faculty," and so forth. All those statements have clear meanings along with the scriptural evidence.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Divine Eye

Now is the Discussion of the Divine Eye (Dibbacakkhukathā). In this discussion, referring to the Andhakas and Sammitiyas who hold the view that the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu) itself, when supported by the fourth jhāna, is called the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), the Sakavādin asks, "Is it the physical eye?" and the Paravādin admits it.

Again, when asked, "Is the physical eye the divine eye, is the divine eye the physical eye?", the Paravādin rejects it because the physical eye alone, without the support of the Dhamma (jhāna), is not that divine eye. In questions such as "Of what nature is it?", they reject it because the two do not share the same nature.

In terms such as "sphere" (visaya), the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) is the object for both eyes. However, the physical eye sees only what has come into range (āpāthagata). The other, the divine eye, can see even what has not come into range, such as what is on the other side of a mountain. Furthermore, the object of the divine eye is an extremely subtle form, whereas the other, the physical eye, does not have such an object. Thus, the power and the range of these eyes are not the same.

When asked, "Being kammically acquired (upādinna), does it become not kammically acquired (anupādinna)?", the Paravādin rejects it because the physical eye is kammically acquired while the divine eye is not, and they do not wish to accept that the physical eye alone is the divine eye. When asked a second time, they admit it because, based on the statement "The arising of the physical eye is the path for the divine eye," the divine eye arises depending on the physical eye, and they accept that it is the sensitivity (pasāda) of the four great elements belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). When asked, "Being of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara)...", they reject it because they do not wish to accept that the physical eye alone is the divine eye. When asked a second time, they admit it, saying it is called fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) because it arises depending on the fine-material sphere jhāna.

When asked, "Being of the fine-material sphere, does it become of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara)?", they reject it because after that, through development (bhāvanā), at the moment of the immaterial sphere, the fine-material sphere mind does not exist. When asked a second time...
174:
He admits with the view that it arises as the clarity (pasāda) of the four great elements produced by formless-sphere jhāna (arūpāvacara-jhāna). However, because he does not desire the supramundane (lokuttara) nature of that divine eye, he rejects it as usual.

'The divine eye is supported by the Dhamma' means it is supported by the sense-sphere Dhamma (meaning it is the fleshly eye). Again, 'supported by the Dhamma' means it is supported by the supramundane Dhamma (meaning it is the wisdom-eye). When asked if there are only two types of eyes, although he does not desire the wisdom-eye nature of the divine eye supported by the supramundane Dhamma, he rejects it because the wisdom-eye exists. When asked again, he admits based on the view that the fleshly eye supported by the fourth jhāna is the divine eye. The remaining words in this Discussion on the Divine Eye are clear in meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion on the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion on the Divine Ear (Dibba-sota-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now is the Discussion on the Divine Ear. In that discussion, when asked if there is only one type of ear, he rejects it because there are two: the fleshly ear and the divine ear. When asked again, since that very fleshly ear is called the divine ear when supported by the fourth jhāna, he admits it. The rest is the same as the method mentioned below in the Discussion on the Divine Eye.

## Commentary on the Discussion on the Divine Ear (Dibba-sota-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion on Knowledge of Beings Passing Away According to Kamma (Yathākammūpagata-ñāṇa-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now is the Discussion on Knowledge of Beings Passing Away According to Kamma. In that discussion, referring to those who wrongly grasp the Sutta, "Thus with the divine eye, purified... he knows beings passing away according to kamma" (DN 1.246, Patis. M. 1.106), and hold the view that the knowledge of passing away according to kamma is itself the divine eye, the Sakavādī asks and the other (Paravādī) admits. Again, when asked if one also attends to the passing away according to kamma, he rejects it because two objects cannot exist in a single mind. When asked a second time, he admits by way of various minds. Again, without giving an opportunity for evasion, when asked if two contacts (phassa) arise, he rejects it. Just as the meaning is understood by this term 'passing away according to kamma' (yathākammūpagata), so too should the meaning be understood in connection with terms such as "Indeed, sirs, these beings," and so on.
175:
"The Venerable Sāriputta knows the knowledge of passing away according to kamma"—the Sakavādī asks this point. This is because the Elder, due to his fewness of wishes (appicchatā), does not use the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā-ñāṇa). Some people not only do not know this, but they also think that those supernormal knowledges do not exist in that Elder's continuum. Therefore, thinking of that Elder as "the Elder who has not attained the divine eye," they ask (the Paravādī). For that very reason, when asked later, "Does the Venerable Sāriputta have the divine eye?", the Paravādī denies it. When asked a second time, he admits, "The Elder has attained all the Dhamma that should be attained by a disciple."

Now, the Sakavādī, wishing to cause confusion (vikkhepa) to that Paravādī, says, "Is it not the Venerable Sāriputta?" and so on. The Elder spoke this verse only because he had no desire to use it, not because of the absence of supernormal knowledge. The Paravādī, however, perceives the meaning as being only due to the absence (of supernormal knowledge). Therefore, according to that Paravādī's view, the Elder has only the knowledge of passing away according to kamma, not the divine eye. Thus it is said, "If so, it should not be said that the knowledge of passing away according to kamma is the divine eye."

## Commentary on the Discussion on Knowledge of Beings Passing Away According to Kamma (Yathākammūpagata-ñāṇa-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion on Restraint (Saṃvara-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now is the Discussion on Restraint (Saṃvara-kathā). In that Discussion on Restraint, starting from the Tāvatiṃsa devas and including the devas above them, because those devas do not practice the five enmities (pañca-vera) such as killing, there is the view of the Paravādī that restraint (saṃvara) exists. This is the Sakavādī's question. It is the admission of the Paravādī who does not see the practice of enmity. Then, since what is called restraint (saṃvara) can only exist when there is non-restraint (asaṃvara) that ought to be restrained, the Sakavādī asks regarding non-restraint. The Paravādī rejects it because killing and so on do not exist among the devas.

The phrase "Does it exist among humans?" and so on was spoken (by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa) for the purpose of showing the occurrence of non-restraint when there is restraint, and the occurrence of restraint when there is non-restraint.

In the questions such as "Abstaining from killing," one should understand the admission by way of not practicing killing and so on, and the rejection because killing and so on do not exist. The reverse question (paṭiloma) has a clear meaning.

At the end, in the question "There is no restraint among devas," the Sakavādī admits, referring to the absence of restraint from killing and so on after having committed killing and so on. Then...
176:
If, by way of the six-fold view (chaḷavāda), there is no restraint, then the question "Are all devas killers?" and so on is the Paravādī's question. The rejection by the Sakavādī is because the practice of enmity (vera-samudācāra) does not exist among devas. Establishing one's own view by merely grasping the words "Na hevaṃ" (It is not so) is the work of the Paravādī. A view established in this way is an unstable view.

## Commentary on the Discussion on Restraint (Saṃvara-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 11. Commentary on the Discussion on Unconscious Beings (Asañña-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now the Discussion on Unconscious Beings will be presented. In that Discussion on Unconscious Beings, according to the word "With formations as condition, consciousness arises," there is no such thing as rebirth without consciousness. According to the word "Because perception arises, those devas pass away from that body," there is the view of the Andhakas who hold that even for unconscious beings (asañña-satta), there is perception at the moment of death and rebirth. Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks a question and the Paravādī admits. Then, the Sakavādī speaks "Perception-existence (saññā-bhava), perception-destination (saññā-gati)," and so on, to challenge: "According to your wish, is that realm a perception-existence?" All these words and the words to follow should be understood according to the method of the Pali text.

## Commentary on the Discussion on Unconscious Beings (Asañña-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 12. Commentary on the Discussion on the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now the Discussion on the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception will be presented. In that discussion, because of the name "Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana," there is the view of the Andhakas who hold that it should not be said "There is perception in that existence." Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks a question and the Paravādī admits. All the remaining points in this discussion should be understood according to the method of the Pali text.

## Commentary on the Discussion on the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## The Third Group (Tatiyo Vaggo).

## 4. Fourth Chapter
## 1. Gihissa Arahati Kathāvaṇṇanā
Now follows the discussion titled "A Layperson can be an Arahant" (Gihissa Arahati Kathā). In this discussion, seeing the attainment of Arahantship by those such as Yasa, the clansman, while still in the lay appearance, the view is held that "A layperson can be an Arahant," as is the current view of the Uttarāpathakas. The question is by the Sakavādin referring to them. In that context, "gihissa" means one who is a layperson because of being associated with lay fetters (gihisaṃyojana); the meaning is that such a person can be an Arahant. The Paravādin, however, without noting the Sakavādin's intention, agrees while looking only at the lay appearance (gihivyañjana).

Now, to make that Paravādin understand that "A layperson is so called because of lay fetters, not merely by appearance," the Blessed One said this:
"Even if adorned, if he walks in peace,
Calm, tamed, established in the holy life,
Having laid aside the stick towards all beings,
He is a Brahmin, he is a Samana, he is a Bhikkhu."
To show this method, the Elder Moggaliputta-Tissa began the passage "Atthi arahato," etc. The meaning of the entire text is clear.

## Gihissa Arahati Kathāvaṇṇanā.

## 2. Upapattikathāvaṇṇanā
Now follows the discussion titled "Discussion on Rebirth" (Upapattikathā). In this discussion, taking the words "He is of spontaneous birth and attains Parinibbāna there" improperly, some hold the view that one becomes an Arahant by way of rebirth in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realms. Or, by changing the term "upahaccaparinibbāyī" to "upapajjaparinibbāyī" and learning it as such, they hold the view that one becomes an Arahant simultaneously with rebirth, as is the current view of the Uttarāpathakas. The question is by the Sakavādin and the admission is by the other. In that context, since the rebirth-consciousness (upapatticitta) is mundane (lokiya), even Stream-enterers and others cannot be attained with that consciousness, let alone an Arahant.
178:
Therefore, to show this method to the Opponent, the text begins with "One is a Stream-enterer simultaneously with rebirth" and so on. The passage "Sāriputto" and so on is stated for the purpose of challenging: "Among these Great Elders, which single one is called an Arahant simultaneously with rebirth?" "Upapattesiyena" means "with the rebirth-consciousness." This is because that rebirth-consciousness seeks (esati) rebirth (upapatti); therefore, it is called "upapattesiya." The remaining words in this Upapattikathā have an obvious meaning.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Rebirth.

## 3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Taintless (Anāsavakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the discourse on the Taintless. In that discourse, there is a view held by the Opponents, such as the current Uttarāpathakas, that all things existing in the continuum of an Arahant, who is free from taints (anāsava), are themselves taintless. The Proponent's question "Arahato" is directed at them, and the other affirms it. Then, for the purpose of challenging the Opponent—that what is called "taintless" refers only to the Path and so on, and asking whether only those things like the Path arise in the Arahant's continuum—the passage "Maggo phalaṃ" and so on is begun. When asked "Is the eye taintless?", the Opponent rejects it because the eye is subject to taints (sāsava). When asked a second time, he affirms it, considering that "this is the eye of an Arahant who is taintless."

In the question regarding robes (cīvara), if it is said that a single thing like a robe is both taintless and subject to taints, he rejects it for fear of contradicting the characteristics (lakkhaṇa). When asked a second time, he affirms it, saying that it can be the property of a taintless Arahant and also the property of a worldling (puthujjana) who is subject to taints. In the two questions "Taññeva anāsavaṃ" and so on, the method is the same. Since the Opponent has affirmed "Taññeva" (that very same thing), the Proponent challenges with the words "Maggo anāsavo hutvā" and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all the questions.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Taintless.

## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Possession (Samannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the discourse on Possession. In that discourse, there are two kinds of possession (samannāgama): possession by presence (samangībhāva-samannāgama), which is being endowed with something at the present moment, and possession by acquisition (paṭilābha-samannāgama), which is the attainment due to reaching a certain plane such as the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). This possession by acquisition is maintained as long as one does not fall away from the specific attainment reached. To make the Uttarāpathakas of the present day—who, setting aside these two kinds of possession, believe there is another kind of possession by the power of the nature of rebirth—understand that there is no such thing as "attainment-nature" (pattidhamma), the Proponent asks, "Is an Arahant possessed of the four fruits?" and the Opponent affirms it, referring to acquisition.

Then, the Proponent begins with "Is an Arahant possessed of the four contacts (phassa)?" and so on, to challenge: "If an Arahant is possessed of the four fruits just as he is possessed of the four aggregates (khandha), then it would follow that the Arahant is possessed of the four contacts and so on that exist in those four fruits." All of that was rejected by the Opponent because four contacts and so on cannot exist at the same single moment. The same method applies to the questions regarding the Non-returner (Anāgāmī) and others.

In the phrase "He has transcended the fruit of stream-entry," it is not like one who has attained the second jhāna transcends the first jhāna; rather, the question is asked to show that it means transcending by way of non-recurrence. The passage "Sotāpattimaggaṃ" and so on was begun to show that the Arahant is no longer possessed of that which he has transcended.

In the question "He has not fallen away from those things," unlike mundane jhānas which fall away due to the occurrence of opposing states, supramundane states do not fall away. Because the defilements that are abandoned by the Path and stilled by the Fruit remain abandoned and stilled in that way, the Proponent affirmed with "Āmantā" (Yes). This meaning is clearly explained later in passages such as "The Arahant has acquired the four paths." The remaining words have an obvious meaning.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Possession.

## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Being a Buddha because of Bodhi (Bodhiyābuddhotikathāvaṇṇanā)
Now follows the discussion "Being a Buddha because of Bodhi" (Bodhiyābuddhotikathā). In this context, "Bodhi" is a designation for both the four Path Knowledges and Omniscience. Therefore, just as for some, one is called "white" because of a white complexion or "dark" because of a dark complexion, likewise, the view that "one is a Buddha because of Bodhi" currently belongs only to the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, there is the questioning and interrogation by the Sakavādī, and the affirmation and rejection by the other (the Paravādī).

In the problem "Is it because of past Bodhi?", he rejects it because it does not exist at that moment, being past. When asked a second time, he affirms it with reference to the attainment of Bodhi. Again, when asked by way of function, he rejects it because of the absence of function. When asked a second time, he affirms the absence of confusion regarding whatever task was to be performed by that Bodhi. Without giving an opening for a hint, when asked in the manner of "Does he fully understand suffering?" etc., he rejects it because of the absence of that function.

In the problem regarding the future, he rejects it because of the absence of Path Knowledge at that moment. When asked a second time, thinking of the state of being a Buddha because of future Bodhi as in "The Buddha went to Rājagaha" (Sn 410), he affirms it. When asked "Does he perform the function of Bodhi?", he rejects it because of the absence of function at that moment. When asked a second time, he affirms it, saying that if he did not perform it, he should not be called "Buddha"; since he will certainly perform it, he is indeed said to perform it. Again, without giving an opening for a hint, when asked, he rejects it. The problem regarding the present is clear in meaning along with the comparison (saṃsandana).

When asked by combining the three types of Bodhi, he affirms it with reference to Omniscience, because one is called a Buddha because of all three types of Bodhi. Again, when asked "Is it because of the three?"...
181:
...he rejects it because all of them cannot exist at a single moment. When asked a second time, he affirms it by way of Omniscience which is past, future, and present. Again, without giving an opening for speech, when asked "Is it constant and continuous?", he rejects it again.

The question "It should not be said 'because of Bodhi'" is the Paravādī's question; the affirmation is the Sakavādī's, because at the moment when Bodhi is absent, the state of not being a Buddha would follow. In the problem "Is it not because of the attainment of Bodhi?", however, in whichever continuity (santāna) the Path Knowledge called Bodhi has arisen, the affirmation is that of the Sakavādī because the conventional designation (sammuti) "Buddha" exists there. Without knowing the Sakavādī's intention, the establishment of the view "If (one is a Buddha because of the attainment of Bodhi)" is the Paravādī's way of establishing the view. Now, to make clear the Paravādī's lack of discernment, the Sakavādī asks, "If one is a Buddha because of the attainment of Bodhi, is one a Buddha because of Bodhi?" The meaning of that question is: "According to your view, since one is a Buddha because of the attainment of Bodhi, is one therefore a Buddha because of Bodhi?" The other, the Paravādī, without discerning this distinction—that "attainment of Bodhi" means the state of having arisen in the continuity even if Bodhi has arisen and ceased, while "Bodhi" is the knowledge at the moment of the Path—affirms it again. Then, when the Sakavādī asks, "Is Bodhi because of the attainment of Bodhi?", he rejects it, having no opportunity for speech.

## Exposition of the Discussion of Being a Buddha because of Bodhi.

Thus, all these three discussions belong only to the Uttarāpathakas.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Marks (Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of Marks. In that context, having improperly grasped this Sutta: "For a Great Man endowed with these marks, only two destinies are possible," those who hold the view that "Only a Bodhisatta is endowed with the marks" are the current Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other affirms.

In the problems "Is it a being who is a Universal Monarch?", since both a Universal Monarch and a Bodhisatta (can be endowed with marks), he rejects it with reference to a Universal Monarch who is not a Bodhisatta. He affirms it with reference to a Bodhisatta.
182:
This Sutta concerning the person endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man is spoken solely with reference to the Bodhisatta. Indeed, in his final birth, he becomes a Buddha, and in other births, he becomes a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). Therefore, even if he is presented as a disciple (sāvaka) [by the opponent], it is as if he is not so presented.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Marks (Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion of Entering the Path of Assurance (Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of Entering the Path of Assurance. In this context, regarding the ordination of the youth Jotipāla in the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta, the Andhakas currently hold the view: 'The Bodhisatta entered the Path of Assurance (niyāma) and practiced the holy life (brahmacariya) under the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.' With reference to them, the question 'Bodhisatta?' is the question of the Proponent (Sakavādī), and the affirmation while standing by one's own view is the response of the Opponent (Paravādī). Furthermore, because both 'niyāma' and 'brahmacariya' are names for the Noble Path (Ariyamagga), there is no such thing as 'entering the path of assurance' for Bodhisattas other than the fulfillment of the Perfections (pāramī). If there were, the Bodhisatta would be a disciple who is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). But this is not the case. In fact, the Buddhas, established in the power of their own knowledge, give the prophecy (byākata): 'This person will become a Buddha.' Therefore, the question 'Bodhisatta?' is again the question of the Proponent. The denial with reference to the final birth is the response of the Opponent. In the second question, the affirmation with reference to the time of Jotipāla is that of the same Opponent. The same method should be understood for the questions beginning with 'Having become a disciple' (sāvako hutvā). 'Anussaviya' means one whose knowledge of the Dhamma is attained through hearsay (anussava). Having denied it with reference to the final birth, the Opponent affirms it with reference to hearsay during the time of Jotipāla.

The phrase 'another teacher' is spoken with reference to Āḷāra [Kālāma] and Rāmaputta [Uddaka]. The passage beginning with 'Venerable Ānanda' is spoken to show that 'only those who have entered the Path of Assurance are true disciples; others who have not entered the Path of Assurance are not such true disciples; only those who have entered the Path of Assurance possess the nature of Venerable Ānanda.'

In the phrase 'the disciple transcends birth,' the question is asked: 'Does he transcend that birth by which he is a disciple and become a non-disciple in another birth?' The Opponent denies this because the state of being a disciple for Stream-enterers and others continues in future births. The rest of the meaning here is clear.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Entering the Path of Assurance (Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā)

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Abandoning All Fetters (Sabbasaṃyojanappahānakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of Abandoning Fetters. In this discussion, the Andhakas currently hold the view: "The Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is the abandonment of all fetters (saṃyojana) in the primary sense." With reference to them, there is the question of the Proponent and the affirmation of the other. Again, when asked "All fetters?", the Opponent denies it with reference to the fetters already abandoned by the three paths mentioned below. When asked a second time, the Opponent affirms it because there are no fetters left unabandoned by that Path of Arahantship. In the problems concerning self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so on, the Opponent denies it with reference to what was abandoned by the first path, and affirms it with reference to the abandonment without remainder by the fourth path, the Path of Arahantship. This same method applies to all problems.
