## 5. The Fifth Chapter (Pañcamavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation (Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of Liberation. In this Discussion of Liberation, the name 'knowledge of liberation' (vimuttiñāṇa) applies to four kinds of knowledge: insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa), path knowledge (maggañāṇa), fruit knowledge (phalañāṇa), and reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa). Among these four, insight knowledge is called 'knowledge of liberation' because it is liberated from the signs of permanence (niccanimitta) and so on, or because it is liberated by way of 'liberation by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅgavimutti).
184:
The Path (magga) is called 'liberation by eradication' (samucchedavimutti); the Fruit (phala) is called 'liberation by tranquilization' (paṭippassaddhivimutti); and reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa) is called 'knowledge of liberation' because it knows liberation. Among these four types of knowledge of liberation, in the primary sense, only the knowledge of the Fruit is liberation. The remaining knowledges should not be called 'liberated' (vimuttāni) or 'unliberated' (avimuttāni). Therefore, without specifying 'this particular knowledge of liberation is liberated,' the Andhakas hold the general view that 'knowledge of liberation is liberated.' With reference to them, there is the question of the Proponent and the affirmation of the Opponent. Again, when asked 'Any [knowledge]?', the Opponent denies it with reference to reviewing knowledge and so on. When asked 'Of one who is practicing?', the Opponent affirms it with reference to the taintless nature (anāsava) of Path knowledge. Because that knowledge of one who is practicing is not the knowledge of a Stream-enterer established in the Fruit, it is not 'liberated' in the true sense; for the purpose of this objection, the Proponent says 'Of a Stream-enterer' (sotāpannassa) and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation (Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā)

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of a Non-learner (Asekhañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of a Non-learner (asekha). In this discussion, because learners (sekha) such as the Elder Ānanda know non-learners (asekha) by way of 'The Blessed One is magnificent' and so on, the Uttarāpathakas hold the view: 'A learner possesses the knowledge of a non-learner.' With reference to them, there is the question of the Proponent and the affirmation of the Opponent. The words 'He knows, he sees' are spoken by virtue of knowing the Dhamma attained by oneself. The words 'To one of the change-of-lineage' (gotrabhuno) and so on are spoken to show the absence of higher knowledges in a person established on a lower plane. The Opponent desires to call that knowledge 'knowledge of a non-learner' because it occurs with reference to the Blessed One, who is a non-learner, saying: 'Does not the Venerable Ānanda, while still a learner, know that "The Blessed One is magnificent"?' However, that knowledge is not the knowledge of a non-learner. Therefore, even if the view is established in this way, it remains unestablished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of a Non-learner (Asekhañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Perversion (Viparitakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of Perversion. In this discussion, there are those who hold the view: 'When a person enters a meditative attainment (samāpatti) perceiving earth in the earth-kasina (pathavīkasiṇa), that knowledge of his is perverted knowledge (viparitañāṇa).'
185:
It is just like the view of the Andhakas. Regarding them, the Sakavādin questions and the Paravādin admits. The reason is that the meditation sign (kasiṇa-nimitta) arising in dependence on earth is not the actual characteristic earth (lakkhaṇa-pathavī) or the composite earth (sasambhāra-pathavī). Yet, in that sign, this person has the perception of "earth." Therefore, that knowledge is perverted knowledge (viparīta-ñāṇa); this is the intention of the Paravādin.

Subsequently, the Sakavādin says, "Characteristic earth, composite earth, the meditation sign of earth, and the earth deity are all just earth. Knowledge that knows them as earth is not perverted. Only perversion such as taking the impermanent as permanent is called perverted knowledge. Is this knowledge of yours one of those, such as taking the impermanent as permanent?" in order to challenge. The Paravādin rejects it, referring to the absence of the characteristic of perversion (vipallāsa-lakkhaṇa), but admits it, referring to the meditation sign of earth.

The term "kusala" (wholesome) is spoken referring to the knowledge of trainees (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas). In the questions "Does an Arahant have it?", he rejects it because of the absence of the characteristic of perversion. He admits it, referring to the meditation sign of earth. With the words "Is all earth?", he asks whether all that earth-kasiṇa is indeed characteristic earth. The Sakavādin rejects it because it is not so. "Is there not earth? Does someone not attain earth through earth?" is the question of the Sakavādin. Its meaning is: "Is there not the meditation sign of earth? Does someone not attain that meditation sign of earth through earth itself, and not through water or fire?" The words "Earth exists," etc., are spoken to show: "If the knowledge of one who attains something as it is, is perverted, then since Nibbāna exists, may the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) of a noble person who attains that Nibbāna and uproots all perversions also be perverted according to your view!"

## Commentary on the Discourse on Perversion (Viparīta-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Certainty (Niyāma-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

428-431. Now is the Discourse on Certainty (Niyāma-kathā). Therein, because the Blessed One knows of a person who will enter the certainty of rightness (sammatta-niyāma), "This person is capable of realizing the Dhamma," there is the view of the Uttarāpathakas at present that "Even while being an unassured worldling (aniyata-puthujjana), there is knowledge in that person's continuity for reaching the certainty (niyāma) of the Path." Referring to them, the Sakavādin questions with "aniyatassa" (of the unassured), etc. Therein, "for reaching certainty" (niyāma-gamanāya) means the Path is called certainty; the meaning is for reaching the Path or for entering the Path. Referring to that knowledge of the worldling, seeing which the Blessed One knows "This person is capable," the Paravādin admits.
186:
Then, the Sakavādin, to show the unreasonableness of the Paravādin's doctrine, speaks the reverse cross-examination starting with "niyatassa" (of the assured). Among those problems, in the first problem, he (the Paravādin) rejects that there is no such thing as knowledge for reaching the "unassured state" (aniyāma) for a noble person who is assured by the Path. In the second problem, he admits it because of its non-existence. In the third problem, because he is asked "Is there not for the unassured person?", he rejects it as it contradicts his own view. Again, making the first problem the fourth, three problems are made by way of the assured noble person reaching certainty (niyāma), etc. Among those problems, in the first, because there is no knowledge for the sake of that same Stream-entry Path for a noble person already assured by the initial Path (Stream-entry), he rejects it. In the second, he admits it because of its non-existence. In the third, he rejects it because it contradicts his own view. Again, making the first problem the eighth, three problems are made by way of the unassured person reaching the "unassured state" (aniyāma), etc. The meaning of those problems should be understood in the same manner as already stated. Again, making the first problem the twelfth, problems such as "There is certainty" (atthi niyāmo), etc., which have that as their root, are made. In those problems, because the knowledge for reaching certainty is indeed the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), it is said "There is certainty" referring to that Path-knowledge. But the Paravādin rejects when it is called "certainty" and admits when it is called "knowledge." The same method applies to the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), etc. The negative (paccanīka) problem has a clear meaning. The phrase "of the one of the lineage" (gotrabhūno), etc., is spoken to show that if a person has not yet reached a certain knowledge, that knowledge does not exist for him. "The Blessed One knows" means He knows by the power of His own knowledge, not because that person's knowledge for reaching certainty is actually present. Therefore, the view of the Paravādin established by this reason is indeed unestablished.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Certainty (Niyāma-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on Analytical Insight (Paṭisambhidā-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

432-433. Now is the Discourse on Analytical Insight (Paṭisambhidā-kathā). Therein, referring to the Paravādins such as the Andhakas who hold the view that "Whatever knowledge noble ones have is entirely supramundane" and "All knowledge is analytical insight (paṭisambhidā)," there are the questions of the Sakavādin and the admissions of the Paravādin. In the problems of conventional knowledge (sammuti-ñāṇa), he rejects referring to the knowledge of attaining meditative absorption in the conventional designation of the earth-kasiṇa, but admits referring to the knowledge of grammar/language (nirutti-ñāṇa). In the problem "Whatever conventional...", he rejects referring to worldlings. In the problems of knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), he rejects referring to the knowledge of a worldling, but admits referring to the knowledge of a noble one. In the problems "All wisdom" (sabbā paññā), etc., he rejects referring to the wisdom that knows the kasiṇa-attainment, but admits referring to supramundane wisdom. The phrase "attainment of earth-kasiṇa" (pathavīkasiṇa-samāpatti), etc., is spoken for the purpose of asking, "Is all the wisdom that exists in these many instances analytical insight?"
187:
Therefore, by the phrase "all knowledge" (sabbaṃ ñāṇaṃ), because all supramundane wisdom is analytical insight (paṭisambhidā), the word "all" is established together with the four fruits which are the results of the path.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Analytical Insight.

## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Knowledge

434-435. Now is the Discussion of Conventional Knowledge. In that discussion, there are two truths: conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) and ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca). However, those opponents (such as the Andhakas) who do not make this distinction and claim that the knowledge of conventional truth also "has only truth as its object" simply because of the common name "truth"—those people hold an improper view. To purify their doctrine, this discussion was initiated (by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa). In this discussion, the question beginning with "It should not be said" (na vattabbaṃ) is the opponent's question, and the one who gives the admission with reference to ultimate truth is the proponent (sakavādin). "In conventional truth" (sammutisaccasmiṃ) means occurring in what is conventionally designated (such as the earth-kasiṇa, etc.). Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative, meaning "conventional truth". The question "Does conventional knowledge have only truth as its object?" is the proponent's question, and the admission is the opponent's. Then, to refute that opponent by saying, "If that knowledge, without distinction, has only truth as its object, then one should be able to perform the comprehension of suffering (dukkha-pariññā), etc., with that knowledge," the proponent said the words beginning with "With that knowledge" (tena ñāṇena).

## Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Knowledge.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Mind as Object

436-438. Now is the Discussion of Mind as Object. In that discussion, taking only the phrase "knowledge of others' minds" (cetopariya-ñāṇa), those opponents (such as the present-day Andhakas) hold the view that "that knowledge has only the mind as its object." With reference to them, the proponent asks and the opponent admits. Then, to refute that opponent by saying, "When one knows a mind by way of lust, etc., lust and so on also become objects for him; therefore, it should not be said that that knowledge has only the mind as its object," the proponent initiated the words beginning with "Is there not anyone?" (nanu atthi koci). "In the object of contact" (phassārammaṇe) means occurring in the object known as contact (phassa). The same method applies to terms like "feeling as object" (vedanārammaṇa), etc. Again, when asked, "Should it not be said that it is knowledge having contact as its object?" for a person who attends to the characteristic of touching (phusana-lakkhaṇa) of contact...
188:
...he admits that contact alone is the object for one who attends to the characteristic of touching. When asked, "Is this knowledge having contact as its object a knowledge in the comprehension of contact?" he denies it because there is no such Sutta passage. The same method applies to feeling (vedanā), etc. Now, to establish their own view by showing the very knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) upon which they rely, they say, "Is there not knowledge of others' minds?" and so on. Although that view is established by firmly adhering to mere words, it remains unestablished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Mind as Object.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Future.

439-440. Now is the Discussion of Knowledge of the Future. In that discussion, the "future" is both immediate (anantara) and non-immediate. Among these two, there is certainly no knowledge of the immediate object. Just as there is no knowledge of the immediate object, there is also no knowledge of a mind included within a single thought-process (vīthi) or a single impulsion (javana). In this discussion, with reference to the opponents like the Andhakas who desire that there is knowledge of the entire future, the proponent asks and the opponent admits. Thereafter, to challenge that opponent by saying, "According to your view, there is knowledge of the future; with that knowledge, do you know the immediate future by way of its root, etc.?" the proponent said the words beginning with "The future from its root" (anāgataṃ mūlato).

In that context, all the words beginning with "from the root" (mūlato) are synonyms for "cause" (kāraṇa). A cause produces its own effect; because that effect is established in that cause, it is called "root" (mūla). Because the effect proceeds from that cause, it is called "condition" (hetu). That same cause is called "source" (nidāna) because it hands over the effect, as if saying, "Here, take this effect." Because the effect arises well from that cause, it is called "origin" (sambhava); because it begins from it, it is called "source" (pabhava). Because the effect originates in that cause, or because that cause makes the effect originate well, it is called "origination" (samuṭṭhāna). Because that same cause brings the effect forward, it is called "nutriment" (āhāra). It is called "object" (ārammaṇa) in the sense of not being discarded by the effect. Because this effect arises depending on that very cause, it is called "condition" (paccaya). Because the effect arises well from that cause, it is called "arising" (samudaya).

Since the immediate mind cannot be known through these modes such as the root, etc., he denies it by saying, "It should not be said so." "The future as root-condition" (anāgataṃ hetupaccayataṃ) means: do you know the state of being a root-condition (hetupaccaya) in the immediate future mind? The meaning is: do you know those states (dhammā) which are root-conditions in that future mind? The same method applies to the remaining terms. The words beginning with "of the change-of-lineage" (gotrabhuno) are spoken to show specifically that future in which knowledge does not arise.
189:
The Sutta beginning with "Pāṭaliputtassa" was brought forward (by the opponent) to show that knowledge arises in the distant future. However, since this Sutta does not establish that knowledge exists in the entirety of the future, it does not constitute a valid proof.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Future

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Present

441-442. Now follows the Discussion on Knowledge of the Present. In this context, based on the statement, "When all formations are seen as impermanent, that seeing knowledge is also seen as impermanent," those such as the Andhakas hold the view that "knowledge exists in the present without distinction." Referring to them, the question "In the present?" (Paṭuppanne) is the question of the proponent (Sakavādī), and the affirmation is that of the opponent (Paravādī).

Then, for the purpose of challenging the opponent, the proponent asks the investigative question beginning with "By that" (Tena): "If knowledge exists in the present without distinction, that knowledge should also exist in the momentary present. If this were so, since two knowledges cannot exist simultaneously, would that knowledge be known by that same knowledge?" Among those questions, in the first question, the rejection that "it is not possible to know that knowledge by that same knowledge" is the rejection of the opponent. In the second question, the affirmation with reference to the continuity present (santati-paccuppanna) is the affirmation of that same opponent. The meaning is that one who sees dissolution (bhaṅga) in succession sees the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution by that very knowledge of contemplation of dissolution. In problems such as "He knows that knowledge by that knowledge," the same method applies. The statements such as "He touches that contact with that contact" are also spoken to prevent the opponent from finding an opening. The opponent stated the words beginning with "In all formations..." to establish their own view. In that statement, the affirmation of the proponent is with the meaning that "that knowledge is seen by way of method (naya), not by way of object (ārammaṇa)." Therefore, even though it is established in this way, the opponent's view remains unestablished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Present

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of Fruition

443-444. Now follows the Discussion on Knowledge of Fruition. In this context, "The Buddhas teach the Dhamma for beings to attain Noble Fruition, and the disciples also teach the Dhamma." Thus, by this similarity, just as the Buddhas...
190:
Just as the Buddhas teach the Dhamma for beings to attain Noble Fruition, the disciples also teach the Dhamma. In this same manner, those such as the Andhakas hold the view that disciples also possess knowledge of the fruition to be attained by various beings, just as the Buddhas do. Referring to them, the question "Does a disciple (have knowledge of fruition)?" is asked by the proponent, and the opponent affirms it. Then, to challenge the opponent, the proponent asks: "If a disciple has knowledge of fruition, just as the Buddhas—even though the Fruition of Stream-entry is the same—designate the distinctions of fruition by the power of their own knowledge as 'This person is an ekabījī, this person is a kolaṅkola, this person is a sattakkhattuparama,' can the disciple also designate in such a way according to your view?" Thus, he asks, "Does the disciple designate the distinctions of fruition?" The opponent rejects this.

The passage beginning with "Does the disciple have the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of fruition (phala-paropariyatti-ñāṇa)?" is spoken to inquire about the causal knowledge, given that there is knowledge of fruition. The meaning here is: The Buddhas possess what is called the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of fruition, which is the understanding of the high or low status of fruitions, such as "This fruition is superior, this fruition is inferior." Likewise, they possess the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties (indriya-paropariyatti) and persons (puggala-paropariyatti). Because of the existence of these knowledges, they know various fruitions by the power of the respective faculties of various persons. The question is: "According to your view, does the disciple also possess these knowledges of superiority and inferiority?"

The passages beginning with "Does the disciple have the designation of aggregates (khandha-paññatti)?" are spoken to challenge: "If, according to your view, the disciple has knowledge of fruition like the Buddhas, then these designations must exist for that disciple. Does the disciple have these designations? Is that disciple able to know or designate these designations by his own power?" The passage beginning with "Is the disciple a Conqueror (Jina)?" is spoken to challenge: "If the disciple has knowledge of fruition like the Buddhas, then in that case, is that disciple himself a Conqueror?" In the problem "Is the disciple one who brings about the unarisen (Path)?" the same method applies. In the problem "Is he one without knowledge (aññāṇī)?" it is rejected because ignorance (avijjā), which is called non-knowledge (aññāṇa), has been destroyed. However, it does not mean that the disciple has knowledge of fruition like the Buddhas. Therefore, the opponent's doctrine is indeed without foundation.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of Fruition

## 6. Chaṭṭhavagga
## 1. Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā
445-447. Now follows the discussion on the Fixed Course (Niyāmakathā). In this discussion, the Noble Path is called the 'Fixed Course' (Niyāma) because of the word: "He is capable of entering the fixed course, the rightness in wholesome states." However, even though that Path arises and then ceases, the person does not become 'unfixed' (aniyata). Therefore, some, such as the Andhakas, hold the view: "That fixed course is unconditioned in the sense of being eternal." With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other (Paravādī) affirms. Then, wishing to show that "If that fixed course were unconditioned, it should be of such a nature (as Nibbāna)," he said "Nibbānaṃ," and so on. The comparative questioning is only for the purpose of making the meaning clear.

The statement beginning with "Atthi keci" is said for the purpose of showing the conditioned nature of the fixed course. To the question "Is the Path unconditioned?", he denies it because that Path has the nature of arising and ceasing. To the question "Is the fixed course conditioned?", he denies it with reference to the persistence of the 'fixed' status even when the Path has ceased. In the problems such as the 'Fixed Course of Stream-entry' (Sotāpattiniyāma), the meaning should be understood in this same way, both by the method of direct order and inverse order. When asked "Are there five unconditioneds?", he denies it as he does not see any Pali passage mentioning five unconditioneds. When asked a second time, he affirms it because of the name 'fixed course' for the four right fixed courses and because of the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna. The problem of the 'Fixed Course of Wrongness' (Micchattaniyāma) is stated for the purpose of showing that it is inappropriate for something to be unconditioned merely by the word 'fixed course'.
## Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā.
## 2. Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā
Now follows the discussion on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādakathā). Therein, some, such as the Pubbaseliyas and the Mahīśāsakas, hold the view: "Dependent Origination is unconditioned," because of the word in the Nidānavagga: "Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element remains stable, the stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitatā)," and so on. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other affirms.
192:
The questions beginning with "Is ignorance unconditioned?" are stated for the purpose of showing that ignorance and so on are themselves Dependent Origination. The reason why each factor among those factors of Dependent Origination is called "Dependent Origination" has already been stated in the Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga.

In the phrase "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), the view was established by a certain sutta mentioning "stability of Dhamma" (dhammaṭṭhitatā) and so on; this is stated for the purpose of refuting that view by showing the true meaning of that very sutta. The meaning here is this: that 'element' which was mentioned below as "That element remains stable, the stability of Dhamma, the fixed law of Dhamma," does not exist as a separate, single element apart from ignorance and so on. Indeed, this name "stability of Dhamma" and so on is merely a name for the conditions such as ignorance. For, whether the Tathāgata arises or does not arise, volitional formations come into being from ignorance, and consciousness and so on come into being from volitional formations and so on. Therefore, in this term "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," ignorance is called "stability of Dhamma" because it stands as the cause for the states of volitional formations. Because it is the fixed law (niyāmatā) for those very states by way of being their cause, ignorance itself is called "fixed law of Dhamma" (dhammaniyāmatā). The Paravādī asks, "Is that ignorance also unconditioned, and is Nibbāna also unconditioned?" The Paravādī affirms according to his own view, and when asked again, "Are there two unconditioneds?", he denies it due to the absence of a sutta, but then affirms it again according to his own view. In the remaining terms, this same method applies. The meaning similar to what was stated below should be understood in the same way as the method already stated.

## Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 3. Saccakathāvaṇṇanā

452-454. Now follows the discussion on the Truths (Saccakathā). In this discussion, based on the sutta, "Monks, these four are true, not false," some, such as the Pubbaseliyas, hold the view: "The Four Truths are eternal and unconditioned." With reference to them, there is the questioning of the Sakavādī and the affirmation of the Paravādī. This is the intention of that Paravādī: in the truths of suffering, origination, and the path, the 'substance-truth' (vatthu-sacca) such as birth and so on is conditioned, but the 'characteristic-truth' (lakkhaṇa-sacca) such as oppression (bādhana) and so on is unconditioned. In the truth of cessation, there is no such thing as 'substance-truth'; it is purely unconditioned. Therefore, he says "Āmantā" (Yes). However, that view is merely the view of that Paravādī. This is because that Paravādī desires the truth of suffering to be the substance-truth; likewise, he desires the truth of origination and the truth of the path to be substance-truths. Those characteristics of oppression, source, and deliverance which belong to these three truths are called 'characteristic-truth'. Nevertheless, there are no such things as suffering and so on apart from the characteristics of oppression and so on. In the Pali passages beginning with "Tāṇāni," the meaning should be understood in the same way as the method already stated.
193:
In the question "Is it the truth of suffering?", one affirms by referring to the characteristic (such as oppression, etc.) according to one's own doctrine. In the question "Is it suffering?", one denies by referring to the basis (such as birth, etc.). After this question, all the pure questions (suddhika-pañhā) and comparative questions (sandandana-pañhā) should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text. The sutta brought forward at the end to establish one's own doctrine is just like one not brought forward, because its meaning has been wrongly grasped.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Truths (Saccakatha-vaṇṇanā)

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Formless (Aruppakatha-vaṇṇanā)

455-456. Now comes the Discussion of the Formless. Therein, for those who, relying on the statement "The four formless states are imperturbable (āneñja)," hold the view that "All those states are also unconditioned (asankhata)," referring to them, the question "Is it the sphere of infinite space?" is the question of the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is that of the other (the Paravādī). The remaining meaning here is clear. The supporting sutta is also just like one not brought forward, because it was brought forward without understanding its meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Formless (Aruppakatha-vaṇṇanā)

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation (Nirodhasamapatti-vaṇṇanā)

457-459. Now comes the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation. Therein, the "attainment of cessation" is the non-occurrence of the four mental aggregates. However, because it is produced when being produced and attained when being attained, it is called "produced" (nipphanna). Yet, due to the absence of the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned, it should not be called either "conditioned" or "unconditioned." Therein, for those who hold the view that "Because it is not conditioned, it is unconditioned," such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas, referring to them, the question "Is it the attainment of cessation?" is the question of the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is that of the other. The words beginning with "they produce" are spoken only in the sense of attainment and acquisition. Just as conditioned things like matter (rūpa) are produced, no one can be said to produce that attainment of cessation in that way. By the Pali "nirodhā vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ," the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) should be understood. As for the unconditioned...
194:
Because emerging from that attainment of cessation does not exist, he denies it. By the words "tena hi" (if so), they hold the view that because it is not conditioned, it is therefore unconditioned. However, although it is said that this reason of not being conditioned is not a reason for the attainment of cessation being unconditioned, it is as if it were not said.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation (Nirodhasamapatti-vaṇṇanā)

## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Space (Akasakatha-vaṇṇanā)

460-462. Now comes the Discussion of Space. Therein, space is of three kinds: delimited space (paricchedākāsa), space abstracted from a kasina (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa), and open space (ajaṭākāsa). The name "empty space" (tucchākāsa) is also a name for that open space. Among those three, delimited space is conditioned (sankhata), while the other two are merely concepts (paññatti). For those, such as the Uttarāpathakas and the Mahisāsakas, who hold the view that "Because the two kinds of space are not conditioned, they are unconditioned," referring to them, the Sakavādī asks "Is space unconditioned?" and the Paravādī affirms. The remaining words in this discussion have a clear meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Space (Akasakatha-vaṇṇanā)

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Space as Visible (Akaso Sanidassano-vaṇṇanā)

463-464. Now comes the Discussion of Space as Visible. Therein, for those such as the Andhakas who, relying on the occurrence of the thought-process that knows in keyholes and so on, hold the view that "All open space is visible (sanidassana)," referring to them, the Sakavādī asks "Is space visible?" and the Paravādī affirms. After that, to challenge that Paravādī, the words beginning with "rūpaṃ" (matter) are spoken, meaning "If it were visible, it would be of such a nature." In the questions beginning with "dependent on the eye," he denies because there is no such sutta (scripture) of this nature, and affirms by relying on the mental apprehension of the space between two beams and so on. In the case of "the interval between two trees," having seen the form of the trees with the eye, because there is no visible form in the interval, only mind-door consciousness (manodvāra-viññāṇa) arises as "space," not eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa). In other cases too, this is the same method. Therefore, this evidence does not constitute valid proof.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Space as Visible (Akaso Sanidassano-vaṇṇanā)
