## 2. Commentary on the Section of the Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā)
33-34. In the Pavattivāra of this Dhamma Yamaka, in the forward method (anuloma-naya) of the section on persons (puggala-vāra) in the present time: "For whom wholesome states arise, do unwholesome states arise for him? Or else, for whom unwholesome states arise, do wholesome states arise for him?" Thus, there are three pairs: two pairs with wholesome states as the root and one pair with unwholesome states as the root. In the reverse method (paṭiloma-naya) of that Pavattivāra, and in the section on locations (okāsa-vāra) etc., it should be understood in this same way. Thus, in all sections of this Dhamma Yamaka, the count of pairs should be understood by way of three pairs each. In the determination of the meaning, there is this following characteristic. How? In this Dhamma Yamaka...
336:
In the Great Chapter on Occurrence (Pavatti-mahāvāra) of the Dhamma Yamaka, in these Chapters on Arising and Ceasing (Uppādavāra and Nirodhavāra) which state "they arise, they cease," wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) states are obtained certainly only at the time of the course of life (pavatti), and not at the times of death (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paᅩisandhi). Indeterminate (abyākata) states, however, are obtained at all three times: during the course of life, at death, and at rebirth-linking. Thus, in this Yamaka, whatever state is obtained in whatever instance, the determination should be understood in those instances by virtue of that state. 

Herein, this is the method-entry (nayamukha): Since wholesome and unwholesome states cannot arise at the same single moment, the negation "No" (no) is made. The statement "and indeterminate states [arise]" is said by virtue of materiality produced by consciousness (cittasamuᅩᅩhāna-rũpa).

35-36. The statement "In whatever place wholesome states do not arise" is said with reference to the non-percipient realm (asaa-bhava). For that reason, the answer "Yes" (āmantā) is given here. The statement "they arise" is also said with reference to the non-percipient realm itself. Since there is no realm or location where indeterminate states do not arise, the rejection "There is none" (natthi) is made.

"In the second unwholesome" means in the second impulsion (javana) among the impulsions of attachment to existence (nikanti-javana) that arise enjoying existence. "When occurring in the second consciousness" means when occurring in the second life-continuum (bhavaᅄga) consciousness after rebirth-linking; or, treating rebirth-linking and the life-continuum as one by virtue of being resultant (vipāka), it refers to the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) that occurs before the impulsion of attachment to existence. Since that mind-door adverting consciousness is a functional (kiriya) consciousness, it is called the "second" after the resultant in the indeterminate class (abyākata-jāti).

The statement "Immediately after which consciousness the Path of Arahatship [will arise]" is said with reference to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhũ) consciousness. The statement "wholesome states will arise" is said with reference to those states of the Path of Arahatship itself.

The statement "at the moment of arising of that consciousness immediately after which they will attain the Path of Arahatship" is said by virtue of the class of consciousness (cittajāti). This characteristic is also obtained at the moment of arising of the preparatory (parikamma), access (upacāra), and conformity (anuloma) consciousnesses which occur below that life-continuum produced by a single adverting of that same class of consciousness.

In the Chapter on Ceasing (Nirodhavāra) as well, since wholesome and unwholesome states cannot cease simultaneously, it is said "No" (no). By this method-entry, the determination in all places should be understood.

## 10. Indriyayamaka

Now, following the explanation of the Dhamma Yamaka, there is the commentary on the Indriya Yamaka, which is taught after the Dhamma Yamaka by encompassing a portion of those states such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, as taught in the Mūla Yamaka, according to what is obtainable. In this Indriya Yamaka, the determination of the Pali text should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Khandha Yamaka and others. Indeed, in this Indriya Yamaka, the three Great Sections (Mahāvāra) such as the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra), as well as the remaining Intermediate Sections (Antaravāra) along with the divisions of time and so forth, are just similar to those appearing in the Khandha Yamaka and others. The distinction, however, is that due to the plurality of the faculties (indriya), there are even more pairs (yamaka) than in the Dhātu Yamaka.

Just as in the Section on Persons (Puggalavāra) and others mentioned below, in the methods based on the eye-base (cakkhāyatana-mūla) and the eye-element (cakkhudhātu-mūla), the tongue-base (jivhāyatana) and body-base (kāyāyatana) were not paired with the eye-base and eye-element, and the pairs based on the tongue-base and body-base were not taken at all; likewise, in this Indriya Yamaka, in the method based on the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya-mūla), the tongue-faculty (jivhindriya) and body-faculty (kāyindriya) are not paired, and the pairs based on the tongue-faculty and body-faculty are not taken. The reason for not taking these pairs should be understood in the same way as stated in that Āyatana Yamaka. As for the mind-faculty (manindriya), just as it is paired with those based on the eye-faculty and so forth, it also reaches a pairing with those based on the female-faculty (itthindriya) and so forth; therefore, it should be understood that it is not paired according to the order set in the matrix (mātikā), but is paired at the end with all faculties starting from the eye-faculty. The female-faculty, male-faculty (purisindriya), and life-faculty (jīvitindriya) are paired with the eye-faculty. The pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya), pain-faculty (dukkhindriya), and displeasure-faculty (domanassindriya) are not taken because they do not exist at the moment of rebirth (paṭisandhi). The joy-faculty (somanassindriya) and equanimity-faculty (upekkhindriya) are taken because of their evident existence at the moment of rebirth. Likewise, the five faculties starting with the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) are taken. The three supramundane (lokuttara) faculties are not taken precisely because of their absence at the moment of rebirth. Thus, the counting of pairs in the method based on the eye-faculty in this Indriya Yamaka should be understood by way of those faculties that are taken. As it is in this eye-faculty method, so it is everywhere. However, the pairs should not be counted by way of those faculties that are not taken. Or, if one wishes to count them, they should be counted by way of void questions (mogha-puccha). Thus, first of all, the determination of the Pali text in all sections should be understood.

## Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā)

1-86. In the determination of the meaning here, this following statement is the opening of the method: The words "For those with eyes who are not women" are spoken by way of the Brahmas of the Retinue of Brahma (Brahmapārisajja) and so forth who possess form, as well as by way of males and neuter beings. Indeed, for those fine-material Brahmas and neuter beings, the female-faculty does not arise. The words "For those with eyes who are not men" are spoken by way of the Brahmas who possess form, as well as by way of females and neuter beings. Indeed, for those fine-material Brahmas, females, and neuter beings, the male-faculty does not arise. The words "For those being reborn without eyes, the life-faculty arises for them" are spoken with reference to beings in the one-constituent (ekavokāra) realm, the four-constituent (catuvokāra) realm, and those in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) who lack eyes. The words "For those with eyes without joy (somanassa)" are spoken by way of the four Great Resultant rebirths accompanied by equanimity...
338:
are spoken by way of the four Great Resultant rebirths accompanied by equanimity. "For those with eyes without equanimity" is spoken by way of beings whose rebirth is accompanied by joy. "For those with equanimity without eyes" is spoken by way of rootless (ahetuka) rebirth. "For rootless individuals" is spoken because of the absence of the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) and so forth along with the rootless rebirth-consciousness. For in that rootless rebirth-consciousness, faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), and wisdom (paññā) are definitely absent. Concentration (samādhi) and energy (vīriya), however, do not reach the status of faculties (indriya). "For those with roots (sahetuka) without eyes" is spoken in connection with womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) individuals and immaterial (arūpī) Brahmas. This is because there are no other rooted individuals without eyes besides the womb-born and immaterial Brahmas. "For those with eyes who are rootless" is spoken in connection with individuals who have spontaneous rebirth (opapātika) in the woeful states (apāya). "For those with eyes dissociated from knowledge" is spoken by way of individuals with double-rooted (duhetuka) rebirth in the sense-sphere. "For those with eyes associated with knowledge" is spoken with reference to Brahmas with form and sense-sphere devas and humans. "For those associated with knowledge without eyes" is spoken with reference to immaterial Brahmas and triple-rooted (tihetuka) womb-born individuals.

In the pairs based on the life-faculty (jīvitindriya-mūlaka), "For those being reborn without joy" is spoken with reference to both types of life-faculties (physical and mental). "At the arising moment of consciousness dissociated from joy during the course of existence (pavatti)" is spoken with reference to the mental life-faculty. By this method, the connection of the life-faculty should be understood in all places by way of rebirth and the course of existence. In the pairs based on the joy-faculty and so forth, the meaning should also be taken only by way of rebirth and the course of existence. In the reverse method (paṭiloma-naya) and in the section on cessation (nirodhavāra), the non-arising and cessation of these and other states should be understood in all three times: death (cuti), rebirth (paṭisandhi), and the course of existence (pavatti), according to what is obtainable.

In the Section on the Future (Anāgatavāra), "by this state only" means by this male state only, without becoming female in the interval, and only by taking rebirth as a male. "Having shown some existences, they will attain Parinibbāna" means that after taking some rebirths and without reaching the female state, they will attain Parinibbāna. In the second question also, this is the same method.

In the Section on the Present and Past (Paccuppannātītavāra), regarding the dissolution moment (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, the phrase "the mind-faculty (manindriya) has also not arisen before" should be understood not by way of passing the arising moment as in the Citta Yamaka, but by way of it never having arisen before in that existence. By this opening of the method, the determination of the meaning in the entire Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) should be understood.

## Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding

435-482. In the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra), among the pairs (yamaka) having the eye faculty as the root, only one pair—the eye as the root and the ear as the object—is shown. Although only this one pair is shown, the remaining mundane indeterminate (lokiya-abyākata) faculties and those mixed with mundane indeterminates are also to be fully understood (pariññeyya). Therefore, even if they are not directly shown, they are indeed shown by means of this eye-ear pair. Because the unwholesome (akusala) must certainly be abandoned, the wholesome (kusala) must certainly be developed within oneself, and the supramundane indeterminate (lokuttara-abyākata) must be realized, it is said: 'He abandons the faculty of grief (domanassindriya),' 'He develops the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya),' and 'He realizes the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya).'

Regarding the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), there is an aspect to be developed and an aspect to be realized; it is taken here only by way of the aspect of development.

In the passage (starting with 'develops the faculty of final knowledge'), 'two persons' refers to the person possessed of the path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimaggasamaṅgī) and the person possessed of the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggasamaṅgī). Among these two, one (the Once-returner) is said not to be abandoning the faculty of grief because he is unable to cut it off completely. The other (the Arahant) is said not to be abandoning it because he has already abandoned hatred. In the passage 'He does not fully understand the eye faculty,' it means he is not currently fully understanding it because he is unable to bring about its non-arising. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all answers.

## Concluding Remarks

By this much sequence of words—
Standing in the instruction of that Blessed One, who has completed his task of the sixteen-fold path, even a group of young women, having well-established discipline, can transcend the authority of Yama.
In the midst of the assembly of devas in the city of devas, by that Supreme Deva of all devas, whose body hairs are pure and grow singly (not in pairs), the text named Yamaka was made known.
To show the method of defining the Pali text and the system of meaning in the questions and answers of that Yamaka, I have undertaken this Yamaka Commentary.

## Commentary on the Book of Paṭṭhāna
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
The Buddha, the God above gods, worshipped by gods and asuras, having a pure restraint of body, speech, and mind, after teaching the Book of Yamaka,

immediately following that Yamaka, which is profound in both meaning and text, the Great Hero, the seventh Sage,

who knows the cessation of mind and matter (Nibbāna), taught the book named Paṭṭhāna, a teaching adorned with extremely profound methods.

Now, as the sequence for the commentary on that Paṭṭhāna has arrived, I shall explain it; listen to that explanation with a concentrated mind.

## Explanation of the Enumeration of Conditions
Indeed, in the Anuloma Paṭṭhāna, the Rightly Self-Awakened One set forth the Tika-paṭṭhāna based on the twenty-two triads (tikas), and the Duka-paṭṭhāna based on the one hundred dyads (dukas). After that, taking the twenty-two triads and inserting them into the hundred dyads, He showed the Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna. After that, taking the hundred dyads and inserting them into the twenty-two triads, He showed the Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna. By inserting triads into triads only, He showed the Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna. And by inserting dyads into dyads only, He showed the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna. Thus—

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna, the supreme Duka-paṭṭhāna,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
In the Anuloma (Positive) mode, there are six extremely profound methods.
342:
In the Paccaṇīya Paṭṭhāna as well, based on the twenty-two triads, it is called Tika-paṭṭhāna; based on the hundred dyads, it is called Duka-paṭṭhāna; by inserting the twenty-two triads into the hundred dyads, it is called Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna; by inserting the hundred dyads into the twenty-two triads, it is called Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna; by inserting triads into triads only, it is called Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna; and by inserting dyads into dyads only, it is called Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna. In this way, in the Paccaṇīya (Negative) mode also, the Paṭṭhāna was shown by six methods. Therefore, it is said:

"The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna, the supreme Duka-paṭṭhāna,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
In the Paccaṇīya mode, there are six extremely profound methods."

After that, in the Anuloma-paccaṇīya (Positive-Negative) mode also, six methods were shown in this same manner. Therefore, He said:

"The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna, the supreme Duka-paṭṭhāna,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
In the Anuloma-paccaṇīya mode, there are six extremely profound methods."

Immediately following that, in the Paccaṇīya-anuloma (Negative-Positive) mode also, it was set forth by these same six methods. Therefore, He said:

"The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna, the supreme Duka-paṭṭhāna,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
In the Paccaṇīya-anuloma mode, there are six extremely profound methods."

Thus, there are 6 Paṭṭhānas in Anuloma, 6 in Paccaṇīya, 6 in Anuloma-paccaṇīya, and 6 in Paccaṇīya-anuloma; this book is called "The Great Book of Paṭṭhāna, the Collection of the Twenty-four Universal Paṭṭhānas" (Catuvisati-samantapaṭṭhāna-samodhāna-paṭṭhāna-mahāpakaraṇa).

Since it is called "The Great Book of Paṭṭhāna, the Collection of the Twenty-four Universal Paṭṭhānas" due to the collection of those twenty-four universal Paṭṭhānas, the meaning of the name of those universal Paṭṭhānas and of this book should first be understood as follows.
343:
In what sense is it called "Paṭṭhāna"? It is called Paṭṭhāna in the sense of being a condition (paccaya) of various types. For the prefix "Pa" indicates the meaning of various types, and the word "ṭhāna" indicates the meaning of condition. Indeed, in such passages as "skillfulness in conditions and non-conditions" (ṭhānāṭṭhāna-kusalatā), the condition is called "ṭhāna". Thus, because it is taught by way of various types of conditions, each one among these twenty-four Paṭṭhānas is called Paṭṭhāna. However, because it is a collection of these Paṭṭhānas, this entire book should be known as Paṭṭhāna.

Another method: In what sense is it called "Paṭṭhāna"? It is called Paṭṭhāna in the sense of analytical division (vibhajana). In the passage that comes as "pointing out, setting forth (paṭṭhapana), opening, analyzing (vibhajana), making clear," Paṭṭhāna is evident in the sense of analytical division. Thus, because states such as the wholesome are analyzed by way of root-condition (hetu-paccaya) and so on, each one among these twenty-four Paṭṭhānas is called Paṭṭhāna. However, because it is a collection of these Paṭṭhānas, this entire book should be known as Paṭṭhāna.

Another method: In what sense is it called "Paṭṭhāna"? It is called Paṭṭhāna in the sense of proceeding (paṭṭhita). The meaning is in the sense of going (gamana). In the passage that comes as "the cows that have proceeded (paṭṭhita) from the cow-pen," by the word "paṭṭhāna" the cows that have proceeded are meant; that word, in meaning, is simply "going". Thus, in books such as the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, which have methods that are not very extensive, the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa), which does not have an unhindered proceeding, gains an extensive method in states such as the wholesome, which are divided by root-condition and so on; because it occurs as a proceeding without hindrance, each one among these twenty-four Paṭṭhānas is called Paṭṭhāna. However, because it is a collection of these Paṭṭhānas, this entire book should be known as Paṭṭhāna.

Among those, in the Anuloma mode, because it is first taught in connection with the triads (tikas), it is called Tika-paṭṭhāna. If that term Tika-paṭṭhāna is analyzed: it is Tika-paṭṭhāna because the various conditions for the triads exist here. The meaning is that in this teaching, there are various types of conditions for the triads. In the second alternative also, it is Tika-paṭṭhāna because it is the teaching that extensively analyzes the triads. In the third alternative, the triads themselves, which have attained extensiveness because they are divided by root-condition and so on, are the Paṭṭhāna, hence Tika-paṭṭhāna. The meaning is that it is the ground for the unhindered proceeding of Omniscient Knowledge. In the Duka-paṭṭhāna and so on, the method is the same. Having thus understood the six Paṭṭhānas in the Anuloma mode, they should be understood in the same way in the Paccaṇīya and other modes.

Since these become twenty-four by being six each in the Anuloma, Paccaṇīya, Anuloma-paccaṇīya, and Paccaṇīya-anuloma modes in their entirety, therefore "the twenty-four..."
344:
They are called the "Twenty-four Universal Relations" (Samantapaṭṭhāna). Thus, by the combination of these twenty-four Universal Relations, also known as the Minor Relations (Khuddakapaṭṭhāna), this treatise is named the Great Treatise of Relations (Paṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇa).

Because this Great Treatise of Relations is presented based on the Triads (Tika) and so forth, it is referred to as the "Relation of Triads (Tikapaṭṭhāna), Relation of Dyads (Dukapaṭṭhāna) ... Relation of Dyad-Dyads (Dukadukapaṭṭhāna)." Without dealing directly with those Triads etc., the Chapter on the Laying Down of the Matrix (Mātikānikkhepavāra)—which sets forth the conditions by which those Triads etc. are analyzed—was taught at the beginning. The name "Chapter on the Analysis of Conditions" (Paccayavibhaṅgavāra) is also a name for that same Mātikānikkhepavāra. That Mātikānikkhepavāra is twofold: by way of Brief Exposition (Uddesa) and Detailed Exposition (Niddesa). This Pali passage of the Nikkhepavāra, "Root-condition (hetupaccaya) ... Non-disappearance-condition (avigatapaccaya)," is the Uddesa, which is the summary of headings.

In that Uddesa, it is called "root-condition" (hetupaccaya) because it is both a root (hetu) and a condition (paccaya). It means it is a condition by being a root, or a condition in the state of a root. The same method should be understood for object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and others. In the term "hetupaccaya," the word "hetu" is a designation for a part of a sentence, a cause, or a source/root. In the world, a part of a sentence is called a hetu. In the Dispensation (Sāsana), however, in such Pali passages as "Those things which arise from a cause (hetuppabhavā)," hetu means cause (kāraṇa). In passages such as "There are three wholesome roots (hetū), three unwholesome roots (hetū)," hetu means root (mūla). It is this meaning of root (mūla) that is intended here.

In the term "paccaya," there is the following linguistic meaning: an effect arises depending on (paṭicca) this cause, therefore it is a condition (paccaya). The meaning is that it occurs without discarding that cause. Whatever state exists or arises depending on another state, the latter is said to be the condition (paccaya) for the former.

By way of characteristic, a condition has the characteristic of being helpful (upakāraka). Whatever state is helpful for the persistence or the arising of another state is called the condition for that state. The terms Paccaya, Hetu, Kāraṇa, Nidāna, Sambhava, and Pabhava are one in meaning but different in phrasing. Thus, it is called "hetu" in the sense of being a root, and "paccaya" in the sense of being helpful. Therefore, in brief, a state that is helpful in the sense of being a root is a root-condition (hetupaccaya).

It is the intention of the Teachers that this root-condition accomplishes the state of being wholesome etc., for wholesome states etc., just as rice seeds etc. accomplish the production of rice etc., and as the color of a gem etc. accomplish the luster of the gem. However, if this were the case, the nature of root-condition would not be established for the material forms produced by those roots. This is because that root-condition cannot accomplish the wholesome nature etc. of those material forms. Yet, it is not that it is not a condition for those material forms. Indeed, the Blessed One taught: "Roots are a condition for states associated with roots..."
345:
"...and for the material forms produced by them, by way of root-condition." (Even if the root-condition cannot accomplish the wholesome nature of those material forms), it is not that it is not a condition. Even without this root-condition, the indeterminate (abyākata) nature of rootless consciousnesses is established.

The wholesome nature etc. of rooted consciousnesses is also connected only with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and so forth; it is not connected solely with the associated root. If the wholesome nature etc. existed inherently only in the associated roots, then non-greed (alobha) associated with such a root would be either wholesome or indeterminate. Since non-greed can be both, one must seek the wholesome nature etc. in the roots just as one does in the associated states (as being dependent on other causes). If one takes the meaning of "root" (mūla) for the roots not by way of accomplishing the wholesome nature etc., but by way of accomplishing the state of being well-established, then there is no contradiction in meaning. For states that have obtained root-condition are firm and well-established like trees with deep roots. Rootless states, however, are not well-established, like moss the size of a sesame seed. Thus, a state that is helpful in the sense of a root, or helpful by accomplishing the state of being well-established, should be known as root-condition (hetupaccaya).

Following that root-condition, a state that is helpful by way of being an object is called object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya). That object-condition begins with "The visible-data base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element" and concludes with "Whatever state those states of consciousness and mental factors arise depending upon, those states are a condition for those states of consciousness and mental factors by way of object-condition." Therefore, there is no state that cannot be an object-condition. Just as a weak man can only rise or stand by leaning on a staff or a rope, so too consciousness and mental factors arise and persist only by taking an object such as a visible object. Therefore, all states that become objects for consciousness and mental factors should be known as object-condition.

A state that is helpful by way of being the chief is called predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya). That condition is twofold: conascent (sahajāta) and object (ārammaṇa). Therein, according to the words, "Desire-predominance is a condition for states associated with desire and the material forms produced by them by way of predominance-condition," the four states known as desire (chanda), energy (viriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā) should be known as conascent-predominance-condition. However, they do not act as predominants all at once. When the mind functions by making desire the leader and the chief, then only desire is the predominant, not the others. This same method applies to the remaining ones. Furthermore, whatever state mental states (arūpadhamma) function by giving it high regard, that state is their object-predominance-condition.
346:
Therefore, it was said: "By giving weight to whatever state, whatever states of mind and mental factors arise, those states are a condition for those states by way of predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya)."

A state that assists by way of being without interval is the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). A state that assists by way of being well-without-interval is the contiguity condition (samanantara-paccaya). Ancient teachers have explained these two conditions in many ways. The essence here is this: the fixed order of consciousness (citta-niyama), such as the arising of the mind-element (mano-dhātu) immediately after eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa), and the arising of the mind-consciousness-element (mano-viññāṇa-dhātu) immediately after the mind-element, is accomplished only by the power of the preceding consciousness and not by any other means. Therefore, only the state that is capable of producing a suitable arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) immediately after itself is called the proximity condition. For this reason, the Buddha said: "The proximity condition: the eye-consciousness-element and its associated states are a condition for the mind-element and its associated states by way of proximity condition," and so forth.

That which is the proximity condition is itself the contiguity condition. Here, there is a difference only in phrasing, as in the cases of 'accumulation' (upacaya) and 'continuity' (santati), or as in the pairs of 'designation' (adhivacana) and 'usage' (nirutti); however, there is no difference in meaning. As for the view of some teachers who say, "It is the proximity condition because of the absence of interval in substance (addhā), and it is the contiguity condition because of the absence of interval in time (kāla)," this contradicts such Pali passages as: "For one emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the wholesome state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) by way of contiguity condition." Even what they say there—that "the capability to produce states does not diminish, but because of being prevented by the power of meditation, states do not arise in immediate contiguity"—only proves the absence of temporal non-interval (i.e., that there is a time gap). We also say the same: that because of the power of meditation, there is no temporal non-interval there. And since there is no temporal non-interval, the status of contiguity condition is not appropriate. This is because, in their view, the contiguity condition exists only when there is no temporal interval. Therefore, without being dogmatic, one should understand the difference in these two conditions as being merely in phrasing and not in meaning. How? They are 'anantara' (proximity) because there is no interval (antara) between these states. They are 'samanantara' (contiguity) because they are 'well' (su) proximate, having no form or shape.

A state that assists by way of arising together while it is arising is the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), just as a lamp assists its light. That conascence condition is of six kinds by way of the mental aggregates and so on. As He said: "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of conascence condition. The four great essentials are a condition for one another... pe... At the moment of conception..."
347:
Mind and matter are for one another... The states of mind and mental factors are for the matter produced by mind... The great essentials are for derived matter (upādā-rūpa)... Material states are a condition for immaterial states at some times by way of conascence condition, and at other times they are not a condition by way of conascence condition (so it was said). This statement was made with reference only to the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu).

A state that assists by way of mutual production and support is the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya). It is like three sticks supporting each other. That mutuality condition is of three kinds by way of the mental aggregates and so on. How was it stated? "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of mutuality condition. The four great essentials... pe... At the moment of conception, mind and matter are a condition for one another by way of mutuality condition."

A state that assists by way of being a foundation and a support is the dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya). It is like the earth for trees or a canvas for a painting. This dependence condition should be understood in the same way as the method stated for the conascence condition: "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of dependence condition." Specifically, the sixth part in this dependence condition is analyzed thus: "The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness-element; the ear, nose, tongue, and body-bases are a condition for the body-consciousness-element and its associated states by way of dependence condition. That matter depending on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element arise, that matter is a condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and their associated states by way of dependence condition."

In this term 'strong dependence condition' (upanissaya-paccaya), first, the word-meaning (vacanattha) is: it is 'nissaya' (dependence) because it is depended upon by its own fruit due to the fruit's occurrence being dependent on that cause, and it is not rejected. Just as intense distress (āyāsa) is called 'upāyāsa', so a strong dependence is called 'upanissaya'. This is a designation for a powerful cause. Therefore, a state that assists by way of being a powerful cause should be understood as the strong dependence condition.

That strong dependence condition is of three kinds: object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya), proximity-strong-dependence (anantarūpanissaya), and natural-strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya). Among these three, object-strong-dependence is first analyzed without making it distinct from the object-predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipati) in the following way: "Having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, having performed the Uposatha duties, one reviews that merit, giving it weight; one reviews former good deeds, giving them weight; having emerged from jhāna, one reviews the jhāna, giving it weight; trainees (sekha) review change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), giving it weight; they review purification (vodāna), giving it weight; trainees, having emerged from the path, review the path, giving it weight." Among those instances of object-predominance and object-strong-dependence, whatever object the mind and mental factors arise giving weight to, that object is certainly the powerful object among the objects of those mind and mental factors.
348:
Thus, it is called ārammaṇādhipati (object-predominance) in the sense of being worthy of great regard, and it is called ārammaṇūpanissaya (object-strong-dependence) in the sense of being a powerful cause; in this way, the distinction between these two should be understood.

Anantarūpanissaya (proximity-strong-dependence) is also analyzed without making a distinction from anantara-paccaya (proximity condition) in such ways as: "Preceding wholesome aggregates are a condition for subsequent wholesome aggregates by way of strong-dependence condition." However, in the layout of the Mātikā (Table of Contents), there is a specific arrangement because anantara is taught as: "The eye-consciousness element and its associated states are a condition for the mind element and its associated states by way of proximity condition," and upanissaya is taught as: "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for subsequent wholesome states by way of strong-dependence condition." Although there is this specific arrangement, in terms of meaning, they reach a state of unity. Nevertheless, the state of anantara should be understood because of the ability to produce a suitable arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) immediately after itself, and the state of anantarūpanissaya should be understood because the preceding mind is powerful in producing the subsequent mind. For example, while a mind can arise without certain conditions like hetu-paccaya (root condition), there is no such thing as the arising of a mind without a preceding mind. Therefore, it is a powerful cause. Thus, it is called anantara-paccaya by virtue of the arising of a suitable consciousness immediately after itself, and it is called anantarūpanissaya by virtue of being a powerful cause; in this way, the distinction between these two should be understood.

Pakatūpanissaya (natural strong-dependence) means a well-prepared powerful cause. "Prepared" (pakata) refers to faith (saddhā), virtue (sīla), etc., produced within one's own continuity, or climate (utu), food (bhojana), etc., that one makes use of. Alternatively, it is called pakatūpanissaya because it is a strong dependence by its very nature; it means a cause that is not mixed with the object or proximity conditions. The variety of this pakatūpanissaya should be understood in many ways, such as: "Pakatūpanissaya—depending on faith, one gives gifts, undertakes virtue, performs the Uposatha duties, produces jhāna, produces insight (vipassanā), produces the Path (magga), produces direct knowledge (abhiññā), produces attainment (samāpatti). Depending on virtue, learning (suta), generosity (cāga), and wisdom (paññā), one gives gifts... produces attainment. Faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom are conditions for faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom by way of strong-dependence condition." Thus, these states like faith are "prepared" (pakata) and are also "strong dependence" (upanissaya) in the sense of being a powerful cause; hence they are called pakatūpanissaya.

A state that assists by having arisen earlier and being currently present is called purejāta-paccaya (pre-nascence condition). That purejāta-paccaya is of eleven kinds in the five doors by way of base (vatthu), object (ārammaṇa), and heart-base (hadayavatthu).
349:
Purejāta-paccaya is of eleven kinds. How is it taught? The eye-base (cakkhāyatana) is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and its associated states by way of pre-nascence condition. The ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, visible-data base, sound-base, odor-base, flavor-base, and tangible-data base are conditions for the body-consciousness element and its associated states by way of pre-nascence condition. The visible-data, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible-data bases are conditions for the mind element and its associated states by way of pre-nascence condition. Depending on which matter (the heart-base) the mind element and mind-consciousness element arise, that matter is a condition for the mind element and its associated states by way of pre-nascence condition. It is taught that for the mind-consciousness element and its associated states, it is a condition by way of pre-nascence condition at some times, and not a condition by way of pre-nascence condition at other times.

A mental state that assists by way of supporting the previously arisen material states is called pacchājāta-paccaya (post-nascence condition). It is like the volition (cetanā) for food in the bodies of young vultures. With reference to this, it is taught: "Post-nascent consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of post-nascence condition."

A state that assists preceding states to have superior quality through the sense of repetition is called āsevana-paccaya (repetition condition). It is like previous practice in scriptures and so on. That āsevana-paccaya is of three kinds by way of wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), and functional (kiriya) impulsion (javana). How is it taught? "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for subsequent wholesome states by way of repetition condition. Preceding unwholesome states... (pe) ... preceding functional indeterminate states are a condition for subsequent functional indeterminate states by way of repetition condition," so it is taught.

A state that assists by way of action, called the exertion of the mind, is called kamma-paccaya (kamma condition). That kamma-paccaya is of two kinds: by way of asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika) wholesome and unwholesome volition, and by way of all co-nascent (sahajāta) volition. How is it taught? "Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for resultant aggregates and kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of kamma condition. Volition is a condition for its associated states and the matter produced by it by way of kamma condition," so it is taught.

A resultant state that assists in reaching a state of tranquility by way of being effortless and tranquil is called vipāka-paccaya (resultant condition). That resultant state [assists] matter produced by consciousness during the course of existence (pavatti), and kamma-produced matter at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)...
350:
That resultant state supports mind-produced matter during the course of existence, kamma-born matter at the moment of rebirth-linking, and associated states at all times during both the course of existence and rebirth-linking, by way of resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya). The Blessed One said: "One resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition for the other three aggregates and for mind-produced matter by way of resultant condition... at the moment of rebirth-linking, one resultant indeterminate aggregate... two aggregates are a condition for the other two aggregates and for kamma-born matter by way of resultant condition. The aggregates are a condition for the physical base by way of resultant condition."

The four nutriments, which support by way of sustaining both material and mental states, constitute the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya). The Blessed One said: "Edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is a condition for this body by way of nutriment condition. Mental nutriments are a condition for their associated states and for mind-produced matter by way of nutriment condition." In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate nutriments are a condition for their associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter by way of nutriment condition."

The twenty faculties, excluding the femininity faculty (itthin-driya) and the masculinity faculty (purisin-driya), which support by way of predominance, constitute the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya). Among those twenty faculties, the five such as the eye-faculty support only mental states. The remaining faculties support both material and mental states. The Blessed One said: "The eye-faculty is a condition for the eye-consciousness element... the ear, nose, tongue, and body-faculty are a condition for the body-consciousness element and its associated states by way of faculty condition. The physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) is a condition for kamma-born matter by way of faculty condition. Mental faculties are a condition for their associated states and for mind-produced matter by way of faculty condition." In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate faculties are a condition for their associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter by way of faculty condition."

The seven jhāna factors of various types such as wholesome, etc., excluding the two feelings of bodily pleasure and bodily pain occurring in the two sets of fivefold consciousness, which support by way of close contemplation, constitute the jhāna condition (jhāna-paccaya). The Blessed One said: "Jhāna factors are a condition for states associated with jhāna and for mind-produced matter by way of jhāna condition." In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate jhāna factors are a condition for their associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter by way of jhāna condition."

The twelve path factors of various types such as wholesome, etc., which support by way of being a means of deliverance from the round of existence, constitute the path condition (magga-paccaya). The Blessed One said: "Path factors are a condition for states associated with the path and for mind-produced matter by way of path condition." In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate path factors are a condition for their associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter..."
351:
"...is a condition for material states by way of path condition." However, it should be understood that both these jhāna and path conditions are not obtained in the two sets of fivefold consciousness and in rootless consciousness, respectively.

Mental states that support by way of association, characterized by having the same physical base, the same object, the same arising, and the same cessation, constitute the association condition (sampayutta-paccaya). It is as the Blessed One said: "The four mental aggregates are a condition for one another by way of association condition."

Material states that support mental states, and mental states that support material states, by way of not being characterized by having the same physical base, etc., constitute the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya). That dissociation condition is of three types: conascent (sahajāta), post-nascent (pacchājāta), and pre-nascent (purejāta). It is said: "Conascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-produced matter by way of dissociation condition. Post-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of dissociation condition." In the section on indeterminate states (abyākata), in the Sahajāta-vibhaṅga, it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate aggregates are a condition for kamma-born matter by way of dissociation condition. The aggregates are a condition for the physical base, and the physical base is a condition for the aggregates, by way of dissociation condition." Pre-nascent dissociation should be understood only by way of the physical bases such as the eye-faculty. It is as the Blessed One said: "The pre-nascent eye-base (cakkhāyatana) is a condition for eye-consciousness... the body-base (kāyāyatana) is a condition for body-consciousness by way of dissociation condition. The physical base is a condition for resultant indeterminate and functional indeterminate aggregates; the physical base is a condition for wholesome aggregates; the physical base is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of dissociation condition."

A state that supports another state of a similar kind by way of its presence, characterized by its existence in the present, constitutes the presence condition (atthi-paccaya). The matrix (mātikā) of that presence condition is laid down in seven ways by way of: mental aggregates, great essentials, mind-and-matter, mind and mental factors, great essentials, bases, and the physical base. It is as the Blessed One said: "The four mental aggregates are a condition for one another by way of presence condition. The four great essentials (mahābhūta) are a condition for one another; at the moment of rebirth-linking, mind-and-matter are a condition for one another; mental and mental factor states are a condition for mind-produced matter; the great essentials are a condition for derived matter (upādā-rūpa); the eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element... the body-base... the sight-base... the tangible-object base is a condition for the body-consciousness element and its associated states by way of presence condition. The sight-base... the tangible-object base is a condition for the mind-element and its associated states by way of presence condition. The material state depending on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness element occur, that material state is a condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness element, and their associated states by way of presence condition." In the Pañhāvāra, conascent, pre-nascent, post-nascent, nutriment, and faculty are also laid down; first, in the conascent section: "One aggregate is a condition for the other three aggregates..."
352:
It has been explained in the way beginning with: "Assists the materiality produced by mind by way of the presence condition" (in the section on conascent presence). In prenascent presence, it has been explained by way of the (base) materiality such as the eye-base which arise earlier. In postnascent presence, it has been explained how the later-arisen consciousness and mental factors assist this material body by way of being a condition. However, in the presence of nutriment and faculty, it has been explained thus: "Nutriment consisting of edible food assists this body by way of the presence condition; the material life-faculty assists the states of materiality produced by kamma by way of the presence condition."

Mental states that have ceased in proximity and assist the mental states arising immediately after them by giving them the opportunity to occur are called the absence condition. Thus, it has been taught: "Consciousness and mental factors that have ceased in proximity assist the presently arising consciousness and mental factors by way of the absence condition."

Because those very states assist by way of their disappearance, they are called the disappearance condition. Thus, it has been taught: "Consciousness and mental factors that have disappeared in proximity assist the presently arising consciousness and mental factors by way of the disappearance condition."

It should be understood that the states of the presence condition themselves are called the non-disappearance condition because they assist by way of their non-disappearance. This dyad (presence and non-disappearance) is taught either by way of the elegance of the teaching or by way of the inclination of the veneyya (those to be taught), just as the dyad of states associated with roots is taught even after teaching the dyad of states accompanied by roots.

For the sake of non-confusion regarding these twenty-four conditions:
The decision should be understood by way of ultimate reality (dhamma), by way of time (kāla), by way of various distinctions, and by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

In that (verse), regarding the ultimate reality: Among these conditions, first, the root condition is only a portion of mentality (nāma) among the states of mentality and materiality. The object condition consists of all states of mentality and materiality along with concepts (paññatti) and Nibbāna which is (in terms of ultimate reality) the absence of conditioned states. In the predominance condition, the conascent predominance is a portion of mentality; likewise are the kamma, jhāna, and path conditions. The object-predominance consists of all object-states that are to be esteemed. The proximity, contiguity, postnascent, repetition, resultant, association, absence, and disappearance conditions are only mental states. Since Nibbāna is not included (in proximity, etc.), it can also be said that they are a portion of mentality. The prenascent condition is a portion of materiality. The remaining conditions are states of mentality and materiality as applicable. Thus, first, the decision regarding these (twenty-four conditions) should be understood by way of ultimate reality.
353:
Regarding time:
Among these conditions, fifteen are only present. Five are only past. One condition depends on both those times (past and present). Three are tri-temporal and also freed from time.

In fact, among those conditions, these fifteen conditions—namely, root, conascent, mutuality, dependence, prenascent, postnascent, resultant, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—are only present states. These five conditions—namely, proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance—are only past states. One kamma condition, however, depends on both those times, present and past. The remaining three conditions—namely, object, predominance, and sufficing condition—are tri-temporal, and because they include Nibbāna along with concepts, they are also freed from time. Thus, in these conditions, the decision should also be understood by way of time.

The meaning of these two terms, "by way of various distinctions" and "by way of conditionally arisen states," will be made clear in the Niddesavāra (the section of detailed exposition).

## Explanation of the Summary of Conditions
## Exposition of Conditions
## 1. Explanation of the Exposition of the Root Condition

Now, in order to show all those conditions by analyzing them in detail according to the order in which they were summarized, he said: "The root condition: roots are a condition for states associated with roots and for the materiality produced thereby by way of the root condition," and so on. In that passage, the term "hetupaccayo" (root condition) is the extraction of the term to be analyzed first of all, according to the order of the matrix (mātikā) laid down among the twenty-four conditions. It should be understood that in the remaining conditions also, the answer is given by extracting the term to be analyzed first in this same manner. The connection (sambandha) here is: the condition which was summarized as "hetupaccayo" in the Summary of Conditions (Paccayuddesa) should be understood by way of the detailed exposition (Niddesa) thus: "Roots are a condition for states associated with roots and for the materiality produced thereby by way of the root condition."
354: [It] should be understood. In this way, the manner of connecting the analyzed term with the explanation in all conditions should be understood. Now, in this context of "hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ," why is it stated as "hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ" instead of just "hetusampayuttakānaṃ"? It is because of the desire to define the condition (paccaya) and the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna) separately. If only "hetusampayuttakānaṃ" were stated, it would mean "to those associated with roots, [it] is a condition by way of root-condition." In that case, the definition of the condition—which state exactly is the condition by way of root-condition—would not be clear. Alternatively, if the meaning "associated with roots" is not taken, and it is understood that for any unspecified associated states, the root is a condition by way of root-condition, then eye-consciousness and so on, which are dissociated from roots, are also associated states [among themselves], just as wholesome states and so on, which are associated with roots, are associated states. In that case, the definition of the conditionally arisen—to which associated state this root is a condition—would not be clear. Therefore, desiring to define both the condition and the conditionally arisen, He said "hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ." Its meaning is: there is a root which is associated with those states such as the wholesome that are associated with roots; that root is a condition by way of root-condition. Even there, the statement "by way of root-condition" (hetupaccayena) instead of just "is a condition" (paccayo) is for the purpose of excluding the root's status as a condition in other ways. For this root is a condition by way of root-condition, and also by way of co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and so on. Among those, the statement "by way of root-condition" is made to exclude its status as a condition in other ways, such as by way of co-nascence condition. Even so, why is it stated as "hetusampayuttakānaṃ" instead of "taṃsampayuttakānaṃ" (associated with that)? It is because the state to be pointed out is not evident. If "taṃsampayuttakānaṃ" were said, that state—associated with which they are called "associated with that"—would not be evident as to which specific state it is. Because it is not evident, He said "hetusampayuttakānaṃ" to show the very form of that state, associated with which they are called "associated with that." In the phrase "taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ," however, the word "taṃ" (that) is used because the state to be pointed out is evident. The meaning here is: those roots and states associated with roots are the origin (samuṭṭhāna) of these [material] states; thus they are "taṃsamuṭṭhāna." It means: to those having that as their origin, which are produced by the roots and by the states associated with roots. By this [term], mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) [is shown].
355: (By this phrase "taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ") He takes the matter that has the mind as its origin. If it is asked, "Does that matter also arise from something other than the mind?" the answer is "Yes, it does." For indeed, all consciousness and mental factors together produce matter. However, in the teaching of mundane phenomena, because of the primary role of the mind, such matter is called mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). Therefore, He said: "States of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for mind-produced matter by way of co-nascence condition." If so, it might be asked: why is it not stated here as "cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ" instead of "taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ"? It is because of the desire to include matter that is not mind-produced. Indeed, in the Question Section (Pañhāvāra), it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate roots are a condition for associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of root-condition." To include that kamma-born matter, "taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ" is said here in this Root-Condition Description (Hetupaccaya-niddesa) instead of "cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ." The meaning of that statement is: even if they do not produce mind-born matter, those roots and states associated with roots are the origin [of matter] by way of co-nascence condition and so on; thus they are "taṃsamuṭṭhāna." Among those material states having that as their origin, it should be understood that roots are a condition by way of root-condition for mind-born matter during the course of existence (pavatti) and for kamma-born matter at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). In this way, the meaning should be understood in other places where "taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ" appears. Why does this root serve as a root-condition for kamma-born matter only at rebirth-linking and not during the course of existence? It is because at rebirth-linking, kamma-born matter has an occurrence connected to the mind. Indeed, at rebirth-linking, the occurrence of kamma-born matter is connected to the mind; they arise and persist only by the power of the mind. At that moment, just as the mind cannot produce mind-born matter, those kamma-born material states cannot arise or persist without the mind. Therefore, He said: "With consciousness as condition, mind-and-matter [arises]; when that consciousness is established, the descent of mind-and-matter occurs." During the course of existence, however, even though the mind exists, those kamma-born material states occur connected only to kamma, not connected to the mind. And even when the mind is absent, in those who have entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), those kamma-born material states continue to arise. Why is the mind unable to produce mind-born matter at the moment of rebirth-linking? It is because it is weak, being hurled by the force of kamma and having no stable physical base (vatthu). Indeed, at that time, it is weak because it is hurled by the force of kamma and because it has no stable physical base, as the physical base is not a pre-nascent condition (purejāta-paccaya). Therefore, just as a man who has just fallen from a cliff cannot perform any craft, [the rebirth-linking mind] cannot produce matter. However, kamma-born matter alone stands in the place of mind-produced matter for that rebirth-linking mind. And that rebirth-linking mind stands in the place of a seed for kamma-born matter. Kamma is like the field for that kamma-born matter.
356: Defilements are like water. Therefore, just as a tree grows due to the power of the seed when the field and water are present at the initial arising, so too, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the group of kamma-born matter arises due to the power of the mind. Just as a tree continues to grow stage by stage through the power of the earth and water even when the seed has disappeared, it should be understood that during the course of existence (pavatti), the occurrence of kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa) happens due to kamma alone, independent of the mind. This has also been taught: 'Kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture' (A. Ni. 3.77). This meaning should be understood only by way of the spheres of existence (okāsa). For there are three kinds of spheres: the sphere of name (nāmokāsa), the sphere of form (rūpokāsa), and the sphere of name-and-form (nāmarūpokāsa). Among these, the formless existence (arūpa-bhava) is called the sphere of name. In that existence, only mental phenomena arise without physical conditions such as the heart-base (hadayavatthu). The non-percipient existence (asañña-bhava) is called the sphere of form. In that existence, only physical phenomena arise without mental conditions such as rebirth-linking consciousness. The five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) is called the sphere of name-and-form. In that existence, at the time of rebirth-linking, mental phenomena cannot arise without the physical base, nor can kamma-born physical phenomena arise without rebirth-linking consciousness. Like oxen yoked together, mind and form arise only in conjunction. Just as one cannot initially enter a palace that has a master, a king, and a doorkeeper without the king's command, but later one can enter by the influence of the previous command even without a new one; similarly, in the five-constituent existence, there is no initial arising of matter by way of rebirth-linking without the support of the rebirth-linking consciousness-king through conditions such as conascence (sahajāta). However, later during the course of existence, although the influence of conditions like conascence from the rebirth-linking consciousness is absent, kamma-born matter, having gained entry through the previous influence, continues to occur due to kamma. Since the non-percipient existence is not a sphere where mental phenomena occur, physical phenomena arise there without mental conditions, because it is a sphere of non-perception. This is like entering an empty house without a master, or like entering one's own house. Since the formless existence is not a sphere where physical phenomena occur, mental phenomena arise there without physical conditions, because it is a different kind of sphere. However, since the five-constituent existence is a sphere of both form and name, there is no arising of physical phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking without mental conditions. Thus, this root (hetu) is a condition that assists kamma-born matter only at the moment of rebirth-linking, and not during the course of existence. 'Roots are a condition for conascent states by way of root-condition'—if it is taught thus, is not all this meaning already included? Why then is it specifically taken as 'to the states associated with roots and the matter produced by them'? It is because of the desire to exclude the conditionality of kamma-born matter and so on during the course of existence. For if it were taken in this way, then during the course of existence...
357: ...at the same moment as the root, kamma-born matter as well as matter produced by temperature (utu) and nutriment (āhāra) arise. It might follow that the root is a root-condition for those physical phenomena as well, but it is not their condition. Therefore, it should be understood that this [specification 'associated with roots...'] is taken for the purpose of excluding their status as conditioned states. Now, the decision should be understood by way of these terms: 'by way of various types' and 'by way of resultant states.' Among them, 'by way of various types' means: this thing called 'root' (hetu) is of four kinds by way of nature (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. Among those four, the wholesome root is of four kinds by way of the difference in planes, such as the sense-sphere and so on. The unwholesome root belongs only to the sense-sphere. The resultant root is of four kinds by way of the difference in planes, such as the sense-sphere and so on. The functional root is of three kinds: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and formless-sphere. Therein, the sense-sphere wholesome root is of three kinds by way of name, such as non-greed (alobha) and so on. The same method applies to the wholesome roots of the fine-material sphere and so on. The unwholesome root is of three kinds by way of greed (lobha) and so on. The resultant and functional roots are each of three kinds by way of non-greed and so on. However, by way of association (sampayoga) with various consciousnesses, there are indeed various types of those respective roots. Thus, first, the decision in this [root-condition] should be understood by way of various types. 'By way of resultant states' means: the decision should also be understood in this way—'these states arise because of this condition; this is the condition for these specific states.' Among those resultant states, in this root-condition, first, the sense-sphere wholesome root is a root-condition for the states associated with itself and for mind-produced matter in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere; in the formless-sphere, it is a condition only for the associated states. The fine-material sphere wholesome root is a root-condition for the associated states and for mind-produced matter only in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere. The formless-sphere wholesome root is just like the sense-sphere wholesome root. Likewise for the supramundane (apariyāpanna) wholesome root, and likewise for the unwholesome root. The sense-sphere resultant root, however, is a root-condition for the states associated with itself only in the sense-sphere, for kamma-born matter at the time of rebirth-linking, and for mind-produced matter during the course of existence. The fine-material sphere resultant root is a root-condition only for the aforementioned types (associated states, kamma-born matter, mind-produced matter) in the fine-material sphere. The formless-sphere resultant root is a root-condition only for the associated states in the formless-sphere. The supramundane resultant root is a root-condition for the associated states and mind-produced matter in the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, and only for the formless states in the formless-sphere. As for the functional roots...
358:
In the functional roots (kiriya-hetu) occurring in the three planes as well, the mode of assistance (condition) is just like that of the wholesome roots (kusala-hetu). Thus, in this Exposition of the Root Condition (Hetu-paccaya-niddesa), the conclusion should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna-dhamma).

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Root Condition

## 2. Explanation of the Exposition of the Object Condition

In the Exposition of the Object Condition (Ārammaṇa-paccaya-niddesa), "rūpāyatanaṃ" refers to the base (āyatana) known as the visible-data object. The same method applies to the remaining bases such as the sound-base, etc. "Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā" means to the element known as eye-consciousness (it is meant that it assists this element). The same method applies to the remaining terms such as the ear-consciousness element, etc. "Taṃsampayuttakānaṃ" means that the visible-data base assists the three mental aggregates associated with that eye-consciousness element, as well as all four mental aggregates that have the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) as their physical base (vatthu), by way of object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). The same method applies to the sound-base and others that follow.

"Manodhātuyā" means that the five bases such as the visible-data base assist the three-fold mind-element (the five-door adverting consciousness and the two types of receiving consciousness) along with its associated states by way of object condition. However, they do not assist all five at the same moment. "Sabbé dhammā" means that these five bases such as the visible-data base, as well as all other knowable states (ñeyya-dhamma), assist the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇa-dhātu) along with its associated states—excluding these six elements such as eye-consciousness—by way of object condition.

By the phrase "yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbha" (depending on whatever state), it is shown that whatever states are mentioned as the objects of these seven consciousness elements, they become the object condition for those consciousness elements only at the moment of arising, by making those states their object. Even though this is the case, they do not assist all at once; it is also shown that depending on whichever object whichever states arise, those respective objects become the object condition for those respective states individually.

Regarding the word "uppajjanti" (they arise), it should be understood as being stated in a way that encompasses all time, just as it is said, "rivers flow, mountains stand." Because of this use of the present tense (denoting a constant occurrence), the meaning is established that all states which have arisen in the past or will arise in the future depending on those objects, have arisen and will arise solely due to the object condition.

The phrase "cittacetasikā dhammā" (states of mind and mental factors) is a direct indication of the states mentioned as "ye ye dhammā" (whichever states). "Te te dhammā" refers to those respective object-states. "Tesaṃ tesaṃ" refers to those respective states of mind and mental factors. This which has been stated is the commentary on the Pali text in this Exposition of the Object Condition.

This which is called an 'object' is of six kinds by way of groups: visible-form object, sound object, smell object, taste object, tangible object, and mental object. Among those six objects, excluding the concept-object (paññatti), the remaining objects...
359:
By way of plane (bhūmi), there are four kinds: sense-sphere object (kāmāvacara), fine-material-sphere object (rūpāvacara), immaterial-sphere object (arūpāvacara), and supramundane object (apariyāpanna). Among those four, the sense-sphere object is of five kinds by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and matter. The fine-material-sphere object is of three kinds by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional. The immaterial-sphere object is likewise of three kinds. The supramundane object is of three kinds by way of wholesome, resultant, and Nibbāna.

Alternatively, all these objects are of seven kinds by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, matter, Nibbāna, and concept (paññatti). Among those seven, wholesome is of four kinds by way of plane. Unwholesome belongs only to the sense-sphere. Resultant occurs in all four planes. Functional occurs in the three planes. Matter occurs only in the sense-sphere plane. Nibbāna also belongs only to the supramundane plane. Concept is free from planes. Thus, in this Exposition of the Object Condition, the conclusion should be understood by way of various classifications.

In these objects thus classified, the sense-sphere wholesome object assists these six groups by way of object condition: sense-sphere wholesome, fine-material-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, sense-sphere resultant, sense-sphere functional, and fine-material-sphere functional. The fine-material-sphere wholesome object assists five groups among those six, excluding the sense-sphere resultant, by way of object condition. The immaterial-sphere wholesome object assists these eight groups by way of object condition: sense-sphere wholesome, fine-material-sphere wholesome, immaterial-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, immaterial-sphere resultant, sense-sphere functional, fine-material-sphere functional, and immaterial-sphere functional. The supramundane wholesome object assists only the wholesome and functional states of the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere by way of object condition. The unwholesome object assists these six groups by way of object condition: sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, sense-sphere resultant, and sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional.

The sense-sphere resultant object assists these six groups by way of object condition: sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, sense-sphere resultant, and sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional. The fine-material-sphere resultant object assists these five groups by way of object condition: sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere functional. The immaterial-sphere resultant object also assists only these same five groups by way of object condition. The supramundane resultant object assists only the wholesome and functional states of the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere by way of object condition.

The sense-sphere functional object assists these six groups...
360:
The groups (rāsi) are assisted by the object condition (ārammaṇapaccayo). The fine-material functional object (rūpāvacarakiriyā-ārammaṇa) assists five of these six groups, excluding the sense-sphere resultant (kāmāvacaravipāka), by way of the object condition. The immaterial functional object (arūpāvacarakiriyā-ārammaṇa) assists those five groups as well as the immaterial functional group; thus, it assists these six groups by way of the object condition.

The visible object (rūpārammaṇa), which is the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha) produced by the four causes, assists these six groups: sense-sphere and fine-material wholesome (kāmāvacara-rūpāvacarakusala), unwholesome (akusala), sense-sphere resultant (kāmāvacaravipāka), and sense-sphere and fine-material functional (kāmāvacara-rūpāvacarakiriyā), by way of the object condition. The object of Nibbāna assists these six groups: sense-sphere and fine-material wholesome, the wholesome resultants from the unincluded (apariyāpanna/supramundane), and sense-sphere and fine-material functional, by way of the object condition. Some teachers do not accept [Nibbāna as an object] for fine-material wholesome and functional states; that view should be examined through logical reasoning. However, the various conceptual objects (paññatti-ārammaṇa) assist these nine groups: wholesome, unwholesome, fine-material resultant, immaterial resultant, and functional states belonging to the three planes, by way of the object condition. Among those objects and object-possessors (ārammaṇika), whichever object is a condition for whichever states, those states are called the conditioned states (paccayuppanna) of that object. Thus, in this object condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditioned states.

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Object Condition (Ārammaṇapaccayaniddesa-vaṇṇanā)

## 3. Explanation of the Exposition of the Predominance Condition (Adhipatipaccayaniddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the exposition of the predominance condition, 'predominance of desire' (chandādhipati) refers to the predominance known as desire (chanda). This is the name for the desire to act (kattukamyatāchanda) that arises at the time of the arising of consciousness, having made desire the precursor and the chief. The same method applies to the remaining predominances. Why is it that, while in the exposition of the root condition it was said, "The roots are [a condition] for the states associated with the roots," here in this predominance condition it is not said, "The predominances are [a condition] for the states associated with the predominances," but instead the teaching is given in the manner, "The predominance of desire is [a condition] for the states associated with desire," and so on? It is because multiple predominances cannot exist in a single moment.

Indeed, in the previous method of the root condition, two or three roots can be a root condition in a single moment by way of being a foundation (mūla), as they do not relinquish their nature of being supportive. However, a predominance assists by way of being the chief (jeṭṭhaka), and many chiefs cannot exist in a single moment. Therefore, even though those states such as desire arise together, they cannot have the nature of the predominance condition in a single moment. Because that nature of the predominance condition cannot exist [simultaneously] in a single moment, the teaching is given here in this manner.
361:
Even though they arise or exist, the nature of the predominance condition does not exist simultaneously for those states like desire. Because this nature of the predominance condition does not exist simultaneously, it is taught in this exposition of the predominance condition by the method starting with 'chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ'. This is the detailed explanation.

Having thus shown the conascence predominance (sahajātādhipati), the passage beginning with 'yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā' is now introduced to show the object predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). In that passage, 'yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ' means whichever object-state. 'Garuṃ katvā' means making it an object that is esteemed, respected, or through the power of attachment—an object that is heavy (significant), to be cherished, to be attained (if not yet attained), not to be relinquished (if already attained), and not to be looked down upon. 'Te te dhammā' refers to those states that should be esteemed. 'Tesaṃ tesaṃ' refers to those states that perform the act of esteeming. 'Adhipatipaccayena' means it is a condition by way of the object predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipatipaccayo). This is first the explanation of the Pali text before the final decision in this exposition of the predominance condition.

This predominance is of two kinds: conascence (sahajāta) and object (ārammaṇa). Among them, conascence predominance is of four kinds by way of desire (chanda) and so on. Each of those four is again of four kinds by way of the planes (bhūmi), such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Among those four planes, the sense-sphere conascence predominance is of three kinds: wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), and functional (kiriyā). Specifically, when it comes to the unwholesome, the predominance of investigation (vīmaṃsādhipati) is not obtained. The fine-material and immaterial spheres are of two kinds each: wholesome and functional. The unincluded (apariyāpanna/supramundane) is of two kinds: wholesome and resultant (vipāka). Object predominance, however, is of six kinds by way of the distinction of class (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, matter (rūpa), and Nibbāna. Thus, the decision should be understood by these various distinctions.

Among these different predominances, first, in conascence predominance, the predominance known as sense-sphere wholesome or functional assists the states associated with itself and mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa) by way of the predominance condition, when it arises making one of the factors like desire the chief in double-rooted or triple-rooted consciousness-arisings. The same method applies to the predominance known as fine-material wholesome or functional. Specifically, this fine-material predominance is obtained invariably (ekanta). Indeed, those states do not arise without conascence predominance. The predominance known as immaterial wholesome or functional is just like the fine-material predominance in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra); but in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra), it assists only the associated states by way of the predominance condition. Likewise, all sense-sphere predominances arising there [in the four-constituent existence] are the same. The unincluded predominance, whether wholesome or resultant, invariably assists the associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence; but in the four-constituent existence, it assists only the mental states. The unwholesome predominance invariably assists the associated states and mind-produced matter in the sense-sphere existence in consciousnesses fixed in wrongness (micchattaniyata). The unwholesome predominance that is not fixed (aniyata) in the sense-sphere existence...
362:
In fine-material existences (rūpabhava), when they are predominant (adhipati), they are the predominance condition for those fine-material states only.
