In immaterial existence (arūpabhava), however, they are the predominance condition for immaterial states (mental states) only. This is the method for conascent predominance (sahajātādhipati).

Regarding object predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara-kusala) object predominance is the object predominance condition for these two groups: sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome associated with greed (lobhasahagata-akusala). The same method applies to fine-material sphere wholesome and immaterial sphere wholesome object predominance. Supramundane (apariyāpanna) wholesome object predominance, however, is the object predominance condition for knowledge-associated wholesome (ñāṇasampayutta-kusala) and knowledge-associated functional (ñāṇasampayutta-kiriya) among sense-sphere states. Unwholesome object predominance refers to the arising of consciousness associated with greed. That (consciousness associated with greed) is the object predominance condition for unwholesome associated with greed only. Sense-sphere resultant (vipāka) object predominance is the object predominance condition for unwholesome associated with greed only. Similarly, fine-material sphere resultant and immaterial sphere resultant object predominance (are the object predominance condition for unwholesome associated with greed only). Supramundane resultant object predominance, however, is the object predominance condition for knowledge-associated wholesome and functional states among sense-sphere states only. The three types of functional object predominance, such as sense-sphere and so on, are the object predominance condition for unwholesome associated with greed only. The materiality aggregate (rūpakkhandha) known as materiality produced by the four causes, as object predominance, is the object predominance condition for unwholesome associated with greed only. Nibbāna is the object predominance condition for these four groups: knowledge-associated wholesome and knowledge-associated functional among sense-sphere states, supramundane wholesome, and supramundane resultant. In this way, the decision should be understood here also by the power of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## Explanation of the Predominance Condition (Adhipatipaccaya-niddesa).

## 4. Explanation of the Proximity Condition (Anantarapaccaya-niddesa)

In the description of the proximity condition, "manodhātuyā" (to the mind-element) refers to the resultant mind-element (receiving). "manoviññāṇadhātuyā" (to the mind-consciousness-element) refers to the rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element having the function of investigation (santīraṇa). After that (investigation), those having the functions of determining (votthabbana), impulsion (javana), registration (tadārammaṇa), and life-continuum (bhavaṅga)...
363:
...the mind-consciousness-elements having the functions of determining, impulsion, registration, and life-continuum should also be stated; although those mind-consciousness-elements are not explicitly mentioned, they should be understood by this very method. Thus, showing the method, the teaching is condensed. In the sixth method (chaṭṭhanaya) taught as "Preceding wholesome states..." and so on, those mind-consciousness-elements are already included, and therefore it should be understood that they are not separately mentioned in this Pali text. In that sixth method, "preceding" (purimā purimā) refers to the wholesome impulsion states that have just passed in the six doors. "Succeeding" (pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ) refers only to those states arising immediately after. "To wholesome states" (kusalānaṃ) refers to similar wholesome states. The phrase "to indeterminate states" (abyākatānaṃ) is taught by way of registration (tadārammaṇa), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) occurring immediately after the wholesome. "To indeterminate states" rooted in unwholesome refers only to those states known as registration and life-continuum. "To indeterminate states" rooted in indeterminate refers to functional and resultant indeterminate states occurring by way of advertence (āvajjana) and impulsion (javana), or by way of life-continuum. This method is also obtained in the cognitive processes (vīthi-citta) occurring from the functional mind-element up to the mind-consciousness-element having the function of determining. "To wholesome states" refers to the first impulsion wholesome states occurring immediately after determining in the five doors, and immediately after advertence in the mind door. The same method applies to the term "to unwholesome states". "Whichever and whichever" (yesaṃ yesaṃ) is a summary definition of all proximity condition states. This is the explanation of the Pali text in this proximity condition description.

This proximity condition should be understood as the group of immaterial states (arūpadhammarāsi) occurring in the four planes, excluding Nibbāna. That proximity condition is divided into four by way of nature (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. Among those four, wholesome is of four types by way of sense-sphere and so on. Unwholesome is only of the sense-sphere. Resultant occurs in all four planes. The functional proximity condition occurs in three planes. Thus, the decision regarding various distinctions should be understood here.

In the proximity condition thus divided, sense-sphere wholesome is a proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome similar to itself. Knowledge-associated sense-sphere wholesome, however, is a proximity condition for these three groups: fine-material sphere wholesome, immaterial sphere wholesome, and supramundane wholesome. Sense-sphere wholesome is a proximity condition for these four groups: sense-sphere resultant, fine-material/immaterial sphere resultant, and if it is knowledge-associated, for supramundane resultant as well. Fine-material sphere wholesome is a proximity condition for these three groups: fine-material sphere wholesome, knowledge-associated sense-sphere resultant, and fine-material sphere resultant. Immaterial sphere wholesome is a proximity condition for those two resultants...
364:
It assists its own wholesome states and resultant states; thus, generally, without distinction, it is a proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) for the four groups. Specifically, here, the wholesome consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-kusala) is also a proximity condition for the supramundane resultant known as the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). Supramundane wholesome consciousness is a proximity condition only for supramundane resultant consciousness. Unwholesome consciousness, generally without distinction, is a proximity condition for unwholesome states and for the resultants of wholesome and unwholesome states. Specifically, among these unwholesome states, those associated with pleasant feeling or neutral feeling are proximity conditions for the resultants of the fine-material and immaterial spheres; thus, it is a proximity condition for these four groups.

The resultant of the sense-sphere, whether associated with knowledge or dissociated from knowledge, is a proximity condition for the sense-sphere functional adverting (āvajjana). Specifically, among these sense-sphere resultants, the one associated with knowledge is also a proximity condition for the fine-material and immaterial sphere resultants arising by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi); thus, it is a proximity condition for these four groups. Fine-material sphere resultant is a proximity condition for sense-sphere resultants accompanied by roots (sahetuka), for fine-material and immaterial sphere resultants, and for sense-sphere functional adverting; thus, it is a proximity condition for these four groups. Immaterial sphere resultant is a proximity condition for triple-rooted (tihetuka) sense-sphere resultants, for immaterial sphere resultants, and for sense-sphere functional adverting; thus, it is a proximity condition for these three groups. Supramundane resultant is a proximity condition for triple-rooted sense-sphere resultants, and for fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane resultants; thus, it is a proximity condition for these four groups.

Sense-sphere functional consciousness is a proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome states, for resultants belonging to the four planes, and for functional states belonging to the three planes; thus, it is a proximity condition for these nine groups. Fine-material sphere functional consciousness is a proximity condition for triple-rooted sense-sphere resultants, for fine-material sphere resultants, and for fine-material sphere functional consciousness; thus, it is a proximity condition for these three groups. Immaterial sphere functional consciousness is a proximity condition for triple-rooted sense-sphere resultants, for fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane resultants, and for immaterial sphere functional consciousness; thus, it is a proximity condition for these five groups. In this way, the decision should also be understood here by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## Explanation of the Proximity Condition (Anantara-paccaya-niddesa).
365:
## 5. Explanation of the Contiguity Condition (Samanantara-paccaya-niddesa)
The explanation of the contiguity condition follows the same course as this explanation of the proximity condition. However, these two conditions are very extensive; therefore, their details should be investigated and noted by way of the arising of all consciousness.

## Explanation of the Contiguity Condition (Samanantara-paccaya-niddesa).

## 6. Explanation of the Co-nascence Condition (Sahajāta-paccaya-niddesa)
In the explanation of the co-nascence condition, "aññamaññaṃ" means one state to another (assisting each other). By this word "aññamaññaṃ," the Teacher shows both the state of being a condition and the state of being conditionally arisen for those states at the same single moment. "Okkantikkhane" refers to the moment of rebirth-linking in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). This is because at that moment, mentality-materiality arises as if descending, as if rushing in, or as if coming from another world and entering this world; therefore, that moment is called "the moment of descent" (okkantikkhana).

In this context, "rūpaṃ" refers only to the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu). That heart-base reaches the state of co-nascence condition for mentality, and mentality for that heart-base, mutually. "Citta-cetasikā" refers to the four mental aggregates during the course of existence (pavatti). In this context of "sahajāta-paccayena," mind-produced matter (citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) does not reach the state of being a condition for consciousness and mental factors; therefore, "aññamaññaṃ" (mutuality) is not mentioned. Similarly, derived matter (upādā-rūpa) does not assist the great essentials (mahābhūta) mutually. "Rūpino dhammā arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ" means the heart-base assists the four mental aggregates. "Kiñci kāle" means at a certain time. The phrase "by co-nascence condition" (sahajāta-paccayena) is said with reference to the time of rebirth-linking. The phrase "not by co-nascence condition" (na sahajāta-paccayena) is said with reference to the course of existence.

This co-nascence condition exists in six portions (koṭṭhāsa) in this manner: "The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by co-nascence condition." Among those six, three portions are stated by way of mutuality (aññamañña), and three are not stated by way of mutuality. Among those six, in the first portion, only mentality is both the condition and the conditionally arisen. In the second portion, only materiality is the condition and the conditionally arisen. In the third portion, mentality-materiality are the condition and the conditionally arisen. In the fourth portion, the condition is mentality and the conditionally arisen is materiality. In the fifth portion, both the condition and the conditionally arisen are materiality only. In the sixth portion, the condition is materiality and the conditionally arisen is mentality. This is the explanation of the Pāḷi text here.

This co-nascence condition is divided into five kinds by way of nature (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and materiality. Among those five, wholesome, by way of plane...
366:
(Wholesome) is of four kinds; unwholesome is of only one kind; resultant is of four kinds; the state called functional is of three kinds; matter is of only one kind, being exclusively of the sense-sphere. In this way, first of all, the decision should be understood by way of various distinctions in this Sahajāta-paccaya (conascence condition).

In this Sahajāta-paccaya thus distinguished, wholesome states belonging to the four planes also assist their own associated mental aggregates and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) by way of conascence condition. Unwholesome states do likewise. Whatever (wholesome or unwholesome) states arise in the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi), those states assist only formless states by way of conascence condition.

Sense-sphere resultant and fine-material sphere resultant assist mind-produced matter and associated states by way of conascence condition. Whatever resultant does not produce matter (the twice five-fold consciousness), that resultant assists only associated states. Whatever resultant arises at the moment of rebirth, that resultant also assists kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of conascence condition. Formless-sphere resultant assists only associated states. Supramundane resultant assists associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence, and only formless states in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava). Sense-sphere functional and formless-sphere functional states assist associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence, and only formless states in the four-constituent existence. Fine-material sphere functional states certainly assist associated states and mind-produced matter by way of conascence condition.

Among the groups of matter having four causes, in kamma-produced matter (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa), one great essential (mahābhūta) assists three great essentials, three assist one, two assist two, and the great essentials assist derived matter (upādā-rūpa) by way of conascence condition. At the moment of sense-sphere and fine-material sphere rebirth, the heart-base (vatthu-rūpa) assists the resultant aggregates (vipāka-kkhandha) by way of conascence condition. However, in matter produced by temperature, mind, and nutriment, the great essentials assist each other and derived matter by way of conascence condition. Thus, in this conascence condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## Sahajātapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā.

## 7. Aññamaññapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the description of mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya), the Pali text appears by way of the first three portions of the description of conascence condition. Since the explanation of that Pali text is identical to what has already been stated in that conascence condition, it is not taken up again. This mutuality condition is also distinguished into five kinds by way of its nature (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and matter. Among those five, wholesome...
367:
...is of four kinds by way of plane. All the discussion on the decision is just the same as the previous discussion. In this way, the decision should be understood by way of various distinctions in this mutuality condition.

In this distinction, in this mutuality condition, all wholesome states belonging to the four planes assist their own associated states by way of mutuality condition. Unwholesome states do likewise. As for resultants, sense-sphere resultant and fine-material sphere resultant assist the heart-base at the moment of rebirth, and only associated states during the course of existence (by way of mutuality condition). Formless-sphere resultant and supramundane resultant assist only their own associated states by way of mutuality condition. All functional states also assist only associated states by way of mutuality condition. In matter produced by the four causes, in kamma-produced matter, one great essential assists three great essentials, three assist one, and two great essentials assist two by way of mutuality condition. At the moment of sense-sphere and fine-material sphere rebirth, the heart-base assists the resultant aggregates by way of mutuality condition. In matter produced by temperature, mind, and nutriment, only the great essentials assist the great essentials by way of mutuality condition. Thus, in this mutuality condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states.

## Aññamaññapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā.

## 8. Nissayapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the description of support condition (nissaya-paccaya), having shown the method of conascence-support (sahajāta-nissaya) by way of the first five portions of the description of conascence condition, the text "The eye-base is for the eye-consciousness element" etc. is undertaken to show the method of prenascence-support (purejāta-nissaya) by way of the sixth portion. In that Pali, the phrase "depending on which matter" (yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya) is stated with reference to the heart-base (vatthu-rūpa). Indeed, depending on that heart-base, these seventy-five types of consciousness arise, namely: the three-fold mind-element (manodhātu) and the seventy-two-fold mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu), excluding formless resultants. This is the initial explanation of the Pali in this support condition. This support condition is also distinguished into five kinds by way of its nature (jāti), such as wholesome and so on. Among those five, wholesome is of four kinds by way of plane, unwholesome is of one kind, resultant is of four kinds, the state called functional is of three kinds, and matter is of only one kind. In this way, the decision should be understood by way of various distinctions in this support condition.

In this distinction, in this support condition, wholesome states belonging to the four planes assist associated aggregates and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence by way of support condition. Likewise...
368:
Unwholesome states also [perform the function of support]. Among these unwholesome states, that which arises in the formless realm (āruppa) is a dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya) only for formless states. Sense-sphere and fine-material sphere resultants (vipāka) are dependence conditions for associated states and mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) during the course of existence, and for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) at the moment of rebirth. Formless sphere resultants are [dependence conditions] only for associated aggregates. Supramundane resultants are dependence conditions for associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra), and only for formless states in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra). Sense-sphere and formless-sphere functional states (kiriya) are dependence conditions for associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence, and only for formless states in the four-constituent existence. Fine-material sphere functional states are definitely dependence conditions for associated states and mind-produced matter.

Regarding matter produced by the four causes: among kamma-produced matter, one great element (mahābhūta) is a dependence condition for the other three, three for one, and two for two; the great elements are dependence conditions for derived matter (upādā-rūpa); the physical base matter (vatthu-rūpa) is a dependence condition for these four groups of states: wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultants of the three planes (excluding formless resultants and the two sets of fivefold consciousness), and functional states of the three planes in the five-constituent existence. The five bases, such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), are dependence conditions for the eye-consciousness and so on, along with their associated states. In the case of matter produced by temperature, mind, and nutriment, the great elements are dependence conditions for the other great elements and for derived matter. Thus, in this dependence condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally produced states.

## Explanation of the Dependence Condition (Nissaya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).

## 9. Explanation of the Decisive Support Condition (Upanissaya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the exposition of the decisive support condition, in the phrase 'preceding, preceding' (purimā purimā), states that have passed away in immediate proximity are obtained in the proximity decisive support (anantarūpanissaya); in the object decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) and natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya), states that occurred earlier by way of various thought-processes (vīthi) [are obtained]. Those three groups are obtained in the wholesome section by way of wholesome states; however, in the case of wholesome states [supporting] unwholesome states, states that have passed away in immediate proximity are not obtained. Therefore, it is said: 'to unwholesome states by some decisive support condition.'
369:
'Condition' (paccayo) means: 'A wholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state by way of decisive support condition; there are object decisive support and natural decisive support. Object decisive support means: having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, having performed the Uposatha observance, one gives weight to that [merit] and enjoys and delights in it; giving weight to that, lust arises, wrong view arises. Giving weight to wholesome states well-practiced in the past, one enjoys and delights in them; giving weight to them, lust arises, wrong view arises. Having emerged from jhāna, one gives weight to the jhāna and enjoys and delights in it; giving weight to that jhāna, lust arises, wrong view arises. Natural decisive support means: depending on faith, one arouses conceit or adopts a wrong view. Depending on virtue, learning, generosity, or wisdom, one arouses conceit or adopts a wrong view. Faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom are conditions for lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, and longing by way of decisive support condition.' This was said with reference to this method. In the case of wholesome [supporting] indeterminate states, all three types of decisive support are obtained; likewise, unwholesome for unwholesome.

In the case of unwholesome [supporting] wholesome states, however, states that have passed away in immediate proximity are not obtained. Therefore, it is said: 'to wholesome states by some decisive support condition.' This also refers only to the natural decisive support mentioned in the Pañhāvāra [Question Section] in this way: 'An unwholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of decisive support condition. Natural decisive support means: depending on lust, one gives a gift, undertakes virtue, performs the Uposatha observance, arouses jhāna, arouses insight, arouses the path, arouses direct knowledge, arouses attainment. Depending on hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, or longing, one gives a gift ... arouses attainment. Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, and longing are conditions for faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom by way of decisive support condition. Having killed a living being, one gives a gift for the sake of counteracting that [act of killing],' and so on. An unwholesome state does not become an object decisive support for a wholesome state. Why? Because one does not give weight to that unwholesome state and let that wholesome state arise. Just as proximity decisive support is not obtained, so too it should be understood that object decisive support is not obtained here. In the section of unwholesome [supporting] indeterminate states, only object decisive support is not obtained. Indeterminate states do not give weight to unwholesome states. However, since the state of being in immediate proximity is obtained, the word 'some' is not used here. In the three methods of indeterminate [supporting] indeterminate, wholesome, and unwholesome, all three types of decisive support are indeed obtained. The two—'person' and 'lodging'—are mentioned by way of natural decisive support. These two are powerful conditions for the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states.
370:
In this natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya), the fact that persons and lodgings (puggala-senāsana) act as causes should also be understood by way of figurative expression (pariyāya). This much is the commentary on the Pāḷi text regarding this decisive support condition.

This decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) consists of all states of the four planes together with certain concepts (paññatti). By way of classification, it is threefold: object decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya), proximity decisive support (anantarūpanissaya), and natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). Among these, since object decisive support is not different from the object predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya), it should be understood in its various aspects according to the method already mentioned below. Proximity decisive support is also not different from the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya); it too should be understood in its various aspects according to the method already mentioned below. The decision regarding the resultants (paccayuppanna) of these object decisive support and proximity decisive support conditions should also be understood according to the method mentioned for those object predominance and proximity conditions. Natural decisive support, however, is fivefold by way of its nature (jāti): wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), and matter (rūpa). By way of the planes of the wholesome and so on, there are many varieties. Thus, the decision regarding the various aspects of this natural decisive support should be understood.

When thus distinguished, in this natural decisive support, the wholesome of the three planes is a natural decisive support condition for the four groups of the four planes: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. Supramundane wholesome is not a natural decisive support for the unwholesome only. However, according to the view of our teacher, by way of the method 'I have produced the supramundane state,' it is a natural decisive support even for the unwholesome of others. Or, for one in whose continuity the supramundane state will arise, if that person arouses longing for the unsurpassed liberations (vimokkha), it is indeed a natural decisive support by this method. The unwholesome is a natural decisive support for the aggregates (khandha) of all four planes. Likewise, the resultant of the three planes (is a natural decisive support for the aggregates of the four planes). Among the supramundane resultants, the three lower fruits are not natural decisive supports for the unwholesome only. The highest, the fruit of Arahatship, (is a natural decisive support) for the wholesome as well. By the method mentioned earlier, whether in the continuity of others or in the continuity of one in whom the supramundane resultant will arise, all supramundane resultants are natural decisive supports for all mental aggregates such as the wholesome. The natural decisive support called functional is also indeed for the aggregates of the four planes, such as the unwholesome. Likewise, the natural decisive support called matter (is for the aggregates of the four planes, such as the wholesome). Matter itself does not obtain the status of a decisive support condition by the method found in this Great Treatise of the Paṭṭhāna; however, it should be said that it does obtain it by the method found in the Suttas. Thus, the decision regarding the resultants in this natural decisive support should be understood.

## Commentary on the Explanation of the Decisive Support Condition.
371:
## 10. Commentary on the Explanation of the Pre-existence Condition

In the explanation of the pre-existence condition, regarding the phrase 'conditioned by way of pre-existence condition' (purejāta-paccayena paccayo), 'pre-existence' refers to matter that, having arisen earlier than the resultant state it assists, has passed the moment of arising (jātikkhana) and reached the moment of presence (ṭhitikkhana). The words beginning with 'eye-base' (cakkhāyatana) are spoken by the Blessed One by way of base pre-existence (vatthu-purejāta). The words beginning with 'visible-form base' (rūpāyatana) are spoken by way of object pre-existence (ārammaṇa-purejāta). The phrase 'sometimes by pre-existence condition' is spoken with reference to the course of existence (pavatti). The phrase 'sometimes not by pre-existence condition' is spoken with reference to rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Thus, in every way, this Pāḷi text occurs by way of base and object pre-existence in the five doors, and by way of base pre-existence only in the mind door. However, in the Question Section (Pañhāvāra), because it is stated: 'Object pre-existence—trainees (sekha) or worldlings (puthujjana) contemplate the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self,' object pre-existence is indeed obtained in the mind door as well. In this Explanation of Conditions (Paccaya-niddesa), however, the teaching is given by way of a remainder (sāvasesa). This is the initial commentary on the Pāḷi text here.

This pre-existence condition is purely matter (rūpa). Furthermore, it is only the eighteen types of concretely produced matter (rūpa-rūpa) that have passed the moment of arising (uppādakkhana) and reached the moment of presence. All that matter is established in two ways: base pre-existence and object pre-existence. Among these, the base matter consisting of the eye-base... etc. ...body-base is called base pre-existence. The twelve types of matter—whether occurring or not occurring in this Pāḷi text of the Explanation of Conditions—namely, color, sound, smell, taste, the four great elements, the three faculties (femininity, masculinity, and life faculties), and edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), are called the object pre-existence condition. Thus, the decision regarding the various aspects here should be understood.

When thus distinguished, in this pre-existence condition, the eye-base is a condition for the two types of eye-consciousness by way of pre-existence condition. Likewise, the other four bases are conditions for the ear-consciousness and so on. Base matter, however, excluding the ten types of sense-consciousness and the four formless resultants, is a pre-existence condition for all other wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousness and mental factors of the four planes. The five objects such as visible form are definitely pre-existence conditions for the ten types of sense-consciousness and the mind-elements (mano-dhātu). These eighteen types of concretely produced matter are also conditions for these six groups: sense-sphere wholesome, super-knowledge wholesome arising from the fine-material sphere, unwholesome, sense-sphere resultant occurring as registration (tadārammaṇa), sense-sphere functional, and super-knowledge functional arising from the fine-material sphere...
372:
Thus, in this pre-nascent condition (purejāta-paccaya), the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## Exposition of the Description of the Pre-nascent Condition (Purejāta-paccaya-niddesa).

## 11. Exposition of the Description of the Post-nascent Condition (Pacchājāta-paccaya-niddesa)

In the description of the post-nascent condition, 'pacchājātā' (post-nascent) refers to those mental states that arise and exist while that group of material forms, for which they serve as a condition, has already arisen and is present. 'Purejātassa' (to the pre-nascent) refers to the material body which arose earlier than those mental states and, having passed the moment of arising (jāti-kkhaṇa), has reached the stage of presence (ṭhiti). 'Imassa kāyassa' (to this body) refers to this group of material forms consisting of the great essentials (bhūta-rūpa) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) produced by four causes (catu-samuṭṭhānika) or three causes (ti-samuṭṭhānika). In this context, 'the body produced by three causes' (ti-samuṭṭhānika-kāya) should be understood as the material body of Brahmas such as the Brahmā-pārisajja, due to the absence of matter produced by nutriment (āhāra). This is the explanation of the Pāḷi text for this post-nascent condition. This post-nascent condition, in brief, consists of the mental aggregates of the four planes, excluding the immaterial resultants (arūpa-vipāka). That conditioning state is divided into four types according to its nature (jāti): wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya). Thus, the decision here should be understood through these various classifications.

When so divided, the wholesome and unwholesome states of the four planes arising in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) are the post-nascent condition for the group of material forms produced by four causes or three causes that have passed the moment of arising and reached the stage of presence. Among resultants, excluding the rebirth-linking resultant (paṭisandhi-vipāka), the remaining resultants of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) and fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) are certainly the post-nascent condition for that same group of material forms. The supramundane resultant (lokuttara-vipāka) arising in the five-constituent existence is also the post-nascent condition for that same group of material forms. The functional states of the three planes arising in the five-constituent existence are also the post-nascent condition for the group of material forms of the aforementioned types. Thus, in this post-nascent condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states.

## Exposition of the Description of the Post-nascent Condition (Pacchājāta-paccaya-niddesa).

## 12. Exposition of the Description of the Repetition Condition (Āsevana-paccaya-niddesa)

In the description of the repetition condition, by the words 'purimā purimā' (preceding, preceding), only those states that have passed away in the immediate proximity (samanantara) in all methods should be understood. Why, in this repetition condition, as in the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya), is the description not made together with states of different classes, such as 'preceding wholesome states (are a condition) for subsequent indeterminate states (abyākata)' and so on?...
373:
...(Because of) the inability to make the subsequent states adopt their own nature (gati). Indeed, although states of different classes may achieve the state of being proficient and powerful through the quality of repetition for mental states of different classes, they are unable to make them adopt their own nature, which is defined as being wholesome and so on. Therefore, without making a description together with those states of different classes, it should be understood that the description is made only with states of the same class—those which are able to make the subsequent states adopt their own nature (wholesome, etc.) characterized by being more proficient and more powerful through repetition, which is called 'habituation' (vāsanā).

If that is so, why is the resultant indeterminate (vipāka-abyākata) not taken? Because of the absence of the power of repetition (āsevana). For the resultant, having reached the state of being a resultant by the power of kamma, exists as something transformed by kamma, being passive (nirussāha) and weak (dubbala). Therefore, it is unable to produce another resultant by perfuming it and making it adopt its own nature through the quality of repetition, nor is it able to arise by taking up the influence of a preceding resultant. It arises like an object that has been thrown and is falling by the momentum of kamma. Thus, because the power of repetition is absent in resultants in every way, the resultant is not taken in the repetition condition. Even though it arises immediately after wholesome, unwholesome, or functional states, this resultant does not take up the quality of repetition because its occurrence is bound to kamma. Therefore, wholesome and other states also do not become the repetition condition for that resultant. Furthermore, because they are of different classes, these states simply do not become the repetition condition. However, by way of plane (bhūmi) or object (ārammaṇa), there is no such thing as being of different classes. Therefore, sense-sphere wholesome and functional states are indeed the repetition condition for sublime (mahaggata) wholesome and functional states; and the adaptation wholesome (anuloma-kusala) which has conditioned states as its object is indeed the repetition condition for the change-of-lineage wholesome (gotrabhū-kusala) which has Nibbāna as its object. This is the initial explanation of the Pāḷi text in this context.

This repetition condition, by way of nature (jāti), exists in three ways: wholesome, unwholesome, and functional indeterminate. Among these three, wholesome is of three types by way of plane: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere. Unwholesome is only of the sense-sphere. Functional indeterminate is also of three types: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere. There is no such thing as a supramundane (lokuttara) repetition condition. Thus, the decision in this repetition condition should be understood through these various classifications.

In this repetition condition thus divided, a sense-sphere wholesome state is (a repetition condition) only for a sense-sphere wholesome state that immediately follows it. Among those sense-sphere wholesome states, one associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) is (a repetition condition) for fine-material wholesome, immaterial wholesome, and supramundane wholesome states that have the same feeling as itself...
374: To these groups, it is a repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya). Fine-material sphere wholesome (rūpāvacara-kusala) is a repetition condition only for fine-material sphere wholesome; immaterial sphere wholesome (arūpāvacara-kusala) only for immaterial sphere wholesome; and unwholesome (akusala) only for unwholesome. Among the functional indeterminates (kiriya-abyākata), that which is called sense-sphere functional (kāmāvacara-kiriya) is a repetition condition only for sense-sphere functional. Among these sense-sphere functionals, that which is associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) is a repetition condition for these groups: fine-material sphere functional and immaterial sphere functional which have similar feeling (vedanā) to itself. That which is called fine-material sphere functional is a repetition condition only for fine-material sphere functional; that which is called immaterial sphere functional is a repetition condition only for immaterial sphere functional. There is no repetition condition for a resultant (vipāka) towards another state, nor for any state towards a resultant. In this way, the decision regarding this repetition condition should be understood by way of its resultants (paccayuppanna).## Commentary on the Description of the Repetition Condition.## 13. Commentary on the Description of the Kamma ConditionIn the description of the kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), 'kamma' refers only to volitional kamma (cetanā-kamma). 'And to the kamma-produced matter' (kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ) means to the matter produced because of the kamma having been performed. 'By way of kamma condition' (kamma-paccayena) means by way of the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) which is capable of producing its own result even after many billions of aeons. Indeed, wholesome or unwholesome kamma does not give its result at the moment of its own occurrence (pavatti-khaṇa). If it were to do so, when a human performs a wholesome kamma that leads to the celestial realm, he would become a deva at that very moment by the power of that kamma. However, at whatever moment that kamma is performed, even though it no longer exists at a different moment from that, it produces its result when there is a meeting with the remaining conditions—whether in the present life, the next life, or in subsequent successions of lives—simply because it has been performed. This is like how a previous act of learning a craft, though it has ceased, assists a subsequent act of learning the craft at a later time. Therefore, it is called the asynchronous kamma condition. 'To the states associated with volition' (cetanā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ) means whatever volition assists the states associated with itself. By the term 'to those originated by it' (taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ), it also includes kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking. The phrase 'by way of kamma condition' is stated here with reference to conascent volition (sahajāta-cetanā). For in wholesome states and so on, whatever conascent volition there is, it assists the remaining states by way of what is called mental exertion (citta-payoga)...
375:
(Volition) is helpful by way of being an action. Therefore, it is called co-nascent kamma condition (sahajāta-kamma-paccaya). This is the explanation of the Pali text regarding this kamma condition.

In terms of meaning, this kamma condition is just volition occurring in the four planes (catubhūmika-cetanā). That kamma condition is divided into four by way of its nature (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. Among them, the wholesome is divided into four by way of planes, such as the sense-sphere and so on. The unwholesome is of only one kind. The resultant is of four kinds, and the functional is of only three kinds. In this way, the decision should be understood in this kamma condition by way of various classifications.

In this kamma condition thus divided, co-nascent sense-sphere wholesome volition is a co-nascent kamma condition for the states associated with itself and for mind-produced matter in the five-constituent plane (pañcavokāra-bhūmi), and for the associated aggregates only in the four-constituent plane (catuvokāra-bhūmi). However, that (sense-sphere wholesome volition) which has arisen and ceased is a condition for its own resultant aggregates and for kamma-born matter by way of asynchronous kamma condition. And that assistance occurs only in the five-constituent plane, not elsewhere. Co-nascent fine-material sphere wholesome volition is invariably a condition for the states associated with itself and for mind-produced matter by way of co-nascent kamma condition. The volition which has arisen and ceased is a condition for its own resultants and for kamma-born matter by way of asynchronous kamma condition. Co-nascent wholesome volition which is both immaterial sphere and supramundane (lokuttara) is a condition for the states associated with itself and for mind-produced matter in the five-constituent plane, and for the associated aggregates only in the four-constituent plane by way of co-nascent kamma condition. These two types of volition which have arisen and ceased are conditions for their respective resultant aggregates only by way of asynchronous kamma condition. Co-nascent unwholesome volition is a condition for the aggregates associated with itself and for mind-produced matter in the five-constituent plane, and for the immaterial aggregates only in the four-constituent plane by way of co-nascent kamma condition. The volition which has arisen and ceased is a condition for the resultant aggregates and for kamma-born matter by way of asynchronous kamma condition.

Resultant volition of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere is a condition for the states associated with itself, for mind-produced matter during the course of existence (pavatti), and for kamma-born matter at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) by way of co-nascent kamma condition. Immaterial sphere resultant volition is a condition for the states associated with itself only by way of co-nascent kamma condition. Supramundane resultant volition is a condition for the states associated with itself and for mind-produced matter in the five-constituent plane, and for immaterial states only in the four-constituent plane by way of co-nascent kamma condition. Functional volition occurring in the three planes...

In the five-constituent realm, it assists the associated states and mind-produced matter by way of conascent kamma condition. That volition which arises in the formless realm assists only the formless states by way of conascent kamma condition. Thus, in this kamma condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states.

## 14. Explanation of the Resultant Condition (Vipāka-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the explanation of the resultant condition, regarding the phrase "the four resultant aggregates," since kamma-produced matter is not a resultant, after saying "resultant," the phrase "four aggregates" is stated. Thus, this Pali text comes by way of the resultant condition for mental states only. However, in the Question Section (Pañhāvāra), because it is stated: "One resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition for three aggregates and mind-produced matter by way of resultant condition. At the moment of rebirth-linking, one resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition for three aggregates and kamma-born matter by way of resultant condition," the resultant condition is also obtained for mind-produced matter and kamma-produced matter. Here, however, the teaching is given in a partial manner (sāvasesa); this is the explanation of the Pali here. This resultant condition is of one kind by way of its nature as a resultant, but by way of the division of planes, it is divided into four by way of the sense-sphere, etc. Thus, the decision should be understood here by way of various types of divisions.

In this division, the sense-sphere resultant and the fine-material sphere resultant are a resultant condition for their associated states, for mind-produced matter during the course of existence (pavatti), and for kamma-born matter at rebirth-linking. The formless-sphere resultant is a condition for associated states only. The supramundane resultant is a resultant condition for associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent realm, and for associated aggregates only in the four-constituent realm. Thus, here too, the decision should be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states.

## 15. Explanation of the Nutriment Condition

In the explanation of the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya), "edible food" (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) refers to the nutritive essence (ojā) contained in matter produced by the fourfold continuity—kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment. Since that nutriment performs the function of nutriment only when it is made into a bolus and swallowed, and not while it remains outside, it is called "edible food" rather than just "nutriment." Or, it is named "edible food" because it has the substance that must be made into a bolus and swallowed. "Immaterial nutriments" refers to contact-nutriment, mental-volition-nutriment, and consciousness-nutriment. In the phrase "produced by those nutriments," kamma-produced matter is also included. For has it not been stated thus in the Pañhāvāra: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant-indeterminate nutriments assist associated aggregates and kamma-produced matter by way of nutriment condition"? This is the explanation of the Pali in this context.

Briefly, this nutriment condition consists of only four states: edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness. Among those four, excluding edible food, the remaining three immaterial nutriments are divided into four by way of their nature (jāti) as wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya). Again, by way of the planes of existence, they are divided into many: wholesome is of four kinds, unwholesome is of one kind, resultant is of four kinds, and functional is of three kinds. Edible food, however, is indeterminate (abyākata) by nature and belongs only to the sense-sphere by plane. Thus, the decision should be understood here by way of various classifications.

In such a classification, the three wholesome nutriments occurring in the four planes assist their associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence by way of nutriment condition. Excluding the fine-material sphere wholesome nutriment, the remaining wholesome nutriments assist only associated states in the formless existence by way of nutriment condition. The same method applies to unwholesome nutriments. Resultant nutriments occurring in the four planes assist associated states in all planes by way of nutriment condition. Among these resultant nutriments, the sense-sphere resultant and fine-material sphere resultant nutriments, when arising in the five-constituent existence, assist mind-produced matter during the course of existence and kamma-produced matter at rebirth-linking by way of nutriment condition. Supramundane resultant nutriments assist only mind-produced matter. Resultant nutriments arising in the formless existence do not serve as a condition for matter. The three functional nutriments occurring in the three planes assist associated states and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence. The sense-sphere and immaterial-sphere functional nutriments assist only associated states in the formless existence by way of nutriment condition...
378:
It is a nutriment condition. Although edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), which has four types of origin (samuṭṭhāna), is taught generally as "for this body" without distinction, specifically, this edible food is a condition by way of nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya) by being both the producer and the sustainer of the nutriment-originated matter in this group of matter. For the remaining matter with three types of origin, it is a condition by way of nutriment condition only by being the sustainer. Thus, in this nutriment condition, the decision should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna).

## 16. Commentary on the Description of Faculty Condition (Indriya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the description of faculty condition, 'cakkhundriyaṃ' means the faculty called the eye. 'Indriya-paccayena' means that, having arisen previously, it is a condition by way of faculty condition for the immaterial states (nāma) from their arising (uppāda) until their dissolution (bhaṅga). The same method applies to the ear-faculty (sotindriya) and so on. In the phrase 'arūpino indriyā', the immaterial life-faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya) is also included. In the phrase 'taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ', kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) is also included by the same method mentioned below. Indeed, it is stated in the Pañhāvāra: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate faculties are a condition by way of faculty condition for the associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter." Thus, first, the commentary on the Pali in this description of faculty condition should be understood.

This faculty condition exists by way of twenty faculties, excluding the feminine faculty (itthindriya) and the masculine faculty (purisindriya). Although the feminine faculty and the masculine faculty are like seeds for the feminine characteristics (itthi-liṅga) and masculine characteristics (purisa-liṅga) etc., and although they exist at the time of the kalala-drop etc., because the feminine and masculine characteristics etc. are absent then, they do not extend the state of faculty condition over those characteristics or over other matter.

In fact, there is no such thing as a faculty condition not extending its state of faculty condition over the inseparable states at the moment of its own existence; therefore, those [two] are not faculty conditions. However, these feminine and masculine faculties are like seeds for those feminine and masculine characteristics etc.; they serve as natural decisive support (pakaṭūpanissaya) for those characteristics. Thus, it should be understood that faculty condition exists by way of twenty faculties. That faculty condition is divided into five types by way of its nature (jāti): wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), and matter (rūpa). Among those five, the wholesome is of four types by way of planes (bhūmi); the unwholesome is only of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara); the resultant is of four types; the state called functional is of three types; and matter is only of the sense sphere. Thus, it is divided in many ways. In this way, the decision in this faculty condition should be understood by way of various divisions.
379:
In this faculty condition thus divided, the wholesome faculty condition occurring in the four planes is a condition by way of faculty condition for the associated states and for mind-originated matter (citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhūmi); the unwholesome is the same. Excluding the fine-material sphere wholesome (rūpāvacara-kusala), the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states are conditions by way of faculty condition only for the associated states in the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhūmi). The resultant faculty condition occurring in the four planes is definitely a condition by way of faculty condition for the associated states. In this faculty condition, the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere resultants, because they arise in the five-constituent existence, are conditions by way of faculty condition for mind-originated matter during the course of existence (pavatti), and also for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking. Supramundane (lokuttara) resultants are conditions only for mind-originated matter. Supramundane resultant faculties arising in the immaterial existence are not conditions for matter. Functional faculties occurring in the three planes are conditions for the associated states and for mind-originated matter in the five-constituent existence (by way of faculty condition); however, the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere functional faculties extend the state of faculty condition only to the associated states in the immaterial existence. Among the six types of physical faculties by way of the eye-faculty etc., the eye-faculty is a condition (by way of faculty condition) for the two types of eye-consciousness which occur with associated states as wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant; the ear-faculty etc. are likewise (conditions) for ear-consciousness etc. The physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) is a condition by way of faculty condition for the co-nascent matter at the moment of its presence (ṭhiti-kkhaṇa). For that physical life-faculty, there is no state of co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya). Thus, the decision in this faculty condition should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states.

## Commentary on the Description of Faculty Condition (Indriya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).

## 17. Commentary on the Description of Jhana Condition (Jhāna-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the description of jhana condition, 'jhānaṅgāni' refers to the seven factors called initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), joy (somanassa), displeasure (domanassa), equanimity (upekkhā), and one-pointedness of mind (cittēkaggatā), which arise in the remaining consciousnesses excluding the two sets of fivefold consciousness (dvi-pañcavijñāna). Because the five groups of consciousness are merely the falling (of the mind) upon the object, the equanimity, pleasure, and pain existing in those consciousnesses are not extracted as jhana factors because they lack the mode of closely contemplating (upanijjhāna). Because the nature of jhana is interrupted in those consciousnesses, jhana factors are also not extracted in the remaining rootless (ahetuka) consciousnesses. By the word 'taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ', it should be understood that kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) is also included in this jhana condition. Indeed, it is stated in the Pañhāvāra: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate jhana factors are [a condition] for the associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter..."
380:
"Jhānapaccayena paccayo"—this statement is first the opening explanation of the text in this Exposition of the Jhana Condition. Although this Jhana condition is established by way of the seven jhana factors, it is divided into four types according to its nature (jāti): wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. Furthermore, it is divided into twelve types according to the planes: four, one, four, and three respectively. Thus, the decision in this Jhana condition should be understood through these various classifications.

In this Jhana condition thus divided, the wholesome jhana factors occurring in the four planes are a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states and for mind-produced matter in the five-constituent plane. Excluding the fine-material wholesome jhana factors, the remaining wholesome jhana factors are a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states only in the immaterial plane. The same method applies to the unwholesome. The sense-sphere and fine-material resultants are a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states and for mind-produced matter during the course of existence (pavatti), and for the associated states and for kamma-born matter at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). The immaterial resultant is a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states only. Whatever supramundane resultant arises in the immaterial plane, that supramundane resultant is also a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states only. In the five-constituent plane, however, that supramundane resultant is also a condition by way of jhana condition for mind-produced matter. The functional jhana factors occurring in the three planes are a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states and for mind-produced matter in the five-constituent plane. Among these functional jhana factors of the three planes, whichever functional jhana factor arises in the immaterial plane, that functional jhana factor is a condition by way of jhana condition for the associated states only. Thus, the decision in this Jhana condition should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## 18. Commentary on the Exposition of Path Condition

In the Exposition of Path Condition, "maggaṅgāni" refers to these twelve factors: wisdom, initial application, right speech, right action, right livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration, wrong view, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood, which arise in the remaining consciousnesses excluding the rootless consciousness-arisings. Because the path has roots as its finality, the path factors are not extracted in rootless consciousnesses. By the word "taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ," kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa) is also included here in this Exposition of Path Condition. Indeed, it is stated in the Pañhāvāra: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate path factors are a condition by way of path condition for the associated aggregates and for kamma-born matter." This stated thus far is first the opening explanation of the text in this Exposition of Path Condition.

Although this path condition is established by way of the twelve path factors, it is divided into four types according to its nature such as wholesome, etc., and into twelve types according to the planes such as sense-sphere, etc. Thus, the decision in this path condition should be understood through these various classifications.

## 19. Commentary on the Exposition of Associated Condition

In the Exposition of Associated Condition, the text has a clear meaning. Briefly, this associated condition refers to all mental aggregates. Extensively, this associated condition is divided into many types according to nature such as wholesome, etc., and according to planes such as sense-sphere, etc. Thus, the decision in this associated condition should be understood through these various classifications. In this division, among the wholesome aggregates occurring in the four planes, one aggregate is a condition for three aggregates, three for one, and two for two; thus, all aggregates are mutually a condition by way of associated condition. The same method applies to unwholesome, resultant, and functional aggregates. Thus, the decision in this associated condition should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states.

## Commentary on the Exposition of Associated Condition.

## 20. Commentary on the Exposition of Dissociated Condition

In the Exposition of Dissociated Condition, the statement "material states [condition] mental states" should first be understood by way of the heart-base (hadayavatthu) and the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya), etc. Among material states, only these six groups are the conditioning states that condition the mental aggregates by way of dissociated condition. Although sense objects such as the visible-data base (rūpāyatana) are dissociated states, they are not dissociated conditions. Why? Because there is no suspicion of association. For the mental aggregates such as eye-consciousness arise as if emerging from within the bases such as the eye-base. In that arising, the suspicion occurs: "Are these [material bases] associated with these [mental aggregates], or are they dissociated?" But since sense objects are merely objects for the mental states that arise depending on a base, there is no suspicion of association regarding those sense objects. Thus...
382:
Because there is no doubt regarding their association (sampayoga), those (object) states are not dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya). This state of dissociation condition should be understood only in regard to the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) and so forth. In the Pañhāvāra (Question Section) also, it is stated: "The base-matter is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of dissociation condition. The base-matter is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of dissociation condition. The eye-base is a condition for eye-consciousness by way of dissociation condition. The ear... nose... tongue... body-base is a condition for body-consciousness by way of dissociation condition. The base-matter is a condition for resultant indeterminate and functional indeterminate aggregates by way of dissociation condition."

This statement, "Mental states (are a condition) for material states," should be understood by way of the four mental aggregates. Among mental states, only the four mental aggregates are dissociation condition for co-nascent (sahajāta) and pre-nascent (purejāta) material states. Although Nibbāna is a mental state (arūpa-dhamma), it is not a dissociation condition for matter. This is because it is taught: "Association with the four (mental aggregates) and dissociation from the four (mental aggregates)." Thus, the state of dissociation condition should be understood only for the four mental aggregates. In the Pañhāvāra also, it is stated: "Co-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-produced matter by way of dissociation condition. Post-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for this pre-nascent body (material group) by way of dissociation condition. At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate aggregates are a condition for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of dissociation condition; the aggregates are a condition for the base-matter (by way of dissociation condition)." Thus, the explanation of the Pali text in this (dissociation condition) should be understood.

This dissociation condition, in brief, refers to the material and mental states occurring in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). Among those material and mental states, matter is divided into six kinds by way of the base-matter and the bases such as the eye and so forth. Mind is divided into four kinds by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states occurring in the five-constituent existence. By way of planes (bhūmi) such as the sense-sphere and so forth, that mind has eleven divisions: four, one, three, and three. Since the immaterial-sphere resultant (arūpa-vipāka) is not a dissociation condition, the decision (vinicchaya) in this (dissociation condition) should be understood by way of various divisions.

In this (dissociation condition) thus divided, the wholesome and unwholesome states of the four planes occurring in the five-constituent existence are a condition for mind-produced matter caused by themselves by way of co-nascent dissociation condition. Having passed the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) and reached the moment of presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa), they are a condition for the pre-nascent material group having four origins or three origins by way of post-nascent dissociation condition. Here, the material group having three origins should be understood as the bodies of Brahmas such as the Brahmapārisajja and so forth, because of the absence of nutriment-produced matter. As for the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere resultants, during the course of existence (pavatti), for mind-produced matter...
383:
At the time of rebirth-linking, they are a condition for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of co-nascent dissociation condition. The supramundane resultant (lokuttara-vipāka) is a condition only for mind-produced matter. That resultant, which has three divisions—sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, and supramundane—is a condition for the pre-existing body having four origins or three origins by way of post-nascent dissociation condition. The functional mind occurring in the three planes is also a condition for mind-produced matter by way of co-nascent dissociation condition, and is a condition for the pre-existing body having four origins or three origins by way of post-nascent dissociation condition. Among the material states existing in six divisions, the base-matter is a condition for sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere resultants at the moment of rebirth-linking by way of co-nascent dissociation condition. During the course of existence, it is a condition for wholesome and unwholesome states of the four planes, and for resultants and functionals of the three planes (excluding the ten-fold sense-consciousness), by way of pre-nascent dissociation condition. The eye-base and so forth are a condition for eye-consciousness and so forth by way of pre-nascent dissociation condition. Thus, the decision in this dissociation condition should be understood also by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## 21. Explanation of the Description of Presence Condition (Atthi-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the description of presence condition, the presence condition is shown by way of co-nascence through the words "the four aggregates" and so forth. It is shown by way of pre-nascence through the words "the eye-base" and so forth. In the phrase "depending on which matter," the presence condition is shown by way of co-nascence and pre-nascence. Thus, this Pali text of the description of presence condition comes by way of presence conditions that are only co-nascent and pre-nascent. In the Pañhāvāra, however, since it comes by way of these conditions—co-nascence, pre-nascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty—the presence condition is also obtained by way of post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty. In this description of presence condition, the teaching is made by way of the remaining (modes). This is the explanation of the Pali text here.

This presence condition is of two kinds: by way of mutuality (aññamañña) and by way of non-mutuality (na-aññamañña). Among those two, mutuality is of three kinds: mind and mind, matter and matter, and mind-and-matter and mind-and-matter. In the phrase "the four immaterial aggregates," mind together with mind is shown as presence condition by way of all arisings of consciousness. In the phrase "the four great essentials," matter together with matter is shown as presence condition by way of all material continuities. In the phrase "at the moment of descent, mind-and-matter," mind-and-matter together with mind-and-matter is shown as presence condition by way of the rebirth aggregates and the base. Non-mutuality is also of three kinds: mind for matter, matter for matter...
384:
Regarding the matter assisting the immaterial (mind) and in the phrase 'citta-cetasikā dhammā' (mental states and mental factors), it is stated that by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra), the immaterial assists matter by the presence condition (atthi-paccaya). In the phrase 'mahābhūtā upādārūpānaṃ' (the great elements [are a condition] for derived matter), matter assists matter by the presence condition by way of the entire continuity of matter. In the phrases such as 'cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā' (the eye-base [is a condition] for the eye-consciousness element), it is stated that matter assists the immaterial by the presence condition by way of base and object.

In another way, this presence condition, in brief, refers to the immaterial and material states that have reached the three sub-moments. It can also be said to be the five aggregates that are currently existing. This presence condition is divided into five types by way of nature (jāti): wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), and matter (rūpa). Among these five, the wholesome presence condition is of two types by way of conascence (sahajāta) and post-nascence (pacchājāta). Similarly, the unwholesome, resultant, and functional presence conditions also have two types each. Among these presence conditions, the wholesome is divided into four types by way of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so on. The unwholesome is only of the sense-sphere. The resultant occurs in the four planes. The functional presence condition occurs in the three planes. The presence condition called matter is only of the sense-sphere. That material presence condition is also of two types by way of conascence and pre-nascence (purejāta). Among those two, the five bases such as the eye and the objects are only pre-nascent which have arisen earlier. The heart-base (hadayavatthu) is either conascent or pre-nascent. The nutriment presence (āhāra-atthi) and faculty presence (indriya-atthi) conditions mentioned in the Pañhāvāra do not receive the distinction of conascence and so on. Thus, the decision should be understood here by way of various distinctions.

When thus divided, the wholesome occurring in the four planes is also a conascent presence condition. In the five-constituent existence, by the method such as 'one aggregate [is a condition] for three aggregates' (eko khandho tiṇṇannaṃ khandhānaṃ), it assists the aggregates mutually and also the mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). Excluding the fine-material sphere wholesome (rūpāvacara-kusala), the remaining wholesome assists only the associated aggregates in the formless plane by way of the conascent wholesome presence condition. This wholesome occurring in the four planes assists the body produced by four causes (catusamuṭṭhānika) or three causes (tisamuṭṭhānika) in the five-constituent existence by way of the post-nascent wholesome presence condition. The same method applies to the unwholesome. For that unwholesome also assists the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence, and only the associated aggregates in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra), by way of the conascent unwholesome presence condition. It assists the body produced by four causes or three causes in the five-constituent existence by way of the post-nascent unwholesome presence condition. As for the resultant, the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere resultant presence condition assists the aggregates and kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) invariably by way of the conascent presence condition.
385:
During the course of existence (pavatti), however, it assists the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter by way of the conascent presence condition. It assists the material group produced by four causes or three causes that has reached the stage of presence (ṭhiti) by way of the post-nascent presence condition. The formless-sphere resultant (arūpāvacara-vipāka) and the supramundane resultant (lokuttara-vipāka) arisen in the formless plane assist only their associated aggregates by way of the conascent presence condition. In the five-constituent existence, the supramundane resultant assists the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter by way of the conascent presence condition. It assists the material group produced by four causes or three causes by way of the post-nascent presence condition. Among functional consciousnesses, the fine-material sphere functional assists the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter by way of the conascent presence condition. It assists the material group produced by four causes or three causes by way of the post-nascent presence condition. The sense-sphere and formless-sphere functionals, however, assist only the associated aggregates in the formless plane, and the mind-produced matter in the five-constituent existence, by way of the conascent presence condition. They assist the material group produced by four causes or three causes by way of the post-nascent presence condition.

The presence condition called matter is of four types: conascent, pre-nascent, nutriment, and faculty. Among those four, the conascent material presence condition exists in four ways by way of the four origins (samuṭṭhāna). Among those four, kamma-produced matter assists as follows: one great element assists three great elements, three assist one, two assist two, and the great elements assist derived matter; thus it assists by way of the conascent presence condition. At the moment of rebirth-linking, the base-matter (vatthu-rūpa) assists the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere resultant aggregates by way of the conascent presence condition. The matter produced by three causes (tisamuṭṭhānika-rūpa) of those resultant aggregates also assists as follows: one great element assists three, three assist one, two assist two, and the great elements assist derived matter; thus it assists by way of the conascent presence condition. The pre-nascent presence condition is of two types: base pre-nascent (vatthu-purejāta) and object pre-nascent (ārammaṇa-purejāta). Both these types should be understood by applying the method already mentioned under the pre-nascent condition (purejāta-paccaya) below. The nutriment presence condition should also be applied according to the method already mentioned under the physical nutriment condition (kabaḷīkārāhāra-paccaya) below. Here, however, it is called the presence condition because of its state of assisting at the moment when it has not yet ceased. The physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) should also be applied according to the method of applying physical life-faculty mentioned under the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya) below. Here also, it is called the presence condition because of its state of assisting only at the moment when it has not yet ceased. Thus, the decision in this presence condition should also be understood by way of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna).

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Presence Condition (Atthi-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).
386: ## 22. Commentary on the Description of the Absence ConditionIn the description of the absence condition (natthi-paccaya), 'ceased without interval' (samanantara-niruddhā) means having ceased immediately after another arising of consciousness without any gap. 'To the present' (paṭuppannānaṃ) means to the presently existing states. By this word, the Buddha establishes the state of being an absence condition by way of giving opportunity for the resultants to arise. Indeed, if the preceding arisings of consciousness did not give opportunity for the succeeding ones to arise by way of their cessation, the present existence of those succeeding ones would not be possible. This is the commentary on the Pali in this context. All the rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). Only the characteristic of the condition is different here; there is no difference in the conditions or the resultants themselves. However, in that proximity condition, the conditions and resultants were shown specifically by way of 'the eye-consciousness element and its associated states are to the mind-element,' and so on. But here, in this absence condition, all of them are shown generally by way of cessation and arising, as 'the mental and concomitant states that have ceased without interval are to the present mental and concomitant states.'## Commentary on the Description of the Absence Condition.## 23. Commentary on the Description of the Disappearance ConditionIn the description of the disappearance condition (vigata-paccaya), 'disappeared without interval' (samanantara-vigatā) means disappeared immediately. By this, the Buddha shows the state of being a condition only by way of the state of disappearing. Thus, between the absence condition and this disappearance condition, there is a difference only in the phrasing (byañjana), not in the meaning (attha).## Commentary on the Description of the Disappearance Condition.## 24. Commentary on the Description of the Non-disappearance ConditionIn the description of the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya), the meaning of the terms 'the four aggregates' and so on should be understood in every way as stated in the description of the presence condition (atthi-paccaya). Indeed, for this condition as well, there is a difference from the presence condition only in the phrasing, not in the meaning.## Commentary on the Description of the Non-disappearance Condition.
