## Paccayaniddesa Pakiṇṇakavinicchayakathā

Now, for the sake of clarity of knowledge regarding these twenty-four conditions shown by way of enumeration (uddesa) and explanation (niddesa), the miscellaneous decision (pakiṇṇaka-vinicchaya) should be understood by way of these ten terms:
(1) The state of many states being a single condition,
(2) The state of a single state being many conditions,
(3) The state of a single condition being many conditions,
(4) The similarity of conditions (paccaya-sabhāga),
(5) The dissimilarity of conditions (paccaya-visabhāga),
(6) By way of pairs (yugaḷaka),
(7) By way of producing and non-producing (janaka-ajanaka),
(8) By way of being a cause for all [mentality-materiality] and not being a cause for all,
(9) By way of variety such as "matter for matter" (rūpaṃ rūpassa), etc.,
(10) By way of difference in existence (bhava-bheda).

Among those ten terms, "the state of many states being a single condition" means that among these twenty-four conditions, excluding the Kamma condition, in the remaining twenty-three conditions, many states together act as a condition. In the Kamma condition, however, only the single state of volition (cetanā) is the condition. Thus, first, the decision by way of many states being a single condition should be understood in this miscellaneous decision.

"The state of a single state being many conditions" means that in the Root Condition (hetu-paccaya), first, non-delusion (amoha) is a single state, yet that non-delusion acts as a condition by way of twenty conditions, excluding the four conditions of Prenascence (purejāta), Kamma, Nutriment (āhāra), and Jhāna. Non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa) are also not Faculty (indriya) or Path (magga) conditions (nor are they the four preceding conditions like Prenascence); they act as conditions by way of the remaining eighteen conditions. Greed (lobha) and delusion (moha) are not Resultant (vipāka) conditions; they act as conditions by way of the remaining seventeen conditions. Hatred (dosa) is not a Predominance (adhipati) condition; it acts as a condition by way of the remaining sixteen conditions.

In the Object Condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), the visible-data base (rūpāyatana) acts as a condition for the eye-consciousness element in four ways: Object, Prenascence, Presence (atthi), and Non-disappearance (avigata). Likewise for the mind-element and rootless mind-consciousness element. For the mind-consciousness element with roots, it also acts as a condition by way of Object-predominance and Object-decisive support. In this way, the state of all object-condition states being many conditions should be understood.

In the Predominance Condition (adhipati-paccaya), the state of Object-predominance being many conditions should be understood in the same way as stated in the Object Condition. Among the Conascence-predominance (sahajāta-adhipati) factors, investigation (vīmaṃsā) acts as a condition in twenty ways, like the non-delusion root. Desire (chanda) is not Root, Prenascence, Kamma, Nutriment, Faculty, Jhāna, or Path condition; it acts as a condition by way of the remaining seventeen conditions. Consciousness (citta) is not Root, Prenascence, Kamma, Jhāna, or Path condition; it acts as a condition by way of the remaining nineteen conditions. Energy (vīriya) is not Root, Prenascence, Kamma, Nutriment, or Jhāna condition; it acts as a condition by way of the remaining nineteen conditions.
388:
In the Proximity Condition (Anantara-paccaya), among the four aggregates taught by the method beginning with "eye-consciousness element" (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) does not become a Root condition, Pre-nascence condition, Kamma condition, Nutriment condition, or Path condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen conditions. The aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) also does not become a Faculty condition or a Jhāna condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining seventeen conditions. In the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the roots are conditions in the same manner as stated under the Root condition (hetu-paccaya); zeal (chanda) and energy (vīriya) are conditions exactly as stated under the Predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya).

Contact (phassa) does not become a Root, Pre-nascence, Kamma, Faculty, Jhāna, or Path condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining eighteen conditions. Volition (cetanā) does not become a Root, Pre-nascence, Faculty, Jhāna, or Path condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen conditions. Initial application (vitakka) does not become a Root, Pre-nascence, Kamma, Nutriment, or Faculty condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining nineteen conditions. Sustained application (vicāra) also does not become a Path condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining eighteen conditions. Rapture (pīti) is a condition only by way of those (eighteen) conditions. One-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) does not become a Root, Pre-nascence, Kamma, or Nutriment condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining twenty conditions. Faith (saddhā) does not become a Root, Pre-nascence, Kamma, Nutriment, Jhāna, or Path condition, but is a condition by way of the remaining eighteen conditions. Mindfulness (sati) is a condition by way of nineteen conditions, namely those (eighteen) and the Path condition. The life faculty (jīvitindriya) is a condition by way of the eighteen conditions stated under faith.

Shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) are conditions by way of the remaining seventeen conditions, having excluded the Faculty condition from those (eighteen) conditions. Likewise, the pairs of states beginning with tranquility of the mental body (kāyapassaddhi), and among the "or-whatever" states (yevāpanaka), decision (adhimokkha), attention (manasikāra), equanimity (tatramajjhattatā), compassion (karuṇā), and appreciative joy (muditā) [are conditions by way of those seventeen conditions]. As for the abstinences (virati), they are conditions in eighteen ways, namely by those (seventeen) and the Path condition. Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is a condition in seventeen ways, having excluded the Resultant condition from those (eighteen) conditions. Wrong speech (micchāvācā), wrong action (micchākammanta), and wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) are conditions in nineteen ways, namely by those (seventeen) and the Kamma and Nutriment conditions.

These states—shamelessness (ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), conceit (māna), sloth (thina), torpor (middha), and restlessness (uddhacca)—do not become Root, Pre-nascence, Kamma, Resultant, Nutriment, Faculty, Jhāna, or Path conditions, but are conditions only by way of the remaining sixteen conditions. Doubt (vicikicchā), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), and worry (kukkucca) are [conditions] of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) in fifteen ways, having excluded the Predominance condition from those (sixteen) conditions. The state of being multiple conditions should be understood exactly by the method stated under the Predominance condition. This same method applies to the Contiguity condition (samanantara-paccaya) as well.

In the Co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), first, the state of being multiple conditions for each single state among the four aggregates should be understood exactly by the method already stated. The four Great Essentials (mahābhūta)...
389:
The four Great Essentials (mahābhūta) are conditions in nine ways: by way of Object, Object-predominance, Co-nascence, Mutuality, Dependence, Strong dependence, Pre-nascence, Presence, and Non-disappearance. The heart-base (hadayavatthu) is a condition in ten ways, by way of those nine conditions and the Dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya). In the Mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya), there is no new condition. In the Dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya), the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so on are conditions in nine ways: by way of Object, Object-predominance, Dependence, Strong dependence, Pre-nascence, Faculty, Dissociation, Presence, and Non-disappearance. In the Strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya), there is no new condition. In the Pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), the visible object, sound, smell, and taste bases (rūpa-sadda-gandha-rasāyatana) are conditions in six ways: by way of Object, Object-predominance, Strong dependence, Pre-nascence, Presence, and Non-disappearance. In this Pre-nascence condition, only the visible object base (rūpāyatana) of such extent is new (from co-nascence-dependence). In the Post-nascence (pacchājāta) and other conditions, there is no new condition. In the Nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya), physical food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is a condition in six ways: by way of Object, Object-predominance, Strong dependence, Nutriment, Presence, and Non-disappearance. In the Faculty (indriya) and other conditions, there is no new condition. Thus, in this miscellaneous analysis (pakiṇṇakavinicchaya), the decision should be understood also by way of a single state becoming multiple conditions.

Regarding "because a single condition becomes multiple conditions": among the Root condition and so on, by whatever primary mode and by whatever sense of being beneficial a certain state is a condition for the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna), without abandoning that mode and that sense, that state at that very moment reaches the state of being multiple conditions for those states by way of other beneficial modes and senses; the decision of that condition should be understood because of such a state of being multiple conditions. This is the meaning. For example—non-delusion (amoha) is a Root condition; that non-delusion, without abandoning its state as a Root condition, reaches the state of being multiple conditions by way of eleven other modes: Predominance, Co-nascence, Mutuality, Dependence, Resultant, Faculty, Path, Association, Dissociation, Presence, and Non-disappearance. Non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa) reach the state of being multiple conditions by way of the remaining conditions, having excluded three conditions—Predominance, Faculty, and Path—from those eleven conditions. This mode is obtained only in the resultant roots (vipāka-hetu); however, in wholesome and functional roots, the state of being a resultant condition is excluded. Greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha) reach the state of being multiple conditions by way of the remaining conditions, having excluded four conditions—those three and the Resultant condition.

The Object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), without abandoning its state as an Object condition, reaches the state of being multiple conditions by way of seven other modes: Object-predominance, Dependence, Strong dependence, Pre-nascence, Dissociation, Presence, and Non-disappearance. This is the maximum limit in this Object condition. If there is the state of being an Object condition for mental states (nāma-dhamma) or for physical states (rūpa-dhamma) that are past or future, only Object-predominance and Object-strong-dependence are obtained in addition to the Object condition.
390:
It can also be obtained beyond the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). In the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), investigation-predominance (vīmaṃsādhipati) is similar to the non-delusion root (amoha-hetu). Desire-predominance (chandādhipati), without abandoning its nature as a predominance condition, also becomes a multiple condition through the power of eight other modes: conascence, mutuality, dependence, resultant, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Energy-predominance (vīriyādhipati) becomes a multiple condition through the power of those eight conditions plus faculty and path conditions, making ten other modes. Consciousness-predominance (cittādhipati), by removing the path condition from those ten and adding the nutriment condition, becomes a multiple condition through the power of these ten conditions, beyond the predominance condition, in ten other modes. As for the multiple conditionality of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), it should be understood in the same way as stated below under the object condition.

Proximity and contiguity conditions (anantara, samanantara-paccaya), without abandoning their nature as proximity and contiguity conditions, also become multiple conditions through the power of five other modes: decisive support, kamma, repetition, absence, and disappearance. Among these proximity and contiguity conditions, only the volition associated with the Noble Path (ariya-magga-cetanā) obtains the nature of kamma condition; the remaining states do not. The conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a conascence condition, also becomes a multiple condition through the power of fourteen other modes: root, predominance, mutuality, dependence, kamma, resultant, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. This is also the maximum limit. It should also be understood that through the power of conascent heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) and so on, there is an absence of root condition and so on in this conascence condition. The same method applies to the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya).

The dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a dependence condition, among the twenty-four conditions, excluding its own nature as dependence condition and the six conditions of proximity, contiguity, post-nascence, repetition, absence, and disappearance, becomes a multiple condition through the power of the remaining seventeen modes. This is also the maximum limit. It should also be understood that through the power of the dependence conditions such as the six bases (vatthu), there is an absence of root condition and so on in this dependence condition.

In the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), object-decisive support (ārammaṇူpanissaya) is similar to object-predominance. Proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya), without abandoning its nature as proximity-decisive support condition, also becomes a multiple condition through the power of six other modes: proximity, contiguity, kamma, repetition, absence, and disappearance. In this proximity-decisive support as well, only the volition associated with the Noble Path obtains the nature of kamma condition; the remaining states do not. Natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) is just natural decisive support. The pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a pre-nascence condition, through the power of the modes of object, object-predominance, dependence, decisive support, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance...
391:
...becomes a multiple condition through eight other modes. This is also an exalted exposition (ukkaṭṭha-niddesa). However, in object pre-nascence (ārammaṇa-purejāta), among these eight conditions, the nature of dependence, faculty, and dissociation conditions is not obtained. Beyond this, what is obtained and what is not obtained should be understood. The post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a post-nascence condition, also becomes a multiple condition through the power of dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance in three other modes. The repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a repetition condition, also becomes a multiple condition through the power of proximity, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance in five other modes.

The kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a kamma condition: first, synchronous kamma (ekakkhaṇika-kamma) becomes a multiple condition through the power of conascence, mutuality, dependence, resultant, nutriment, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance in nine other modes. Asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma) becomes a multiple condition through the power of decisive support, proximity, contiguity, absence, and disappearance in five other modes. The resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a resultant condition, becomes a multiple condition through the power of root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance in fourteen other modes. In the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya), physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra), without abandoning its nature as a nutriment condition, becomes a multiple condition through the power of presence and non-disappearance in two other modes. The remaining three mental nutriments, without abandoning their nature as nutriment conditions, become multiple conditions as appropriate through the power of predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, kamma, resultant, faculty, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance in eleven other modes.

In the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya), the five physical faculties, without abandoning their nature as faculty conditions, become multiple conditions through the power of dependence, pre-nascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance in five other modes. Physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) also, without abandoning its nature as a faculty condition, becomes a multiple condition through the power of presence and non-disappearance in two other modes. Mental faculties also, without abandoning their nature as faculty conditions, become multiple conditions as appropriate through the power of root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, resultant, nutriment, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance in thirteen other modes. The jhāna condition (jhāna-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as a jhāna condition...
392: As appropriate, by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), resultant (vipāka), faculty (indriya), path (magga), association (sampayutta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata), it reaches the state of being multiple conditions in ten other ways. The path condition (magga-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as path condition, reaches the state of being multiple conditions in twelve other ways as appropriate, by way of the ten conditions mentioned in the absorption condition (jhāna-paccaya) and by way of root (hetu) and predominance (adhipati). The association condition (sampayutta-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as association condition, reaches the state of being multiple conditions in thirteen other ways as appropriate, by way of root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, action (kamma), resultant, nutriment (āhāra), faculty, absorption, path, presence, and non-disappearance. The dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as dissociation condition, excluding the six conditions called proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), repetition (āsevana), association, absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata), reaches the state of being multiple conditions in seventeen other ways as appropriate, by way of the remaining conditions. In this dissociation condition, the analysis of conditions for matter (rūpa) and mind (nāma) should be understood. The presence condition (atthi-paccaya), without abandoning its nature as presence condition, excluding the five conditions called proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance, reaches the state of being multiple conditions in eighteen other ways as appropriate, by way of the remaining conditions. The absence condition and disappearance condition are similar to the proximity condition. The non-disappearance condition is just like the presence condition. Thus, in this miscellaneous decision (pakiṇṇaka-vinicchaya), the decision should be understood from the fact that a single condition can become multiple conditions. By way of similarity of conditions (paccaya-sabhāga): Among these twenty-four conditions, proximity, contiguity, proximity-dependence (anantarūpanissaya), repetition, absence, and disappearance are similar (sabhāga). Likewise, object (ārammaṇa), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), and object-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) are also similar. In this way, the decision should be understood here by way of similarity of conditions. By way of dissimilarity of conditions (paccaya-visabhāga): Here, the prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya) is dissimilar (visabhāga) to the postnascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). Likewise, the association condition is dissimilar to the dissociation condition, the presence condition to the absence condition, and the disappearance condition to the non-disappearance condition. In this way, the decision should be understood here by way of dissimilarity of conditions. By way of pairs (yugaḷaka): Among these conditions, the decision should be understood by way of pairs through these reasons: similarity of meaning, similarity of terms, opposition of time, cause and effect relationship, and mutual opposition. Proximity and contiguity are called one pair because of similarity of meaning. Dependence (nissaya) and decisive dependence (upanissaya) are called one pair because of similarity of terms. Prenascence and postnascence are called one pair because of opposition of time. Action (kamma)
393: Prenascence and postnascence are called one pair because of being opposite in terms of time; action (kamma) and resultant (vipāka) are called one pair because of being cause and effect; association (sampayutta) and dissociation (vippayutta) are called one pair because of mutual opposition. Likewise, presence (atthi) and absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) and non-disappearance (avigata) are also pairs. Thus, in this section on conditions, the decision should be understood by way of pairs (yugaḷaka). By way of producer (janaka) and non-producer (ajanaka): Among these conditions, proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), proximity-dependence (anantarūpanissaya), natural decisive dependence (pakatūpanissaya), repetition (āsevana), asynchronous action (nānākkhaṇika-kamma), absence, and disappearance are only producing conditions (janaka), not non-producers. The postnascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is only a supportive condition (upatthambhaka), not a producer. The remaining conditions are both producers (janaka) and non-producers (ajanaka/upatthambhaka). Thus, in this section on conditions, the decision should be understood by way of producer and non-producer. By way of universal (sabbaṭṭhānika) and non-universal (asabbaṭṭhānika): Among these conditions, conascence (sahajāta), dependence (nissaya), presence, and non-disappearance are called universal (sabbaṭṭhānika). This means they are the basis and cause for all conditioned (saṅkhata) material and mental phenomena. There is not a single phenomenon that arises without these conditions. Object (ārammaṇa), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), proximity, contiguity, proximity-dependence, natural decisive dependence, repetition, association, absence, and disappearance are called non-universal (asabbaṭṭhānika). This means they are not the basis for all material and mental phenomena, but only for mental aggregates (nāma-kkhandha). This is because only mental phenomena arise due to these conditions, not material phenomena. Prenascence and postnascence are also non-universal because they are conditions only for mind and matter respectively in their order. The remaining conditions are also not universal because they are causes for the arising of only some material and mental phenomena. Thus, in this section on conditions, the decision should be understood by way of universal and non-universal. By way of various classifications such as 'matter to matter' etc.: Among these twenty-four conditions, there is no single condition that is always matter and conditions only matter. However, there is a condition that is always matter and conditions only mind. Which one is that? It is the prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya). The prenascence condition is always matter and conditions only mind. There is also no condition that is always matter and conditions both matter and mind. However, there is a condition that is always mind and conditions only mind. Which one is that? There are six kinds: proximity, contiguity, repetition, association, absence, and disappearance. All these are always mind and condition only mind. There is also a condition that is always mind and always conditions only matter. Which one is that? It is the postnascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). That postnascence condition...
394:
(That condition of sixfold variety) being invariably mentality, is a condition only for mentality. There is also a condition which, being invariably mentality, is a condition only for materiality. What is that condition? It is the post-existence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). That post-existence condition, being invariably mentality, assists only materiality. There is also a condition which, being invariably mentality, is a condition for both materiality and mentality. What is that condition? It is fivefold by way of root (hetu), karma (kamma), resultant (vipāka), jhāna, and path (magga). All those conditions, being invariably mentality, assist both material phenomena and mental phenomena. There is no condition which, being invariably both materiality and mentality, is a condition only for materiality; rather, it is a condition only for mentality. What is that condition? It is the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya). These two conditions, being invariably both materiality and mentality, assist only mentality. There is also a condition which, being invariably both materiality and mentality, is a condition for both materiality and mentality. What is that condition? It is ninefold by way of predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). All these conditions, being invariably both materiality and mentality, assist both materiality and mentality. Thus, in this section on conditions, the decision should be understood through various classifications such as "materiality for materiality," and so on.

The decision should be understood by way of the different planes of existence (bhava). Among these twenty-four conditions, in the five-constituent plane (pañcavokāra-bhava), there is no condition that is not obtained (all are obtained). In the four-constituent plane (catuvokāra-bhava), however, excluding the three conditions of pre-existence (purejāta), post-existence (pacchājāta), and dissociation (vippayutta), only the remaining twenty-one conditions are obtained. In the one-constituent plane (ekavokāra-bhava), only seven conditions are obtained by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), karma (kamma), faculty (indriya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). In external materiality not bound up with the faculties (anindriyabaddha-rūpa), only five conditions are obtained by way of conascence, mutuality, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, the decision should be understood here also by way of the different planes of existence.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Description of Conditions (Paccayāniddesavāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## The Section of Questions (Pucchāvāra)
## 1. The Explanation of the Analytical Order of Conditions (Paccayānuloma-vaṇṇanā)

Thus, in the Great Book of Conditional Relations (Paṭṭhāna-mahāpakaraṇa), which is the collection of the twenty-four conditional relations in their entirety by way of the Triad Paṭṭhāna (Tika-paṭṭhāna) and so on, this Paṭṭhāna is called "Triad Paṭṭhāna" (Tika-paṭṭhāna), "Dyad Paṭṭhāna" (Duka-paṭṭhāna)... "Dyad-Dyad Paṭṭhāna" (Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna) because it is taught based on those triads and so on. Before dealing with those triads and so on, those conditions by whose power those triads were analyzed are first shown by way of the section known as the Analysis of Conditions (Paccaya-vibhaṅga) and the Laying Down of the Matrix (Mātikā-nikkhepa), both in brief and in detail. Now, because it is taught based on those triads and so on, this Paṭṭhāna is called "Triad Paṭṭhāna," "Dyad Paṭṭhāna"... "Dyad-Dyad Paṭṭhāna."
395: In order to show those triads and so on in detail by the power of these conditions, the teaching was given through the seven Great Chapters (Mahāvāra) based on each triad and dyad. The names of those chapters are: the Chapter on Dependence (Paṭiccavāra), the Chapter on Conascence (Sahajātavāra), the Chapter on Conditions (Paccayavāra), the Chapter on Support (Nissayavāra), the Chapter on Admixture (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra), the Chapter on Association (Sampayuttavāra), and the Chapter on Questions (Pañhāvāra). Among those seven Great Chapters, the one taught in connection with the word "dependent on" (paṭicca), such as "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises," is called the Chapter on Dependence (Paṭiccavāra). The one taught in connection with the word "conascent with" (sahajāta), such as "Conascent with a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises," is called the Chapter on Conascence (Sahajātavāra). This Chapter on Conascence does not differ in meaning from the preceding Chapter on Dependence. The first was taught for the sake of those who understand easily through the word "dependent on," and the second was taught for the sake of those who understand easily through the word "conascent with." In both these chapters, the conditions and the conditionally arisen states should be understood by way of material and mental phenomena. Furthermore, these are only conascent (sahajāta) states; pre-existent (purejāta) and post-existent (pacchājāta) states are not obtained. The one taught in connection with the word "conditioned by" (paccaya), such as "Conditioned by a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises," is called the Chapter on Conditions (Paccayavāra). This chapter, like the previous two, should be understood by way of material and mental phenomena. However, in this Chapter on Conditions, the condition of pre-existence (purejāta) is also obtained. This is the distinction of this chapter from the previous two. Immediately following that, the one taught in connection with the word "depending on" (nissāya), such as "Depending on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises," is called the Chapter on Support (Nissayavāra). This chapter does not differ in meaning from the preceding Chapter on Conditions. The first was taught for the sake of those who understand easily through the word "condition," and the second was taught for the sake of those who understand easily through the word "depending on." After that, the one taught in connection with the word "mixed with" (saṃsaṭṭha), such as "Mixed with a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises," is called the Chapter on Admixture (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra). The one taught in connection with the word "associated with" (sampayutta), such as "Associated with a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises," is called the Chapter on Association (Sampayuttavāra). This Chapter on Association does not differ in meaning from the preceding Chapter on Admixture. The first was taught for the sake of those who understand easily through the word "mixed with," and the second for the sake of those who understand easily through the word "associated with." In both these chapters, the conditions and the conditionally arisen states should be understood only by way of mental phenomena. In the seventh chapter, however, because various questions are raised in the manner of "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of root-condition," and so on, and then all those questions are analyzed and made free from entanglement and confusion in the manner of "Wholesome roots are [a condition] for the associated aggregates," and so on, that chapter is known as the Chapter on Questions (Pañhāvāra) because the questions are thoroughly analyzed. In this Chapter on Questions also, both the conditions and the conditionally arisen states should be understood by way of material and mental phenomena.
396:
Among those seven sections (vāra), this so-called Paṭiccavāra, which is the very first of all sections, is twofold by way of summary (uddesa) and exposition (niddesa). Of these two, the summary section (uddesavāra) is first; it is also called the question section (pucchāvāra). It is also named the designation section (paṇṇattivāra). Indeed, it is called uddesavāra because it is briefly stated by way of root condition (hetupaccaya), etc., of wholesome states, etc., depending on wholesome states, etc. It is called pucchāvāra because it asks about the arising of wholesome states, etc., by way of root condition, etc., depending on wholesome states, etc. It is also called paṇṇattivāra because it makes known (designates) in various ways the arising of wholesome states, etc., by way of root condition, etc., depending on wholesome states, etc.

25-34. In that summary section, the question "Dependent on a wholesome state, might a wholesome state arise because of root condition?" is a hypothetical question (parikappapucchā) asked by way of planning and formulation. The meaning in this question is: There is a certain wholesome state that arises because of root condition; does that state arise depending on a wholesome state? Or else: There is a certain wholesome state that arises depending on a wholesome state; does that state arise because of root condition? This is the meaning here. Among those words, the word 'paṭi' occurs in the sense of 'similarity'. For a similar person is called a counterpart (paṭipuggala), and a similar part is called a counterpart (paṭibhāga). 'Icca' is a word expressing the effort to connect the verb of going (gamana) with a subsequent verb. Combining these two as 'paṭicca', it means having reached a state of similarity known as co-arising, and having reached the state of arising together as one with that condition. By the text 'kusalo dhammo', it asks: "Dependent on a wholesome state in such a way of co-arising, might a wholesome state arise because of root condition?" Alternatively, 'paṭicca' means 'having made a condition'. That making of a condition is obtained in a pre-nascent (purejāta) condition and also in a co-nascent (sahajāta) condition. Here in this Paṭiccavāra, however, only the co-nascent (sahajāta) condition is intended. In the texts such as "Dependent on a wholesome state, might an unwholesome state arise...", the method is the same. Therein, although an unwholesome state does not exist depending on a wholesome state by way of co-nascence, in this question section, whether it is obtainable in reality or not when being answered, all of it is brought forth by way of the question. But in the subsequent answering, having discarded what is not obtainable, only what is obtainable is answered.

Thus, having known the meaning of the questions and the course of the questions in this question section, the delimitation of the questions by way of counting should now be understood. Here, starting with the term 'wholesome' as "Dependent on a wholesome state," there are 3 questions ending with wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Again, starting with that same term, there are 3 questions ending with the dyad (duka) divisions such as wholesome and indeterminate. Again, starting with that same term, there is 1 question ending with the triad (tika). Thus, "Dependent on a wholesome state"...

In this 23-mūlaka method, it should be known that by way of counting, there are only ninety-eight (98) interrogations.

The 24-mūlaka method, however, should be known by way of the combination of all conditions; for that very reason, it is called the 'all-root' (sabba-mūlaka). In that sabba-mūlaka method, there are only 49 interrogations. Thus, taking only the root condition (hetu-paccaya) term, the interrogations which the Teacher analyzed in detail among the assembly of devas by way of the methods beginning with the single-root (eka-mūlaka) and ending with the all-root (sabba-mūlaka), are shown here in brief in this Pucchāvāra Pali.

The sum total of the count of all those interrogations is as follows: In the eka-mūlaka method, one thousand one hundred and seventy-six (1,176) interrogations occur. In the hetu-paccaya method, by making 49 with that very root, they should be taken in this hetu-paccaya-mūlaka; the remaining interrogations should be included in the remaining root methods of conditions such as the object condition (ārammaṇa). In the du-mūlaka method, one thousand one hundred and twenty-seven (1,127); in the ti-mūlaka method, one thousand and seventy-eight (1,078); in the catu-mūlaka method, one thousand and twenty-nine (1,029); in the pañca-mūlaka method, nine hundred and eighty (980); in the cha-mūlaka method, nine hundred and thirty-one (931); in the satta-mūlaka method, eight hundred and eighty-two (882); in the aṭṭha-mūlaka method, eight hundred and thirty-three (833); in the nava-mūlaka method, seven hundred and eighty-four (784); in the dasa-mūlaka method, seven hundred and thirty-five (735); in the ekādasa-mūlaka method, six hundred and eighty-six (686); in the dvādasa-mūlaka method, six hundred and thirty-seven (637); in the terasa-mūlaka method, five hundred and eighty-eight (588); in the cuddasa-mūlaka method, five hundred and thirty-nine (539); in the pannarasa-mūlaka method, four hundred and ninety (490); in the soḷasa-mūlaka method, four hundred and forty-one (441); in the sattarasa-mūlaka method, three hundred and ninety-two (392); in the aṭṭhārasa-mūlaka method, three hundred and forty-three (343); in the ekūnavīsati-mūlaka method, two hundred and ninety-four (294); in the vīsati-mūlaka method, two hundred and forty-five (245); in the ekavīsati-mūlaka method, one hundred and ninety-six (196); in the dvāvīsati-mūlaka method, one hundred and forty-seven (147); in the tevīsati-mūlaka method, ninety-eight (98); and in the sabba-mūlaka method, forty-nine (49). Thus, in the methods beginning with eka-mūlaka analyzed starting with the root term (hetu-paccaya):

By way of the different methods beginning with eka-mūla, the interrogations of the root term (hetu-paccaya) alone are fourteen thousand and seven hundred (14,700).
403:
39-40. Having thus shown the variations of questions starting from the root condition (hetu-paccaya), beginning with the single-root method (ekāmūlaka) up to the all-root method (sabbamūlaka), now, to show them starting from the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), the text says: "Could a wholesome state arise dependent on a wholesome state through object condition and root condition?" and so on. In that passage, by the extent of the words "through object condition and root condition," the single-root method starting with the object condition and ending with the root condition is shown. After that, the double-root method (dukamūlaka) starting with "through object condition and predominance condition" is undertaken. In that double-root method, this first dyad (duka) as well as the object-non-disappearance dyad are shown, and the remaining object-proximity dyad and others are summarized. This final dyad, "through object condition and root condition," is also not shown. However, if it is found in any recitational sequence (vācanāmagga), that recitational sequence should be accepted. After that, without showing the triple-root method (tikamūlaka) and others by way of the object condition, to show the single-root method and others starting with the predominance condition, only this much is said: "through predominance condition, proximity condition, contiguity condition, conascence condition, mutuality condition." This should be understood by way of the single-root method or the all-root method.

After that, to show the double-root method starting with the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya), the text begins with "through non-disappearance condition and root condition," and so on. There, having stated the three dyads in order—the non-disappearance-root dyad, the non-disappearance-object dyad, and the non-disappearance-predominance dyad—at the end, one dyad, the non-disappearance-disappearance dyad, is shown. After that, to show the triple-root method by way of the non-disappearance condition itself, the three triads (tika) are stated in order: "through non-disappearance condition, root condition, and object condition," "through non-disappearance condition, root condition, and predominance condition," and "through non-disappearance condition, root condition, and proximity condition." Then the final triad, "through non-disappearance condition, root condition, and disappearance condition," is stated. After that, to show the quadruple-root method (catumūlaka) by way of the non-disappearance condition itself, the two quadruplets (catukka) are stated: "through non-disappearance condition, root condition, object condition, and predominance condition" and "through non-disappearance condition, root condition, object condition, and proximity condition." Then the term "through disappearance condition" is extracted and placed, and all the rest is summarized. To show that summarization, it is said: "The single-root, double-root, triple-root, and all-root methods of each term should be expanded without confusion." Therefore, just as starting from the root condition, by way of the terms beginning with root, there are 1,176 questions in the single-root method... [pe]... 49 in the all-root method; similarly, in the object condition and others, starting with each condition, by way of the terms beginning with object, in the variations of the single-root method and others of each term, there are 14,700 questions. The numerical determination of those questions in all twenty-four conditions is as follows: In the positive method (anuloma-naya) of the Wholesome Triad (kusala-ttika), 352,800 questions have been well analyzed. Likewise, it occurs in the Feeling Triad (vedanā-ttika) and others. Thus, in all twenty-two triads, 7,761,600 variations of questions have been shown in the recitational sequence.
404:
In the single-root method of each term, there are 1,176 questions... [pe]... in the all-root method, there are 49 questions. Thus, by way of the variations such as the single-root method of each term, there are 14,700 questions. The numerical determination of those questions in all twenty-four conditions is as follows:

In the positive method of the Wholesome Triad, 352,800 questions have been well analyzed.

As in the Wholesome Triad, so it is in the Feeling Triad and others. Thus, in all twenty-two triads:

By way of the variations of the triads, 7,761,600 questions have been shown in summary in the recitational sequence.

In the dyads (duka), however: "Dependent on a root state, does a root state arise because of root condition?" Thus, (1) root dependent on root, (2) non-root dependent on root, (3) root and non-root dependent on root, (4) non-root dependent on non-root, (5) root dependent on non-root, (6) root and non-root dependent on non-root, (7) root dependent on root and non-root, (8) non-root dependent on root and non-root, and (9) root and non-root dependent on root and non-root—thus, in each dyad, there are 9 questions for each condition such as the root condition. Among those conditions, starting with the root condition, there are 216 questions in the single-root method. Among those questions, the 9 questions of the root condition alone, unmixed with other conditions, should be taken. The remaining questions have been taken by way of the turns (vāra).

In the twenty-three turns starting from the double-root method of those questions, subtracting the groups of nine each, the numerical determination up to the all-root method is as follows: First, in the double-root method, subtracting 9 from the 216 questions shown in the single-root method, there are 207 questions. Subtracting 9 from that, there are 198 in the triple-root method. Thus, subtracting 9 from each preceding one, there are 189 in the quadruple-root method, 180 in the quintuple-root method (pañcamūlaka), 171 in the sextuple-root method (chamūlaka), 162 in the septuple-root method (sattamūlaka), and 153 in the octuple-root method (aṭṭhamūlaka).
405:
In the nine-root (nava-mūlaka), there are 144; in the ten-root, 135; in the eleven-root, 126; in the twelve-root, 117; in the thirteen-root, 108; in the fourteen-root, 99; in the fifteen-root, 90; in the sixteen-root, 81; in the seventeen-root, 72; in the eighteen-root, 63; in the nineteen-root, 54; in the twenty-root, 45; in the twenty-one-root, 36; in the twenty-two-root, 27; in the twenty-three-root, 18; and in the all-root, there are 9 each.

Just as there are 216 in the one-root... and so on, up to 9 in the all-root by the power of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya), so also in the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and others, starting with each one, by the power of the terms such as 'object', there are 216 in the one-root... and so on, up to 9 in the all-root for each term. Thus, for each term, in the various divisions such as the one-root, there are 2,700 questions each. Among all those questions, this is the numerical determination for the twenty-four conditions:

Sixty-four thousand and eight hundred questions
Are known in the forward method (anuloma-naya)
Of the Root Couplet (hetu-duka) alone.

As it is in the Root Couplet, so it is in the Couplet with Roots (sahetuka-duka) and others. Therefore, in the entire hundred couplets:

Six million, four hundred
And eighty thousand questions
In the hundred couplets are known by the wise.

This is the numerical determination of the questions in the Pure Triplets (Suddhika Tika-paṭṭhāna) and the Couplets (Duka-paṭṭhāna).

Furthermore, in the text taught under the name of Couplet-Triplets (Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna), which takes the twenty-two triplets and includes them in the hundred couplets, such as: "Dependent on a wholesome state which is a root, does a wholesome state which is a root arise because of root-condition?"—in this way, each triplet among the twenty-two triplets is to be combined with each of the hundred couplets, and the determination of the questions should be understood by counting them through the power of the one-root and so on, according to the method mentioned below.

Furthermore, in the text taught under the name of Triplet-Couplets (Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna), which takes the hundred couplets and includes them in the twenty-two triplets, such as: "Dependent on a wholesome root-state, does a wholesome root-state arise because of root-condition?"—in this way, in the hundred couplets...
406:
The determination of the questions to be shown by combining each couplet with the twenty-two triplets should be understood by counting them through the power of the methods such as the one-root, according to the method mentioned below.

Furthermore, in the text taught under the name of Triplet-Triplets (Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna), which includes triplets within triplets themselves, such as: "Dependent on a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling, does a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling arise because of root-condition?"—in this way, the determination of the questions to be shown by combining each triplet among the twenty-two triplets with the remaining twenty-one triplets should be understood by counting them through the power of the methods such as the one-root, according to the method mentioned below.

Furthermore, in the text taught under the name of Couplet-Couplets (Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna), which includes couplets within couplets themselves, such as: "Dependent on a state that is both a root and accompanied by roots, does a state that is both a root and accompanied by roots arise because of root-condition?"—in this way, the determination of the questions to be shown by combining each couplet among the hundred couplets with the remaining ninety-nine couplets should be understood by counting them through the power of the methods such as the one-root, according to the method mentioned below. Indeed, the Tathāgata taught the Dhamma to the assembly of devas only after showing all these divisions. To the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), however, the teaching was declared merely by showing the method in brief, saying, "Today, I have taught this and that."

The Elder (Sāriputta) also maintained the lineage of recitation (vācanāmagga) only in brief. That lineage of recitation was included in the collection (sangaha) at the time of the Council (Sangīti) exactly according to the method maintained by the Elder.

To show that summary method, this verse beginning with "Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ" was established. Its meaning is:

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna,
The especially noble Duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna,
The Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna,
The Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna,
And the Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna—
These six methods, which are very profound in the forward order (anuloma), should be known.

In that forward order, there are two types: the forward order of states (dhamma-anuloma) and the forward order of conditions (paccaya-anuloma). Among those two, in the forward order of states, which is summarized by the terms of the Abhidhamma Mātikā such as "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises"...
407:
The teaching that proceeds by way of the conformity of states is called Dhammānuloma. The teaching that proceeds by way of the conformity of the twenty-four conditions, such as "root-condition, object-condition," is called Paccayanuloma.

Among those two types of conformity, in the commentary below, this verse: "The excellent Paṭṭhāna, the triads... the six methods in the conformity are very profound," is spoken with reference to Dhammānuloma. However, in this Paṇṇattivāra, this verse is spoken with reference to Paccayanuloma within that Dhammānuloma. Therefore, in the commentary verse "the six methods in the conformity are very profound," the meaning should be understood as: the six methods such as the Triad Paṭṭhāna (Tikapaṭṭhāna) in Dhammānuloma are very profound. In the context of this Paṇṇattivāra, the meaning should be understood as: in the Paccayanuloma which proceeds as "root-condition, object-condition," these six methods such as the Triad Paṭṭhāna of this Dhammānuloma are very profound. Among those six Paṭṭhānas, in the Anuloma Triad Paṭṭhāna, the classification of questions is shown in brief in the Paṭiccavāra of this Paṇṇattivāra only by way of the Wholesome Triad (Kusalattika). In the remaining triads and the remaining Paṭṭhānas, not even a single question is shown. In the subsequent sections such as the Sahajātavāra, even by way of the Wholesome Triad, the questions are not extracted, but only the answers (vissajjanā) are shown according to what is obtainable. Because of the statement "the six methods in the conformity are very profound," in this Paccayanuloma, all these six Paṭṭhāna methods should be extracted and shown by way of questions. For this is the responsibility of the teachers who explain the Paṭṭhāna text.

## 2. Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā
42-44. Now it is the Negative Conditionality (Paccanīya). To show that Paccanīya, the passage beginning with "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state may arise, not due to root-condition" is commenced. In that Paccanīya, the extent of the questions is exactly equal to the Anuloma questions. Therefore, in this Paccanīya, after saying "Just as the root-condition is expanded in the Anuloma, so should the non-root-condition (na-hetupaccaya) be expanded in the Paccanīya," it is said again at the end: "Just as in the Anuloma, for each term, it is expanded from the single-root (ekamūlaka), double-root (dumūlaka), triple-root (timūlaka), quadruple-root (catumūlaka) up to the twenty-three-root (tevisatimūlaka), so should it be expanded in the Paccanīya." This word "tevisatimūlaka" is spoken here with reference only to the double-root (dumūlaka). At the end, however, there is indeed the twenty-four-root (caturvīsatimūlaka) which has all roots. It should be noted that all that textual procedure is only a summary.
408:
In this verse, "In the excellent Paṭṭhāna, the triads... the methods in the negative (paccanīya) are very profound," there are also two kinds of negative: Dhammapaccanīya and Paccayapaccanīya. Among those two, the method that proceeds by way of the negative teaching of states categorized by the Abhidhamma matrix terms such as "wholesome states," as in "Dependent on a non-wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises," is called Dhammapaccanīya. The method that proceeds by way of the negative teaching of the twenty-four conditions such as "not due to root-condition, not due to object-condition," is called Paccayapaccanīya. Among those two, in the commentary mentioned below, this verse: "In the excellent Paṭṭhāna, the triads... the methods in the negative are very profound," is spoken with reference to Dhammapaccanīya. In this Paṇṇattivāra, however, this verse is spoken with reference to Paccayapaccanīya within Dhammānuloma itself. Therefore, in the commentary verse "the methods in the negative are very profound," the meaning should be noted as: in Dhammapaccanīya, the six methods such as the Triad Paṭṭhāna are very profound. In this context, however, the meaning should be noted as: in the Paccayapaccanīya which proceeds as "not due to root-condition, not due to object-condition," these six methods such as the Triad Paṭṭhāna within this Dhammānuloma itself are very profound.

Among those methods, in the Anuloma Triad Paṭṭhāna itself, the classification of questions is shown in brief in the Paṭiccavāra of this Paṇṇattivāra only by way of the Wholesome Triad. In the remaining triads and the remaining Paṭṭhānas, not even one kind of question is shown. In the subsequent sections such as the Sahajātavāra, even by way of the Wholesome Triad, the questions are not extracted, but only the answers (vissajjanā) are shown according to what is obtainable. Because of the statement "the methods in the negative are very profound," in this Paccayapaccanīya, all these six Paṭṭhāna methods should be extracted and shown by way of questions. For this is the responsibility of the teachers who explain the Paṭṭhāna text.

## 3. Anulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā

45-48. Now it is the Positive-Negative Conditionality (Anulomapaccanīya). To show that Anulomapaccanīya, it is commenced with: "Dependent on a wholesome state, does a wholesome state arise due to root-condition but not due to object-condition?" etc. In that passage "due to root-condition but not due to object-condition... due to root-condition but not due to non-disappearance-condition," by way of combining the root-term (hetu-pada) with each of the remaining twenty-three conditions, there are twenty-three single-root (ekamūlaka) Anulomapaccanīyas beginning with the root-term. Among those twenty-three, by making forty-nine for each, there are 1127 (one thousand one hundred and twenty-seven) questions. In the double-root (dumūlaka), the terms root and object are combined with each of the remaining twenty-two conditions...
409:
In all the methods such as Ekamūlaka (Single Root) mentioned in the Anuloma (Positive) method, the number of questions should be understood by excluding one term at a time and proceeding with the remaining terms. In this Paccaya-anuloma-paccanīya (Condition Positive-Negative) method, among the methods such as Ekamūlaka, all the questions that appear in the Pali text and those that do not appear should be understood exactly according to the method stated below.

Regarding the statement, "The noble text of Tika-paṭṭhāna... the six methods in the Anuloma-paccanīya are very profound," here also, by the method stated below, there are two types of Anuloma-paccanīya: Dhamma-anuloma-paccanīya and Paccaya-anuloma-paccanīya. Among these two, the method that proceeds by the power of the Anuloma-paccanīya teaching on the states encompassed by the Abhidhamma Mātikā terms such as "Kusalā dhammā" (Wholesome states), as in "Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca na kusalo dhammo" (Dependent on a wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises), is called Dhamma-anuloma-paccanīya. The method that proceeds by the power of the Anuloma-paccanīya teaching on the terms obtained among the twenty-four conditions, as in "Hetupaccayā na-ārammaṇapaccayā" (By way of root condition, not by way of object condition), is called Paccaya-anuloma-paccanīya. Among these two, in the lower Commentary, this verse "Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ... cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā" was spoken with reference to Dhamma-anuloma-paccanīya. However, in this Paṇṇatti-vāra, this verse is spoken with reference to Paccaya-anuloma-paccanīya within the Anuloma itself. Therefore, in the Commentary verse, "The six methods in the Anuloma-paccanīya are very profound," the meaning should be understood as: the six methods such as Tika-paṭṭhāna in the Dhamma-anuloma-paccanīya are very profound. But in the context of this Paṇṇatti-vāra Pali text, the meaning should be understood as: in the Paccaya-anuloma-paccanīya which proceeds as "Hetupaccayā na-ārammaṇapaccayā", these six methods such as Tika-paṭṭhāna within this Dhamma-anuloma itself are very profound.

Among those methods, in the Anuloma Tika-paṭṭhāna itself, the classification of questions is shown in brief in this Paṇṇatti-vāra of the Paṭicca-vāra by way of only the Kusala-tika (Wholesome Triad). Not a single question is shown in the remaining Triads or in the remaining Paṭṭhānas. In the subsequent sections such as Sahajāta-vāra (Co-nascence Section), the answers (vissajjanā) are shown only by way of what is obtainable, without extracting the questions even by way of the Kusala-tika. Because of the statement, "The six methods in the Anuloma-paccanīya are very profound," all these six Paṭṭhāna methods should be extracted and shown by way of questions in this Paccaya-anuloma-paccanīya. This is indeed the responsibility of the teachers who explain the Paṭṭhāna text.
410:
## 4. Description of the Negative-Positive (Paccanīya-anuloma-vaṇṇanā)

49-52. Now, the Paccanīya-anuloma (Negative-Positive) method occurs. In that method, the extent of the questions is exactly the same as the Anuloma-paccanīya questions. Among these two, the method that proceeds by the power of the Paccanīya-anuloma teaching on the states encompassed by the Abhidhamma Mātikā terms such as "Kusalā dhammā", as in "Nakusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo" (Dependent on a non-wholesome state, a wholesome state arises), is called Dhamma-paccanīya-anuloma. Among these two, in the lower Commentary, this verse "Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ... cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīရာ" was spoken with reference to Dhamma-paccanīya-anuloma. However, in this Paṇṇatti-vāra, this verse is spoken with reference to Paccaya-paccanīya-anuloma within the Anuloma itself. Therefore, in the Commentary, in the statement "The six methods in the Paccanīya-anuloma are very profound," the meaning should be understood as: the six methods such as Tika-paṭṭhāna in the Dhamma-paccanīya-anuloma are very profound. But in the context of this Paṇṇatti-vāra, the meaning should be understood as: in the Paccaya-paccanīya-anuloma which proceeds as "Nahetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā", these six methods such as Tika-paṭṭhāna within this Dhamma-anuloma itself are very profound.

Among those methods, in the Anuloma Tika-paṭṭhāna itself, the classification of questions is shown in brief in this Paṇṇatti-vāra of the Paṭicca-vāra by way of only the Kusala-tika. Not a single question is shown in the remaining Triads or in the remaining Paṭṭhānas. In the subsequent sections such as Sahajāta-vāra, the answers are shown only by way of what is obtainable, without extracting the questions even by way of the Kusala-tika. Because of the statement, "The six methods in the Paccanīya-anuloma are very profound," all these six Paṭṭhāna methods should be extracted and shown by way of questions in this Paccaya-paccanīya-anuloma.
