411:
## 1. Commentary on the Triplets of Wholesome States
## 1. Commentary on the Section on Dependence
## 1. Analytical Enumeration of Conditions
## 1. Section on Analysis
Now, in the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra), based on the Triplets of Wholesome States (Kusalatika), by way of root condition (hetupaccaya) and so forth, forty-nine questions have been shown as a method, thereby presenting an immeasurable number of questions. Among those questions, because wholesome states and unwholesome states do not arise together, the question "Depending on a wholesome state, an unwholesome state arises through root condition" does not receive an answer. Discarding those questions that do not receive an answer, the Explanatory Section (Niddesavāra) of the Section on Dependence (Paṭiccavāra) is begun with the method: "Depending on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises through root condition," and so forth, in order to answer only those that do receive an answer.

In that Explanatory Section, a question might arise: "If these forty-nine questions by way of root condition and so forth do not receive an answer in every respect, why are they shown? Should not only those that receive an answer be shown?" Yes, they should indeed be shown. However, if only those were shown, they would have to be shown without abbreviation in every single triplet (tika), couplet (duka), couplet-triplet (dukatika), triplet-couplet (tikaduka), triplet-triplet (tikatika), and couplet-couplet (dukaduka) in all the Tikapaṭṭhāna, Dukapaṭṭhāna, and so forth. Why? Because the questions that receive an answer in the Kusalatika do not necessarily receive an answer in the Triplets of Feeling (Vedanātika) and so forth. Furthermore, in the Dhammānulomapaccanīya Tikapaṭṭhāna, in the answers for the Triplets of Initial Application (Vitakkatika) and the Triplets of Rapture (Pītitika), all these forty-nine questions receive an answer. Therefore, as an extreme limit, all the questions that should exist in each triplet are shown in the Kusalatika. When all are shown in this way, by discarding those that do not receive an answer and answering only those that do, they can be easily understood. Thus, all are shown in the Kusalatika for the sake of easy understanding. It should be understood that here, discarding the questions that do not receive an answer, only those that receive an answer are answered.

In that Explanatory Section, "Depending on a wholesome state" (Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca) means: depending on one state among the wholesome states of the four planes, such as the feeling aggregate and so forth, having reached it in a similar state known as co-arising, and having reached the state of arising together as one with that state. "A wholesome state" (Kusalo dhammo) refers to one state among the wholesome states of the four planes, such as the perception aggregate and so forth. "Arises" (Uppajjati) means: from the moment of arising (uppāda) until before reaching cessation (nirodha), it arises upwards; it also means it is produced.
412:
The meaning is: it gains its own nature; it is said that it reaches all three moments, beginning with arising. "Through root condition" (Hetupaccayāti) means: by means of a wholesome root, accomplishing the state of root condition.

Having thus given the answer "it arises" to the question "would it arise?", the text now says "one wholesome aggregate..." and so forth, to show by way of aggregates which state arises depending on which state. In that statement, "one" means any one among the four aggregates such as feeling and so forth. "Three aggregates" refers to the remaining three aggregates, excluding whichever one was taken as the condition. "Three aggregates [arise]" means the remaining three, excluding the one aggregate that was taken as "arises" among the aggregates such as feeling and so forth. "Depending on two aggregates" means depending on any two aggregates among the six pairs such as the feeling-perception couplet and so forth. "Two aggregates" means the remaining two aggregates, excluding whichever ones were taken as the condition, arise by means of a wholesome root, accomplishing the state of root condition.

The reason is that there is no such thing as one aggregate being a condition for only one or only two, nor two aggregates being a condition for only one. Therefore, it is not said: "Depending on one aggregate, one aggregate [arises]; depending on one aggregate, two aggregates [arise]; depending on two aggregates, one aggregate [arises]." In places such as "Depending on a wholesome state, an indeterminate state arises," the meaning should be understood in the same manner as already stated. The phrase "mind-produced matter" (cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ) is stated to show that matter which is co-nascent with the wholesome and receives the root condition, because the meaning of the word "depending" (paṭicca) is co-nascence (sahajāta). In the future as well, this same method should be applied in such places.

In the phrase "resultant indeterminate, functional indeterminate," the rootless (ahetuka) should not be taken because of the absence of root condition, and the immaterial resultant (āruppavipāka) should not be taken because it does not arise together with matter. The phrase "at the moment of rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhikkhaṇe) is stated to show the arising of an indeterminate state depending on an indeterminate state known as kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa). "Resultant indeterminate" is stated by way of the indeterminate states existing at that moment. The phrase "Depending on aggregates, the base; depending on the base, aggregates" is stated to show the arising of aggregates depending on the base, even though the base (hadayavatthu) is already included by taking kamma-produced matter.

The phrase "one great essential" (ekaṃ mahာbhūtaṃ) and so forth is stated to show the arising of material indeterminate states depending on material indeterminate states. The connection of meaning here should be understood in the same manner as stated for "one aggregate" and so forth. Having thus stated the arising of great essentials depending on the great essentials which are material indeterminates, now...
413:
To demonstrate the arising of derived matter (upādārūpa) depending on the great essentials (mahābhūta), the statement beginning with "depending on the great essentials, mind-produced matter..." is taught. This being so, only the term "derived matter" (upādārūpa) should have been mentioned; why were the other two terms (mind-produced matter and kamma-produced matter) taught? It is for the purpose of showing their arising depending also on the great essentials. The reason is that the matter shown below as "mind-produced matter and kamma-produced matter" does not arise depending on the aggregates alone, but it should be understood that this was taught to show that it arises depending on the great essentials as well. Among those types of matter, mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) occurs only during the course of existence (pavatti), while kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) occurs also at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). The term "derived matter" (upādārūpa) is a qualifier for both of them.

In this Pāḷi passage, "depending on wholesome aggregates and the great essentials," only the mind-produced great essentials are taken. However, in the passage "mind-produced matter," both primary matter (bhūtarūpa) and derived matter (upādārūpa) are taken. According to the method "depending on one great essential, three great essentials [arise]," primary matter also arises depending on the aggregates and the great essentials. By the method already mentioned, "depending on the great essentials, derived matter [arises]," derived matter also (arises depending on the aggregates and the great essentials). The same method applies to the answers for the questions on the unwholesome and the indeterminate. Thus, in the root condition (hetu-paccaya), nine questions are answered. Only these nine are obtained here; the remaining forty questions are void questions (mogha-pucchā) and are therefore not answered. By this means, the meaning of the answers to the questions in the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and so forth should also be understood. However, we shall examine only those points that are worthy of examination in each respective condition.

In the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), first of all, because matter does not arise by way of the object condition, those questions mixed with matter among the nine questions are excluded, and only three questions are answered. For that very reason, it is stated, "depending on the base, the aggregates arise," but it is not taught that "depending on the aggregates, the base arises." The reason is that the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) does not arise by way of the object condition.

In the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), the term "resultant indeterminate" (vipākābyākata) is taught with reference only to the supramundane resultant. Therefore, in this predominance condition, "at the moment of rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhikkhaṇe) is not taken. The rest of the arrangement is exactly the same as the root condition.

In the proximity (anantara) and contiguity (samanantara) conditions, because matter is not obtained, only three questions are answered, just as in the object condition.

In the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), the phrase "at the moment of rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhikkhaṇe) is taught by way of rebirth-linking in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhūmi). Below, in the analysis of conditions (paccaya-vibhaṅga), the term "at the moment of descent" (okkantikkhaṇe) appears; that term is also identical in meaning to this "at the moment of rebirth-linking," and there is only a difference in phrasing. Alternatively, "due to the conjunction of three factors..."
414:
Based on the teaching, "Due to the conjunction of three factors, there is the descent of the embryo" (from the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, Mūlapaṇṇāsa), this name "descent" (okkanti) is a name for rebirth-linking in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-paṭisandhi) only. The name "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) is a term common to all existences. However, in this conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), because of the teaching of the words "and kamma-produced matter" and so forth, only rebirth-linking in the five-constituent realm is intended. The reason is that such rebirth-linking in the five-constituent realm encompasses both the state of being a condition and the state of being conditionally arisen for both matter and mind. Therefore, because it provides a complete answer involving the five aggregates, only that rebirth-linking in the five-constituent realm is taken.

The phrase "one external great essential" is taught with reference to the great essentials residing in earth, stones, and so forth, which are not connected with the life-faculty (anindriya). The reason is that in the explanation of conditions (paccaya-niddesa) within the analysis of conditions (paccaya-vibhaṅga), the internal great essentials and external great essentials are taken together by the text "the four great essentials." That teaching in the Paccaya-vibhaṅga-vāra is a brief teaching (saṅkhepa-desanā). This detailed teaching (vitthāra-desanā), however, because it intends to show everything by analyzing it in detail, states "one external great essential" and so forth. The phrase "depending on one great essential of the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta)" is stated by way of the great essentials produced by the two continuities of kamma and temperature (utu). This statement, "depending on the great essentials, kamma-produced matter [arises]," is stated only by way of kamma-produced matter (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa). The term "derived matter" (upādārūpa) is stated only by way of temperature-produced matter (utu-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa).

In the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya), the statement "depending on the aggregates, the base; depending on the base, the aggregates" is taught to show the state of mutuality condition of the four aggregates together with the heart-base matter.

In the support condition (nissaya-paccaya), because the meaning of "depending on" (paṭicca) is the meaning of "conascent" (sahajāta), the support condition of the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth shown below in the explanation of conditions (paccaya-niddesa) is not taken here. The reason is that the eye-base and so forth become conditions by being prenascent (purejāta), whereas in this "depending-on" section (paṭicca-vāra), only that which is conascent (sahajāta) is obtained. For that very reason, it is said, "The support condition is similar to the conascence condition."

In the strong support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), because there is no strong support condition for matter, only three answers are obtained; therefore, it is said, "It is similar to the object condition." In that strong support condition, although not all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states obtain the object-strong support condition (ārammaṇūpanissaya-paccaya), it should be understood that this is stated by way of those states that do obtain it.

In the prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), the statement "the base [is a condition] by way of prenascence condition" means that they arise by way of the prenascence condition through the base, depending on the base. In this context of "one aggregate that is a resultant indeterminate," that base which is a conascence condition for the resultant indeterminate at the moment of rebirth-linking should not be taken here, because it belongs to the analysis of the prenascence condition. That which...
415:
Wholesome states and so forth do not obtain the pre-existence condition (purejāta-paccaya) in the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi). These wholesome states, which do not obtain the pre-existence condition in the formless realm, should also not be included here in this Exposition of Pre-existence (Purejāta-niddesa), which is the analysis of the pre-existence condition. Furthermore, the object does not invariably obtain the status of a pre-existence condition. Why? Because the sense-base of forms (rūpāyatana) and so forth can only fulfill the status of pre-existence condition for eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) and so forth; however, for the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇa-dhātu), past and future forms and so forth also certainly become objects. Therefore, the object pre-existence condition is not taken here in this Purejāta-niddesa. This teaching is given by way of the aggregates (khandha), not by way of the consciousness elements (viññāṇa-dhātu). In the teaching beginning with 'One resultant indeterminate aggregate' (vipākābyākataṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ), all seven consciousness elements are included; it should be understood that it is not only eye-consciousness and so forth that are included.

The post-existence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is not a condition for wholesome and unwholesome states; it is merely a supporter of indeterminate matter and not a producer. Therefore, since there is not even a single state that should be taught as 'it arises because of the post-existence condition,' the answer is not given by way of the post-existence condition.

In the repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), although all functional (kiriya) states certainly do not obtain the repetition condition, it is taught as 'functional indeterminate' (kiriyābyākataṃ) in connection with those functional states that do obtain it. Therefore, it should be understood that only functional states performing the function of impulsion (javana) are taken in this Exposition of Repetition (Āsevana-niddesa).

In the kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), the synchronous kamma condition (ekakkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) should be understood in wholesome and unwholesome states; it should be understood similarly in functional indeterminate states. In resultant indeterminate states, however, the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) should also be understood; it should be understood similarly for the great essentials (mahābhūta) at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). For mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), the synchronous kamma condition should be understood. For kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa), only the asynchronous kamma condition should be understood; it should be understood similarly for the matter of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta-rūpa). In the context of this matter of non-percipient beings, the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) is taught as kamma-born matter. The remaining group of matter is not taught as derived matter (upādā-rūpa) because it is certainly kamma-produced matter (kammasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). Even so, in the context of this matter of non-percipient beings, only kamma-produced matter is intended.

In the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya), since wholesome, unwholesome, and functional states are not obtained, the answer is given only by way of the indeterminate. 'Mind-produced' (cittasamuṭṭhāna) refers only to the matter that has resultant consciousness as its cause. 'Kamma-born matter' (kaṭattā-rūpa) refers to the faculty-matter (indriya-rūpa) and base-matter (vatthu-rūpa) as applicable. 'Derived matter' (upādā-rūpa) refers to the derived matter existing at that moment, which remains after excluding that faculty-matter and base-matter.

In the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya), the arising of all wholesome and other aggregates, as well as mind-produced matter, by way of mental nutriment (nāma-āhāra) should be understood; it should be understood similarly for the great essentials at the moment of rebirth-linking. 'Mind-produced' refers to the matter that has consciousness such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as its cause. 'Nutriment-produced' (āhārasamuṭṭhāna) refers to the matter that has edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) as its cause. Mind-produced...
416:
It is the (matter) produced by edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra). 'Mind-produced' (cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ) refers only to the (matter) produced by wholesome and unwholesome consciousness. In the Chapter on the Analysis of Conditions (Paccaya-vibhaṅga-vāra), edible food was shown first according to the sequence of nutriments. However, in this (Chapter on the Dependent Origination - Paṭicca-vāra), it should be understood that mental nutriments are shown first by way of the question beginning with 'Wholesome state' (kusalaṃ dhammaṃ).

In the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya), in the Paccaya-vibhaṅga-vāra, the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) and so forth were shown first according to the sequence of faculties. However, in this (Paṭicca-vāra), the status of mental faculties as conditions was shown first by way of the question on wholesome states and so forth. Among those (mental and physical faculties), mental faculties should be taken in wholesome and other states as applicable. In the case of the essential matter of non-percipient beings, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) (is taken).

In the jhāna condition (jhāna-paccaya) and path condition (magga-paccaya), the answer is just the same as the answer for the root condition (hetu-paccaya). For that very reason, it is stated here as 'similar to the root condition' (hetupaccaya-sadisa).

In the association condition (sampayutta-paccaya), the answer follows the mode of the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). For that very reason, it is stated here as 'similar to the object condition' (ārammaṇapaccaya-sadisa).

In the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya), 'depending on the base, by way of dissociation condition' (vatthuṃ vippayutta-paccayā) means that (the aggregates arise) by way of dissociation condition depending on the base. The meaning is that they arise because of the base which fulfills the status of dissociation condition. 'Depending on the aggregates, by way of dissociation condition' (khandhe vippayutta-paccayā) means that (the base arises) by way of dissociation condition depending on the aggregates. The meaning is that (the base) arises because of the aggregates which fulfill the status of dissociation condition. 'Aggregates, depending on the base, by way of dissociation condition' (khandhā vatthuṃ vippayutta-paccayā) means that the aggregates arise by way of dissociation condition depending on the base. The meaning is that they arise because of the base which fulfills the status of dissociation condition. 'Mind-produced matter, depending on the aggregates, by way of dissociation condition' (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpaṃ khandhe vippayutta-paccayā) means that mind-produced matter arises by way of dissociation condition depending on the aggregates. The meaning is that mind-produced matter arises because of the aggregates which fulfill the status of dissociation condition. In the remaining answers as well, such as 'depending on the base, by way of dissociation condition,' the meaning should be understood in the same manner as already stated. In this resultant indeterminate state of the dissociation condition, the physical bases such as the eye-base are included by the taking of 'base' (vatthu). The statement beginning with 'one great essential' (ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ) is made to show the status of the matter-indeterminate state as a condition. 'Mind-produced' (cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ) refers to the (matter) produced by indeterminate consciousness as well as that produced by wholesome and unwholesome consciousness.

In the presence condition (atthi-paccaya), the entire answer follows the mode of the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). For that very reason, it is stated here as 'similar to the conascence condition' (sahajātapaccaya-sadisa).

71-72. The absence condition (natthi-paccaya) and disappearance condition (vigata-paccaya) follow the mode of the object condition. The non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya) follows the mode of the conascence condition. For that very reason, it is stated here as 'similar to the object condition, similar to the conascence condition' (ārammaṇapaccaya-sadisaṃ, sahajātapaccaya-sadisaṃ).
417: The statement "these twenty-three conditions" is spoken by way of the conditions shown in brief. "Should be expanded" means they should be expanded by way of those questions that receive an answer. This is the explanation of the meaning in the answering of the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-ttika) of the Dependent Chapter (Paṭiccavāra) in the direct order of conditions (Paccayānuloma), having the Root Condition (Hetu-paccaya) as the single root (Ekamūlaka). ## ၂။ သင်္ချာဝါရ Now, in order to show by way of calculation those answering-sections (vissajjanavāra) obtained in each condition among these root conditions and so forth, the passage beginning with "Hetuyā nava" (nine in root) is undertaken. Therein, "Hetuyā nava" means there are nine answering-sections of questions in the root condition. Those nine are: wholesome with wholesome, wholesome with indeterminate, wholesome with wholesome and indeterminate; unwholesome with unwholesome, unwholesome with indeterminate, unwholesome with unwholesome and indeterminate; indeterminate with indeterminate; wholesome and indeterminate with indeterminate; and unwholesome and indeterminate with indeterminate. "Ārammaṇe tīṇi" (three in object) means: wholesome with wholesome, unwholesome with unwholesome, and indeterminate with indeterminate. "Adhipatiyā nava" (nine in predominance) is just the same as what was said for the root condition. Indeed, it is said that there are nine each in twelve conditions. In all those, the answering of questions is just like the root condition. However, there is a distinction in the Analysis (Vibhaṅga/Niddesavāra). It is said that there are three each in ten conditions. In all those, the answering of questions is just like the object condition. However, there is a distinction in the Analysis. For in the answering of the indeterminate term in the Mutuality Condition (Aññamañña-paccaya), matter (rūpa) is also obtained; likewise, there is a distinction in the Pre-nascent Condition (Purejāta-paccaya). In the Repetition Condition (Āsevana-paccaya), resultant states (vipāka) and functional process-minds (vīthi-citta) [noted as non-vīthi functional in Myanmar] are not obtained. In the Resultant Condition (Vipāka-paccaya), "one" means it is only the indeterminate. Thus, in this Enumeration Chapter, in brief, there are only three types of section-limits: nine, three, and one. In detail, there are 12 conditions with nine, 10 conditions with three, and 1 condition with one; thus, in all twenty-three conditions, there are one hundred and thirty-nine (139) sections, and there are one hundred and thirty-nine questions. "One hundred and thirty-nine question-answers" is also the name of that same section. Having thus shown the calculation in the single-root (Ekamūlaka) beginning with the root condition, and having summarized the detailed teaching in the double-root (Dumūlaka) and so forth that follow, the passage beginning with "Hetu-paccayā ārammaṇe tīṇi" is spoken first in the double-root to show the section-limits by taking the same calculation obtained in the teaching shown in the single-root. In that passage, this is the characteristic to be noted.
418:
The characteristic to be noted is—a condition with a large number [of counts], when combined with a condition that does not have a large number, has a number equal to that [smaller] one. Therefore, it was said: 'From Root condition, three in object condition.' The meaning is that in the Root-Object dyad (hetu-ārammaṇa-duka), only the three answers mentioned in the Object condition are obtained. But a condition with an equal number, when combined with a condition with an equal number, has a number that is not diminished. Therefore, it was said: 'From Root condition, nine in predominance condition.' The meaning is that in the Root-Predominance dyad (hetu-adhipati-duka), only nine answers are obtained. 'One in Resultant' means that in the Root-Resultant dyad (hetu-vipāka-duka), only the one answer mentioned in the Resultant condition is obtained. Thus, first, the cycle-limit in the double-root should be understood.

In the triple-root (ti-mūlaka) and so on, this same characteristic is the rule. Therefore, it was said: 'From Root condition, from Object condition, three in Predominance.' The meaning is that in the Root-Object-Predominance triad (hetu-ārammaṇa-adhipati-tika), only the three answers mentioned in the Object condition are obtained. In this way, the method should be applied in all cases.

76-79. Specifically, in the twelve-root (dvādasa-mūlaka), the Resultant condition is not obtained; therefore, after saying 'From Repetition condition, three in Kamma condition,' and without touching upon the Resultant condition, it was said: 'Three in Nutriment condition.' In the thirteen-root (terasa-mūlaka) and so on, this same method applies. Having summarized those thirteen-root and so on, only the twenty-three-root (tevīsati-mūlaka) is shown here. That [twenty-three-root] is of two types: either with repetition (sāsevana) or with resultant (savipāka). Among them, the one with repetition is shown first; it receives only three answers. Therefore, it was said: 'From Repetition condition, three in Non-disappearance condition.' But the one with resultant does not receive the Repetition condition; therefore, having set aside that Repetition condition, in order to show the calculation connected with the Resultant condition, immediately after the one with repetition, a single method was shown: 'From Root condition... from Resultant condition, one in Nutriment condition,' and afterwards the twenty-three-root itself was shown. Among those two types of twenty-three-root, although the Resultant condition is absent in one, and the Repetition condition is absent in the other, and the Post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is absent in both, they should be known as 'twenty-three-root' by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī-sadda). Among them, in the one with repetition, there are only three answers in all cycles by way of the Repetition condition; in the one with resultant, there is only one by way of the Resultant condition. This is the calculation in the single-root and so on, starting with the Root condition.

As for the statement made immediately after the Root-root (hetu-mūlaka), 'One who stands in the Object condition has only three questions in all methods,' that statement [refers to] the single-root starting with the Object condition, and also the double-root and so on...
419:
In the entire section on the Object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya-pada), and in the Pali passages where the Object condition is combined with the remaining conditions, it was stated [by the teachers of the Sangīti] to show that where there should be nine questions, there are only three. In the Resultant section (vipāka-pada), and in combinations of the Resultant section with the remaining conditions, it should be noted that there is only one question. Thus, because of the Pali statement that there are only three questions in combination with the Object condition, what we said below—'Even a condition with a large count, when combined with a condition of a small count, becomes equal in count to that [smaller] one'—is well-said indeed.

80-85. Now, regarding the methods such as the Single-root (ekamūlaka) which should be shown by the power of conditions like Object, etc.; among those, the Single-root method is not shown for other conditions because it is identical to the Single-root method of the Root condition (hetu-paccaya). To show the enumeration in the Double-root method (dumūlaka) by the power of the Object condition, it is stated: "Because of Object condition, three in Root, three in Predominance ...pe... three in Non-disappearance."

Here, although it should have been taught in order as "Because of Object condition, three in Predominance ...pe... three in Non-disappearance," the Root condition, which stands before the Object condition, is placed after the Object condition, stating "Because of Object condition, three in Root," in order to show the enumeration obtained when conditions with large counts, such as the Root condition, are mixed with conditions of fewer or equal counts. By teaching out of order in this way, this meaning is made clear: In whatever way the Object condition reaches distinctions such as Doublets (duka) and Triplets (tika) together with a condition of a larger or equal count, in all those distinctions, three question-answers should be understood. However, in mixing with the Resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya), only one question-answer is obtained; since the fact that only one is obtained in mixing with the Resultant condition will become clear in the enumeration of the Resultant condition, etc., it is not shown here in the Double-root method connected with the Object condition. This enumeration shown in the Double-root method is the same in methods such as the Triple-root (timūlaka); therefore, the Triple-root etc. are not expanded by the power of the Object condition.

Now, to show the enumeration in the Double-root etc. by the power of the Predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), etc., it is stated: "Because of Predominance condition, nine in Root," and so on. In that statement "nine in Root because of Predominance condition," the arrangement of conditions should be understood by the method already mentioned. Just as there are nine in Root because of Predominance condition, likewise there are only nine in the conditions remaining from the Root condition which have an equal count to the Root. Thus, whichever condition stands at the beginning, in mixing it with conditions of equal count, the enumeration occurs by the power of the condition standing at the beginning. But in mixing that [initial] condition with conditions of fewer counts, it should be understood that the enumeration occurs only by the power of the conditions with fewer counts. Just as the Triple-root etc. were not expanded by the power of the Object condition, likewise they are not expanded by the power of the Predominance condition, nor by the power of conditions such as Proximity (anantara) which follow that Predominance condition. Therefore...
420:
In all methods, [the counts] should be completed by the power of the counts already shown in the Double-root method (dumūlaka-naya). For that very reason, because the counts in all methods should be completed in connection with the counts shown in the Double-root method, it was stated [by the teachers]: "Each single condition should be made the root and counted by way of the sequence of recitation."

## Section on Dependent Origination.

## Commentary on the Negative Method of Conditions.

86-87. As for the Negative Method (paccanīya-naya), it is not obtained in the Wholesome section (kusala-pada) because wholesome states cannot arise without the Root condition (hetu-paccaya). Therefore, [the Buddha] began [the teaching] with "Dependent on an unwholesome state" (akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca), and so on. In that [unwholesome section], "by non-root condition" (na-hetu-paccaya) means the rejection of the Root condition, signifying that it arises by a condition other than the Root condition. Delusion (moha) associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) is itself a Root condition for its associated states and for mind-produced matter (citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa); however, because there is no other associated root (sampayutta-hetu), it arises without the Root condition. Therefore, setting aside the Root condition, it arises by the remaining conditions suitable to itself. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all statements that reject conditions. This statement, "the rootless resultant indeterminate" (ahetukaṃ vipākābyākataṃ), should be understood only by way of the power that produces matter. In other similar Pali passages, this same method applies.

In the "non-predominance condition" (na-adhipati-paccaya), a predominant state (adhipati) is indeed obtained as "non-predominance" because there is no second predominant state together with itself. However, just as delusion associated with doubt and restlessness is rootless (ahetuka, i.e., having no associated root), it is not that only the predominant states are without predominance (niradhipati). In fact, at the time of the arising of wholesome states, etc., without making any one of the states such as desire (chanda) a predominant factor, all wholesome states etc. are without predominance (niradhipatino). Therefore, without extracting and showing only the predominant states separately like delusion, it should be understood that this teaching was given as "Dependent on one aggregate, three aggregates," etc., by way of including all states without predominance.

In the "non-proximity" (na-anantara) and "non-immediate proximity" (na-samanantara) conditions, just as in "non-object" (na-ārammaṇa), only matter is the conditionally arisen state (paccayuppanna). Therefore, it was stated: "It is similar to the non-object condition" (na-ārammaṇa-paccaya-sadisaṃ). The Co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) is excluded. Just as this Co-nascence condition is excluded, so too are the Dependence (nissaya), Presence (atthi), and Non-disappearance (avigata) conditions excluded. For what reason? Because without these [Co-nascence, etc.] conditions, not even a single state can arise. Indeed, by setting aside the Co-nascence, Dependence, Presence, and Non-disappearance conditions, not even a single state of matter or mind can arise; therefore, those conditions are excluded.
421:
In the classification of the non-mutuality condition (na-aññamaññapaccaya), in the phrase "dependent on the resultant indeterminate aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking, there is kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa)," it should be understood as rebirth-linking kamma-born matter excluding the heart-base (hadayavatthu).

In the classification of the non-decisive support condition (na-upanissayapaccaya), only matter is the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna), because that matter does not obtain the decisive support condition. Although mental phenomena might not obtain object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) or natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya), there is no mental phenomenon free from proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya). Therefore, it is said, "It is similar to the non-object condition (na-ārammaṇapaccaya)."

In the non-prenascence condition (na-purejātapaccaya), the phrase "mind-produced matter" (cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ) is stated by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra).

In the non-postnascence condition (na-pacchājātapaccaya), the conascence condition (sahajātapaccaya) and prenascence condition (purejātapaccaya) are included. Therefore, the Pali text here is similar to the conascence condition; since that Pali text has already been explained in detail under the non-predominance condition (na-adhipatipaccaya), it is presented here in brief. In the non-repetition condition (na-āsevanapaccaya), wholesome and unwholesome states should be understood by way of the first impulsion (pathamajavana); likewise, the functional indeterminate (kiriyābyākata) should be understood. The Pali text in this non-repetition condition should also be understood as explained in detail under the non-predominance condition. For this reason, it is said: "The non-postnascence condition and the non-repetition condition are both similar to the non-predominance condition."

94-97. In the non-kamma condition (na-kammapaccaya), resultant volition (vipāka-cetanā) is not taken (as a conditionally arisen state) because it obtains the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇikakammapaccaya). In the non-nutriment condition (na-āhārapaccaya), only certain matter is the conditionally arisen; the same should be understood for the non-faculty condition (na-indriyapaccaya).

In the non-jhāna condition (na-jhānapaccaya), the fivefold consciousness (pañcavijñāṇa) and certain matter are the conditionally arisen. In the fivefold consciousness, feeling (vedanā) and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) are weak and thus do not reach the characteristic of close contemplation (upanijjhānalakkhaṇa); therefore, they are not taken in the jhāna condition.

99-102. In the non-path condition (na-maggapaccaya), rootless resultant and functional [states] as well as certain matter are the conditionally arisen. In the non-association (na-sampayutta), non-absence (no-natthi), and non-disappearance (no-vigata) conditions, only matter is the conditionally arisen. Therefore, it is said, "It is similar to the non-object condition."

The statement "two in non-root" (na-hetuyā dve) follows the Pali text exactly in the single-root (ekamūlaka) counting.

In the double-root method (dumūlakanaya), regarding the phrase "one in non-root and non-object" (na-hetupaccaya na-ārammaṇe ekaṃ), although there should be two as in the non-root condition when comparing the condition with a larger number and the condition with a smaller number, it is stated as "one" with reference to the arising of indeterminate matter dependent on indeterminate [mental states], because mental phenomena decrease by way of the non-object condition.
422:
...has been stated (previously). The same method applies to all single (ekaka) methods. However, in the place where "two" is stated, it should be understood as two cycles (vāra) by way of the power obtained through the non-root condition.

105-106. In all methods starting from the triple-root (timūlaka) and so on, since the non-object condition does not decrease, the answer is only one. This is the counting in the negative [method] in the single-root and subsequent methods, starting with the non-root condition.

107-130. The non-object condition and others are not shown here because they are similar to the previous [single-root method] in the single-root counting. In the double-root method by way of the non-object condition, the statement "one in non-root from the non-object condition" (na-ārammaṇapaccayā na-hetuyā ekaṃ) should be understood as already stated in the non-root double-root method. In the phrase "five in non-predominance" (nādhipatiyā pañca), the counting should be understood by way of the power obtained in the non-object condition. Thus, in all comparisons (saṃsandana), the counting should be understood by way of the condition that has the lesser number. Wherever the non-object condition enters, only matter is the conditionally arisen state. The same method applies where the non-proximity, non-contiguity, non-mutuality, non-decisive support, non-nutriment, non-faculty, non-association, non-absence, and non-disappearance conditions enter. The non-nutriment, non-faculty, non-jhāna, and non-path conditions have similar answers in all places. The group of four starting with non-conascence (na-sahajāta) also decreases here; this is the characteristic to be noted in this context. By this characteristic, in all double-root and subsequent methods, one should note: "This condition is the root, this is the double-root here, this is the triple-root, this is the all-root," and the counting should be understood by way of the condition with the lesser number.

## Explanation of the Negative Conditions (Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā).

## Explanation of the Positive-Negative Conditions (Paccayānulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā)

131-189. Now, to show the counting in the positive-negative [method], the section beginning with "Hetupaccayā na-ārammaṇe pañca" (From the root condition, five in non-object) is commenced. There, while the root, predominance, and path conditions are present in the positive way, the four universal conditions (sabbaṭṭhānikapaccaya) starting with conascence, and the four conditions—nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path—these eight conditions cannot be obtained in the negative way. This is because there is no state arising by way of the root condition and others that does not obtain these eight conditions. However, while the object, proximity, contiguity, decisive support, association, absence, and disappearance conditions are present in the positive way, those belonging to the formless [states] (arūpaṭṭhānika)...
423:
They cannot be obtained as negative. It is not that states arising through object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), etc., do not obtain proximity (anantara) and contiguity (samanantara) conditions, etc.; they do indeed obtain them. When conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), kamma, nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions are established as positive (anuloma), only the four universal conditions (sabbaṭṭhānika) cannot be obtained as negative. This is because among the states arising by the power of these conditions, there are no states that do not obtain the universal conditions. There is no such thing as a basis for post-nascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) as positive. Thus, while the remaining conditions are established as positive, one should note which conditions are obtained and which are not. In all methods such as the two-rooted (dumūlaka), etc., the counting should be understood by the power of the reduced numbers when comparing those various conditions.

## Commentary on the Positive-Negative Method of Conditions

## Commentary on the Negative-Positive Method of Conditions

Now, to show the counting in the negative-positive method, the passage beginning with "With non-root condition, two in object" (na-hetupaccayā ārammaṇe dve) is commenced. Therein, when root condition (hetu) is established as negative, the remaining conditions except for predominance condition (adhipati) are obtained as positive. Post-nascent condition, however, is not obtained as positive in any instance. Among the nine conditions said to "support only mental states" (arūpānaññeva), when the seven conditions—excluding pre-nascent (purejāta) and repetition (āsevana)—are established as negative, the remaining conditions that are bases for mental states cannot be obtained as positive. This is because if a state does not arise through object condition, etc., it cannot obtain proximity condition, etc. However, although resultant rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-vipāka) does not arise through pre-nascent condition, it does obtain proximity condition, etc. And although all resultants (vipāka), together with the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu), do not arise through repetition condition, they do obtain proximity condition, etc. Therefore, it is said, "excluding pre-nascent and repetition."

When pre-nascent, post-nascent, repetition, resultant, and dissociation (vippayutta) conditions are established as negative, the remaining conditions except for one are obtained as positive. When kamma condition is established as negative, the remaining conditions except for resultant condition are obtained as positive. When nutriment and faculty conditions are established as negative, the remaining conditions except for the universal conditions and mutuality, kamma, nutriment, and faculty conditions cannot be obtained as positive. The others are obtained by way of their appropriate association. When jhāna condition is established as negative...
424:
...root, predominance, repetition, and path (magga) conditions are not obtained as positive. When path condition is established as negative, root and predominance conditions are not obtained as positive. When dissociation condition is established as negative, the remaining conditions except for pre-nascent condition are obtained as positive. Thus, when those various conditions are established as negative, one should know which ones are not obtained as positive, and the counting should be understood by the power of the reduced numbers in the comparison of those various conditions.

191-195. In the methods such as the two-rooted (dumūlaka), etc., starting from whichever condition and showing whichever dyads (duka), etc., those dyads, etc., should be well noted as they are shown by the power of the conditions that are obtained or not obtained. Among those methods, when showing the two-rooted methods by the power of non-root (na-hetu), it is said: "By non-root condition, by non-object condition... pe... by non-repetition condition," and then "all are the same up to repetition." The similarity of that statement with "By non-mutuality condition, one in conascence," etc., should be understood. As for the statement written in the Sinhala language (Sīhaḷa-bhāsā), "When non-kamma is counted, it takes five," the meaning is: starting from non-root condition, thus with non-kamma condition, in conascence connected with non-kamma condition, only the five conditions shown as "one" are obtained as positive, and not others. Thus, in other such places as well, one should not focus on the literal phrasing (byañjana) but should grasp only the intended meaning (adhippetattha). For ancient teachers wrote such phrasing in their own languages to fix their own notations (saññā).

Furthermore, in this negative-positive method, among the conditionally arisen states, there is a state that obtains kamma condition but does not obtain faculty condition. That state should be understood by the power of the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) in non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) and during the course of existence (pavatti) in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra). There is a state that obtains path condition but does not obtain root condition. That state should be understood by the power of delusion (moha) associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca). There is a state that obtains jhāna condition but does not obtain path condition. That state should be understood by the power of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the rootless mind-consciousness-element (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu). Where kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) obtains kamma condition only by the power of asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma), there the material states do not obtain root, predominance, resultant, faculty, jhāna, and path conditions; the universal negatives do not occur. In the rootless (ahetuka), there is no predominance condition. Thus, by the power of these miscellaneous determinations, the section on counting (gaṇanā-vāra) should be understood without confusion.
425:
In this (combined determination), this is the method: In the phrase "Na-hetu-paccayā ārammaṇe dve" (two in object condition by way of non-root condition), first, rootless delusion (delusion associated with the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion) and rootless resultants and rootless functionals are the conditionally arisen states. Therefore, it is said "two" here, referring to unwholesome arising because of unwholesome, and indeterminate arising because of indeterminate. In the remaining phrases as well, this same method applies. However, in the repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), resultant is not obtained; likewise, the functional mind-element (five-door adverting) is not obtained. Therefore, by virtue of the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element (mind-door adverting and smile-producing consciousness), indeterminate arising because of indeterminate should be understood here. "One" in resultant means only indeterminate arising because of indeterminate. "One" in path means only unwholesome arising because of unwholesome.

196-197. The statement "Na-ārammaṇa-mūlake hetuyā pañca" (five in root condition with non-object as the root) is said with reference only to matter (rūpa). That matter arises depending on five groups: wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate, wholesome and indeterminate, and unwholesome and indeterminate. In all pentads (pañcaka), this same method applies. The statement "Aññamaññe ekaṃ" (one in mutuality) is said with reference to the primary elements (bhūtarūpa) and the heart-base (hadayavatthu). Those states arise due to the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya) which is not an object condition. In the triple-root (ti-mūlaka) as well, this same method applies.

198-202. The statement "Na-adhipati-mūlake hetuyā nava" (nine in root condition with non-predominance as the root) refers to the same answers (vissajjanā) already mentioned in the root condition of the analytical order (anuloma). The answers beginning with "three" (tīṇi) are also similar to those mentioned below in the analytical order. The answers "two" (dve) in the triple-root are similar to those mentioned below in "Na-hetu-paccayā ārammaṇe".

203-233. The statement "Na-purejāta-mūlake hetuyā satta" (seven in root condition with non-prenascence as the root) refers to those already shown in prenascence (purejāta) by the method beginning with "depending on one wholesome aggregate in the formless realm" below. In all heptads (sattaka), this same method applies. In the problems beginning with "Na-kamma-mūlake hetuyā tīṇi" (three in root condition with non-kamma as the root), only volition (cetanā) is the conditionally arisen state. Therefore, "three" is said with reference to the arising depending on wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. By this method, the counting in places where "one, two, three, five, seven, nine" occur should be understood. These three counts—"four, six, eight"—do not exist at all.

## Explanation of the Negative-Analytical Order (Paccaya-paccanīyānuloma).
## The explanation of the meaning of the Section on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccavāra) is finished.
426:
## 2. Explanation of the Section on Co-nascence (Sahajātavāra-vaṇṇanā)

234-242. In the Section on Co-nascence, "being co-nascent with a wholesome state" means having arisen together with that wholesome state, depending on it. The remaining collection of words in this Section on Co-nascence should be understood in the same way as mentioned in the Section on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccavāra). At the end, however, the statement "What is called the state of dependence (paṭiccattaṃ) is the state of co-nascence (sahajātattaṃ); what is called the state of co-nascence is the state of dependence" is said for the purpose of showing that these two sections are not different in meaning. In terms of meaning, these two are indeed not different (they are identical). Even though they are not different, they are stated for the purpose of defining the mutual meaning. For in the Pali passages such as "depending on the eye and visible forms," it is taught that [consciousness] arises depending even on states that are not co-nascent (asahajāta). Also, co-nascent derived matter (upādārūpa) is not a condition for the primary elements (bhūtarūpa). Therefore, both these sections are stated: by the Section on Dependent Origination, to define the nature of the co-nascence condition; and by the Section on Co-nascence, to define the co-nascent nature of the state called "dependent" (paṭicca). Furthermore, both these sections are stated by virtue of the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of the veneyya (those to be taught) who will understand in that way, by virtue of the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa), and by virtue of knowing the divisions of the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).

## The explanation of the Section on Co-nascence is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Section on Conditions (Paccayavāra-vaṇṇanā)

In the Section on Conditions, "because of a wholesome state (kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayā)" means being established in a wholesome state, making the wholesome state a condition in the sense of support (nissaya). "Because of one wholesome aggregate" means that by making one wholesome aggregate a dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya), three aggregates arise due to the root condition (hetu-paccaya). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. "Because of the base-matter (vatthu), resultant indeterminate and functional indeterminate aggregates [arise]"—this is said by virtue of the course of existence (pavatti) in the five-aggregate realm (pañcavokāra). For in the course of existence in the five-aggregate realm, the pre-nascent (purejāta) base-matter is the dependence condition for the aggregates. Since the meaning of "dependent" (paṭicca) has the meaning of "co-nascent" (sahajāta), this method is not obtained in the Section on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccavāra); therefore, at the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), referring only to the co-nascent base-matter, it is said "depending on the base-matter (vatthuṃ paṭicca), aggregates [arise]." In the Pali passages such as "because of one wholesome aggregate and the base-matter, three aggregates [arise]," the meaning should be understood by this same method.
427:
The statement "Dependent on an indeterminate state, wholesome and indeterminate states arise" is spoken with reference to the simultaneous arising of wholesome and indeterminate states by way of root-condition (hetu-paccaya). Indeed, at the moment of the arising of the wholesome, the wholesome aggregates arise depending on the physical base (vatthu), and the mind-produced derived matter (upādā-rūpa) arises depending on the mind-produced great essentials (mahābhūta) by way of root-condition. Thus, it should be understood that although there is diversity in the indeterminate states which are the conditions, this is spoken with reference to the simultaneous arising of the conditionally arisen states (paccayuppanna) by way of root-condition. In other similar instances, the same method applies. Thus, in this root-condition, seventeen questions are answered by making the conascence (sahajāta) and pre-existence (purejāta) states the condition in the sense of support (nissaya). Among those questions, the mental aggregates and the great essentials are taken by way of conascence, while the physical base is taken by way of both conascence and pre-existence. In the Paṭiccavāra (Dependent Section), however, the condition is obtained only by way of conascence; therefore, only nine questions are answered there. Among the seventeen questions answered in this Paccayavāra, in the explanation (vissajjanā) starting with one and ending with one, one conditionally arisen state arises due to one kind of condition among wholesome states, etc. In the explanation starting with one and ending with two, various conditionally arisen states arise due to one kind of condition. In the explanation starting with two and ending with one, one conditionally arisen state arises due to various kinds of conditions. In the explanation starting with two and ending with two, various conditionally arisen states arise due to various kinds of conditions.

248-252. In the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), etc., the variety of answering questions should be understood in this same way. The statement in the object condition, "Dependent on the physical base, mental aggregates arise," is spoken with reference only to the resultant aggregates (vipāka-khandha) at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Eye-consciousness, etc., are spoken of to show the distinction of states arising by way of object condition depending on indeterminate states. Again, the statement "Dependent on the physical base" is spoken to show the arising of resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriya) indeterminate states during the course of existence (pavatti). The rest should be understood according to the previous method. Thus, in this object condition, seven questions are answered by making conascence and pre-existence states the condition. Among those questions, the mental aggregates are taken by way of conascence, the physical base by way of conascence and pre-existence, and the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), etc., only by way of pre-existence. In the Paṭiccavāra, however, the condition is obtained only by way of conascence. Therefore, only three questions are answered there.

253-254. In the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), the resultant indeterminate state (vipākābyākata) should be understood as only the supramundane resultant (lokuttara-vipāka). Proximity (anantara) and contiguity (samanantara) conditions are similar to the object condition due to the absence of matter (rūpa). The same method applies to the subsequent repetition (āsevana), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) conditions.
428:
In the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), "kamma-born matter, derived matter" (kaṭattārūpaṃ upādārūpaṃ) refers to kamma-born matter which is called derived matter. This is spoken with reference only to the matter of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). The eye-base (cakkhāyatana), etc., are spoken of by way of five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra).

256-257. In the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya), the statement "just as in the object condition" is spoken with reference to the similarity of the answers (vissajjanā). However, there is diversity among the conditionally arisen states.

In the strong support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), the statement "it is similar to the object condition" is spoken both because of the absence of matter and because of the similarity of the answers.

259-260. The meaning of the Pali passages such as "Dependent on the physical base by way of pre-existence condition" (vatthuṃ purejātapaccayā) should be taken according to the method stated in the Paṭiccavāra.

261-266. In the kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), "three" means that three answers should be understood: dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state, an indeterminate state, and both wholesome and indeterminate states arise. The same method applies to unwholesome states.

267-268. In the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya), "dependent on the aggregates by way of dissociation condition" (khandhe vippayuttapaccayā) means they arise by way of dissociation condition depending on the mental aggregates. "The aggregates arise by way of dissociation condition depending on the physical base" (khandhā vatthuṃ vippayuttapaccayā) means the mental aggregates arise by way of dissociation condition depending on the physical base. The rest should be understood according to the method stated below.

269-276. Now, to show the answers obtained by way of enumeration, he said "seventeen in root" (hetuyā sattarasa), etc. In that context, "seventeen in root condition" means: wholesome with wholesome, wholesome with indeterminate, wholesome with wholesome and indeterminate—thus, by way of wholesome, there are two answers starting with one term and ending with one term, and one answer ending with two terms, making three. The same applies by way of unwholesome. Indeterminate with indeterminate; with that same indeterminate, wholesome, unwholesome, wholesome and indeterminate, unwholesome and indeterminate; with wholesome and indeterminate, wholesome, indeterminate, wholesome and indeterminate; with unwholesome and indeterminate, unwholesome, indeterminate, unwholesome and indeterminate—thus, seventeen should be understood.

In the object condition, "seven" means: wholesome with wholesome, unwholesome with unwholesome, indeterminate with indeterminate, wholesome, unwholesome; wholesome and indeterminate with wholesome; unwholesome and indeterminate with unwholesome—thus, there are seven.
429:
In the case of result (vipāka), the 'one' refers only to the explanation where an indeterminate state arises dependent on an indeterminate state. Thus, in this Paccayavāra, there are three divisions of sections: seventeen, seven, and one. Among these divisions, there are 12 sections of seventeen, 10 sections of seven, and 1 section of one. Having carefully noted all these, one should understand the method of counting by way of the minimum number when comparing and combining conditions through dyads (duka), triads (tika), and so on. Since the divisions of sections in the dyad-roots and so forth can be known by this counting, the division of sections is shown by the power of counting alone, without re-examining the phrase 'Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises,' starting with 'By way of root-condition, there are seven in object-condition,' and so forth.

In that passage (starting with 'By way of root-condition, there are seven in object-condition'), a wholesome state arises dependent on a wholesome state through root-condition and through object-condition. The explanations obtained in the object-condition should be expanded in this manner: 'Dependent on one wholesome aggregate, three aggregates arise.' This is the method first shown in the analytical order (anuloma).

277-285. In the negative method (paccanīya), however, since the wholesome is not obtained, the explanation is started by taking only the unwholesome as the beginning, thus: 'Dependent on an unwholesome state.' That explanation follows the meaning exactly as in the Pāḷi text. Whatever needs to be said in this negative method has already been stated in the negative method of the Paṭicca-vāra.

286-287. Regarding the statement 'In non-root (na-hetu), there are four,' and so forth, which is said to show the division of explanations obtained in the negative method by way of counting, there are six divisions: four, seventeen, seven, five, three, and one. By way of these divisions, the counting should be understood when comparing and combining conditions in dyads, triads, and so forth. Whichever condition obtains seventeen explanations, when comparing it with a condition of equal count, seventeen are obtained; when comparing it with a condition of lower count, all the remaining six divisions are obtained. Thus, in the remaining conditions as well, excluding the higher divisions, the equal and lower divisions are obtained.

In this negative method, the fact that higher divisions are not obtained is the fixed rule (niyama) here. However, equal and lower divisions are obtained if there is no contradiction in meaning. Therefore, it is stated here: 'By way of non-root condition, there is one in non-object (na-ārammaṇa),' and so forth. In this non-root non-object dyad, since four occur in non-root and five occur in non-object, it should be stated as 'four' by the power of non-root. However, because it is combined with non-object, the object-state is contradictory; therefore, 'Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises; dependent on an indeterminate state, an unwholesome state arises...'
430:
The three explanations (answers) beginning with the sentence 'Dependent on an unwholesome state and an indeterminate state, an unwholesome state arises' are lost (not obtained). However, the explanation 'Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises' is taught as only one, by way of matter (rūpa) [such as rootless mind-produced matter, rootless rebirth kamma-produced matter, external matter, nutriment-produced matter, temperature-produced matter, kamma-produced matter of non-percipient beings, and kamma-produced matter during the course of existence]. Thus, in all conditions, the obtainable division should be understood by way of both contradictory and non-contradictory states. A slight distinction to be noted here is that this is merely a demonstration of the method. 'In non-predominance (na-adhipati), there are four' refers to the same explanations obtained in non-root (na-hetu). In the remaining tetrads (sections of four) as well, this same method applies.

'In non-proximity (na-anantara), there is one' means an indeterminate state arises dependent on an indeterminate state by way of rootless mind-produced matter and the remaining matter (such as rootless rebirth kamma-produced matter). Thus, in all sections where 'one' occurs, the matter that is suitable to be associated as the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna) should be understood. In 'In non-prenascence (na-purejāta), there are two,' it should also be stated as 'four' by the power of non-root. However, because it is connected with non-prenascence, the two explanations by way of base-prenascence (vatthu-purejāta)—namely, unwholesome arising dependent on an indeterminate state, and unwholesome arising dependent on unwholesome and indeterminate states—are lost. In the formless realm (arūpabhūmi), however, two explanations are taught by way of rootless delusion (ahetuka-moha) and rootless functional [mind-door adverting] which lack associated roots. 'In non-dissociation (na-vippayutta), there are two' means there are two in the formless realm by way of rootless unwholesome (delusion associated with the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion) and rootless functional. 'In non-non-existence (no-natthi) and non-disappearance (no-vigata), there is one' should be understood as an indeterminate state arising dependent on an indeterminate state by way of all matter. In the triads (tika) and so forth, there is nothing new or special to be said.

In the non-object root section (na-ārammaṇa-mūlaka), 'In non-predominance, there are five' refers to the same explanations obtained in non-object. In 'In non-kamma (na-kamma), there is one,' it should be understood as an indeterminate state arising dependent on an indeterminate state by way of the remaining matter, without taking mind-produced matter and kamma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa).

289-296. In the non-predominance root section (na-adhipati-mūlaka), 'In non-prenascence, there are seven' refers to those obtained in non-prenascence. These seventeen explanations in 'In non-postnascence (na-pacchājāta), there are seventeen' are also the same seventeen obtained in that (non-predominance) condition. The sections of non-proximity root, non-contiguity root, non-mutuality root, non-sufficing condition root, non-association root, non-non-existence root, and non-disappearance root are just the same as the non-object root section. By thus showing the mere method, the problems that appear or do not appear, and the states that are obtainable or not obtainable in all conditions, should be understood.

## The Explanation of the Negative Method is concluded.

297-328. By this very method, the counting of numbers, the problems that appear or do not appear, and the states that are obtainable or not obtainable should be understood in the analytical-negative (anuloma-paccanīya) where the analytical is placed first, and in the negative-analytical (paccanīya-anuloma) where the negative is placed first.

## The Explanation of the Chapter on Conditions is concluded.
431: ## ၄။ နိဿယဝါရဝဏ္ဏနာ ၃၂၉-၃၃၇။ In the Support Chapter (Nissayavāra), 'Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ nissāya' (depending on a wholesome state) means having made a wholesome state a support (nissaya) in the sense of a foundation. The rest in this chapter should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Condition Chapter (Paccayavāra). However, at the end of this Support Chapter, the statement 'the state of being a condition is the state of being a support; the state of being a support is the state of being a condition' is spoken to show that these two chapters are not different in meaning. In terms of meaning, these chapters are not different, just like the Dependent Chapter (Paṭiccavāra) and the Co-nascence Chapter (Sahajātavāra). Even though they are not different, they are taught to define the mutual meaning. This is because in passages such as 'Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā' (with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise), a state that arises at a different moment without depending [on the condition] is also said to 'arise because of a condition.' Just as among pieces of wood that stand leaning against each other, one is not the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the other, and likewise, derived matter (upādā-rūpa) is not the support-condition for the great elements (mahābhūta). Thus, both these chapters are taught to define the state of support-condition by the Condition Chapter, and the state of co-nascence and pre-nascence of the state called 'condition' by the Support Chapter. Furthermore, both these are taught according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those who can understand in that way, by the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa), and to make known the distinctions of the analytical insight into language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). ## နိဿယဝါရဝဏ္ဏနာ။ ## ၅။ သံသဋ္ဌဝါရဝဏ္ဏနာ ၃၃၈-၃၄၆။ In the Conjoined Chapter (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra), 'Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ saṃsaṭṭho' (conjoined with a wholesome state) means having made a wholesome state a condition by way of association (sampayoga) characterized by arising together and so forth. 'Conjoined with one wholesome aggregate' means that by making one wholesome aggregate an association-condition (sampayutta-paccaya), three aggregates arise through the root condition (hetu-paccaya). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. In this root condition, three questions are answered by making only mental states (arūpa-dhamma) a condition by way of association. As in the root condition, so it is in the object condition and so forth; however, in the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya), there is only one answer. ၃၄၇-၃၅၀။ Now, in order to show the answers obtained by way of calculation, the passage beginning with 'Hetuyā tīṇi' (three in root) is spoken. Therein, among all the triads (tika), the arising of wholesome by wholesome...
432:
...unwholesome by unwholesome, and indeterminate by indeterminate—this alone is the fixed rule. But in the case of the single indeterminate, only indeterminate by indeterminate is obtained. Thus, in this Saṃsaṭṭha-vāra, among the twenty-two conditions, there are two divisions: three (in conditions other than resultant) and one in the resultant-condition. In the post-nascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), there is no positive (anuloma) method. Therefore, by way of these divisions of three and one, in the combination of conditions in the dyads and triads (duka-tika) etc., the counting should be understood as one where the resultant-condition is included, and three in the remaining places. The meaning of the remaining words in this positive chapter is clear.

351-354. In the negative chapter (paccanīya-vāra), since the wholesome is not obtained, the answer is given starting only with the unwholesome. That statement is also clear in meaning.

In this negative chapter, to show the divisions of answers by way of number, 'nahetuyā dve' (two in non-root) and so on are taught. Therein, there are three divisions: two, three, and one. By way of those divisions, the counting in the combination of conditions in the dyads and triads etc. should be understood. Here too, when combining conditions with a higher count with those of a lower count, only the lower count is obtained; when combining with an equal count, the equal count is obtained. In this negative chapter, since only mental states are the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna), only ten conditions are shown as negative: by way of na-hetu, na-adhipati, na-purejāta, na-pacchājāta, na-āsevana, na-kamma, na-vipāka, na-jhāna, na-magga, and na-vippayutta. The remaining fourteen conditions are not obtained. Among the obtained conditions, when there is a resultant conditionally arisen state, na-kamma and na-vipāka are not obtained.

360-368. 'Two in non-predominance because of non-root condition' refers to the same set of two obtained in non-root. The same method applies to the remaining sets of two. 'One in non-kamma' is the answer where indeterminate arises from indeterminate, having made the volition of rootless functional (ahetuka-kiriya-cetanā) the conditionally arisen state. 'Two in non-resultant' refers to the two by way of rootless delusion (ahetuka-moha) and rootless functional. 'One in non-jhāna' should be understood as the indeterminate answer by way of the rootless fivefold sense-consciousness (ahetuka-pañcavijñāṇa). 'One in non-path' is the indeterminate answer by way of rootless resultant and rootless functional. In this way, the meaning should be understood in the combination of all conditions.

369-383. In the positive-negative (anuloma-paccanīya), only the ten conditions mentioned below, such as na-hetu, are obtained as negative; the rest are not. Among the obtained conditions, when the root-condition (hetu-paccaya) is present in the positive, jhāna and magga are not obtained as negative. All this should be understood in the same manner as stated below.
433:
384-391. In the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma) section, among the resultants of the non-root condition (na-hetu-paccaya), only rootless delusion (ahetuka-moha) obtains the jhāna condition and the path condition; the remaining resultants do not. In the non-jhāna condition, the eight rootless consciousnesses (excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness) also do not obtain them. In the non-kamma, non-root, non-predominance, and non-pre-existence conditions, within the object condition, an indeterminate state arises because of an indeterminate state by way of rootless functional volition (ahetuka-kiriya-cetanā) specifically in the formless realm (arūpabhūmi). In this manner, one should understand the calculation in all sections according to what is obtained and what is not obtained, whether it be a condition or a resultant.

## Commentary on the Conjoined Section (Saṃsaṭṭhavāravaṇṇanā)

## 6. Commentary on the Associated Section (Sampayuttavāravaṇṇanā)

392-400. In the Associated Section (Sampayuttavāra), the phrase "kusalā dhammā sampayuttā" means "making wholesome states the associated condition (wholesome states arise)." The remaining points in this Associated Section should be understood in the same way as stated in the Conjoined Section. However, at the end of this section, the statement "being conjoined is being associated; being associated is being conjoined" is said to show that there is no difference in meaning between these two sections. In terms of meaning, these sections are without distinction, just like the Dependent Section (Paṭiccavāra) and the Co-nascence Section (Sahajātavāra), or like Condition (Paccaya) and Support (Nissaya). Even though there is no distinction, they are stated to define each other's meaning. In passages such as "Horses conjoined (saṃsaṭṭhā) and harnessed, equal in color, strength, and speed" (Jātaka 2.22.70), even things that are not associated (asampayutta) are called "conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭha). In passages such as "That investigation (vīmaṃsā) which is accompanied by sloth, associated (sampayuttā) with sloth" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.832), even states that are mixed (vokiṇṇa) without being conjoined (asaṃsaṭṭha) are called "associated" (sampayutta). Thus, both sections are taught: the Conjoined Section to define the conjoined nature of associated states characterized by arising together (ekuppāda), and the Associated Section to define the associated nature of conjoined states characterized by arising together, etc. Furthermore, both are stated according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of those who can understand in that way, according to the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa), and for the purpose of making known the divisions of the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).

## Commentary on the Associated Section (Sampayuttavāravaṇṇanā)

In these six sections, some conditions do not exist solely in the positive (anuloma) way but exist only in the negative (paccanīka) way. Some conditions do not exist solely in the negative way but exist only in the positive way. Some conditions are not exclusive and exist both in the positive and negative ways. This miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) determination should be understood. Among those three types of conditions, the first...
434:
The first question should be understood by way of the post-existence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), the second by way of the Great Four (mahācatukka—the group of four conditions: sahajāta, nissaya, atthi, and avigata), and the third by way of the remaining applicable conditions.

## 7. Commentary on the Analysis of the Question Section (Pañhāvāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā)

401-403. In the Question Section (Pañhāvāra), the teaching "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of root condition (hetu-paccaya)," etc., is given to show the possible answers to the questions raised in the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-tika). A wholesome state, when it arises, arises due to twenty-two conditions, excluding the post-existence condition and the resultant condition. When it acts as a condition for a wholesome state, it acts as a condition through twenty conditions, excluding the pre-existence, post-existence, resultant, and dissociation conditions. Therefore, to show those conditions in order by which a wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state, the passage beginning with "by way of root condition" is undertaken (taught).

In that phrase "by way of root condition," etc., there is this special purpose in teaching "roots are [a condition] for associated aggregates (khandhānaṃ)" instead of saying "for associated states (dhammānaṃ)" as in the Analysis of Conditions (Paccaya-vibhaṅga). In that Analysis of Conditions, "for states (dhammānaṃ)" was taught to show the meaning of emptiness (suññata). In this Question Section, "for aggregates (khandhānaṃ)" is taught to show the meaning of a group (rāsi), indicating that states arising due to conditions arise as a group and not individually. Alternatively, since the teaching of resultants by way of aggregates has already been presented in the Dependent Section (Paṭiccavāra), etc., it is presented here in the Question Section in that same order. Why is it presented in this way in those sections? It is for the purpose of showing the division without confusion (asaṅkara).
