If it were taught in the manner "Dependent on one state, the remaining states [arise]," etc., it would not be possible to know the condition and the resultant without confusion, such as "depending on such-and-such a state, such-and-such states [arise]." In such a case, the summary (uddesa) and the explanation (niddesa) would be without distinction. Therefore, it should be understood that it is presented in this way for the purpose of showing the division without confusion. The phrase "for those produced by mind (cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ)" is stated to show specifically those indeterminate states for which a wholesome state is a condition by way of root condition. In the Analysis of Conditions, however, without making a division by way of wholesome states, etc., the phrase "for those produced by that (taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ)" is used instead of "for those produced by mind" to show the matter produced by all roots in general. Therefore, in that Analysis of Conditions, matter produced by indeterminate roots as well as karma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) at the moment of rebirth are included. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in other such answers.
435:
"Dānaṃ datvā" means having relinquished objects worthy of being given. Alternatively, the volition (cetanā) by which that gift is given is called dāna. "Datvā" means having purified that volition, making it clean. "Sīlaṃ samādiyitvā" means having undertaken permanent virtue (nicca-sīla) by way of the five precepts and so forth. By this phrase, only abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati) is shown. Abstinence from encountered circumstances (sampatta-virati) and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati) are not mentioned because they are not well-known as "virtue" in the world. Although they are not mentioned, they do occur by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). Among those types of abstinence, abstinence by eradication is an object only for the wholesome states of trainees (sekhas), and not for others (worldlings). "Uposathakammaṃ katvā" means having performed the eightfold observance (uposatha) on observance days, as taught in the words, "One should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given," and so forth. "Taṃ paccavekkhati" means that a trainee (sekha) or a worldling (puthujjana) reviews that wholesome state; an Arahant also reviews it. For an Arahant, the wholesome deeds performed in the past before becoming an Arahant are indeed wholesome, but the mind with which he reviews them is called a functional mind (kiriya-citta). Therefore, in this context of "this wholesome state is for a wholesome state," (the Arahant's reviewing mind) is not included. "Pubbe suciṇṇāni" means that while the words "datvā, samādiyitvā, katvā" refer to acts of giving, etc., performed recently (near to the reviewing mind), the phrase "pubbe suciṇṇāni" refers to acts of giving, etc., that were not performed recently. Alternatively, this is said to show other sense-sphere wholesome states (kāmāvacara-kusala) remaining from giving and so forth. "Jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā" means having emerged from jhāna. Alternatively, this very phrase "jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā" is the Pāḷi text. The phrase "sekkhā gotrabhuṃ" is said with reference to a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). That stream-enterer reviews the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) mind. The word "vodānaṃ" is said with reference to once-returners (sakadāgāmis) and non-returners (anāgāmis). For those individuals, that gotrabhū mind is called purification (vodāna). "Sekkhā" refers to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. "Maggā vuṭṭhahitvā" means having emerged from the path (magga) attained by oneself by way of surpassing the path, fruition (phala), and life-continuum (bhavaṅga). There is no such thing as reviewing by emerging from the path alone without fruition and life-continuum.

In the phrase "kusalaṃ anicccato," one should understand only the wholesome states of the three planes that have come into insight (vipassanā). Insight-wholesome (vipassanā-kusala) is only of the sense-sphere. By the phrase "cetopariyañāṇena," fine-material sphere wholesome (rūpāvacara-kusala) is shown. By the words "ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ" and so forth, immaterial sphere wholesome (arūpāvacara-kusala) is shown, which arises by way of taking immaterial wholesome as an object. By the words "kusalā khandhā iddhi-vidhañāṇassa" and so forth, it is shown by way of phenomena (dhamma) without referring to a person. For this reason, the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), which was already taken below, is mentioned again here.

"Assādeti" means he experiences and is attached to it with minds associated with greed and accompanied by joy. "Abhinandati" means he delights by way of craving accompanied by zest (pīti).
436:
(That person) becomes exceedingly joyful, or delights with a view (diṭṭhi) that is prone to delighting. "Lust (rāga) arises" means lust arises for one who enjoys. This is said taking all eight greed-associated minds. "View (diṭṭhi) arises" means for one who delights, view associated with the four minds (associated with views) arises by way of taking it as "self, belonging to self," and so forth. For one who cannot reach a conclusion regarding these (acts of giving, virtue, and observance), doubt (vicikicchā) arises. For one with a distracted mind, restlessness (uddhacca) arises. For one who regrets, thinking "Alas, I have not done good," displeasure (domanassa) arises. "Taṃ ārabbha" means taking those well-practiced acts of giving, virtue, and observance as an object. This singular term "taṃ" is used as a substitute for the plural, or it is used as a singular by way of the class (jāti) of well-practiced deeds.

"An Arahant emerging from the path" means emerging by way of surpassing the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) that immediately follows fruition (phala) in the path-process (magga-vīthi). However, his reviewing minds (paccavekkhaṇā-citta) are functional-indeterminate (kiriya-abyākata). Having thus shown the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for functional-indeterminate, he says "sekkhā vā" and so forth to show it for resultant-indeterminate (vipāka-abyākata). "When wholesome has ceased" means when the insight-impulsion process (vipassanā-javana-vīthi) is cut off. "Resultant" (vipāka) refers to sense-sphere resultant. "Tadārammaṇatā" means by way of registration (tadārammaṇa); it means arising by taking the wholesome state seen by insight, which was the object of that wholesome impulsion, as an object. It arises not only by way of registration, but also by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti). This is because the resultant of one who takes rebirth by taking kamma as an object definitely has a wholesome object; however, because that resultant is difficult to understand, it is not shown in this Pāḷi text.

"Enjoys wholesome" and so forth is said to show the resultant with a wholesome object at the end of unwholesome impulsions. The phrase "of the resultant of the sphere of infinite consciousness" is said because, although it is difficult to understand, immaterial resultant is obtained by way of not occurring as registration (tadārammaṇa). "For functional" refers to the functional jhāna in the sphere of infinite space attained by one who has reached Arahantship, either in reverse order or by skipping one stage, having not entered it before. The terms "cetopariyañāṇassa" and so forth should be connected with the subsequent "adverting" (āvajjana). The meaning here is that wholesome aggregates are a condition for that adverting by way of object-condition.

## 407-409. "Lust" (rāga) means one's own lust or another's lust. However, the explanation by way of one's own lust is clear here.

"Assādeti" and other terms have the meanings already stated. However, for the three states such as doubt (vicikicchā), the word "assādeti" (enjoys) is not used because they are not things to be enjoyed. Nevertheless, view arises in these states; that view, because of the deficiency of the word "assādeti"...
437:
(Wrong view) is not taught first in the sequence as it arrives, because it is diminished from the term "enjoys" (assādeti). Only in the case of states such as doubt (vicikicchā), etc., having first taught doubt, etc., which have a similar nature to those respective objects, is (wrong view) taught immediately after those similar states. In these states such as greed (rāga), etc., the arising of displeasure (domanassa) should be understood as occurring either through intolerance (akkhanti), thinking "Why do these evil states arise in me?", or through the power of remorse (vippaṭisāra), etc., thinking "I have done evil, I have done a cruel deed."

In the sequence of insight (vipassanā), starting with "the eye as impermanent," the eleven types of matter consisting of the gross sense spheres (āyatana) and the physical bases (vatthu-rūpa) are taken because they are evident. Again, the sense spheres of forms (rūpāyatana), etc., are taken because they are the objects of eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa), etc. Since this teaching is taught in connection with the group of consciousness (viññāṇakāya) and not in connection with the elements (dhātu), the mind-element (manodhātu) is not taken. Thus, in all answers, the states that are taken and those that are not taken should be understood.

"They review the fruition, they review Nibbāna" is taught for the purpose of showing the object of the wholesome state of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-kusala).

413-416. In the explanation of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati-niddesa), the wholesome states occurring in the four planes are shown by way of trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana); likewise in the explanation of co-nascence-predominance (sahajātādhipati-niddesa). Since an Arahant has attained the supreme state (the path and fruit of Arahantship), there is no regarding mundane wholesome states as significant; therefore, only the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) is shown.

In the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya), by the phrase "preceding, preceding," wholesome states are taught collectively, whether they are of the same plane or different planes. The statement "the conformity (anuloma) is to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), the conformity is to the cleansing (vodāna)" is taught because of the variety of objects. The statement "the change-of-lineage is to the path, the cleansing is to the path" is taught because of the variety of planes. In this context, "wholesome is to emergence (vuṭṭhāna)," wholesome refers to the wholesome states of the three planes. Emergence (vuṭṭhāna) refers to the resultants (vipāka) of the three planes. Those resultants emerge from the wholesome impulsion process (javana-vīthi); therefore, they are called "emergence." That emergence is of two kinds: registration (tadārammaṇa) and life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Among those two, for sense-sphere wholesome states, both registration and life-continuum are emergence; for sublime (mahaggata) wholesome states, only the life-continuum is emergence. As for the statement "the path is to the fruition," since the supramundane resultant is included within the impulsion process (javana-vīthi), it is not called "emergence" and is thus taught separately. In the statement "the conformity is to the trainee," because wholesome is not a proximity condition for the non-trainee (fruition attainment), a distinction is made. "To fruition attainment" means to the attainment of the fruition of Stream-entry, Once-return, and Non-return. The (second) "to fruition attainment" refers to the attainment of the fruition of Non-return. In the case of the unwholesome, both kinds of emergence (registration and life-continuum) are obtained. In this context of "resultant indeterminate, functional indeterminate," the resultant indeterminates (assist) only the resultant indeterminates (by way of proximity condition); the functional indeterminates...
438:
...should be understood (to assist) only the functional indeterminates (by way of proximity condition). The statement "life-continuum is to advertence," etc., is taught by way of mixing (condition and conditionally arisen states). In that statement, "functional" (kiriya) refers to sense-sphere functional (excluding five-door advertence). That sense-sphere functional is a proximity condition for both kinds of emergence (registration and life-continuum); the sublime (mahaggata) functional is for the life-continuum only. Thus, in the explanation of the classification of conditions (paccaya-vibhaṅga-niddesa) below, starting with "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for subsequent wholesome states by way of proximity condition," seven turns (vāra) were shown: wholesome to wholesome, wholesome to indeterminate, unwholesome to unwholesome, unwholesome to indeterminate, indeterminate to indeterminate, indeterminate to wholesome, and indeterminate to unwholesome. By way of those seven turns, the proximity condition is classified here in brief.

In detail, however, in this proximity condition:

The detailed explanation should be well noted
As ten-fold, seventeen-fold,
And by way of exactly sixty kinds,
And also in many other ways.

Indeed, this proximity condition does not obtain an explanation only by way of seven kinds. Wholesome is to wholesome, (wholesome is) to resultant, unwholesome is to unwholesome, (unwholesome is) to resultant, resultant is to resultant, (resultant is) to functional, functional is to wholesome, (functional is) to unwholesome, (functional is) to resultant, and (functional is) to functional—thus it obtains an explanation by way of ten kinds. It does not obtain it only by way of ten kinds; wholesome is to wholesome, to wholesome resultant, to unwholesome resultant; unwholesome is to unwholesome, to unwholesome resultant, to wholesome resultant; wholesome resultant is to wholesome resultant, to unwholesome resultant, to functional; unwholesome resultant is to unwholesome resultant, to wholesome resultant, to functional; functional is to functional, to wholesome, to unwholesome, to wholesome resultant, to unwholesome resultant—thus it obtains an explanation by way of seventeen kinds.

And it does not obtain it only by way of seventeen kinds; it also obtains an explanation by way of exactly sixty kinds. How? Sense-sphere wholesome is a proximity condition for four kinds of wholesome states by way of the difference of planes. Fine-material and immaterial wholesome states are (conditions) only for (wholesome states) occurring in their respective planes. Thus, wholesome is a proximity condition for wholesome in six ways. Sense-sphere wholesome (is a condition) for sense-sphere wholesome resultant, unwholesome resultant, fine-material resultant, immaterial resultant, and supramundane resultant. Fine-material wholesome is for fine-material resultant and sense-sphere wholesome resultant. Immaterial wholesome is for sense-sphere wholesome resultant, fine-material resultant, immaterial resultant, and supramundane resultant. Supramundane wholesome is for supramundane resultant. Thus, wholesome is to resultant in twelve ways...
439:
Proximity Condition. Unwholesome is a proximity condition for unwholesome, for unwholesome resultant, and for wholesome resultant belonging to the three planes; thus, it is a proximity condition in five ways.

Sense-sphere wholesome resultant is a proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome resultant, for unwholesome resultant, for fine-material sphere resultant, and for immaterial sphere resultant; thus, sense-sphere wholesome resultant is a proximity condition for resultant in four ways. Fine-material sphere resultant is a proximity condition for wholesome resultant belonging to the three planes in three ways. Immaterial sphere resultant is a proximity condition for immaterial sphere resultant and for sense-sphere wholesome resultant; thus, it is a proximity condition in two ways. Supramundane resultant is a proximity condition for wholesome resultant belonging to the four planes in four ways. In this way, wholesome resultant is a proximity condition for resultant in thirteen ways. Unwholesome resultant is a proximity condition for unwholesome resultant and for sense-sphere wholesome resultant; thus, it is a proximity condition in two ways. Thus, in every way, resultant is a proximity condition for resultant in fifteen ways. Furthermore, sense-sphere wholesome resultant is a proximity condition for sense-sphere functional; likewise, unwholesome resultant, likewise fine-material sphere resultant, and likewise immaterial sphere resultant; thus, resultant is a proximity condition for functional in four ways.

Sense-sphere functional is a proximity condition for functional belonging to the three planes; fine-material and immaterial sphere functional are proximity conditions only for fine-material and immaterial sphere functional; thus, functional is a proximity condition for functional in five ways. Sense-sphere functional is a proximity condition for unwholesome resultant and for wholesome resultant belonging to the four planes; fine-material sphere functional is a proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome resultant and fine-material sphere resultant; immaterial sphere functional is also a proximity condition for wholesome resultant belonging to the four planes; thus, functional is a proximity condition for resultant in eleven ways. Sense-sphere functional is a proximity condition for sense-sphere wholesome and for unwholesome; thus, it is a proximity condition for wholesome and unwholesome in two ways. In this way, it also receives an explanation in sixty equal ways.

It is not only in sixty equal ways that it receives an explanation, but also in many ways. How? Firstly, the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere is a proximity condition for itself, for the four fine-material sphere wholesome consciousnesses, and for the sixteen joyful supramundane consciousnesses through association as a basis (pādaka); thus, it is a proximity condition for twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses. At the end of impulsion (javana), it is a proximity condition for the eleven sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses that arise by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) and life-continuum (bhavaṅga); for the fine-material and immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses that occur by way of life-continuum only; and for the twelve [consciousnesses] that occur by way of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)...
440:
...supramundane resultant consciousnesses. Thus, the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere is a proximity condition for twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses and thirty-two resultant consciousnesses, totaling fifty-three consciousnesses. Similarly, the second great wholesome consciousness is also a proximity condition for fifty-three consciousnesses. The third and fourth great wholesome consciousnesses, however, excluding wholesome consciousnesses of higher planes and supramundane resultant consciousnesses, are proximity conditions for the remaining twenty-one consciousnesses. The fifth and sixth great wholesome consciousnesses are proximity conditions for themselves as wholesome consciousness, for the nine equanimity-associated wholesome consciousnesses of higher planes, and for twenty-three resultant consciousnesses, totaling thirty-three consciousnesses. The seventh and eighth great wholesome consciousnesses are proximity conditions for only twenty-one consciousnesses.

The five fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousnesses are proximity conditions for their respective subsequent fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, for the four knowledge-associated great resultant consciousnesses, and for the five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses, totaling ten consciousnesses. In this same way, among immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousnesses: the first is a proximity condition for eleven consciousnesses including its own resultant; the second for twelve; the third for thirteen; the fourth for fourteen; and including the attainment of fruition, for fifteen consciousnesses. Supramundane wholesome consciousness is a proximity condition for its own respective resultant consciousness only. Among the eight consciousnesses associated with greed, each unwholesome consciousness is a proximity condition for eleven sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements, for nine sublime resultant consciousnesses, and for its own subsequent unwholesome consciousness, totaling twenty-one consciousnesses. The two consciousnesses associated with aversion are proximity conditions for six equanimity-associated sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements and for their own subsequent consciousness, totaling seven consciousnesses. The two consciousnesses associated with doubt and restlessness are proximity conditions for eleven sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements including joyful rootless resultant, for nine fine-material and immaterial resultant consciousnesses, and for their own subsequent consciousness, totaling twenty-one consciousnesses.

Wholesome resultant five-fold sense-consciousness is a proximity condition for wholesome resultant mind-element. Mind-element is a proximity condition for two resultant mind-consciousness elements. Among those two, the joyful mind-consciousness element is a proximity condition for ten resultant mind-consciousness elements that are life-continuum, for the subsequent registration consciousness at the time of registration, and for the functional determining consciousness, totaling twelve consciousnesses. The equanimity-associated rootless mind-consciousness element is a proximity condition for the functional advertence mind-element, for the functional advertence mind-consciousness element occurring in two positions (advertence and determining), and for ten resultant mind-consciousness elements, totaling twelve consciousnesses. The three-rooted great resultant consciousnesses, excluding joyful rootless resultant, are proximity conditions for ten sense-sphere resultant mind-consciousness elements, for fine-material and immaterial resultant consciousnesses, and for the two advertence consciousnesses, totaling twenty-one consciousnesses. The two-rooted resultant consciousnesses, excluding sublime resultants, are proximity conditions for the remaining twelve consciousnesses. The five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses are proximity conditions for the wholesome resultant rooted rebirth-linking consciousnesses of the three planes...
441:
(The five fine-material sphere resultants) assist 17 types of triple-plane wholesome resultant rooted rebirth-linking consciousness and 2 types of adverting consciousness, totaling 19, by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). Among the immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses, the first, the resultant of the sphere of infinite space, assists 4 types of sense-sphere wholesome resultant triple-rooted rebirth-linking consciousness, 4 types of immaterial sphere resultant consciousness, and 1 mind-door adverting consciousness, totaling 9. The second, the resultant of the sphere of infinite consciousness, assists 8 types of consciousness, excluding the lower resultant of the sphere of infinite space. The third, the resultant of the sphere of nothingness, assists 7 types of consciousness, excluding the two lower ones. The fourth, the resultant of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, assists 6 types of consciousness, excluding the three lower ones. The 4 supramundane resultant consciousnesses assist 13 types of triple-rooted resultant consciousness and the resultant consciousness occurring after themselves, totaling 14.

The unwholesome resultant fivefold sense-consciousness assists the unwholesome resultant mind element. The mind element assists the unwholesome resultant rootless mind-consciousness element. That unwholesome resultant rootless mind-consciousness element, when occurring as registration (tadārammaṇa), assists the registration consciousness occurring after itself; when occurring as decease (cuti), it assists 12 types of consciousness: the remaining 9 sense-sphere resultants occurring by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and 2 sense-sphere functional consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity. The functional mind element assists the 10 types of sense-consciousness. The smile-producing functional consciousness assists 13 types of consciousness: 9 triple-rooted resultants occurring as life-continuum in the five-constituent plane, 5 resultants accompanied by joy occurring as registration, and the consciousness occurring after itself, by way of including what was not previously included (aggahitaggahaṇa), totaling 13. The determining functional consciousness assists 45 types of consciousness: 10 sense-sphere functional consciousnesses (excluding the functional mind element), sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, and 15 resultant consciousnesses occurring as life-continuum in the five-constituent plane, totaling 45.

The 2 sense-sphere triple-rooted functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy assist 22 types of consciousness: 13 triple-rooted resultants occurring as life-continuum, 5 resultants accompanied by joy occurring as registration, 4 fine-material sphere functional consciousnesses occurring as preliminary (parikamma), the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, and the consciousness occurring after itself, by way of including what was not previously included, totaling 22. The 2 double-rooted functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy assist 17 types of consciousness: the aforementioned 13 life-continuum consciousnesses, 5 registration consciousnesses, and the consciousness occurring after itself, by way of including what was not previously included, totaling 17. The 2 sense-sphere triple-rooted functional consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity assist 24 types of consciousness: those same 13 life-continuum consciousnesses, 6 resultants accompanied by equanimity occurring as registration, 1 fine-material sphere functional consciousness occurring as preliminary, 4 immaterial sphere functional consciousnesses, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, and the consciousness occurring after itself, by way of including what was not previously included, totaling 24. The 2 double-rooted functional consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity assist those same 13 life-continuum consciousnesses...
442:
...6 life-continuum consciousnesses, 6 registration consciousnesses, and the final consciousness (pacchima-citta) of its own, totaling 18 consciousnesses (by way of proximity condition), through the method of including what was not previously included (aggahitaggahaṇa). Among the fine-material sphere functional consciousnesses, each assists 10 consciousnesses: 9 triple-rooted life-continuum consciousnesses in the five-constituent plane and its own final consciousness. Among the immaterial sphere functional consciousnesses, the first (functional of the sphere of infinite space) assists 11 consciousnesses: 9 life-continuum consciousnesses in the five-constituent plane, 1 life-continuum of the sphere of infinite space in the four-constituent plane, and its own final consciousness. The second (functional of the sphere of infinite consciousness) obtains 2 life-continuum consciousnesses in the four-constituent plane. The third obtains 3, and the fourth obtains 4 and also the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Among those immaterial sphere functional consciousnesses, each is a proximity condition for 11, 12, 13, and 15 consciousnesses respectively. In this way, the explanation is obtained in various ways. Therefore, it is said:

"In ten ways, in seventeen ways, and in sixty-eight ways,
And also in many other ways, the explanation should be well noted."

The proximity condition (samanantara-paccaya) and others have meanings that are quite clear.

In the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya), "depending on faith" (saddhaṃ upanissāya) means making faith a strong dependence regarding kamma, the results of kamma, this world, the world beyond, and so forth. Just as a man, believing there is water underground, digs the earth; similarly, a son of good family, believing in the root-benefit and the consequence of giving and so forth, performs acts of giving and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "depending on faith."

In the phrases "depending on virtue" (sīlaṃ upanissāya) and so forth, the meaning is making these states such as virtue a strong dependence. For a virtuous person, being skilled in the power and benefits of virtue, gives gifts to the virtuous depending on virtue, undertakes higher virtue to be perfectly pure and unbroken, performs the Uposatha observance on the lunar days such as the fourteenth, and depending on the perfection of virtue, produces absorptions (jhāna) and so forth. One of great learning (bahussuta), also being established in the realization through wisdom born of learning (sutamaya-paññā) regarding all attainments connected with meritorious actions such as giving, and the distinctions of defilement and purification of giving and so forth, performs giving and so forth depending on learning (suta). One who is generous (cāgavā), being inclined towards liberality, gives gifts depending on his own perfection of generosity; (thinking) "giving by one who is virtuous is of great fruit," he undertakes virtue, performs the Uposatha, and with a mind purified by that practice, produces absorptions and so forth. A wise person, also investigating the welfare of this world and the world beyond, and the means to transcend the world, performs giving and so forth depending on wisdom, (thinking) "through this practice, the welfare of this world, the welfare of the world beyond, and the means to transcend the world can be accomplished." Because...
443:
States such as faith and so forth are not only decisive supports for giving and so forth that will occur in the future, but they are also decisive supports for faith and so forth that arise in one's own future. Therefore, it is said that faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom are [decisive supports] for faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Regarding 'preliminary work' (parikamma), one should not take the preliminary work immediately preceding [the jhāna], but the preliminary work in the preceding stage. For the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa) and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa), the preliminary work of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) itself is their preliminary work; there is no separate preliminary work. These knowledges are merely peripheral knowledges (paribhaṇḍa-ñāṇa) of the divine eye; when that divine eye is accomplished, they are also accomplished. Even so, the preliminary work of the divine eye, together with the state of being inclined towards those [knowledges], should be understood as their preliminary work. In truth, these knowledges do not occur with uniform accomplishment for all who possess the divine eye. Therefore, it should be noted that there must be a distinction in the preliminary work here. 'The divine eye is a decisive support for the divine ear element' means that for one who, having seen forms at a distance, wishes to hear the sounds of those [who possess those forms], the divine eye is a decisive support for the purification of the ear element (the divine ear). Again, by way of wishing to go to that place after hearing the sounds of those [forms], the divine ear element is a decisive support for the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa). Thus, in all cases, the nature of being a decisive support condition should be understood by way of its helpfulness to each respective resultant state.

Regarding 'depending on the path, one produces an unarisen attainment,' because the obstacles have been weakened or abandoned by that respective path, they can produce that respective attainment; thus, the path of those trainees (sekha) is a decisive support for attainment. 'They practice insight' means they practice insight specifically as impermanent, suffering, and non-self for the sake of the higher paths. It is said that the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) such as the analytical knowledge of meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā) are accomplished only by the attainment of the path. For those who have thus accomplished them, the path itself is the decisive support for their occurrence in various objects later on.

Regarding 'depending on faith, one arouses conceit,' one arouses conceit by thinking, 'I am one who has faith, a devotee [of the Triple Gem].' Regarding 'one grasps a view,' it means going by the power of faith alone in various words, without investigating or reflecting on the meaning with wisdom, one grasps a view such as 'A person exists in the ultimate sense.' Regarding virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom as well, one arouses conceit by thinking, 'I am one who is virtuous, learned, generous, and endowed with wisdom.' Just like the imagining of conceit, one produces the imagining of a view and grasps a view regarding virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. In the context of 'decisive support for lust (rāga)' and so forth, when one exalts oneself depending on the achievement of faith and so forth, each of those states is a decisive support for lust; when disparaging others, it is a decisive support for hatred (dosa); for delusion (moha) associated with both; and for the aforementioned conceit and views. Depending on the achievement of faith and so forth, it is a decisive support for the aspiration for success in existence (bhava-sampatti) and success in wealth (bhoga-sampatti).
444:
In this way, in this context (where wholesome states are a decisive support for unwholesome states), only mundane wholesome states are shown. Supramundane wholesome states, however, are peaceful, sublime, excellent, and destroy unwholesome states. Therefore, just as the moon is not [a support] for the mass of darkness, supramundane wholesome states are not a decisive support for unwholesome states; thus, they are not included (not taught).

The words "causes torment" and so forth are spoken for the purpose of showing indeterminate states by way of physical suffering. Indeed, a person with faith, relying on that faith, does not shrink back thinking "it is too cold" or "it is too hot," but performs various types of new construction work (navakamma), service (veyyāvacca), and so on, thereby tormenting and distressing himself. Thinking, "I will produce wealth and perform meritorious deeds," he experiences suffering rooted in seeking. A virtuous person also, for the sake of protecting virtue, torments and distresses himself by way of the open-air dweller's practice (abbhokāsika) and so forth. He experiences suffering rooted in seeking by way of the alms-food eater's practice (piṇḍapātika) and so forth. A learned person also, practicing in the manner already described with the thought "I will practice in accordance with my great learning," torments and distresses himself and experiences suffering rooted in seeking. A generous person also, because of his devotion to generosity, gives up even his own meager requisites without remainder, or gives up his limbs and so forth, thereby tormenting and distressing himself. He experiences suffering rooted in seeking for the purpose of producing the objects to be given away. A wise person also, thinking "I will increase my wisdom further and further," relies on his wisdom and, disregarding cold, heat, and so forth, applies himself to recitation and reflection, thereby tormenting and distressing himself. Seeing the danger in wrong livelihood and the benefit in right livelihood, he abandons wrong livelihood and, while seeking a living through pure livelihood, experiences suffering rooted in seeking.

"For physical pleasure" refers to physical pleasure at the time of using the means of happiness that have arisen relying on the fulfillment of faith and so forth; for one whose body is pervaded by refined matter produced by faith and so forth; for one whose body is pervaded by matter produced by gladness and rapture rooted in non-remorse by power of that faith and so forth; at the time when pleasure arises; and at the time of resultant pleasure (vipāka-sukha) that arises because of having performed those wholesome deeds. (In these cases, faith and so forth are a condition by way of decisive support for physical pleasure.) In the same manner, at the time when suffering arises, and at the time of being killed or bound, etc., by those who cannot endure his possession of qualities like faith, etc., (faith and so forth are a condition by way of decisive support) for physical suffering. However, at the time of Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti) which occurs relying on faith and so forth, it should be understood that each of these (faith, etc.) is a condition for Fruition Attainment by way of decisive support condition.

"Wholesome kamma" means wholesome volition is a decisive support condition for its own result. That volition, however, is obtained only as strong volition, not weak. In this regard, there is this story: It is said that a certain woman, wishing to hang herself, tied a rope to a tree and made the necessary preparations. Then a thief approached that house at night, thinking, "I will tie something with this rope and take it," and went near to cut it with a knife. At that moment, a swift, venomous snake raised its hood and made a "hissing" sound. The thief fled in fear. The woman then came out of the house, put her neck in the noose, and died by hanging. In this way, strong volition prevents obstacles to the ripening of results and becomes a decisive support condition for its own result. However, this statement "it is obtained only as strong volition, not weak" should not be taken as universally applicable. For, once the opportunity for the result to be given has been granted...
445:
A thief approached that house at night, thinking, "I will bind something with this rope and take it away," and went near to cut it with a knife. At that moment, the rope became a cobra and made a "hissing" sound. The thief, being frightened, retreated. That woman came out of her house, put her neck into the noose of the rope, and died by hanging. In this way, strong intention (balava-cetanā) prevents obstacles and becomes a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for its own result (vipāka). However, this point should not be taken as an absolute rule. Only kamma that has gained the opportunity to produce a result can prevent obstacles and ripen. It should not be said that kamma which produces a result is not a decisive support condition for that result. Here, kamma should be understood as kamma occurring in the four planes. The statement mentioned later, "The path is [a decisive support] for the attainment of fruition," occurs by way of non-volition. Therefore, it shows this meaning: whatever state produces a result is a decisive support condition for its own result.

"One kills a living being depending on lust (rāga)" means one kills a living being either because of being attached to a certain object, or against someone who opposes that object, or for the sake of that object. In the case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and so on, the meaning should be understood in the same way. "One breaks into a house (cuts the joint)" is said by way of taking what is not given. There, sandhi means the joint of a house. "One carries away plunder (nillopaṃ harati)" means one steals by hiding. "One commits a single-house robbery (ekāgārikaṃ karoti)" means one surrounds and plunders a single house together with many people. "One stands in ambush (paripanthe tiṭṭhati)" means one performs the act of highway robbery. In "depending on hatred (dosa)" and so on, one performs killing etc. by making hatred—which arises in the form of "he has done me harm"—the decisive support. "Depending on delusion (moha)" means making delusion—which conceals the danger in killing living beings and so on—the decisive support. "Depending on pride (māna)" means making pride—in the form of "Why should I not be able to kill? Why should I not be able to take?"—the decisive support. Alternatively, it also means making low-esteem (omāna) the decisive support when one is despised, oppressed, or insulted by someone. "Depending on wrong view (diṭṭhi)" means making wrong view the decisive support, like the Brahmins in sacrifices or like forest-dwellers and barbarians. "Depending on aspiration (patthanā)" means making aspiration the decisive support, such as requesting deities: "If this matter of mine succeeds, I will perform such an offering to you," or "Kill such a person for me," or "Bring the property of such a person," or "Come and be my companion while I perform these acts." Lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, and aspiration are [decisive supports] for lust.
446:
In this context, lust (rāga) is a decisive support condition for lust itself, as well as for hatred (dosa) and so on. The same method applies to hatred and so on.

"Killing living beings is for killing living beings (pāṇātipāto pāṇātipāssa)" means that because a killer is established in lack of restraint, he kills other beings as well. Or, he kills someone else among the relatives and friends of the person he killed because he is harassed by them. In this way, killing living beings is a condition for killing living beings by way of decisive support condition. Furthermore, killing living beings is a decisive support for taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and so on, in cases such as: killing the owner or the guard to take another's property; killing the husband to commit adultery with his wife; telling a lie saying "I did not kill"; using slander to conceal a committed act of killing or to facilitate an uncommitted one; similarly, uttering harsh speech or frivolous talk; killing another and then coveting their wealth and possessions which ought to be considered; thinking "May the friends and ministers of the one I killed be destroyed"; or when one adopts a wrong view through difficult practices, thinking "By doing this, my act of killing will be worn away without producing a result." By this method, the meaning should be understood in the cycles where taking what is not given and so on are the root.

"The act of matricide is for the act of matricide (mātughātikammaṃ mātughātikammassa)" means: by the power of one who kills his own mother after seeing another person kill their mother and thinking "It is proper to do so"; or by the power of killing the mother in one life and then killing her again in another life; or by the power of repeatedly ordering in a single life, "Go, kill my mother"; or by the power of giving a second blow to a mother whose death is certain from two blows. The remaining acts, such as patricide (pitughāta), should also be understood in this same way as applicable. Some say that the teaching is given only by way of ānantariya-kamma (kamma with immediate result) that reaches the path of action (kammapatha), because a strong unwholesome state cannot be a decisive support for a weak unwholesome state. That statement should not be taken as absolutely true. This is because after committing killing and so on, when one is accused and asked "Why did you do this?", one may act out of mere anger. Remorse (vippaṭisāra) also occurs. Even when a small defilement arises, one may increase that defilement and commit a transgression. Therefore, a strong state is indeed a decisive support for a weak one, and a weak state is also a decisive support for a strong one. As for the statement in the explanation of the summary of the Paccaya-vibhaṅga, "It is a decisive support condition in the sense of being a strong cause," that was said only regarding the strength of the nature of being a cause, not regarding the strength of the states that are decisive support conditions. For kamma and defilements, whether strong or weak, are indeed strong causes.
447: In the phrases such as "gives a gift depending on lust," one gives a gift depending on lust for rebirth-existence or for wealth, thinking, "Oh, would that I might reach the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings!" The same method applies to actions such as undertaking virtue and observing the Uposatha. However, one who produces jhāna for the purpose of suppressing lust, insight for the purpose of abandoning lust, and the Path for the purpose of eradicating lust, is said to produce them depending on lust. One who produces supernormal knowledge and attainment for the purpose of being free from lust is also said to produce them depending on lust. By producing such supernormal knowledge and attainment, one becomes free from lust. "By faith" means by faith occurring in connection with giving and so forth [it assists by way of strong dependence condition]. The same method applies to virtue and so forth. Just as one who produces faith and so forth by the power of giving and so forth is said to produce them depending on lust, so also lust and so forth should be understood as strong dependence conditions for faith and so forth. "For the purpose of obstructing that kamma" means for the purpose of warding off that kamma of taking life, with the meaning: for the purpose of not giving an opportunity for its result. Let it be so in the case of kammas that can be obstructed from giving results. But why is it said "for the purpose of obstructing that" in the case of the ānantariya kammas which are not capable of being obstructed from giving results? It is said according to that person's intention. Taking the intention of that person who thinks, "I will perform giving and so forth for the purpose of obstructing this kamma," it is thus stated. "Depending on lust, he torments himself" means where there is attachment, seeing that it can only be obtained through difficulty, he acts in this way; everything should be understood according to the previous method. "To bodily pleasure" means [it is a strong dependence condition] for pleasure obtained by performing wholesome deeds through the overcoming of lust and so forth, or for pleasure arisen through the enjoyment of sensual pleasures without seeing the danger by the power of lust and so forth. "To pain" means for pain arisen through self-torment and so forth, or for pain arisen through being killed or bound and so forth, occurring due to lust and so forth. "To fruition attainment" means for fruition attainment produced by eradicating lust and so forth, or for that which is attained by one who is oppressed by those [lust and so forth]. In the phrases "bodily pleasure" and so forth, when pleasure arises, for one who enjoys that pleasure and produces it again and again through such causes, the preceding [pleasure] is a strong dependence condition for the subsequent [pleasure]. For one who excessively indulges in warming oneself by a fire when cold and so forth, the pleasure in the earlier stage is a strong dependence condition for the pain in the later stage. "Oh, how pleasant is the touch of the soft, hairy arm of this young female wanderer," for one who indulges in sensual pleasures in this way, the bodily pleasure in this life is a strong dependence condition for the bodily pain of a hell-being. For one who, being healthy and happy, enters fruition attainment, bodily pleasure is a strong dependence condition for fruition attainment.
448: is a strong dependence condition. For one who makes use of pleasure to dispel pain, and for one who, like the Blessed One, suppresses illness to enter fruition attainment for the purpose of dispelling pain, bodily pain is a strong dependence condition for both bodily pleasure and fruition attainment. Suitable weather is [a strong dependence condition] for both bodily pleasure and fruition attainment. Unsuitable weather is [a strong dependence condition] for bodily pain. Or, for one who wishes to experience the pleasure arisen by the power of the materiality produced by attainment after overcoming unsuitable weather, even unsuitable weather is a condition for fruition attainment. The same method applies to food and lodging. Again, the terms "bodily pleasure" and so forth are shown together simply as conditions. However, their nature as conditions should be understood by the method mentioned below. "Fruition attainment for bodily pleasure" means [assisting] pleasure arisen by the power of materiality having attainment as its cause. For that person experiences that pleasure after emerging from attainment. "Depending on bodily pleasure, one gives a gift" and so forth, the nature of pleasure and pain as strong dependence should be understood by the power of not wanting the obtained pleasure to diminish, thinking "Oh, may this pleasure of mine not diminish," or by the power of desiring to obtain unobtained pleasure, thinking "Oh, may I obtain such pleasure in the future." In the case of pain, it is by the power of wanting the obtained pain to diminish, thinking "Oh, may my pain diminish," or by the power of wishing for it not to arise, thinking "May such pain not arise in the future." Weather, food, and lodging are just as previously mentioned. Again, in the words "bodily pleasure" and so forth, faith arises for those who have reached pleasure, thinking "Excellent indeed, friend Moggallāna, is the taking of refuge in the Buddha," and for those who have reached pain, thinking "The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One, who teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding of such pain." Furthermore, they fulfill virtue and so forth for the sake of association with pleasure and dissociation from pain. Therefore, pleasure and pain are shown as strong dependence conditions for faith and so forth. Weather and so forth should also be applied as appropriate. In the words "depending on bodily pleasure, one kills a living being" and so forth, the nature of pleasure and so forth as strong dependence should be understood according to the mentioned method. In this classification of the strong dependence condition, the wholesome is a strong dependence condition for the wholesome in three ways, for the unwholesome in two ways, and for the indeterminate in three ways. The unwholesome is [a strong dependence condition] for the unwholesome in three ways, for the wholesome in one way, and for the indeterminate in two ways. The indeterminate is also [a strong dependence condition] for the indeterminate in three ways, and likewise for the wholesome [in three ways].
449:
Likewise, for the unwholesome (it is a decisive support). Thus, it should be understood that the decisive support condition is analyzed in twenty-three ways: wholesome in eight ways, unwholesome in six ways, and indeterminate in nine ways.

In the prenascent condition, the eye and so forth are stated by way of the gross material form. However, the water element and so forth are also prenascent objects. The phrase "The eye-base is a prenascent base" is stated to show that which, having become a physical base, is prenascent. The phrase "The base [is a condition] for resultant indeterminate [states]" is stated with reference to the prenascent condition during the course of existence (pavatti).

In the postnascent condition, "for this body" means for the body consisting of the four great elements. "Conditioned by way of postnascent condition" means being a condition by arising later by way of support. Because it conditions in the sense of supporting, this postnascent condition appears in this Question Section (Pañhāvāra) by way of the analytical order (anuloma).

In the repetition condition, the reason for taking terms such as "in analytical order, for the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū)" separately should be understood in the same way as mentioned below (in the proximity condition).

In the kamma condition, in the phrase "wholesome volition for associated states," the word "conascent" (sahajāta) is not mentioned because there is no division between conascent and asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika). However, in the explanation of the indeterminate, that division exists; therefore, it is mentioned there. The taking of rebirth is done by way of the kamma-born material forms (kaṭattā-rūpa). The phrase "volition for the base" is stated to show that although mental states dependent on the base at the moment of rebirth arise due to the base condition, volition is also a condition for the base.

In the resultant condition during the rebirth section, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

429-438. In the nutriment condition, "for this body" means it is a condition by way of nutriment for this body of the four great elements proceeding by way of the four continuities (santati), by way of producing the nutriment-originated material form, and by way of supporting the remaining material forms. In the faculty condition and so forth, the rebirth section should be understood in the same way as already mentioned. All the remaining words have an obvious meaning in all places.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Question Section is finished.
450:
## The Enumeration in Analytical Order in the Combination of the Question Section

Now, in order to show the explanations (vissajjanā) obtained in this Analysis Section (Vibhaṅgavāra) by way of enumeration, it is said: "Seven in root condition," and so forth. In that word "seven," there are 3 explanations: wholesome for wholesome, for indeterminate, and for wholesome-and-indeterminate. Likewise, 3 for the unwholesome, and 1 for indeterminate for indeterminate alone; thus there are 7. "Nine in object condition" refers to the 9 explanations starting with one term and ending with another. "Ten in predominance condition": Wholesome conditions wholesome by way of conascence and object; unwholesome by way of object only; indeterminate by way of conascence and object; and wholesome-and-indeterminate by way of conascence only—thus there are 4 explanations with wholesome as the root. Unwholesome conditions unwholesome by way of conascence and object; indeterminate by way of conascence; and likewise unwholesome-and-indeterminate—thus there are 3 explanations with unwholesome as the root. Indeterminate conditions indeterminate by way of conascence and object; wholesome by way of object only; and likewise unwholesome—thus there are 3 explanations with indeterminate as the root. In this way, there are 10. In this predominance condition, object-predominance is obtained in 7 ways, and conascence-predominance is also obtained in 7 ways.

"Seven in proximity condition": 2 explanations with wholesome as the root, likewise 2 with unwholesome as the root, and 3 with indeterminate as the root; thus there are 7. In the contiguity condition (samanantara), these same explanations occur. "Nine in conascence condition": 3 with wholesome as the root, 3 with unwholesome as the root, 1 with indeterminate as the root, likewise 1 with wholesome-and-indeterminate as the root, and 1 with unwholesome-and-indeterminate as the root; thus there are 9. "Three in mutuality condition": wholesome for wholesome, unwholesome for unwholesome, indeterminate for indeterminate; thus there are 3. "Thirteen in dependence condition": by way of conascence-dependence alone, there are 3 with wholesome as the root, likewise 3 with unwholesome as the root, and likewise 3 with indeterminate as the root. In this indeterminate root, prenascent-dependence is also obtained. Indeed, indeterminate is both conascence-dependence and prenascent-dependence for indeterminate. For the wholesome, it is prenascent-dependence only; likewise for the unwholesome. Again, wholesome-and-indeterminate conditions wholesome by way of conascence and prenascent, and indeterminate by way of conascence only; likewise unwholesome-and-indeterminate conditions; in this way, there are 13. "Nine in decisive support condition" refers to the 9 explanations starting with one term and ending with another. In the Analysis Section of those 9 explanations, twenty-three varieties were shown. Among those 23, there are 7 in object-decisive support, 7 in proximity-decisive support, and 9 in natural-decisive support. "Three in prenascent condition": indeterminate conditions indeterminate, wholesome, and unwholesome; in this way, there are 3.
451:
In the post-existence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), there are three ways: wholesome to indeterminate, unwholesome to indeterminate, and indeterminate to indeterminate. In the repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), there are three answers similar to the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya). In the kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), there are seven ways similar to the root condition (hetu-paccaya). Among those seven answers, asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma) is included in two answers (wholesome to indeterminate, and unwholesome to indeterminate); in the remaining five, only conascent kamma (sahajāta-kamma) is included. In the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya), there is only one way: indeterminate to indeterminate. In the nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), jhāna, and path (magga) conditions, there are only seven ways similar to the root condition. However, in this faculty condition, it is included by way of conascent faculty (sahajātindriya) and pre-existent faculty (purejātindriya). In the association condition (sampayutta-paccaya), there are three ways similar to the mutuality condition. In the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya), there are five ways: one from wholesome to indeterminate by way of conascence and post-existence; one from unwholesome to indeterminate; one from indeterminate to indeterminate by way of conascence, pre-existence, and post-existence; one from indeterminate to wholesome by way of base pre-existence (vatthu-purejāta); and similarly, one to unwholesome. Thus, there are five: one wholesome-root, one unwholesome-root, and three indeterminate-roots.

In the presence condition (atthi-paccaya), there are thirteen ways: three wholesome-roots, namely, wholesome to wholesome by way of conascence, wholesome to indeterminate by way of conascence and post-existence, and wholesome to wholesome and indeterminate by way of conascence. Similarly, there are three unwholesome-roots. There is one from indeterminate to indeterminate by way of conascence, pre-existence, post-existence, nutriment, and faculty; one from indeterminate to wholesome by way of base-object pre-existence (vatthārammaṇa-purejāta); similarly, one to unwholesome; one from wholesome and indeterminate to wholesome by way of conascence and pre-existence; one from those same wholesome and indeterminate to indeterminate by way of conascence, post-existence, nutriment, and faculty; one from unwholesome and indeterminate to unwholesome by way of conascence and pre-existence; and one from those same unwholesome and indeterminate to indeterminate by way of conascence, post-existence, nutriment, and faculty. Thus, there are thirteen ways. In the absence (natthi) and disappearance (vigata) conditions, there are seven ways similar to the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). In the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya), there are thirteen ways similar to the presence condition. Thus, in this fivefold section (pañcavāra), there are seven numerical limits: one, three, five, seven, nine, ten, and thirteen. Among these numerical limits, there is one 'single' (ekaka) by way of the resultant condition; five 'triads' (tika) by way of mutuality, pre-existence, post-existence, repetition, and association conditions; one 'pentad' (pañcaka) by way of the dissociation condition; ten 'septads' (sattaka) by way of root, proximity, contiguity, kamma, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, absence, and disappearance conditions; three 'nonads' (navaka) by way of object, conascence, and decisive support conditions; one 'decad' (dasaka) by way of the predominance condition; and three 'thirteen-folds' (terasaka) by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Thus, having well noted the sections (vāra) shown in each condition by way of numerical calculation, the calculation should be understood when comparing conditions in dyads (duka), triads (tika), and so on, by way of those sections.

Those conditions which are dissimilar (visabhāga) or contradictory (viruddha) to certain conditions should not be combined with those [dissimilar or contradictory] conditions. What are those dissimilar and contradictory conditions? Firstly, of the root condition...
452:
The object (ārammaṇa), proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), decisive support (upanissaya), pre-existence (purejāta), post-existence (pacchājāta), kamma, repetition (āsevana), nutriment (āhāra), jhāna, absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) conditions, and the predominance (adhipati) condition excluding investigation-predominance (vīmaṃsādhipati), are dissimilar (visabhāga) [to the root condition]. The conascence (sahajāta) and other such conditions are similar (sabhāga). Why? Because of the existence or non-existence of such a state. For when the root condition (hetu-paccaya) assists certain states by way of root condition, the conascence and other such conditions also occur for those states, but the object and other such conditions do not occur. Therefore, the object and other such conditions are called dissimilar (visabhāga) to that root condition. Thus, that root condition should not be combined with those object and other conditions, nor should those object and other conditions be combined with that root condition.

The pre-existence, post-existence, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance conditions are also mutually contradictory (viruddha). These conditions should also not be combined with one another. Among those conditions, for the purpose of showing in brief the sections (vāra) obtained when combining the combinable conditions while excluding the non-combinable ones, it is said: "Four in the predominance condition because of the root condition," and so forth.

In that context, although there should be seven sections by way of the condition with the smaller number when comparing the root condition with the predominance condition, since among the predominances only investigation-predominance (vīmaṃsādhipati) is a root condition and the others are not, the dissimilar ones are excluded and it is stated as "four" by way of the similar investigation-predominance. Those sections should be understood thus: A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of root condition and by way of predominance condition; wholesome investigation (vīmaṃsā) assists the associated aggregates (sampayuttaka-khandha). A wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of root condition and by way of predominance condition; wholesome investigation assists mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state and an indeterminate state by way of root condition and by way of predominance condition; wholesome investigation assists the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter. An indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of root condition and by way of predominance condition; resultant indeterminate and functional indeterminate investigation assists the associated aggregates and mind-produced matter.

And here, the resultant indeterminates should be taken only from the supramundane (lokuttara). The object condition, proximity condition, and so forth, are not combined because they are dissimilar conditions. By this method, having understood the conditions that are obtainable and not obtainable in all methods, the sections (vāra) should be extracted by way of the obtainable conditions.

In conascence, the "seven" are the same as those obtained in the root section. In mutuality, the "three" are the same as those obtained in the pure mutuality condition. In support, the "seven" are the same as those obtained in the root section. In resultant, the "one" is the same as that obtained in the pure resultant condition. In faculty and path, the "four" are according to the same method already stated in the root-predominance dyad (hetu-mūla adhipati-duka) mentioned below.
453:
They are just as in the methods already stated. The three in the association condition (sampayutta-paccaya) are the same as the answers (vissajjanā) obtained in the pure association condition (suddhika-sampayutta-paccaya). The three in the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya) should be understood by taking matter produced by consciousness such as wholesome [consciousness] as the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna). The seven in the presence condition (atthi-paccaya) and the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya) are the same as the answers obtained in the root chapter (hetu-vāra).

441-443. In this way, the root condition (hetu-paccaya) enters into association with eleven conditions such as the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya). Having shown the numerical calculation in the two-root method (dūmūlaka-naya) by means of those eleven conditions, [the teacher] now sets down the characteristic to show that calculation in the three-root method (timūlaka) and so on, saying: "Seven in root, conascence, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance," and so forth. In books, however, they write the names of the conditions with omitted letters such as Nissa, Upanissa, and Adhipa; such writing is done merely for the sake of recognition. Therefore, in such places, the Pali should be made complete. By this characteristic that is set down, this meaning is shown: when this root condition is compared with the four conditions such as conascence, it obtains only the seven answers obtained in its own analysis chapter (vibhaṅga-vāra). If the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya) is included here, it obtains the three obtained in mutuality. If the association condition is included, it obtains those same three. If the dissociation condition is included, it obtains the three obtained in the root-dissociation dyad (hetu-vippayutta-duka). If the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya) is included, when compared with all similar resultant conditions (vipāka-sabhāga), it obtains the answers in this same way. If the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya) and path condition (magga-paccaya) are included here, it obtains only the four obtained in the two-root [method] with those conditions. If the mutuality condition is included with those conditions, among the four answers shown in the root-predominance dyad (hetādhipati-duka), it obtains the remaining two after removing the two: "wholesome state is to indeterminate" and "wholesome state is to wholesome and indeterminate." If the association condition is included there, it obtains those same two. If the dissociation condition is included, it obtains the other two. If the resultant condition is included among those conditions, it obtains only one in all chapters. However, together with the predominance condition, if conditions with a lower count than the root-predominance dyad are not included, it obtains only four. If conditions with a lower count are included, it obtains two or one by means of those conditions. Thus, having known the numerical calculation obtainable in the combination of various conditions, the calculation in the three-root method and so on should be extracted.
454:
Among those combinations (ghaṭanā), the first four counts are generally taught by way of the nine roots without the resultant condition (avipāka). However, among these first four counts, in the answer of "indeterminate by indeterminate", the resultant root (vipāka-hetu) is also obtained.

The five counts following that are taught by way of the resultant root. In those five counts, all conascent resultants (sahajāta-vipāka) and matter conascent with resultants (vipāka-sahajāta-rūpa) are obtained. Among those five, in the first count, resultants and matter produced by those resultants are obtained. In the second count, resultants and the base matter (vatthu-rūpa) occurring at the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) are obtained. In the third count, only mental states (arūpa-dhamma) are obtained. In the fourth count, only matter produced by resultant consciousness is obtained. In the fifth count, only base matter is obtained.

The fifteen counts following that are taught by way of the non-delusion root (amoha-hetu) in association with the faculty condition and path condition. Among those fifteen, the first nine are without the predominance condition (nirādhipati). The last six are with the predominance condition (sādhipati). Among the counts without predominance, the first four are generally taught by way of non-delusion in all chapters. The five following them are taught by way of resultant non-delusion. Among those counts without predominance, the first four are the same as those shown below in the root-predominance dyad (hetādhipati-duka). In the second count, mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa) is omitted. In the third count, base matter (vatthu-rūpa) is omitted. In the fourth count, only matter is obtained, as in: "wholesome state (is a condition) for mind-produced matter; indeterminate state (is a condition) for those mind-produced matter." The five counts associated with resultants following that are just as in the method stated below.

Among the counts with predominance, the first three counts are generally taught by way of the non-delusion root that is resultant and the non-delusion root that is not resultant. Among those three, in the first count, the four answers are just as in the method stated. In the second count, matter is omitted. In the third count, mind (arūpa) is omitted. The three counts following that are taught by way of the resultant root. Among those three, in the first count, matter and mind are obtained. In the second count, only mind is obtained. In the third count, only matter is obtained. In this way, having known the numerical calculation obtainable in the combination of various conditions, the calculation in the three-root method and so on should be extracted.

## The Root-Origin (Hetu-mūlaka) is finished.

In the Object-Origin (Ārammaṇa-mūlaka) as well, seven conditions such as the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) are compatible (sabhāga) with the object condition. The remaining sixteen conditions are incompatible (visabhāga). Therefore, those incompatible conditions are not associated, and only the seven are associated. Among those seven, the seven in predominance are: "wholesome state (is a condition) for wholesome state, for unwholesome state, for indeterminate state"—thus there are seven, consisting of three wholesome-roots, one unwholesome-root, and three indeterminate-roots. The three in the dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya) are only indeterminate-roots by way of the base (vatthu). The seven in the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) are the same seven shown below. The three in the pre-nascent condition (purejāta-paccaya) are indeterminate-roots by way of the object-base (vatthārammaṇa). In the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya)...
455:
(In the dissociation condition,) the 'three' is by way of the physical base only. In the presence and non-disappearance conditions, the 'three' is by way of the physical base as object. Just as combinations (ghatanā) are established in the root-based method to show the characteristics, so too are combinations established in the object-based method and others.

In that object-based method, five combinations are established. Among those five, the first combination is one with predominance by way of object-predominance. In that first combination, the 'seven' are the same answers obtained in the object-predominance dyad. The second combination is one without predominance. In that second combination, the 'three' are indeterminate roots by way of the physical base as object, or by way of the object only. The third combination is stated by way of the support condition. There, the 'three' are indeterminate roots by way of the physical base. The fourth and fifth combinations are those with predominance. Among those two, in the fourth combination, the 'one' is an unwholesome state with an indeterminate root by way of the physical base as object, or by way of the object only. In the fifth combination, the 'one' is an unwholesome state with an indeterminate root by way of support. Thus, in this object-based method as well, the counting in triads and so on should be understood according to what is obtainable. The same applies to the predominance-based method and others. Without elaborating on the application by way of object, faculty, and resultant, I shall only state what is appropriate to be said in those respective conditions.

In the conascence condition of the predominance-based method, the 'seven' are three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and one indeterminate root by way of conascence-predominance. Object-predominance cannot be obtained together with conascence-predominance, nor conascence-predominance with object-predominance. In the mutuality condition, the 'three' are by way of conascence-predominance only. In the support condition, the 'eight' are three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and two indeterminate roots. For an indeterminate predominance is a support condition for an indeterminate state by way of both conascence and object; but for an unwholesome state, it is a support condition by way of object only. For a wholesome state, however, it does not occur in either way; therefore, there are only two indeterminate roots, and thus there are eight. In the decisive support condition, the 'seven' are just the same as in the object condition. In the prenascence condition, the 'one' is the indeterminate predominance being a condition for an unwholesome state by way of object. In the resultant condition, the 'one' is the supramundane indeterminate [conditioned] by the indeterminate. In the conditions such as nutriment, the 'seven' are those already obtained below in the single-root method. In the dissociation condition, the 'four' are: wholesome with indeterminate, likewise unwholesome with [indeterminate], and indeterminate with both indeterminate and wholesome. In the presence and non-disappearance conditions, the 'eight' are just the same as in the support condition.

447-452. In this predominance-based method, the combinations are not associated with conditions such as object in sequence, but are first associated with the presence and non-disappearance conditions. For what reason? Because they are mixed with both types of predominance. Among those combinations, in the first combination, the physical base as object is obtained by way of object-predominance.
456:
(In the second combination,) it is obtained. In the second combination, for one who enjoys it by giving weight to it as a support, only the heart-base is obtained. In the third combination, by way of conascence-predominance, wholesome states and so on are conditions for matter; by way of object-predominance, the physical base is a condition for the unwholesome. After that, three combinations are stated by way of object-predominance. Among those three, in the first, the 'seven' are those already stated below. In the second, the 'one' is the prenascent physical base as object being a condition for the unwholesome. In the third, only the physical base is a condition for the unwholesome. After that, three combinations connected with resultant and non-resultant are stated by way of conascence-predominance. Among those three, in the first, both matter and mind are obtained; in the second, only mind is obtained; in the third, only matter is obtained. After that, three combinations are stated by way of resultant-predominance. Among those three as well, in the first, matter and mind are obtained; in the second, mind; in the third, only matter. After that, six combinations associated with the nutriment and faculty conditions are stated by way of predominance of consciousness. Among those six, three are without resultant and three are with resultant. In those six, the counting is clear. After that, six combinations are stated likewise by way of predominance of energy. Should they not have been stated first by way of predominance of energy according to the sequence of predominances? If it is asked why they were not stated so: it is because they are similar to the combinations stated later by way of root (hetu). Indeed, the combinations that occur later by way of root are associated with the path condition because non-delusion is the predominance of investigation and because investigation is right view. Energy is also called a path factor because it is right effort or wrong effort; therefore, the combinations associated with that path condition are similar to the combinations stated later by way of root, and thus they are stated in a reversed order. In those energy-predominance combinations as well, the counting is clear.

453-456. In the proximity and contiguity-based methods, the 'seven' means: wholesome is a condition for wholesome and indeterminate; likewise unwholesome; and indeterminate is a condition for all three; thus there are seven. In the kamma condition, the 'one' means: the wholesome path volition is a condition for its own resultant indeterminate. In these methods, there are only three combinations each. Those combinations are stated according to the sequence of the greater number.

457-460. In the conascence, mutuality, and support-based methods, only those conditions stated in the dyad-based method are similar in nature to the condition standing at the beginning. Therefore, having known the counting in the dyad-based method, the counting in all combinations should be understood by way of the condition with the lesser number among the conditions combined above. In that conascence-based method, there are ten combinations. Among those ten, five are without resultant and five are with resultant. Among those combinations without resultant, first, in the first combination, wholesome is a condition for wholesome.
457:
Among the non-resultant combinations (avippāka-ghaṭanā), in the first combination, there are four answers (vissajjanā): wholesome is a condition for wholesome, for indeterminate, and for wholesome-and-indeterminate. Similarly, unwholesome also has four, and indeterminate is a condition only for indeterminate; thus there are nine. Among these nine answers, in the eight answers starting with wholesome and unwholesome, mental phenomena (nāma) and mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa) are obtained. In the indeterminate answer, the base-matter (vatthu-rūpa) is also obtained. In the indeterminate answer of the second combination, among matters, only the base-matter is obtained. In the third combination, in all three answers, only mental phenomena are obtained. In the fourth combination, only mind-produced matter is obtained. In the fifth combination, at the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), mental phenomena along with base-matter are obtained. Among the resultant combinations (savippāka-ghaṭanā), in the first, resultant phenomena (vipāka), mind-produced matter caused by resultant consciousness, and rebirth-linking karma-produced matter (paṭisandhi-kammaja-rūpa) are obtained. In the second, resultant phenomena and base-matter are obtained. In the third, only resultant phenomena are obtained. In the fourth, only resultant mind-produced matter is obtained.
