In the fifth, only base-matter is obtained.

In the Mutuality-root method (aññamaññamūlaka-naya), there are six combinations. Among these six, the first three are non-resultant, and the last three are resultant. The numbering in these non-resultant and resultant combinations is indeed clear.

In the Dependence-root method (nissayamūlaka-naya), from the Dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya) to the Object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), 'three' refers to what should be understood by way of wholesome etc. arising by taking the base (vatthu) as an object (at the time of death-proximity). In the Decisive Support condition (upanissaya), 'one' refers to unwholesome arising by making the base an object-decisive support (ārammaṇူpanissaya). The remaining procedure should be understood according to the method already stated in the Dual-root method (dumūlaka-naya) below.

462-464. In this Dependence condition, there are twenty combinations. Among these twenty, the first six combinations are stated by way of Prenascence-dependence (purejāta-nissaya) and Co-nascence-dependence (sahajāta-nissaya). Besides those, four are by way of Prenascence only, and ten are by way of Co-nascence only. Among those six, in the first combination, 'thirteen' refers to the answers taught in the Analysis of the Dependence Condition (Nissaya-paccaya-vibhaṅga). In the second, 'eight' refers to seven by way of Co-nascence-predominance (sahajātādhipati) and one unwholesome arising by giving weight to the base; totaling eight. In the third, the seven are the answers obtained in the Faculty condition (indriya-paccaya). In the fourth, five are obtained in the Dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya). In the fifth, 'four' refers to wholesome etc. being a condition for mind-produced matter, and the base being a condition for unwholesome. In the sixth, 'three' refers to wholesome etc. being a condition for mind-produced matter. Among the four by way of Prenascence, in the first, 'three' refers to the base being a condition for wholesome etc., and the eye-base etc. being a condition for indeterminate. In the second, only the base is a condition for wholesome etc. In the third, 'one' refers to the base being a condition for unwholesome. In the fourth, the eye-base etc. are conditions for the fivefold consciousness (viññāṇa-pañcaka). The ten by way of Co-nascence should be understood by dividing them into two types as resultant and non-resultant, according to the method stated in the Co-nascence-root method (sahajātamūlaka-naya).

In the Decisive Support-root method (upanissayamūlaka-naya), in the Object condition, 'seven' refers to the answers obtained in Object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya). In the Predominance condition (adhipati), 'seven' also refers to the answers obtained in that Object-decisive support. In the Proximity (anantara) and Contiguity (samanantara) conditions, they are the answers obtained in Proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya). In the Dependence condition, 'one' refers to the base being a condition for unwholesome. In the Prenascence condition...
458:
(One [way] means) the heart-base (hadayavatthu) which is highly esteemed, or the desirable present produced-matter (nipphanna-rūpa) object which is highly esteemed, is a condition for that very greed-rooted unwholesome consciousness which highly esteems it. In the repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), three ways are taught by way of proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya). In the kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), two ways are taught by way of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). Specifically, supramundane wholesome volition (cetanā) is also a proximity-decisive support. In the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya), one way is taught by way of object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya); likewise, in the presence condition (atthi-paccaya) and the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya), it is taught by way of object-decisive support. In the absence condition (natthi-paccaya) and the disappearance condition (vigata-paccaya), the seven ways are exactly the same as the explanations in the proximity condition.

In the method of decisive support as the root (upanissaya-mūlaka-naya), there are seven combinations (ghaṭanā). Among these seven combinations, the first three combinations are taught by way of object-decisive support. Among those three combinations, in the first combination, 'seven' means: wholesome is a condition for wholesome, etc.; likewise, indeterminate is a condition; and unwholesome is a condition for unwholesome only; thus, there are seven. In the second combination, 'one' means: the highly esteemed present produced-matter indeterminate such as the eye-base, etc., is a condition for the greed-rooted unwholesome consciousness which highly esteems it. In the third combination, the base (vatthu) is a condition for the greed-rooted death-proximate impulsion (maraṇāsannajavana) unwholesome consciousness which highly esteems it. After that third combination, two more combinations are taught by way of proximity-decisive support. In those two combinations, the method of counting is clear. After that, two more are taught by way of proximity-natural-decisive support. Among those two combinations, in the first combination, mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions should be taken as the condition; in the second combination, only supramundane wholesome volition should be taken as the condition.

## 467-468. In the method of pre-existence as the root (purejāta-mūlaka-naya), in the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), 'three' means: present produced-matter indeterminate is a condition for wholesome, etc. In the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), 'one' means: highly esteemed present produced-matter indeterminate is a condition for the greed-rooted unwholesome consciousness which highly esteems it. In the remaining conditions, the method is the same. Here, in this pre-existence-rooted method, there are seven combinations. Among those seven combinations, the first is taught by way of the base and the present produced-matter object; the second by way of the base only; the third by way of the object; the fourth by way of the time when the base becomes an object; the fifth by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati); the sixth by way of the time when the base becomes an object-predominance condition; the seventh by way of the eye-base, etc.

## 469-472. In the method of post-existence as the root (pacchājāta-mūlaka-naya), twenty conditions do not apply; only three conditions—dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—attain application. In this post-existence-rooted method, there is only one combination; that combination should be understood by way of wholesome, etc., for the body produced in four ways (catusamuṭṭhānika-kāya). In the method of repetition as the root (āsevana-mūlaka-naya) also, there is only one combination.

## 473-477. In the method of kamma as the root (kamma-mūlaka-naya), in the proximity condition, the word 'one' is taught by way of path-volition (magga-cetanā). In the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya), in the text 'three,' the base (vatthu) at the moment of rebirth-linking should also be taken. In the decisive support condition, 'two' refers to those already taught in the lower dyad (duka) by way of proximity-decisive support and natural decisive support. In this way, the remaining combinations should also be understood according to the method taught in the lower dyad. Here, in this kamma-rooted method, there are eleven combinations. Among those eleven combinations, the first two are taught by way of asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma) as distinguished into natural decisive support and proximity-decisive support. After those two combinations, the next four are taught by way of synchronous kamma (ekakkhaṇika-kamma) as resultant and non-resultant. Among those four combinations, in the first combination, mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) is obtained together with mental states (nāma)...
459:
In the second combination (ghaṭanā), the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) along with immaterial states (nāma) is obtained; in the third combination, only immaterial states are obtained; in the fourth combination, only mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) is obtained. At the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), however, karma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) is also obtained. Following that, there are five combinations associated with resultants (vipāka); these are exactly as per the method mentioned below. In the resultant-rooted method (vipāka-mūlaka-naya), the five combinations have clear meanings.

478-483. In the nutriment-rooted method (āhāra-mūlaka-naya), the combinations with qualifiers such as 'seven' (satta) and so on are exactly as per the method already mentioned. In this nutriment-rooted method, there are thirty-four combinations. Among those combinations, the first five are stated in terms of being common to both resultant and non-resultant. Among those five, in the first combination, all four nutriments are obtained; in the second combination, only the three immaterial nutriments are obtained. In the third combination, the heart-base is also the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna); in the fourth combination, that heart-base is excluded. In the fifth combination, only matter (mind-produced matter and rebirth karma-produced matter) is the conditionally arisen. Following that, there are five combinations associated with resultants; these are exactly as per the method mentioned below. Following that, nine combinations are stated by way of volition-nutriment (cetanāhāra). Following that, nine combinations are stated by way of consciousness-nutriment (viññāṇāhāra) without predominance (anadhipati). Following that, six combinations are stated by way of consciousness-nutriment with predominance (sadhipati). Among those six, three are stated by way of being common to both resultant and non-resultant. Three are stated by way of resultant only. In those three, due to the absence of mundane resultants, the heart-base is excluded.

484-495. In the faculty-rooted method (indriya-mūlaka-naya), in the pre-nascence cycle (purejāta-vāra), it is certain that an indeterminate state arises due to an indeterminate condition by way of the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) and so on. The remaining double-rooted method (dumūlaka-naya) should be understood exactly as per the method mentioned below. In this faculty-rooted method, there are seventy-six combinations. Among those combinations, in the first combination, all faculties are obtained by way of condition. In the second combination, the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) is excluded. This is correct because that physical life-faculty does not become a support condition (nissaya-paccaya). In the third combination, immaterial faculties are conditions for material states. In the fourth combination, the eye-faculty and so on are conditions for eye-consciousness and so on. Following that, nine combinations are stated by way of co-nascent immaterial faculties; following that, nine are by way of faculties that are path-factors (magga); following that, nine are by way of faculties that are absorption-factors (jhānaṅga); following that, nine are by way of faculties that are both absorption and path factors; following that, nine are by way of the mind-faculty (manindriya) only; following that, six are with predominance; following that, six are associated with the path by way of energy (vīriya); following that, nine are without predominance by way of the non-delusion root (amoha-hetu); and six are with predominance. Among all those combinations, those not associated with the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya) and those associated with it should be understood exactly as per the method mentioned below.

496-500. In the absorption-rooted method (jhāna-mūlaka-naya) as well, the double-rooted method should be understood exactly as per the method mentioned below. In this absorption-rooted method, there are thirty-six combinations. Among those combinations, the first nine, without considering them as faculties or path factors...
460:
...are taught only in connection with the common factors of absorption (jhānaṅga). Following those nine combinations, another nine are taught in connection with absorption factors that have become faculties (indriya); following those, another nine in connection with absorption factors that have become path factors (magga); and following those, another nine in connection with absorption factors that have become both faculties and path factors. Among these four sets of nine, the first four combinations in each set are common to both resultant and non-resultant states. The final five combinations in each set are resultants only; these are exactly as per the method mentioned below.

501-508. In the path-rooted method (magga-mūlaka-naya) as well, the double-rooted method should be understood as per the method already mentioned. In this path-rooted method, there are fifty-seven combinations. Among those fifty-seven combinations, the first nine are taught only in connection with the pure path, without considering them as faculties or absorptions. Following those, another nine are taught in connection with the path that has become a faculty; following those, another nine in connection with the path that has become an absorption; following those, another nine in connection with the path that has become both a faculty and an absorption; following those, another six in connection with the path that has become a predominant factor (adhipati); following those, nine in connection with the path-root without predominance; and following those, six in connection with the path-root with predominance. Among those combinations, in the sets of nine, five each are resultants; and in the sets of six, three each are resultants. The remaining combinations are common; these are exactly as per the method mentioned below.

509-510. In the association-rooted method (sampayutta-mūlaka-naya), the meaning of the double-rooted method is very clear. In this method, there are only two combinations. Among those two, one is taught by way of being common, and one is taught by way of being a resultant.

511-514. In the dissociation-rooted method (vippayutta-mūlaka-naya) as well, the meaning of the double-rooted method is very clear. In this method, there are thirteen combinations. Among those thirteen, in the first combination, the 'five' refers to: a wholesome state being a condition for an indeterminate state; likewise, an unwholesome state for an indeterminate state; and an indeterminate state for all three (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate). In this first combination, these conditions such as dissociation (vippayutta) are co-nascent (sahajāta), and also post-nascent (pacchājāta) and pre-nascent (purejāta). In the second combination, only pre-nascent and co-nascent occur. In the third combination, those same pre-nascent and co-nascent states occur by way of predominance (adhipati). In that third combination, a wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state; likewise, an unwholesome state for an indeterminate state; and an indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state, and also for an unwholesome state by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati)—thus there are four. In the fourth combination, the 'three' refers to wholesome and other states being conditions for indeterminate states. In this fourth combination, the faculties are both material faculties and immaterial faculties. In the fifth combination, the conditions are immaterial states only. In the sixth combination, only material states occur by way of the base (vatthu). In the seventh combination, the base alone is the condition for wholesome and indeterminate states by way of insight (vipassanā), and for unwholesome states by way of the enjoyed object (assādana). In the eighth combination, that same base is the condition for unwholesome states. In the ninth combination, the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so on are conditions for indeterminate states. In the tenth combination, wholesome and other states are conditions for mind-produced matter. In the eleventh combination, at the time of rebirth-linking, the base is a condition for the aggregates (khandha). In the twelfth combination, at the time of rebirth-linking, the aggregates are conditions for karma-produced matter (kaṭattā-rūpa). In the thirteenth combination, at the time of rebirth-linking, the aggregates are conditions for the base (vatthu).
461: 515-518. In the Atthi-paccaya-mūlaka method, regarding the Upanissaya condition, there is one ghaṭanā where an indeterminate state (abyākata) is a condition for an unwholesome state (akusala) by way of object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya). In the remaining methods with two roots (du-mūlaka), the meaning is very clear. In this Atthi-paccaya-mūlaka method, there are 29 ghaṭanās. Among these ghaṭanās, in the first ghaṭanā, the conditions of conascence (sahajāta), pre-nascence (purejāta), and post-nascence (pacchājāta) are obtained by way of mental states (nāma), base (vatthu), object (ārammaṇa), great elements (mahābhūta), faculties (indriya), and nutriment (āhāra). In the second ghaṭanā, post-nascence and physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) conditions are not obtained. The first and second ghaṭanās themselves, together with the predominance (adhipati) condition, have been made into the third and fourth ghaṭanās above. Again, the first ghaṭanā itself, together with the four nutriments, is made into the fifth ghaṭanā; together with the physical faculties (rūpindriya), it is made into the sixth ghaṭanā; and together with both physical and mental faculties, it is made into the seventh ghaṭanā. Alternatively, the second ghaṭanā itself, together with the faculties, is made into the seventh ghaṭanā. The first and second ghaṭanās themselves, together with the dissociation (vippayutta) condition, are made into the eighth and ninth ghaṭanās. Among those eighth and ninth, the ninth ghaṭanā, together with the predominance condition, is made into the tenth ghaṭanā. After that, in the eleventh ghaṭanā, the base (vatthu) decreases by way of condition. In the twelfth ghaṭanā, only mental states are the conditions. In the thirteenth ghaṭanā, the base and the object are the conditions. In the fourteenth ghaṭanā, only the base is the condition. In the fifteenth ghaṭanā, only the object is the condition. In the sixteenth ghaṭanā, only the base is the object. In the seventeenth ghaṭanā, that same object is the condition by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). In the eighteenth ghaṭanā, that same object is the condition by way of object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya). In the nineteenth ghaṭanā, only the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so on are the conditions. These 19 ghaṭanās are called miscellaneous combinations (pakiṇṇaka-ghaṭanā) because they are taught without taking the conascence (sahajāta) condition. After that, 10 ghaṭanās are taught by way of conascence. In the Natthi-mūlaka and Vigata-mūlaka methods, there are only 3 ghaṭanās each by way of decisive support (upanissaya), repetition (āsevana), and kamma, just as in the Anantara-mūlaka and Samanantara-mūlaka methods. The Avigata-mūlaka method is very similar to the Atthi-mūlaka method. All the ghaṭanās taught in this Question Section (Pañhāvāra) are of only two types: miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) and conascent (sahajāta). Therein, the ghaṭanās taught at the beginning of all methods such as Ārammaṇa-mūlaka, without taking the conascence condition, are called miscellaneous combinations (pakiṇṇaka-ghaṭanā). These miscellaneous ghaṭanās are: 5 in Ārammaṇa-mūlaka, 6 in Adhipati-mūlaka, 3 in Anantara-mūlaka, 3 in Samanantara-mūlaka, 10 in Nissaya-mūlaka, 7 in Upanissaya-mūlaka, 7 in Purejāta-mūlaka, 1 in Pacchājāta-mūlaka, 1 in Āsevana-mūlaka, 2 in Kamma-mūlaka, 1 in Āhāra-mūlaka, 4 in Indriya-mūlaka, 9 in Vippayutta-mūlaka, 19 in Atthi-mūlaka, 3 in Natthi-mūlaka, 3 in Vigata-mūlaka, and 19 in Avigata-mūlaka, making a total of 103. These ghaṭanās are taught as miscellaneous combinations (pakiṇṇaka-ghaṭanā) by way of conascence-dependence (sahajāta-nissaya).
462:
Those ghaṭanās that obtain the conascence (sahajāta) condition are called conascent combinations (sahajāta-ghaṭanā). These conascent ghaṭanās are not obtained in the Ārammaṇa-mūlaka, Anantara-mūlaka, Samanantara-mūlaka, Purejāta-mūlaka, Pacchājāta-mūlaka, Āsevana-mūlaka, Natthi-mūlaka, and Vigata-mūlaka methods. This is because those conditions such as Ārammaṇa are not conditions for the states that arise together with the conditioning state (sahajāta-paccayuppanna). Just as those conditions such as Ārammaṇa are not conditions for conascent resultants, likewise, the conditions of root (hetu), conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), resultant (vipāka), jhāna, path (magga), and association (sampayutta) are not conditions for non-conascent (asahajāta) resultants.

In the Hetu-mūlaka method, all 24 ghaṭanās are only conascent ghaṭanās. Likewise, there are 24 in Adhipati-mūlaka, 10 in Sahajāta-mūlaka, 6 in Aññamañña-mūlaka, 10 in Nissaya-mūlaka, 9 in Kamma-mūlaka, 5 in Vipāka-mūlaka, 33 in Āhāra-mūlaka, 72 in Indriya-mūlaka, 36 in Jhāna-mūlaka, 57 in Magga-mūlaka, 2 in Sampayutta-mūlaka, 4 in Vippayutta-mūlaka, 10 in Atthi-mūlaka, and 10 in Avigata-mūlaka; thus, all conascent ghaṭanās are 312. In this way, the 103 ghaṭanās mentioned previously and the 312 ghaṭanās mentioned now, when combined, make a total of 415 ghaṭanās appearing in the Question Section (Pañhāvāra).

Among those ghaṭanās, whichever conditioning states (paccaya-dhamma) are not clearly known by name, those conditioning states should also be shown in the ghaṭanās taught by way of the commonality of being resultant or non-resultant, starting from the beginning of the methods such as Hetu-mūlaka. The 12 roots (hetu), 6 objects (ārammaṇa), 4 predominances (adhipati), 4 nutriments (āhāra), 20 faculties (indriya), 7 jhāna factors (jhānaṅga), and 12 path factors (maggaṅga) are called conditioning states (paccaya-dhamma). Among those conditioning states, whichever states are always wholesome, always unwholesome, always wholesome-resultant, always unwholesome-resultant, always resultant, or always non-resultant (avipāka)—having carefully considered those respective states, those that are resultants should be appropriately associated with the resultant ghaṭanās (vipāka-ghaṭanā), and those that are non-resultants with the non-resultant ghaṭanās (avipāka-ghaṭanā).

## Anuloma Counting of Ghaṭanās in the Pañhāvāra.

## Paccanīyuddhāravaṇṇanā

Now is the time for the Negative Section (Paccanīyavāra). In that Negative Section, in the way of the Dependent Section (Paṭiccavāra) and so on, such as: "Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises by way of the non-root condition (na-hetu-paccaya)" and so on...
463:
The questions obtained have been expanded in detail according to the power of the conditions (paccaya) obtained. To show the negative (paccanīya) briefly by a single characteristic without such expansion, the compilers of the scriptures (Dhamma-sangāhakas) have extracted the conditions of the resultants (paccayuppanna) such as wholesome (kusala) in the forward order (anuloma), in the manner of "Wholesome state is a condition for wholesome state by way of object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya)," and so forth. These conditions are extracted by way of groups, not by way of individual conditions. Therefore, where these conditions are shown as a group, they should be understood by analyzing them.

In fact, all these twenty-four conditions are subsumed into eight conditions. Which eight? They are: Object condition (ārammaṇa), Conascence condition (sahajāta), Decisive Support condition (upanissaya), Prenascence condition (purejāta), Postnascence condition (pacchājāta), Kamma condition (kamma), Nutriment condition (āhāra), and Faculty condition (indriya). How? Indeed, setting aside these eight conditions, among the remaining sixteen conditions, these six—Root condition (hetu), Mutuality condition (aññamañña), Resultant condition (vipāka), Jhāna condition (jhāna), Path condition (magga), and Association condition (sampayutta)—are definitely conascent (sahajāta) and, because they benefit only conascent resultants, they are subsumed under the Conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya).

The five conditions—Proximity (anantara), Contiguity (samanantara), Repetition (āsevana), Absence (natthi), and Disappearance (vigata)—having arisen and ceased, benefit only the resultants that arise immediately after them; therefore, they are subsumed under the Decisive Support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) by the characteristic of Proximity-Decisive Support (anantarūpanissaya).

Dependence condition (nissaya) is of two kinds: Conascence-dependence (sahajāta-nissaya) and Prenascence-dependence (purejāta-nissaya). Of these two, Conascence-dependence is subsumed under the Conascence condition because it benefits only conascent resultants as a dependence condition; Prenascence-dependence is subsumed under the Prenascence condition.

Predominance condition (adhipati) is also of two kinds: Conascence-predominance (sahajātādhipati) and Object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). Of these two, Conascence-predominance is subsumed under the Conascence condition because it benefits only conascent resultants as a predominance condition. Object-predominance, being indeed an Object-Decisive Support condition, is subsumed under the Decisive Support condition by the characteristic of Object-Decisive Support (ārammaṇūpanissaya).

Dissociation condition (vippayutta) is of three kinds: Conascence-dissociation (sahajāta-vippayutta), Prenascence-dissociation (purejāta-vippayutta), and Postnascence-dissociation (pacchājāta-vippayutta). Of these three, Conascence-dissociation is subsumed under the Conascence condition because it benefits only conascent resultants as a dissociation condition. Prenascence-dissociation is subsumed under the Prenascence condition because it arises before and benefits the resultants that arise later. Postnascence-dissociation is subsumed under the Postnascence condition because it arises after and benefits the resultants that have already arisen before by way of support.

Presence condition (atthi) and Non-disappearance condition (avigata) exist in six varieties: by way of Conascence, Prenascence, Postnascence, Nutriment, and Faculty, and by way of each of Presence and Non-disappearance. Among these six, Conascence-presence and Conascence-non-disappearance benefit only conascent resultants as Presence and Non-disappearance conditions...
464:
...(states that are conascent) are subsumed under the Conascence condition. Prenascence conditions are subsumed under the Prenascence condition because they have arisen before and are conditions for states that will arise later. Postnascence conditions are subsumed under the Postnascence condition because they arise later and are conditions for states that have already arisen before by way of support. States that are nutriments are subsumed under the Edible Food Nutriment condition (kabaḷīkārāhāra-paccaya). States that are faculties are subsumed under the Physical Life-faculty condition (rūpajīvitindriya-paccaya). Thus, it should be understood that these sixteen conditions are subsumed under these eight conditions.

Furthermore, there is also mutual subsumption among these eight conditions. The Object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) mentioned at the beginning is of two kinds: Predominance (adhipati) and Non-predominance (anadhipati). Of these two, the Object condition that is Predominance is subsumed under the Decisive Support condition by the characteristic of Object-Decisive Support (ārammaṇūpanissaya). The Object condition that is Non-predominance is merely the pure Object condition. Kamma condition (kamma-paccaya) is also of two kinds: Conascence-kamma (sahajāta-kamma) and Asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma). Of these two, Conascence-kamma is subsumed under the Conascence condition itself because it is a kamma condition only for states that arise together with itself. Asynchronous kamma is of two kinds: Strong kamma (balava-kamma) and Weak kamma (dubbala-kamma). Of these two, Strong kamma is subsumed under the Decisive Support condition because it benefits resultant states by being a Decisive Support. However, Strong kamma for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) and Weak kamma for mental states (arūpa) are conditions only by way of the Asynchronous kamma condition.

Nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya) is also of two kinds: Physical nutriment (rūpāhāra) and Mental nutriment (arūpāhāra). Of these two, Mental nutriment is subsumed under the Conascence condition because it is a condition only for states that arise together with itself. Physical nutriment does not reach the state of Conascence, Prenascence, or Postnascence conditions. It fulfills the state of Nutriment condition only when it has passed its arising moment (uppāda-kkhaṇa) and reached its static moment (ṭhiti-ppatta); thus, it is merely the Nutriment condition.

Faculty condition (indriya-paccaya) is also of two kinds: Physical faculty (rūpindriya) and Mental faculty (arūpindriya). Of these two, the Mental faculty condition is subsumed under the Conascence condition itself because it fulfills the state of Faculty condition only for states that arise together with itself. Physical faculty condition is of two kinds: Internal (ajjhatta) and External (bahiddha). Of these two, the Internal faculty condition is subsumed under the Prenascence condition itself because it has arisen before and is the faculty condition for the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) etc., along with their associated states, which arise later. What is called the External faculty condition is the Physical life-faculty (rūpajīvitindriya). Although that physical life-faculty is a condition for conascent states, it is so only by way of maintenance (anupālana), not by way of generation (janaka); therefore, it is merely the Faculty condition. Thus, it should be understood that these eight conditions also mutually subsume one another. This is the method of subsumption of the remaining sixteen conditions into the eight conditions, and the mutual subsumption among those eight conditions themselves.
465:
Now, it should be understood which of the twenty-four conditions are included in each of these eight conditions. Among those eight conditions, in the very first, the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), only the object condition is included; the remaining twenty-three conditions are not included.

In the second, the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), these fifteen conditions are included: root condition (hetu), conascence-predominance condition (sahajātādhipati), conascence condition (sahajāta), mutuality condition (aññamañña), conascence-dependence condition (sahajātanissaya), conascence-kamma condition (sahajātakamma), resultant condition (vipāka), conascence-nutriment condition (sahajātāhāra), conascence-faculty condition (sahajātindriya), jhāna condition (jhāna), path condition (magga), association condition (sampayutta), conascence-dissociation condition (sahajātavippayutta), conascence-presence condition (sahajātatthi), and conascence-non-disappearance condition (sahajātāvigata).

In the third, the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), these nine conditions are included: the object condition which has become predominant (adhipatibhūta-ārammaṇa), the predominance condition which has become an object (ārammaṇabhūta-adhipati), proximity condition (anantara), contiguity condition (samanantara), decisive support condition (upanissaya), repetition condition (āsevana), the powerful kamma condition which is asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika-balavakamma), absence condition (natthi), and disappearance condition (vigata).

In the fourth, the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), these six conditions are included: pre-nascence-dependence condition (purejātanissaya), pre-nascence condition (purejāta), pre-nascence-faculty condition (purejātindriya), pre-nascence-dissociation condition (purejātavippayutta), pre-nascence-presence condition (purejātatthi), and pre-nascence-non-disappearance condition (purejātāvigata).

In the fifth, the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), these four conditions are included: post-nascence condition (pacchājāta), post-nascence-dissociation condition (pacchājātavippayutta), post-nascence-presence condition (pacchājātatthi), and post-nascence-non-disappearance condition (pacchājātāvigata).

In the sixth, the kamma condition (kamma-paccaya), only the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) is included.

In the seventh, the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya), by way of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) only, these three conditions are included: nutriment condition (āhāra), nutriment-presence condition (āhāratthi), and nutriment-non-disappearance condition (āhāra-avigata).

In the eighth, the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya), these three conditions are included: physical life-faculty condition (rūpajīvitindriya-paccaya), faculty-presence condition (indriyatthi), and faculty-non-disappearance condition (indriyāvigata).

In this way, having known that in each of these eight conditions, such and such conditions are included, it should be understood that those which are included therein are taken by the count of that [category].

Thus, by the power of these eight conditions which encompass all conditions, out of the forty-nine questions, these fifteen questions such as "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of object condition" etc., are extracted and answered in this Negative (paccanīya) section. Among those fifteen questions, there are four questions starting with wholesome: wholesome to wholesome, wholesome to unwholesome, wholesome to indeterminate, and wholesome to wholesome-and-indeterminate. Likewise, there are four questions starting with unwholesome. As for indeterminate, [it is] to indeterminate...
466:
...indeterminate to wholesome, and indeterminate to unwholesome—thus there are three questions starting with indeterminate. There are four questions ending with a single term but having dual roots: wholesome and indeterminate to wholesome, and likewise to indeterminate; unwholesome and indeterminate to unwholesome, and likewise to indeterminate.

Among those [fifteen] questions, in the first question, all conditions that should be present are included and three conditions are stated. In the second, two; in the third, five; in the fourth, only one; in the fifth, three; in the sixth, two; in the seventh, five; in the eighth, only one; in the ninth, seven; in the tenth, three; in the eleventh, three; in the twelfth, two; in the thirteenth, four; in the fourteenth, two; and in the fifteenth, also only four. These conditions are stated as "conascence, post-nascence" (sahajātaṃ pacchājātaṃ) without saying "by way of conascence condition" (sahajātapaccayena). We shall explain the reason for this later.

In brief, here there are six classifications of conditions: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7. This is the classification of questions by way of the maximum in the Negative section of the Question Chapter (Pañhāvāra), as well as the classification of conditions shown by encompassing those respective conditions. In the twenty-four negative conditions such as "not-root condition" (na-hetupaccayo) etc., even in a single negative condition, questions or conditions are not obtained above this [limit of five/seven], but are obtained below. 

Therefore, in those questions where only a single condition appears, such as "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome and indeterminate state by way of conascence condition," if that condition is excluded, those questions are eliminated. However, in a question where two conditions appear, such as "A wholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state by way of object condition and decisive support condition," even if one condition is excluded by saying "not-object condition," that question is still obtained by the power of the other condition. That section (vāra) is cut off only when both conditions are excluded.

In the same way, in those questions where 3, 4, 5, or 7 conditions are obtained, setting aside the excluded conditions, those questions are still obtained by the power of the remaining conditions. All those sections are cut off only when all conditions are excluded; this is the characteristic here in this Negative section. By this characteristic, the variety of conditions stated in brief in those respective questions from the beginning, and the elimination of those respective questions in those respective negative sections, should be understood.
467: In those (divisions of loss/pabhedaparihāni), this is the detailed explanation. Firstly, in the first question, nineteen conditions are shown by means of three conditions (Object, Conascence, and Decisive Support). How? Wholesome states are not conditions for wholesome states only by way of Prenascence, Postnascence, Resultant, and Dissociation conditions; they are conditions by the remaining twenty conditions. Among those twenty conditions, the Object condition is just one. In the Conascence condition, however, fifteen conditions are included by way of all-inclusive power. Among those fifteen conditions, if the Root condition is excluded, there are fourteen. Since wholesome states are neither Resultant nor Dissociation conditions for wholesome states, excluding those two and referring to the remaining twelve, it is said they are conditions by way of Conascence condition. In the Decisive Support condition also, nine conditions are included by way of all-inclusive power. Among those nine, the Object condition that has become Predominance and the Predominance condition that has become Object are included within the Decisive Support condition by way of Object-Decisive Support. Since wholesome states are not Asynchronous Kamma conditions for wholesome states, excluding that Asynchronous Kamma condition and referring to the remaining six, it is said they are conditions by way of Decisive Support condition. Thus, it should be understood that in the first question, nineteen conditions are shown by means of three conditions. Among those conditions, in this Negative Root (hetu-paccanīya) section, in the turn (vāra) 'A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of non-root condition,' the Pali text should be shown by extracting it in the same manner as mentioned in the Object condition etc., such as: 'Having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, having performed the Uposatha observance, one reflects on it; one reflects on deeds well-done in the past.' When the Object condition is excluded, the detail of that Object condition is removed, the detail of the Root condition is inserted, and that same Pali text is shown. In the exclusion of the remaining conditions, this same method applies. As for the turns (vāra) that are lost when that condition is excluded, we shall explain them later. In the second question, three conditions are shown by means of two conditions. How? Wholesome states are not conditions for unwholesome states by way of Contiguity etc. Therefore, excluding those conditions like Contiguity, and referring to Object-Predominance and Natural Decisive Support which are included by way of Object-Decisive Support, it is said they are conditions by way of Decisive Support condition. Therefore, it should be understood that in the second question, these three conditions—pure Object condition, Predominance condition by way of Object-Predominance, and Decisive Support condition—are shown by means of two conditions.
468: In the third question, eighteen conditions are shown by means of five conditions. How? Wholesome states are not conditions for indeterminate states only by way of Mutuality, Prenascence, Repetition, Resultant, and Association conditions; they are conditions by the remaining nineteen conditions. Among those nineteen conditions, the Object condition is one. Because wholesome states are not conditions for indeterminate states by way of Mutuality, Resultant, and Association, and because the Root condition is excluded and the Kamma condition is taken separately, excluding these five, ten conditions are shown by way of Conascence condition. By way of Decisive Support condition, among the six mentioned below (in the first question), excluding Repetition, the remaining five are shown. The Postnascence condition is just one; likewise, the Kamma condition, which is twofold by way of Conascence and Asynchronous, is also just one. Thus, it should be understood that in the third question, these eighteen conditions are shown by means of five conditions. In the fourth question, ten conditions are shown by means of a single condition. How? Among the fifteen conditions mentioned in the Conascence condition for wholesome-indeterminate states, wholesome states are not conditions by way of Mutuality, Resultant, Association, and Dissociation, and the Root condition is also excluded. Therefore, excluding these five, it should be understood that the remaining ten conditions are shown here in this fourth question by means of a single condition. Just as it is shown in these four questions starting with the wholesome term (kusala-pada), so also in the four questions starting with the unwholesome term (akusala-pada), it should be understood that those respective conditions are shown by those respective conditions. Among the three questions starting with the indeterminate term (abyākata-pada) that follow, in the first question, twenty-three conditions are shown by means of seven conditions. How? Indeterminate states are conditions for indeterminate states by all twenty-four conditions. However, when the Root condition is excluded, there are twenty-three. Among those twenty-three, the Object condition is just one. But here in this first question of the indeterminate term, the Nutriment and Faculty conditions are taken separately in order to include those that are not conascent. Therefore, excluding these three, twelve conditions are shown by way of Conascence condition. By way of Decisive Support condition, the six mentioned below, one Prenascence condition, and likewise Postnascence, Nutriment, and Faculty conditions—thus, it should be understood that in this question, these twenty-three conditions are shown by means of seven conditions. In the second question, twelve conditions are shown by means of three conditions. How? The Object condition is one; by way of Decisive Support condition, by way of Object-Decisive Support, there are Object-Predominance, Contiguity, Immediate Contiguity, Absence, Disappearance, and Decisive Support conditions...
469:
Six conditions have been shown. By way of the pre-nascent condition (purejāta-paccaya), five conditions are shown: pre-nascent (purejāta), dependence (nissaya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). In this way, in the second question beginning with the indeterminate term (abyākata), it should be understood that these twelve conditions are shown by means of three conditions. In the third question, the method is the same.

Among the four questions having the two terms as their root following the third question, in the first question, without saying "by way of conascent condition, by way of pre-nascent condition," three conditions are shown by means of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance through the two terms "conascent" (sahajāta) and "pre-nascent" (purejāta). The explanation is: when wholesome states (kusala-dhammā) together with the base (vatthu—the heart-base) accomplish the state of being a condition for the wholesome, although they are conascent with the resultants, they do not become conascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya) because they are mixed with the base. Therefore, they are called "conascent" by way of those conascent conditions of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance. The same method applies to the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu). Although that heart-base arises before the resultants, it does not become a pre-nascent condition (purejāta-paccaya) because it is mixed with the aggregates (khandha). It is called "pre-nascent" only by way of the conditions of dependence, etc., which arise before the resultants without being joined with the pre-nascent condition.

In the second question, by the four terms "conascent, post-nascent, nutriment, faculty," four conditions are shown by way of conascent, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance. Indeed, in this second fivefold section (pañcavāra), the conascent condition is obtained, but the post-nascent condition, etc., are not obtained. However, this is stated by way of the conditions of presence and non-disappearance, which are called nutriment and faculty, arising after the resultants. Wholesome aggregates and indeterminate great essentials (mahābhūta) are conditions for derived matter (upādā-rūpa) in four ways: as conascent condition, dependence condition, presence condition, and non-disappearance condition. Wholesome states arising later, together with those great essentials, are conditions for those same derived matters by way of presence and non-disappearance. Edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), together with wholesome states arising later, is a condition for the physical body (rūpa-kāya) that arose earlier, only by way of presence and non-disappearance. The physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya), together with wholesome states arising later, is a condition for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) only by way of presence and non-disappearance.

Thus, intending this state of being a condition in four ways, the statement "conascent, post-nascent, nutriment, faculty" is made. However, in this second fivefold section, the conditions of post-nascent, nutriment, and faculty are not actually obtained. It should be understood that the same method applies to the two subsequent questions mixed with the unwholesome (akusala-missaka). In this way, the distinctions of the conditions stated in brief in those various questions should be understood. We shall clarify later the decrease or non-decrease of those questions in each respective condition.

## Explanation of the Meaning of the Negative Excerpt.
470:
## Explanation of the Negative Enumeration (Paccanīya-gaṇanā-vaṇṇanā)

Now, the fifteen methods (vāra) by way of the positive (anuloma), such as "Wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state," have been shown. In the negative (paccanīya) also, only these methods exist; there are none above this, but there are some below. Therefore, in order to show by way of enumeration from the beginning which methods are obtained in the negative of each condition, the passage beginning with "In non-root, fifteen" (na-hetuyā pannarasa) is commenced.

In that passage, in the non-root condition (na-hetu-paccaya), fifteen methods are obtained by way of all the conditions already shown. In the non-object condition (na-ārammaṇa-paccaya), the root condition (hetu-paccaya) enters into the conascent (sahajāta). In each respective method, the pure object condition (suddha-ārammaṇa-paccaya) without other conditions is decreased; those methods obtain an answer (vissajjanā) by way of the remaining conditions. As in the non-object, so it is in the remaining conditions. The root condition enters into the conascent. In each respective method, the conditions established by way of the negative, such as "in non-sufficing condition, in non-proximity condition" (na-upanissaye na-anantare), are decreased; those respective methods obtain an answer by way of the remaining conditions.

In the non-conascent (na-sahajāta), however, these four methods are decreased: "Wholesome state for wholesome and indeterminate," "Unwholesome state for unwholesome and indeterminate," "Wholesome and indeterminate states for wholesome," and "Unwholesome and indeterminate states for unwholesome." The reason is that among these four methods, in the first two methods, a single synthesis of conditions (paccaya-saṅgaha) is stated by way of eleven conditions as "condition by way of conascent condition." When that conascent condition is excluded, they do not obtain an answer in any other way. In the latter two methods, the statement "conascent, pre-nascent" is made intending the conditions of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance. When that conascent condition is excluded, they do not obtain an answer by way of the remaining conditions like root, etc., nor by way of the pre-nascent conditions of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance. Therefore, these four methods are also decreased. By way of the remaining methods, "eleven" is stated.

In that statement, there might be a question: "Just as when the root condition is excluded, those methods are obtained by way of the remaining conditions like predominance (adhipati), etc., why are they not obtained by way of the remaining conditions like root, etc., when the conascent condition is excluded?" It is because it is comprehensive (nippadesa). Since conditions like root, etc., are only a portion of the conascent conditions, they are partial (sappadesa). Therefore, when those conditions like root, etc., are excluded, those methods are obtained by way of other conditions. But the conascent condition is comprehensive (nippadesa) and includes all conditions like root, etc. Therefore, when that conascent condition is excluded, all those conditions like root, etc., are also excluded. There are no root conditions, etc., that are not conascent.
471:
Because the conascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya) is exhaustive, if that conascent condition is excluded, both of those preceding cycles (vāra) cannot be obtained. However, in the cycles answered as 'conascent, prenascent,' even if the conascent condition itself is absent, the mental aggregates (nāma-kkhandha) that are conascent in these cycles serve as conditions by way of dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). When the conascent condition is excluded, the conascent dependence, presence, and non-disappearance are also invariably excluded. Therefore, because that conascent condition is excluded, those subsequent cycles also cannot be obtained. Thus, in every respect here, these four cycles decrease. It is said that there are eleven by way of the remaining cycles.

In non-mutuality (na-aññamañña), non-dependence (na-nissaya), and non-association (na-sampayutta) as well, those same cycles decrease. Why? Because they share the same nature as the conascent condition. Just as the conascent condition, which is a mental phenomenon, exhaustively takes the four mental aggregates, so too do mutuality, dependence, and association take the four mental aggregates. Therefore, it should be understood that because they share the same nature as the conascent, if these conditions of mutuality, dependence, and association are excluded, those cycles cannot be obtained. Hence, it is said: 'eleven in non-mutuality, eleven in non-dependence, eleven in non-association.'

In that regard, there might be this objection: It is true that these conditions of mutuality, dependence, and association share the same nature as the conascent because they encompass the four aggregates divided into wholesome and so on without distinction. However, a wholesome state does not become a condition for wholesome and indeterminate states in any other way except as a conascent condition. Therefore, if that conascent condition is excluded, let that cycle decrease. But a wholesome state also does not become a mutuality condition for wholesome and indeterminate states. That being the case, why does that cycle decrease when the mutuality condition is excluded? It is because its occurrence is evident in connection with the phenomena of the mutuality condition. Just as wholesome and indeterminate states do not even become conascent conditions for a wholesome state, yet because their occurrence is evident through dependence condition and so on in connection with conascent phenomena, that cycle decreases when the conascent condition is excluded. Similarly, here in non-mutuality, because its occurrence is evident through conascent and so on in connection with the phenomena of the mutuality condition, that cycle decreases when the mutuality condition is excluded. The meaning of the phrase 'not a condition by way of mutuality condition' (na-aññamaññapaccayena paccayo) is this: those phenomena which have entered the group of mutuality conditions do not act as conditions. When a wholesome state becomes a condition for wholesome and indeterminate states by way of conascent and so on, it becomes a condition only through the phenomena of the mutuality condition. Therefore, if that mutuality condition is excluded, that cycle decreases. Just as that cycle decreases, so do the other three cycles; thus, all four of those cycles decrease.
472:
In this text 'eleven in non-dependence' (na-nissaye ekādasa), since in those cycles only the conascent condition phenomena are indeed the dependence (nissaya), those cycles decrease when the dependence condition is excluded. 'Thirteen in non-prenascent' (na-purejāte terasa) means thirteen after removing the two dual-root cycles (vāra) which have the answer 'conascent, prenascent.' For just as those cycles, when the conascent condition is excluded, cannot obtain an answer by way of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance which are purely prenascent, so too when the prenascent condition is excluded, they cannot obtain an answer by way of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance which are purely conascent. Therefore, it should be understood that there are thirteen after removing those cycles.

In this phrase 'fifteen in non-postnascent' (na-pacchājāte pannarasa), those questions can be obtained by way of the remaining conditions even if the postnascent condition is removed from the places where it occurs as 'condition by way of postnascent condition' or 'conascent, postnascent, nutriment, faculty'; therefore, it is said to be fifteen. In the phrases beginning with 'non-kamma' (na-kamma), kamma, result (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), jhāna, and path (magga) are also only a portion of the four aggregates divided into wholesome and so on. Therefore, because conascent phenomena can be conditions by way of the remaining phenomena even if those phenomena are removed, not even a single answer to a question is lost. In the text 'eleven in non-association' (na-sampayutte ekādasa), it should be understood that because associated phenomena in those four cycles serve as conditions by way of conascent and other conditions, those same cycles decrease by the exclusion of the association condition. 'Nine in non-dissociation' (na-vippayutte nava) refers to these six cycles: the four dual-root cycles ending in one (ekāvasāna) and the two single-root cycles ending in two (dukāvasāna), which are invariably associated with dissociation condition phenomena. Since those phenomena serve as conditions by way of conascent and so on, if the dissociation condition is excluded, all those cycles decrease, and only nine are obtained. Therefore, it is said 'nine in non-dissociation.' The same should be understood for 'non-presence' (no-atthi) and 'non-disappearance' (no-avigata). For those cycles are invariably associated with the presence and non-disappearance condition phenomena; therefore, they decrease upon the exclusion of those conditions. In the cycles that can be obtained, the answers should be made by way of object (ārammaṇa) or by way of proximity (anantara) and so on. They should not be made by way of the five presence and non-disappearance conditions—namely conascent, prenascent, postnascent, nutriment, and faculty—or by way of dissociation phenomena.

Having thus shown the cycles obtained in the negative (paccanīya) by way of count, the text 'fifteen in non-root condition, in non-object' (na-hetupaccayā na-ārammaṇe pannarasa) and so on is begun to show the count of conditions by way of dual-root and so on. In that context, among the dual-roots of the non-root group, when a condition with a higher count is combined with one with a lower count, only the lower count remains.
473:
In the triple-root (ti-mūlaka), in the statement of 13 methods (vāra) in non-decisive support (na-upanissaya), the two methods 'wholesome for unwholesome' and 'unwholesome for wholesome' are excluded. Why? Because the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and the non-decisive support condition (na-upanissaya-paccaya) are connected. Indeed, the occurrence of these two methods is by way of object and by way of decisive support. And both that object and decisive support have been negated. Object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) is also already included by the inclusion of object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya).

In the sixfold-root (cha-mūlaka) as well, the 13 methods in non-decisive support are the same 13 methods mentioned in the triple-root. In the sevenfold-root (satta-mūlaka), however, the 7 methods in non-decisive support are due to the connection with the non-conascence condition (na-sahajāta-paccaya); together with the 4 methods that are excluded in that non-conascence, a total of 8 methods are excluded—namely, these 4 methods occurring by way of proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya) and natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya): 'wholesome for wholesome', 'wholesome for unwholesome', 'unwholesome for unwholesome', and 'unwholesome for wholesome'. Therefore, it is stated as 7 methods by way of the remaining methods. In non-prenascence (na-purejāta), there are 11 methods because of the connection with non-conascence. In non-postnascence (na-pacchājāta), the 9 methods are obtained by removing the 2 methods ending in indeterminate (abyākata) of the double-root (du-mūlaka) among those 11 methods which have answers obtained as conascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty. Indeed, although those methods negate conascence, they are not excluded by way of postnascence. When postnascence is negated together with conascence, they are excluded. Therefore, it is stated as 9 methods by way of the remaining methods.

In the eightfold-root (aṭṭha-mūlaka), the entire procedure starting with 11 methods in non-dependence (na-nissaya) is just the same as the procedure mentioned previously. In the ninefold-root (nava-mūlaka), the 5 methods in non-decisive support consist of 3 methods starting with wholesome and ending with indeterminate, and 2 methods of the double-root ending with indeterminate; thus there are 5 methods. In those 5 methods, the answer (vissajjanā) should be understood in connection with the states of asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma), edible nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra), physical life-faculty (rūpajīvitindriya), and postnascence (pacchājāta).

In the tenfold-root (dasa-mūlaka), in the Pali passages starting with 5 methods in non-prenascence, they are those same 5 methods obtained in the ninefold-root non-decisive support. In non-postnascence, the 3 methods are the remaining methods after removing the 2 methods of the double-root ending with indeterminate obtained by way of postnascence. In non-dissociation (na-vippayutta) as well, there are those same 3 methods. In non-presence (no-atthi), the 2 methods are wholesome and unwholesome for kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of asynchronous kamma. Resultant (vipāka), however, is not obtained here because of the connection with non-decisive support. In the elevenfold-root (ekādasa-mūlaka), the calculation is just the same as mentioned previously. In the twelvefold-root (dvādasa-mūlaka), the 1 method in non-kamma (na-kamma) is indeterminate for indeterminate. In that indeterminate, the answer should be understood by way of nutriment and faculty. In the thirteenfold-root (terasa-mūlaka) and so on, in all places where 1 method occurs in the Pali, only this indeterminate for indeterminate should be taken. In non-nutriment (na-āhāra), however, the answer should be understood by way of faculty. In non-faculty (na-indriya), it should be understood by way of nutriment. In the fourteenfold-root (cuddasa-mūlaka) and so on, because of the connection with non-kamma, non-presence (no-atthi) and non-disappearance (no-avigata) are not obtained...
474:
...it is not stated that they are obtained. The statement "not by way of nutriment condition, not by way of jhāna condition" is made by excluding non-faculty (na-indriya). Therefore, in that place, one answer (vissajjanā) should be understood by way of faculty (indriya). The statement "not by way of resultant condition, not by way of faculty condition" is made by excluding nutriment (āhāra). Therefore, in that place, one answer should be understood by way of nutriment (āhāra). When these two, nutriment and faculty, exist by way of the negative method (paccanīya), there is no such count. Therefore, they are not shown together.

## End of the Non-Root (Na-hetu) Root-group.

In the object-root (ārammaṇa-mūlaka) and so on, there are only four types of root-number divisions in all dyads (duka), namely 15, 13, 11, and 9. In the triads (tika) and so on, in the combination of many conditions, answers with defined numbers such as 7, 5, 3, 2, and 1 are indeed obtained. In those object-roots and so on, whatever answer is obtained in the combination of whichever conditions, that answer should be extracted after carefully considering it according to the method mentioned previously. In all these object-roots and so on, the cycles (cakka) have been constructed by first coupling terms such as object (ārammaṇa) with the preceding root (hetu) term. However, since those cycles are identical to the cycles mentioned in the non-root (na-hetu) root-group, they are shown only in brief without being shown in detail. In that context, just as in the non-root root-group, object and non-decisive support each obtain 15 methods separately but obtain 13 methods in combination, so too in all places they obtain only 13 methods. And just as there are 7 methods in non-decisive support together with object and non-conascence, so too there are 7 methods in non-conascence together with non-decisive support and object.

"Not by way of dependence condition, not by way of decisive support condition, 3 in non-postnascence" refers to the answers starting with wholesome and ending with indeterminate. In those answers, kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) and nutriment-produced matter (āhārasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) are the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna).

543-544. In the tetrads (catukka) of the non-nutriment root and non-faculty root, since they are not associated with non-kamma, they are obtained definitely as in the non-root root-group. In the non-faculty root-group, excluding non-decisive support and non-prenascence, it should be stated as "3 in non-nutriment". Starting from the non-faculty condition, coupling these two conditions, the counting in the nutriment condition should be done as: "Not by way of faculty condition ...pe... not by way of decisive support condition, 3 in non-nutriment"; and "Not by way of faculty condition ...pe... not by way of prenascence condition, 3 in non-nutriment".
475:
(In the nāhāra condition, there are three) means it should be performed as such. Those (three in nāhāra) are the three, such as wholesome, etc., towards the indeterminate. Among those three, wholesome and unwholesome assist kaṭattā (kamma-born) matter (by way of kamma condition) and assist the mind-produced matter group that arose earlier by way of post-nascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). Indeterminate consciousness and mental factors assist only by way of post-nascent condition. Thus, by the power of these conditions, three answers (vissajjanā) should be made. Later, however, because of being combined with the napacchājāta (non-post-nascent) condition, it is said that there are two in the nāhāra condition. In those (two), only this much is obtained: wholesome assists the indeterminate by the power of kaṭattā matter, and likewise, unwholesome assists the indeterminate. Because the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya) is excluded, physical food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) cannot obtain the state of a condition even by the power of presence (atthi) or non-disappearance (avigata).

In the four-root (catumūlaka) of the non-dissociated-root (navippayutta-mūlaka), in non-decisive support (naupanissaya), the five are: wholesome assists conascent wholesome; wholesome assists the indeterminate called kaṭattā matter; unwholesome assists conascent unwholesome; likewise, unwholesome assists the indeterminate called kaṭattā matter; and indeterminate assists conascent indeterminate—thus there are five. From the non-dissociated condition (navippayutta-paccaya) etc., in non-decisive support (naupanissaya), the three are: the three, wholesome etc., assist the indeterminate, just as in the method mentioned below.

In non-presence condition (noatthi-paccaya) and non-root (nahetu), the nine are the same nine mentioned in the non-root condition and non-presence dyad. The reason is that all of them are single-root (ekamūlaka) and single-end (ekāvasāna), and are obtained by the power of proximity-decisive support (anantara-pakatūpanissaya). In non-object (nārammaṇa), the nine are also those same nine. Staying in non-object, two should be made in non-decisive support. "Up to dependence" (nissaya) means: in the non-presence-root method, by the way of circular linking (cakkabandha) as "non-presence condition, non-root condition, non-object condition," staying in the non-object condition, and proceeding either with these three or with any other condition such as non-predominance (nādhipati) etc., until reaching the dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya), two answers (vissajjanā) should be made in non-decisive support.

Having thus established the characteristic, again starting from non-object up to dependence, taking seven conditions, it is said there are two in non-decisive support. In saying so: non-presence condition, non-root condition, non-object condition, two in non-decisive support; non-presence condition, non-root, non-object, non-predominance condition, two in non-decisive support—thus, the connection should be made with all terms starting from non-object and ending with dependence, which occur before and after. Here, the two are: wholesome to indeterminate, unwholesome to...
476:
...to indeterminate—this should be understood as the condition for kaṭattā matter by the power of asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇikakamma). In all conditions such as non-pre-nascent (napurejāta) etc., which are associated with the term non-decisive support (naupanissaya), there are two sections (vāra) each. However, the non-kamma condition (nakamma-paccaya) is not taken here. The reason is that if that non-kamma condition were taken, those two sections would also be cut off, and even an answer (vissajjanā) would not be obtained. Thus, in comparing whichever condition with whichever condition, whatever answer is obtained and whatever answer is lost, all such obtained and lost answers should be carefully noted, and the calculation (gaṇanā) for all negative conditions (paccanīya) should be extracted.

## Explanation of the Calculation of Negative Conditions (Paccanīyagaṇanāvaṇṇanā)

## Explanation of Positive-Negative Conditions (Anulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā)

In the positive-negative (anuloma-paccanīya), such as "seven in root, nine in object," etc. in the positive (anuloma), and "fifteen in non-root, fifteen in non-object," etc. in the negative (paccanīya), among the conditions with obtained numbers, the calculation should be known by the power of those similar sections (vāra) among the sections obtained in the negative of a condition standing by way of negative, together with the sections obtained in the positive of a condition standing by way of positive. For in the positive, in the root condition (hetu-paccaya), seven sections are obtained as "seven in root"; in the negative, in the non-object condition (nārammaṇa-paccaya), fifteen sections are obtained as "fifteen in non-object." Among those sections, among the fifteen sections mentioned in the non-object condition together with the seven sections mentioned in the root condition, these seven are similar: "wholesome to wholesome, to indeterminate, to wholesome-indeterminate; unwholesome to unwholesome, to indeterminate, to unwholesome-indeterminate; indeterminate to indeterminate." Referring to those seven similar sections, it is said: "seven in non-object from the root condition." In the texts such as "seven in non-predominance," etc., the method is the same.

In non-conascent (nasahajāta), however, because there is no root condition, not even a single section is obtained; therefore, the connection of the root condition with that non-conascent condition is not made. In non-mutuality (na-aññamañña), three sections are obtained, such as wholesome etc. being the condition for matter-indeterminate (rūpābyākata); referring to those sections, it is said "three." In non-associated (nasampayutta), it is the same. In non-dissociated (navippayutta), however, three answers (vissajjanā) should be known by the power of immaterial states (arūpadhamma), as "wholesome to wholesome, unwholesome to unwholesome, indeterminate to indeterminate." Non-dependence (nanissaya), non-presence (noatthi), non-disappearance (noavigata), and non-conascent (nasahajāta) (are not obtained).
477:
Just as the non-conascence condition (na-sahajāta) is not obtained, so too the non-dependence (na-nissaya), non-presence (no-atthi), and non-disappearance (no-avigata) conditions cannot be obtained; therefore, the root condition (hetu) should not be combined with those conditions. Thus, in this Anuloma-Paṭṭhāna, there are only two types of numerical limits: seven and three. By means of these numerical limits, the count of the greater number should be reduced along with the lesser number, and the count in the combinations of conditions should be understood.

(551) In those combinations of conditions, when the root, conascence, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions exist, the 'seven' in the non-object condition (na-ārammaṇa) means: a wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of root condition, conascence condition, dependence condition, presence condition, non-disappearance condition, and object condition. The root conditions are conditions for the associated aggregates by way of root condition, conascence condition, dependence condition, presence condition, non-disappearance condition, and object condition—in this manner, the seven ways (vāra) should be extracted. In the texts beginning with "seven in the non-predominance condition" (nādhipatiyā satta), the method is the same. In the second combination, because the mutuality condition (aññamañña) is included, the non-associated condition (na-sampayutta) is excluded, and it is stated as 'three' in the remaining conditions. In the non-associated condition, however, 'one' is stated with reference to the rebirth-linking mind-and-matter (paṭisandhi-nāmarūpa) associated with mutuality and dissociation conditions. In this second combination, because the mutuality condition is included in the positive (anuloma) combination, it cannot be obtained from the negative (paccaṇီya) side; therefore, it is not stated as "non-mutuality" (na-aññamañña). Just as in this second combination, in the remaining combinations also, the conditions included in the positive are not stated because they cannot be obtained from the negative side. In the third combination, because the association condition (sampayutta) is included, there are only three in all conditions. In the fourth combination, because the dissociation condition (vippayutta) is included, the three ways of mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) such as wholesome, etc., should be understood. In the fifth combination, because the resultant condition (vipāka) is included, only one way—indeterminate for indeterminate—should be understood in all conditions. In the combinations associated with resultants following this fifth one, the method is the same.

(552) In the conditions of root, conascence, dependence, faculty, path, presence, and non-disappearance, the 'four' in the non-object condition should be understood by way of these explanations: wholesome for wholesome, wholesome for indeterminate, wholesome for wholesome-and-indeterminate, and indeterminate for indeterminate. In the remaining combinations also, the method is the same. The 'two' in "non-mutuality" (na-aññamañña) means: wholesome for indeterminate, and likewise indeterminate for indeterminate. In the two subsequent combinations, the method is the same. By this means, the count should be understood according to what is obtainable in all combinations. In this Anuloma-Paccaṇīya, by way of the conascence group and the miscellaneous group, all these combinations are said to be four hundred and fifteen (415). Among those combinations, not even one of the conditions established by way of the positive in each respective combination can be obtained from the negative side. In this Anuloma-Paccaṇīya, in the first combination which is root-based (hetu-mūlaka), because five conditions are established by way of the positive, nineteen conditions come from the negative side. Thus...
478:
In the remaining root-based combinations, the conditions remaining from those established by way of the positive (anuloma) come by way of the negative (paccaṇīya). In this Anuloma-Paccaṇīya, although many conditions are established by way of the positive, it should be understood that they come only one by one by way of the negative. Just as in the root-based (hetu-mūlaka), all this arrangement in the object-based (ārammaṇādi-mūlaka) and others should be understood accordingly.

## Commentary on Anuloma-Paccaṇīya

## Commentary on Paccaṇīya-Anuloma

In Paccaṇīya-Anuloma as well, in the conditions with obtained counts such as "7 in root, 9 in object" in the positive, and "15 in non-root, 15 in non-object" in the negative, whichever condition is established as negative, the count should be understood by way of the ways (vāra) obtained from the negative of that condition which are similar to the ways obtained from the positive of the condition established as positive.

Indeed, in the negative, fifteen ways have been obtained in the non-root condition (na-hetu) as "15 in non-root"; in the positive, nine ways have been obtained in the object condition (ārammaṇa) as "9 in object". Among those ways, in the 15 ways stated in the non-root condition, whichever ways are similar to the 9 ways stated in the object condition, the count should be understood by way of those ways. Among those ways, the 9 ways stated in the object condition are similar to these 9 ways among the 15 ways stated in the non-root condition: wholesome for wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; unwholesome for unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate; and indeterminate for indeterminate, wholesome, and unwholesome. With reference to those 9 ways, it is stated: "9 in object in the non-root condition". In places such as "10 in predominance" (adhipati), the method is the same.

It should be understood that the ways stated in the positive count of conditions such as object, etc., are all obtainable even when compared with the non-root condition. The Pali text of those ways should be extracted in this manner: "A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of non-root condition and by way of object condition; having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, having performed the observance-day duty, one reflects on that gift, etc.; one reflects on states well-practiced in the past."

In the phrase "10 in predominance because of non-root condition", the ways that come in the positive analysis (Anuloma-vibhaṅga) should be extracted by way of the remaining predominance conditions, excluding the investigation-predominance (vīmaṃsādhipati). Thus...
479:
There are six categories of counting: 9, 10, 7, 3, 13, and 1. By means of these categories of counting, one should understand the calculation in all combinations of conditions such as the triple-root (ti-mūlaka) and so forth, within the methods starting with the non-root (na-hetu) as the base, by excluding the count of conditions with higher numbers along with those with lower numbers. This is first of all the general characteristic. However, this characteristic does not apply to all combinations of conditions. In the combination of certain conditions with others, where certain cases (vāra) are contradictory, those cases should be excluded, and the counting here should be understood by means of the remaining conditions.

In this case, "In the non-root condition and non-object condition, there are seven in predominance (adhipati)," the three cases obtained by the power of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati)—namely, wholesome to unwholesome, indeterminate to wholesome, and indeterminate to unwholesome—are contradictory. Why? Because it is stated as "non-object condition" (na-ārammaṇa-paccaya). Therefore, excluding those three cases, by the method of conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati) alone, seven cases should be understood here: "wholesome to wholesome, to indeterminate, to wholesome and indeterminate; unwholesome to unwholesome, to indeterminate, to unwholesome and indeterminate; indeterminate to indeterminate." Even those, because of the statement "non-root condition," should be understood by the power of the remaining predominances, excluding investigation-predominance (vīmaṃsādhipati). Thus, in all places, the counting should be understood by the power of conditions with lower counts and by the power of non-contradictory counts.

Furthermore, when certain conditions are established by way of the negative method (paccaṇīya), those conditions which do not stand by way of the analytical method (anuloma) should also be known. For example—when the proximity condition (anantara) is established by way of the negative method, the contiguity (samanantara), repetition (āsevana), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata) conditions do not stand by way of the analytical method. When the conascence condition (sahajāta) is established by way of the negative method, the root (hetu), mutuality (aññamañña), resultant (vipāka), jhāna, path (magga), and association (sampayutta) conditions do not stand by way of the analytical method. When the dependence condition (nissaya) is established by way of the negative method, the base-prenascence condition (vatthu-purejāta) does not stand by way of the analytical method. When either the nutriment condition (āhāra) or the faculty condition (indriya) is established by way of the negative method, the root, mutuality, resultant, jhāna, path, and association conditions do not stand by way of the analytical method. When the object condition (ārammaṇa) is established by way of the negative method, the predominance (adhipati) and sufficing condition (upanissaya) do not stand by way of the analytical method; however, object-predominance and object-sufficing condition are not obtained. In this manner, having known what is obtained and what is not obtained among all conditions, the cases (vāra) should be extracted by the power of those that are obtained.
