Among those cases, in all methods such as the triple-root (ti-mūlaka) and so forth, the cases such as "seven in proximity" are only those cases obtained in the double-root (du-mūlaka). However, in the methods such as the sevenfold-root (satta-mūlaka), in the non-conascence condition, there are three in dependence (nissaya); by the power of prenascence (purejāta), there are three in base-dependence (vatthu-nissaya). In the kamma condition, there are two, only by the power of asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma).
480:
In the nutriment condition (āhāra), there is one explanation (visajjanā) by the power of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra). In the faculty condition (indriya), there is one by the power of the physical faculty (rūpindriya). Proceeding in order, the "three" in the dissociation condition (vippayutta) are the explanations starting from wholesome and ending with indeterminate by the power of post-nascence (pacchājāta). The "five" in the presence (atthi) and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions consist of those three, plus these two: "wholesome and indeterminate to indeterminate" and "unwholesome and indeterminate to indeterminate" by the power of post-nascence nutriment and post-nascence faculty. Furthermore, starting from the negative state of the post-nascence condition, the "one" in the presence and non-disappearance conditions should be understood as "indeterminate to indeterminate" by the power of nutriment and faculty. When the non-nutriment condition (na-āhāra) is taken, the "non-faculty condition" (na-indriya) should not be taken; likewise, when the non-faculty condition is taken, the "non-nutriment condition" should not be taken. Why? Because if those two are taken together, there is no case (vāra) to be counted. Also in jhāna, path, and so forth, when they are established by way of the negative method, without making a single analytical method (anuloma) from nutriment or faculty, it is stated at the end: "one in faculty, one in presence, one in non-disappearance; one in nutriment, one in presence, one in non-disappearance." The remaining meaning here is quite clear.

## The Root of Non-Root (Nahetumūlakaṃ)

In the methods starting with non-object as the base (nārammaṇamūlaka), etc., within the non-mutuality base (na-aññamaññamūlaka), "three in the root (hetu) for the non-mutuality condition" refers to wholesome and so forth which have mind-produced matter (citta-samuṭṭhāna). The "eight" in predominance (adhipati) refers to the remaining eight after excluding two cases—"wholesome to wholesome and indeterminate" and "unwholesome to unwholesome and indeterminate"—from the ten stated in the predominance condition. The "five" in conascence (sahajāta) refers to these two cases: "wholesome and indeterminate to indeterminate" and "unwholesome and indeterminate to indeterminate," together with the three stated in the root condition. The "seven" in dependence (nissaya) refers to these two cases: "indeterminate to wholesome" and "indeterminate to unwholesome" by the power of the base (vatthu), together with those five. The "three" in kamma are the same as those stated in the root condition. This same method applies to the remaining triads (tika). The "three" in predominance are the same as those stated below.

In the non-nutriment base (na-āhāramūlaka), excluding the three in mutuality (aññamañña), they should be understood in the nutriment condition by the power of the remaining mental factors (cetasika). As explained below, here too, only one of either non-nutriment or non-faculty is taken, not both together.
481:
In the root condition (hetu-paccaya) by way of the non-association condition (na-sampayutta-paccaya), the 'three' are the same as the answers already mentioned below under the non-mutuality condition (na-aññamañña-paccaya). In the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), the 'eight' are also those already mentioned. In the kamma condition with non-dissociation as the root (na-vippayutta-mūlaka), the 'five' are: wholesome volitions (cetanā), etc., which are conditions for co-nascent wholesome states, etc., and for resultants; and asynchronous wholesome and unwholesome volitions which are conditions for kamma-produced matter (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa). Thus, there are five. In the nutriment (āhāra) and faculty (indriya) conditions, the 'three' are similar to the answers in the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). In the absorption (jhāna) and path (magga) conditions, etc., the 'three' are similar to the root condition.

In the non-presence root method (no-atthi-mūlaka-naya), because there is no root condition (hetu-paccaya) called non-presence (no-atthi) or non-disappearance (no-avigata)—as it is invariably present—therefore, without taking that root condition, it is said 'nine in object' (nārammaṇe nava). Just like the root condition, other conditions possessing the characteristics of the presence condition (atthi-paccaya) do not stand here by way of the positive method (anuloma). The phrase 'two in kamma' (kamme dve), however, is stated by way of asynchronous kamma (nānākkhaṇika-kamma). By way of the negative method (paccanīya), all conditions are obtained. Although a condition may be obtained by way of the positive method, if it is not yet taken and the conditions preceding it are taken by way of the negative method, that condition receives its connection later. Therefore, it is said here: 'From non-presence condition, non-root condition... non-disappearance condition, two in kamma.' Why is that kamma condition not taken in its own place? Because when all the remaining conditions stand by way of the negative method, only the single kamma condition is obtained by way of the positive method. This is the characteristic in this negative-positive method (paccanīyānuloma): when all conditions stand by way of the negative method, whichever single condition is obtained by way of the positive method is mentioned later. In the phrase 'From non-presence condition, non-root condition... non-disappearance condition, nine in decisive support (upanissaya),' the method is the same. This, however, is stated by way of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). By this means, what should be obtained, what should not be obtained, what is mentioned before, and what is mentioned after in all places should be understood.

## Explanation of the Negative-Positive Method of the Investigation Chapter (Pañhāvāra).
## The Explanation of the Triad of Wholesome States (Kusala Tika) is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Triad of Feeling (Vedanā Tika)

In the Triad of Feeling, these states—the three feelings, matter (rūpa), and Nibbāna—are not obtained [as the subject of the triad]; therefore, it is taught as 'dependent on one aggregate, two aggregates,' etc. The phrase 'by way of pleasant feeling at the moment of rebirth-linking' is stated by way of rebirth-linking with roots (sahetuka-paṭisandhi). Painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is not obtained at rebirth-linking...
482:
Because painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is not obtained at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the inclusion of rebirth-linking is not made in the second section (vāra). In the third section, the phrase 'at the moment of rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhikkhane) is stated by way of rebirth-linking with roots. In this root condition and in the conditions following this, the rest of the collection of words can bring out the meaning exactly according to the Pali text. In all conditions, three sections each are stated. Therefore, it is said: 'three in root... three in non-disappearance.'

In the combination of conditions (paccaya-saṃsandana), however, because there is no resultant painful feeling with roots, it is said 'two in resultant' (vipāke dve) in the root-based method (hetu-mūlaka-naya). Even in combinations with predominance (adhipati) and other conditions, there are only two in resultant. Why? Because in resultants, there is no predominance, absorption (jhāna), or path (magga) for painful feeling. In whichever conditions two sections are obtained in resultant when combined, only two are obtained in those conditions when combined with resultant.

In the negative method (paccanīya), in the non-prenascence condition (na-purejāta-paccaya), two sections occur because painful feeling is absent in the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi) and at the time of rebirth-linking. In the non-dissociation condition (na-vippayutta-paccaya) also, only two occur because painful feeling is absent in the formless realm. The conditions such as co-nascence (sahajāta), etc., which encompass all mental states, diminish in this negative method. Why? Because a state associated with feeling cannot arise without co-nascence and other conditions depending on a state associated with feeling, and because it arises only by excluding the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya).

In the combination of conditions, the word 'one' (ekaṃ) in non-prenascence is stated with reference to the mental aggregates associated with rootless neutral feeling (ahetuka-adukkhamasukha-vedanā) in the formless realm and at the time of rebirth-linking. In non-kamma (na-kamma), the word 'two' (dve) is stated by way of volition associated with rootless functional (ahetuka-kiriya) consciousness. Indeed, rootless functional volitions associated with those feelings arise depending on states associated with pleasant feeling and neutral feeling. In the non-resultant dyad (na-vipāka-duka) with non-root condition as the base, the method is the same. In non-dissociation (na-vippayutta), the word 'one' (ekaṃ) is stated by way of mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) in the formless realm. By this means, the way of counting in all combinations of conditions should be understood.

25-37. In the positive-negative method (anuloma-paccanīya), only the conditions obtained in the negative method of conditions stand as negative. In the negative-positive method (paccanīyānuloma), all conditions such as co-nascence, etc., which encompass all mental states, stand only as positive, not as negative. However, because there is no predominance (adhipati) for rootless consciousness (ahetuka-cittuppāda), the predominance condition does not stand as positive. In the dependence chapter (paṭicca-vāra), etc., the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is simply not obtained as positive, and thus it diminishes. Those conditions which are obtained here as positive, together with those obtained as negative...
483:
They are also to be applied inversely. In those associated conditions, there are only three types of section-delimitations: three, two, and one. These section-delimitations should be noted accordingly in all conditions. The method of explanation for feelings stated in the *Paṭiccavāra* (Section on Dependent Origination) is the same for the *Sahajātavāra* (Section on Conascence) and so on.

In the *Pañhāvāra* (Section on Investigation), however, "to the associated aggregates" (*sampayuttakānaṃ khandhānaṃ*) means to the aggregates associated with that state, either by way of those roots (*hetu*) or by way of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and so on (meaning it is a condition by way of root condition).

"For one who is remorseful" (*vippaṭisārissa*) refers first to one who has mental unease regarding acts of giving and so on, thinking, "Why did I do this? I have done poorly; it would have been better if I had not done it" (thus *domanassa* or displeasure arises). In the case of the decline of *jhāna*, it refers to one who has mental unease thinking, "My *jhāna* has declined; I have indeed suffered a great loss" (thus *domanassa* arises). "Delusion arises" (*moho uppajjati*) refers to delusion associated with aversion (*dosa*). Likewise, "taking delusion as an object" (*mohaṃ ārabbha*) also refers to delusion associated with aversion.

"The life-continuum associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for the life-continuum associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" means the posterior life-continuum (*piṭṭhibhavaṅga*) known as registration (*tadārammaṇa*) is a condition for the original life-continuum (*mūlabhavaṅga*) (by way of proximity condition). "For emergence" (*vuṭṭhānassa*) refers to either registration or the life-continuum. In fact, both registration and life-continuum are called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) because they emerge from wholesome or unwholesome impulsion (*javana*). In the phrase "functional consciousness is a condition for emergence" (*kiriyaṃ vuṭṭhānassa*), the same method applies. "Fruition is a condition for emergence" (*phalaṃ vuṭṭhānassa*) means fruition consciousness is a condition for the life-continuum. Indeed, by means of the life-continuum, one is said to have emerged from fruition attainment (*phala-samāpatti*). In other places where "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) appears later, the same method should be understood.

"Aggregates associated with painful feeling" (*dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā khandhā*) refers to unwholesome aggregates associated with displeasure (*domanassa*). "For emergence associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" (*adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttassa vuṭṭhānassa*) refers to either the adventitious life-continuum (*āgantukabhavaṅga*) known as registration, or the original life-continuum associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*). If, however, the original life-continuum is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) and there is no cause for the arising of registration, then an unwholesome resultant (*akusala-vipāka*) investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) having neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises in an object other than the object of the impulsion (*javana*). That unwholesome resultant is also called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) because it emerges from the impulsion. The expositions (*niddesa*) of conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so on have clear meanings. There is nothing here that cannot be understood by the method stated below; therefore, it should be well noted.

Now, in order to show the count by summarizing all the sections (*vāra*) obtained in each condition, it is stated: "Three in root condition" (*hetuyā tīṇi*) and so on. Therein, all...
484:
In the pure section (*suddha-vāra*), three answers (*vissajjanā*) should be understood by way of the three terms such as "associated with pleasant feeling" (*sukhāya vedanāya sampayutto*). In the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), there are nine answers starting with one term as the root and ending with another term. In the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), there are five: three unmixed answers by way of conascence-predominance (*sahajātādhipati*), and by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), there are two: "a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling" and "a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling." These two should not be counted separately. However, these two answers: "a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" and "a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling" should be counted. Thus, there are five in predominance. In the proximity (*anantara*) and contiguity (*samanantara*) conditions, there are seven: a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for two states; likewise, a state associated with painful feeling for two; and a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling for all three. Thus, there are seven.

In the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), there are nine: a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling by all three types of decisive support; for a state associated with painful feeling by way of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) only; and for a state associated with equanimity by all three types of decisive support. A state associated with painful feeling is a condition for a state associated with painful feeling by way of proximity and natural decisive support; for a state associated with pleasant feeling by way of natural decisive support; and for a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling in two ways. A state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling by all three ways; likewise for a state associated with pleasant feeling by all three ways; and for a state associated with painful feeling by way of proximity and natural decisive support. Thus, there are nine. By way of the varieties of conditions, there are twenty decisive supports: nine natural decisive supports, seven proximity decisive supports, and four object decisive supports. In this Triad of Feeling, the prenascence (*purejāta*) and postnascence (*pacchājāta*) conditions are cut off. This is because mental states (*arūpa-dhamma*) do not condition mental states by way of prenascence or postnascence conditions.

In the kamma condition (*kamma-paccaya*), there are eight: a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling in both ways (conascence and asynchronous); for a state associated with painful feeling by way of asynchronous kamma (*nānākkhaṇika*) only; and likewise for the other (neither-painful-nor-pleasant). A state associated with painful feeling is a condition for a state associated with painful feeling in both ways; there is no kamma condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling; and for the other (neither-painful-nor-pleasant) by way of asynchronous kamma only. A state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling in both ways; and for the other states associated with pleasant and painful feelings by way of asynchronous kamma. Thus, there are eight. By way of the varieties of conditions, there are eleven kamma conditions: eight asynchronous and three conascence. Just like prenascence and postnascence, the dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*) is also cut off here. This is because mental states do not become dissociation conditions for mental states. In the absence (*natthi*) and disappearance (*vigata*) conditions, the seven are similar to the proximity condition. Thus, there are five count-delimitations here: 3, 5, 7, 8, and 9. By way of these count-delimitations, when comparing conditions, one should understand the method of counting by removing the excess answers and the unobtainable answers in comparisons with lower counts.
485:
63-64. The object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is not obtained together with the root condition (hetu-paccaya); likewise, the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth are also not obtained. In the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya), the 'two' refers to the remaining two terms (the term associated with pleasant feeling and the term associated with neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling), excluding the term associated with painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Indeed, there is no such thing as a root (hetu) associated with painful feeling that is a predominance; therefore, that root associated with painful feeling is excluded because it is not obtained. The same method applies to the remaining two combinations. Thus, in the root-based (hetu-mūlaka) section, there are only two numerical limits; by means of those numbers, six combinations (ghaṭanā) are taught.

Among those six, the first combination is taught by way of non-resultant (avipāka) roots that are dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta) and without predominance (nirādhipati). The second is taught by way of those same resultant (vipāka) states. The third and fourth are taught by way of those same states associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), both non-resultant and resultant. The fifth is taught by way of non-resultant non-delusion (amoha) with predominance (sādhipati). The sixth is taught by way of resultant non-delusion with predominance. Alternatively, the first is taught by way of all roots; the second by way of all resultant roots; the third by way of all non-delusion roots; the fourth by way of all resultant non-delusion roots; the fifth by way of all non-delusion with predominance; and the sixth by way of all resultant non-delusion with predominance.

In the object-based (ārammaṇa-mūlaka) section, the 'four' in the predominance condition means that by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling, and for a state associated with neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling; and a state associated with neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling is a condition for a state associated with neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, and for a state associated with pleasant feeling—thus there are four. In the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) also, four are taught by way of object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya). In this object-based section, there is only one combination (ghaṭanā). In the predominance-based (adhipati-mūlaka) section and others, one should understand the comparison of conditions, combinations, and numbering by carefully considering what is obtained and what is not obtained, according to the method already stated below.

83-87. In the negative method (paccanīya-naya), just as in the method stated for the Triad of Wholesome States (Kusala-ttika), the conditions are extracted from the analytical method (anuloma), and by way of the chapters (vāra) obtained in that extraction, and by way of counting in the negative method, "nine in non-root" (na-hetuyā nava) is shown for nine chapters in all conditions. Those chapters should be shown by extracting the Pali text according to the method: "A state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with pleasant feeling by way of non-root condition; having given a gift with a mind associated with pleasant feeling..." and so forth, by way of the nine answers (vissajjanā) starting with one term as the root and ending with one term. In the comparison of conditions, the 'eight' in non-root condition... up to... non-decisive support (na-upanissaya) should be understood by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya). This is because weak kamma is not a decisive support (upanissaya) for a resultant. It is a condition merely by way of asynchronous kamma condition. The remaining answers in this analytical-negative (anuloma-paccanīya) and negative-analytical (paccanīya-anuloma) methods can be counted according to the method stated below, by way of the chapters obtained in the combination of those respective conditions; therefore, they are not elaborated.

## 3. Commentary on the Triad of Resultants (Vipāka-ttika-vaṇṇanā)

1-23. In the Triad of Resultants, 13 chapters (vāra) are taught in the root condition (hetu-paccaya) as: "Dependent on a resultant state, a resultant state arises through root condition." To show the count of these chapters in brief, it is said: "13 in root" (hetuyā terasa). The same method applies to the 5 chapters in the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and so forth. Thus, there are six numerical limits here: 13, 5, 9, 7, 3, and 2. In the comparison of conditions by way of these numerical limits, the method of counting should be understood just as stated below (in the Triad of Wholesome States).

24-52. In the negative (paccanīya) section also, 10 chapters are taught in the non-root condition (na-hetu-paccaya) as: "Dependent on a resultant state, a resultant state arises through non-root condition." To show the count of these chapters in brief, it is said: "10 in non-root" (na-hetuyā dasa). The same method applies to the 5 chapters in the non-object condition (na-ārammaṇa) and so forth. Thus, there are eight numerical limits here: 10, 5, 13, 12, 2, 1, 9, and 3. In the comparison of conditions by way of these numerical limits, the method of counting should be understood in detail just as stated below. The Pali text itself is abbreviated; however, the analytical-negative (anuloma-paccanīya) and negative-analytical (paccanīya-anuloma) methods should be understood by comparing them by way of the chapters of these obtained numerical limits.

The Co-nascence Chapter (Sahajāta-vāra) follows the same course (Pali structure) as this Dependent Chapter (Paṭicca-vāra). The Condition Chapter (Paccaya-vāra), Support Chapter (Nissaya-vāra), Conjoined Chapter (Saṃsaṭṭha-vāra), and Associated Chapter (Sampayutta-vāra) can be understood in meaning according to the Pali text itself.

In the Investigation Chapter (Pañhā-vāra), "When wholesome and unwholesome states have ceased" (kusalākusale niruddhe) means when this wholesome state occurring by way of insight (vipassanā) and this unwholesome state occurring by way of attachment (rāga) and so forth have ceased. "A resultant arises as registration" (vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjati) means a sense-sphere resultant arises in the role of registration (tadārammaṇa). Those teachers who say, "At the end of insight-impulsions (vipassanā-javana) and at the end of impulsions associated with doubt or restlessness, registration does not occur," should be refuted by this canonical Pali sequence. The statement, "Wholesome infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-kusala) is a condition for functional infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-kiriya) by way of object condition," is said by way of an Arahant who, having attained Arahantship, enters the attainments (samāpatti) that were not previously attained, in reverse order (paṭiloma). By this means, the meaning should be understood by carefully investigating the Pali text in all answers (vissajjanā).

In the sections such as "7 in root, 9 in object, 10 in predominance," etc., it is by way of co-nascence-predominance (sahajātādhipati), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), co-nascence-support (sahajāta-nissaya), base-decisive-support (purejāta-nissaya), and proximity-decisive-support (anantarūpanissaya)...
487:
By way of object-strong-dependence, natural-strong-dependence, conascent dissociation, and prenascent and postnascent dissociation, wherever and in whatever manner as many answers (vissajjanā) as are obtained, in those places and in that manner, all those should be noted. Similarly, in the negative sections (paccaṇīya), etc., the extraction of the turns (vāra) by way of the positive (anuloma), the counting by way of the negative of the turns obtained from the positive, the comparison of conditions, and in the positive-negative and negative-positive, as well as in the pure sections (suddhika), the number of turns obtained in the root-condition (hetu-mūlaka), etc., which occur by way of comparison, and the non-obtaining of those that are not obtained—all should be understood in the same manner as stated below (in the Kusala Triad). Just as in this Resultant Triad (everything should be understood in the same manner as stated below), so too in the Triads and Dyads that follow. Indeed, the Great Book of Paṭṭhāna is endless and immeasurable in its Pali text alone. Even for a person with a very long life who strives to explain the meaning according to the sequence of words of that Paṭṭhāna, the lifespan would not be sufficient. It is not that the meaning cannot be known if one explains a part of that Paṭṭhāna and shows the rest by way of method (it can indeed be known). Therefore, after this Resultant Triad, without saying even this much, I will state only those words that must definitely be said because they have different aspects not yet mentioned below in the remaining Triads and Dyads. As for the words that I will pass over without mentioning, they should be understood according to the method of the Pali text. 

## Explanation of the Resultant Triad (Vipāka-ttika-vaṇṇanā)

## 4. Explanation of the Clung-to Triad (Upādinnattika-vaṇṇanā)

In the Question Section (Pañhāvāra) of the Clung-to and Favorable to Clinging Triad, the statement "the base is a condition for the clung-to and favorable to clinging aggregates by way of prenascent condition" is said with reference to the course of existence (pavatti). At the moment of rebirth-linking, however, that base is not a prenascent condition.

In the passage "Edible food that is clung-to and favorable to clinging is a condition for the body that is clung-to and favorable to clinging by way of nutriment condition," what is called "edible food that is clung-to and favorable to clinging" is the nutritive essence (ojā) existing within the kamma-produced matter. "For the body that is clung-to and favorable to clinging" means it is a condition by way of nutriment condition for that very physical body of kamma-produced matter. Just as the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) assists the kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of guarding and supporting, (that nutritive essence) also assists by way of supporting, not by way of producing (janaka). The nutritive essence in the bodies of living creatures such as frogs, which exists in the bodies of snakes, etc., that have swallowed them...
488:
...is said to be related by way of nutriment condition; that statement should not be accepted. Indeed, it is true that the nutritive essence in a living body cannot fulfill the function of being a nutriment condition for another body. In the phrase "to the not clung-to but cluable body" (anupādinnupādāniyassa kāyassa), however, the nutriment condition is obtained also by way of production (janaka). In the Pali "to the clung-to and cluable and to the not clung-to but cluable" (upādinnupādāniyassa ca anupādinnupādāniyassa ca), it is said to be related by way of nutriment condition to one group of clung-to and cluable matter by way of support, and to another group of not clung-to but cluable matter by way of production; or else, it is said to be related to both by way of support only. When two nutriments become a single condition, they are only supporters, not producers. The remaining meaning here should be understood by carefully looking at the Pali text itself.

## Commentary on the Upādinna Triad.

## 5-22. Commentary on the Saṅkiliṭṭha Triad and Others.

In the Saṅkiliṭṭhasaṅkilesika Triad, the entire arrangement should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Kusala Triad.

In the Vitakka Triad, regarding the statement "preliminary work (parikamma) for the knowledge of beings passing away according to kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa)," the preliminary work of the divine-eye (dibbacakkhu) superknowledge is itself the preliminary work for the sake of producing that yathākammūpagañāṇa. This statement is made with reference to the preliminary work at the time of using the already arisen yathākammūpagañāṇa. The remaining collection of words here yields the meaning according to the Pali text itself.

In the Pīti Triad, the statement "the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) accompanied by joy relates to the life-continuum accompanied by equanimity by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya)" is said by way of the registration (tadārammaṇa) bhavaṅga and the original (mūla) bhavaṅga. All remaining meanings here should be understood by way of the Pali text itself.

In the Dassana Triad, in the Pali passages such as "lust to be abandoned by vision arises," the state to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (dassana) arises in the continuity of a worldling (puthujjana). The state to be abandoned by the three higher paths (bhāvanā) arises also in the continuity of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). In this way, it should be understood that the lower states to be abandoned do not arise in the continuity of the respective higher persons. The state to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry is not related to the state to be abandoned by the three higher paths by even a single condition. The remaining meaning here should be understood by following the Pali text and by way of the characteristics stated in the Kusala Triad.

In the Dassanenapahātabbahetuka Triad, the analysis of states having roots to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, etc., should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Section on Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa). Delusion (moha) accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) enters into the third clause because it lacks associated roots (sampayutta-hetu). Thus, in this...
489:
Those states that have roots to be abandoned by the path of vision (dassana) and the three higher paths (bhāvanā) are called states with roots to be abandoned (pahātabbahetuka). Those states that do not have such roots to be abandoned are called states with roots to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development (nevadassanena nabhāvanāya pahātabbahetuka). Having understood this classification of pahātabbahetuka, the remaining arrangement should be understood according to the characteristics already shown in the Dassanenapahātabba Tika and the Kusala Tika.

In the Ācayagāmi Tika, within the Paṭiccavāra and Saṃsaṭṭhavāra, the forward order (anuloma-naya) is just the same as in the Kusala Tika. The remaining answers (vissajjanā) and the method of counting (gaṇanā) proceed according to the Pali text itself.

In the Sekkha Tika, an Asekkha state does not assist a Sekkha state by any condition. However, a Sekkha state assists an Asekkha state by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya). The remaining meaning in this Tika is just as in the Pali text. It is the same in the Paritta Tika.

In the Parittārammaṇa Tika, "volition with immeasurable object" (appamāṇārammaṇā cetanā) refers to the change-of-lineage volition (gotrabhū-cetanā) of Sekkha individuals; it can also be said to be reviewing volition (paccavekkhaṇā-cetanā). "Resultants with limited objects" (vipākānaṃ parittārammaṇānaṃ) refers to resultant states that arise by taking kamma as an object at the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), or by taking objects such as visible forms through the power of eye-consciousness etc. during the course of existence (pavatti), or by taking a limited object grasped by the impulsion (javana) through the power of registration (tadārammaṇa). Those teachers who say, "There is no rebirth-linking with change-of-lineage consciousness," should be refuted by this Pali text. The remaining meaning in this Tika should be understood according to the method in the Pali text. The Hīna Tika is similar to the Saṅkiliṭṭha Tika.

In the Micchatta Tika, a wrongly fixed state (micchattaniyata) does not assist a rightly fixed state (sammattainiyata), nor does a rightly fixed state assist a wrongly fixed state by any condition. In either wrongly fixed or rightly fixed states, there is no state devoid of the conascent predominance condition (sahajātādhipati-paccaya). In rightly fixed states, the object-prenascence condition (ārammaṇapurejāta-paccaya) is never present. In wrongly fixed states, however, some object-prenascence condition may exist. Fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) can arise by taking an unfixed (aniyata) mind as an object. Taking other fixed states as an object, a fixed state does not arise. No state arises by giving weight to a wrongly fixed state. A wholesome state (kusala) does not assist a wrongly fixed state by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). The remaining meaning in this Tika should be understood according to the method stated in the Pali text.

In the Maggārammaṇa Tika, in the forward order of the Paṭiccavāra, there is no resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya). In the kamma condition of this Tika, the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) is not obtained. Likewise, it is not obtained in the Uppanna Tika and the Atīta Tika. In the negative order (paccanīya-vāra), the phrase "rootless state with the path as object" (ahetukaṃ maggārammaṇaṃ) is said with reference to the rootless adverting consciousness (āvajjana) which has the path as its object. The remaining meaning in this Tika should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text.
490:
In the Uppanna Tika and the Atīta Tika, the Paṭiccavāra and other sections do not exist; only the question section (pañhāvāra) is obtained. Why? Because the Paṭiccavāra and other sections occur only for conascent (sahajāta) and prenascence (purejāta) conditions. These Tikas, however, consist of states mixed with the past and future. In this Uppanna Tika, conditions that belong to the proximity (anantara) category are also not obtained. Why? Because in the Uppanna Tika, past states do not exist. In this Uppanna Tika, these two states—the arisen (uppanna) and the not arisen (anuppanna)—do not serve as conditions for these two—the arisen and the not arisen—by any condition. However, these two—the not arisen (anuppanna) and the about to arise (uppādī)—serve as conditions for the arisen state by way of two conditions: object (ārammaṇa) and decisive support (upanissaya). The rest here should be understood according to the method presented in the Pali text.

In the Atīta Tika, a present state does not serve as a condition for past and future states, nor does a past or future state serve as a condition for past and future states by any condition. Nibbāna, however, is not obtained in either of these two Tikas, neither as a condition nor as a conditionally arisen state. The rest here also should be understood according to the method presented in the Pali text.

In the Ajjhatta Tika, the internal-external (ajjhattabahiddhā) term is not taken. Both those groups called internal and external do not together become conditions, nor do they become conditionally arisen. Therefore, it should be understood that the color of a mustard seed placed on the palm of the hand does not become a single object together with the color of the palm. Just as with the internal-external term, in this Ajjhattārammaṇa Tika, the internal-external object (ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇa) term is not obtained. The rest proceeds according to the Pali text.

In the Sanidassana Tika also, the meaning should be taken only by the power of the Pali text. The method of counting (gaṇanā) here should also be understood by summarizing the sections (vāra) that appear in the Pali text and by comparing them in the comparison of conditions according to the method mentioned below.

## Commentary on the Tika-paṭṭhāna in the Dhamma-anuloma.

## 2. Commentary on the Duka-paṭṭhāna

In the Duka-paṭṭhāna also, the answers to the questions and the method of counting in all the Dukas should be understood according to the method presented in the Pali text. However, here the answers for the Sahetuka Duka and the Hetusampayutta Duka are similar to the answer for the Hetu Duka. Likewise, the answers for the Hetucevasahetuka Duka and the Hetucevahetusampayutta Duka, as well as the answers for the Sappaccaya Duka and the Saṅkhata Duka, are also similar (to the Hetu Duka). The statement that "this Duka should be treated like the Sappaccaya Duka" was made (by the compilers) because, just as a conditioned state (sappaccaya) cannot be associated with an unconditioned state (appaccaya), so also a conditioned state (saṅkhata) cannot be associated with an unconditioned state (asaṅkhata). The Sārammaṇa Duka, the Cittasampayutta Duka, and the Cittasaṃsaṭṭha Duka also have answers that are similar to each other. The Āsava, Ogha, and Yoga groups (gocchaka) are also the same...
491:
Just as it is impossible to combine the unconditioned (appaccaya) with the conditioned (sappaccaya), it is also impossible to combine the conditioned (saṅkhata) with the unconditioned (asaṅkhata); therefore, it is said (by the commentators). The Sārammaṇa-duka, Cittasampayutta-duka, and Cittasaṃsaṭṭha-duka also have identical explanations (vissajjanā). Similarly, the Āsava-gocchaka, Ogha-gocchaka, and Yoga-gocchaka are also identical. Indeed, these three groups have identical explanations among themselves. Furthermore, the Lokiya-duka, Sāsava-duka, Saṃyojaniya-duka, Ganthaniya-duka, Nīvaraṇiya-duka, Parāmaṭṭha-duka, and Saṅkilesika-duka, as well as the Āsavavippayutta-sāsava-duka, Saṃyojanavippayutta-saṃyojaniya-duka, Ganthavippayutta-ganthaniya-duka, Nīvaraṇavippayutta-nīvaraṇiya-duka, Parāmāsavippayutta-parāmaṭṭha-duka, Kilesavippayutta-saṅkilesika-duka, Pariyāpanna-duka, and Sauttara-duka—these dyads also have identical explanations.

The Kilesa-duka is similar to the Saṃyojana-duka. The Saṅkiliṭṭha-duka, Kilesasampayutta-duka, Nīvaraṇasampayutta-duka, Dassanenapahātabba-duka, and Saraṇa-duka are also identical. Similarly, the Kilesā-ceva-saṅkiliṭṭha-duka, Nīvaraṇā-ceva-nīvaraṇasampayutta-duka, and Kilesā-ceva-kilesasampayutta-duka are also identical. In this way, it should be understood that the explanations for all dyads that are identical in meaning are themselves identical. However, in the entire Paṭṭhāna, the Kenaciviññeyya-duka is not found. In dyads such as the Āsavā-ceva-āsavasampayutta-duka, Saṃyojanā-ceva-saṃyojanasampayutta-duka, Ganthā-ceva-ganthasampayutta-duka, Nīvaraṇā-ceva-nīvaraṇasampayutta-duka, and Kilesā-ceva-saṅkiliṭṭha-duka, the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya) and the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) are not found. In the Nahetu-sahetuka-duka and Nahetu-ahetuka-duka, the root condition (hetu-paccaya) does not exist. In the Hetū-ceva-hetusampayutta-duka, Āsavā-ceva-āsavasampayutta-duka, and Ganthā-ceva-ganthasampayutta-duka, the non-root condition (na-hetu), non-jhāna condition (na-jhāna), and non-path condition (na-magga) are not found. However, in the Saṃyojanā-ceva-saṃyojanasampayutta-duka, Nīvaraṇā-ceva-nīvaraṇasampayutta-duka, Kilesā-ceva-kilesasampayutta-duka, and Kilesā-ceva-saṅkiliṭṭha-duka, the non-root condition (na-hetu) can be found by virtue of the delusion (moha) associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca), but the non-jhāna and non-path conditions are not found. Thus, by investigating the conditions that are available and not available in all dyads, the number of turns (vāra) should be understood according to the Pāḷi text.

## Commentary on the Dyad Patthana (Duka-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā).

## 3. Commentary on the Dyad-Triad Patthana (Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)

In the Dyad-Triad Patthana (Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna), the teaching is given in brief by extracting the set of questions (pañhā-mattu-ddhāra) as follows: "Dependent on a wholesome state which is a root, a wholesome state which is a root arises through the root condition."
492:
The teaching has been given. The detailed explanation should be stated in the manner of: "Dependent on wholesome non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa) and non-delusion (amoha) arise," and so forth. Even if that detail is not stated here, it can be understood by the method shown below; therefore, not even a single condition is mentioned for a single term. It should be understood that the teaching which was given in brief was presented in this way.

Indeed, by combining the wholesome term with the Root Dyad (Hetu-duka), all the conditions that can be obtained in the Dependent Section (Paṭicca-vāra) by way of the forward (anuloma) and reverse (paccanīya) methods have been shown. However, the forward-reverse (anuloma-paccanīya) and reverse-forward (paccanīya-anuloma) methods, as well as the Conascence Section (Sahajāta-vāra) and others, have not been shown. It was merely stated: "The detail should be expanded just like the Dependent Section." In the Question Section (Pañhā-vāra), without answering the questions, only the extraction of questions (pañhuddhāra) was performed, and the conditions obtainable only by way of the forward and reverse methods were shown. Just as the wholesome term was combined with the Root Dyad, so too should the unwholesome and indeterminate terms be combined with the Root Dyad to explain the Root-Wholesome Dyad-Triad (Hetu-kusala-duka-tika) in detail.

Thereafter, twenty-one dyad-triads such as the Root-Feeling Dyad-Triad (Hetu-vedanā-duka-tika) were shown in the manner of: "A state associated with pleasant feeling which is a root," and so forth. Since what is called a 'root' (hetu) is neither visible-and-impingent (sanidassana-sappaṭigha) nor invisible-and-impingent (anidassana-sappaṭigha), the terms 'visible-and-impingent' and 'invisible-and-impingent' were not combined with the term 'root'. In this way, by combining the twenty-two triads with the Root Dyad according to what is obtainable, those triads were again combined with all the dyads, starting from the Associated-with-Root Dyad (Sahetuka-duka) and ending with the Saraṇa Dyad (Saraṇa-duka). In such combinations, it was stated that whichever term does not go together with another term is not found in the Pāḷi text itself. Thus, in this Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna, by combining twenty-two triads with one dyad, then twenty-two triads with another dyad, and another twenty-two with another, and so on, the twenty-two triads were combined with the obtainable dyad-terms in the one hundred dyads. Thus, the Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna was taught by taking the twenty-two triads and incorporating them into the one hundred dyads. In that Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna, wherever the Pāḷi text was summarized by showing the method, the detailed expansion of that Pāḷi text should be understood according to the method shown in those places.

## Commentary on the Dyad-Triad Patthana (Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā).
493:
## 4. Commentary on the Triple-Double Patthāna (Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)
In the Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna as well, the teaching is delivered solely by way of the mere enumeration of questions (pañhā-mattuddāra), such as: "Dependent on a wholesome state that is a root, a wholesome state that is a root arises by way of root-condition." In this teaching, just as previously (in the Dukatika-paṭṭhāna) the wholesome term was combined with the root-double and taught briefly in all chapters by way of all conditions, so too in this Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna, the root-term is combined with the wholesome triple and taught briefly in all chapters by way of all conditions. Just as the root-term is combined with the wholesome triple, similarly, the non-root-term is also combined with the wholesome triple, thus completing the Wholesome Triple Root-Double (Kusala-ttika-hetu-duka). Following that Wholesome Triple Root-Double, twenty-one Triple-Doubles such as the Feeling Triple Root-Double (Vedanā-ttika-hetu-duka) are shown by way of the method starting with "a root-state associated with pleasant feeling," and so on.

In this way, the root-double is combined with the twenty-two triples; then, all the doubles starting from the "with-root double" (sahetuka-duka) and ending with the "with-fault double" (saraṇa-duka) are combined with those same triples as far as they are applicable. In this Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna also, whatever term does not admit of combination is rejected in the Pali text itself. Thus, taking the hundred doubles and inserting them into the twenty-two triples, that which is called the Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna is taught. In that Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna also, whatever method the Pali text has been abbreviated by, that method should be understood in detail.

## Commentary on the Triple-Double Patthāna.

## 5. Commentary on the Triple-Triple Patthāna (Tikatika-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)
In the Tikatika-paṭṭhāna as well, the teaching is delivered briefly solely by way of the enumeration of questions (pañhuddāra), such as: "Dependent on a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling, a wholesome state associated with pleasant feeling arises by way of root-condition." In this Tikatika-paṭṭhāna, triples are inserted into triples, such as the wholesome triple with the feeling triple and others, and the feeling triple and others with the wholesome triple. Whatever term does not admit of combination with another term is excluded, and the chapters (vāra) and methods of counting (gaṇana-naya) are shown for all conditions only as they are applicable; therefore, those chapters and methods of counting should be understood by carefully investigating the Pali text. Just as the wholesome triple should be understood as combined with the feeling triple and others, and the feeling triple and others with that wholesome triple, so too each triple should be understood as combined with the remaining triples, and the remaining triples with each of those triples.

## Commentary on the Triple-Triple Patthāna.
494:
## 6. Commentary on the Double-Double Patthāna (Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)
In the Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna as well, the teaching is delivered briefly solely by way of the enumeration of questions (pañhuddāra), such as: "Dependent on a state that is a root and has a root (hetu-sahetuka), a state that is a root and has a root arises by way of root-condition." In that Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna, the root-double is combined with the "with-root double" (sahetuka-duka) and others, and the "with-root double" and others are combined with that root-double. Each double should be combined with the remaining doubles, and the remaining doubles with each of those doubles in due order. This so-called Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna is the text taught by "inserting doubles into doubles." Therefore, in this Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna, the combination of all doubles with all doubles should be understood. The Pali text, however, is merely an abbreviation. Whatever term does not admit of combination with another term is excluded from the teaching.

## Commentary on the Double-Double Patthāna.

By this much sequence of words—
The excellent Tikapaṭṭhāna and the supreme Dukapaṭṭhāna,
The Dukatika-paṭṭhāna and the Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna,
The Tikatika-paṭṭhāna and the Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna,
In the Anuloma (Positive), there are these six profound methods.—
This is shown by the verse stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). In the Dhammānuloma-paṭṭhāna, the six methods have been shown in detail. By way of conditions, however, among these six Patthānas, there are four methods each, such as Anuloma (Positive) and so on; thus, in one way, the Anuloma-paṭṭhāna should be understood as being adorned with twenty-four methods in total.

## 7-12. Commentary on the Negative Patthāna (Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)
Now, in order to show the Negative Patthāna (Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna), which receives its name because of the negativity of states by way of rejecting terms such as wholesome (kusala), the text begins: "Dependent on a state that is not wholesome (na-kusala), a state that is not wholesome arises by way of root-condition." In that Pali, by the phrase "dependent on a state that is not wholesome," the conditionality of the wholesome is prohibited. By the phrase "a state that is not wholesome arises," the arising of the wholesome is prohibited. Therefore, in this Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna, the answer is given by way of the method: "Dependent on one unwholesome or indeterminate aggregate, three unwholesome or indeterminate aggregates and mind-produced matter arise." The number of counts obtained for each respective condition is already stated in the Pali text. Those chapters which have similar answers are also shown therein. Therefore, all the meanings here [refer to] below...
495:
One should understand by investigating the Pāḷi text according to the method already stated. Just as in this (Dhammapaccanīya-tika-paṭṭhāna), so also in the Duka-paṭṭhāna, Duka-tika-paṭṭhāna, Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna, Tika-tika-paṭṭhāna, and Duka-duka-paṭṭhāna (it should be understood in the same way).

To this extent—

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the supreme Duka,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
These six methods in the Paccanīya are very profound—

this has been shown by the verse stated in the Commentary. In the Dhammapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna, six methods are pointed out. However, by way of conditions, since there are four methods such as Anuloma in each of these Paṭṭhānas, in one sense, it should be known as the Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna adorned with twenty-four methods.

## Commentary on the Paccanīya-paṭṭhāna.

## 13-18. Commentary on the Anulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna

Now, in order to show the Anulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna, which has received its name because of the 'positive-negative' nature of states—by way of not rejecting the conditioning state (paccaya-dhamma) among states such as wholesome (kusala) but rejecting the conditioned state's (paccayuppanna) nature of being wholesome etc.—the text beginning with "Dependent on a wholesome state, a non-wholesome state arises due to root-condition" etc. is commenced. In that Pāḷi, by the phrase "Dependent on a wholesome state", the status of the wholesome as a condition is permitted. By the phrase "a non-wholesome state arises", the arising of the wholesome itself is prohibited. Therefore, the answer is shown by the method: "Dependent on wholesome aggregates, mind-produced matter arises" etc.; all that Pāḷi text should be observed and well noted. Which explanation is similar to which, which explanation is obtained in which condition, and what the numerical limit of which explanations in which conditions is—all that has been shown in the Pāḷi text. Therefore, in this Anulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna, the Pāḷi text itself is the meaning. Just as in this case, so also in the Duka-paṭṭhāna etc.

To this extent—

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the supreme Duka,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
These six methods in the Anulomapaccanīya are very profound (has been shown).
496:
In the Dhammānulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna, six methods are pointed out by the verse stated in the Commentary. In this Dhammānulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna, by way of conditions, there are four methods such as Anuloma in each Paṭṭhāna; thus, in one sense, it should be known as the Anulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna adorned with twenty-four methods.

## Commentary on the Anulomapaccanīya-paṭṭhāna.

## 19-24. Commentary on the Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna

Now, in order to show the Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna, which has received its name because of the 'negative-positive' nature of states—by way of rejecting the conditioning state (paccaya-dhamma) among states such as wholesome but not rejecting the conditioned state's (paccayuppanna) nature of being wholesome etc.—the text beginning with "Dependent on a non-wholesome state, an unwholesome state arises due to root-condition" etc. is commenced. In that statement, by the Pāḷi "Dependent on a non-wholesome state", the status of the wholesome as a condition is prohibited. By the Pāḷi "an unwholesome state arises", the arising of the unwholesome is permitted.

Indeed, a non-wholesome state is either unwholesome or indeterminate (abyākata). There is no such thing as a wholesome state arising by making that unwholesome or indeterminate state a conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). Therefore, the teaching is given by way of the unwholesome and indeterminate. Therein, the answer to "Dependent on a non-wholesome state" should be understood as: "Dependent on one unwholesome aggregate, three aggregates arise". As for this question, "An indeterminate state arises due to root-condition", it has already been answered as: "Dependent on one resultant indeterminate or functional indeterminate aggregate, three aggregates and mind-produced matter arise". Thus, in all questions, there is the answer that is appropriate to the meaning of a question not yet answered, and the answer that is exactly as it appears in the Pāḷi text for a question already answered. The entire arrangement of the varieties of sections (vāra) and the counting of conditions in each Tika-duka should be understood exactly according to the method stated below.

To this extent—

The noble Tika-paṭṭhāna and the supreme Duka,
Duka-tika and Tika-duka,
Tika-tika and Duka-duka,
These six methods in the Paccanīyānuloma are very profound—

these have been shown by the verse stated in the Commentary. In the Dhammapaccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna, six methods are pointed out. In this Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna, by way of conditions, there are four methods such as Anuloma in each Paṭṭhāna; thus, in one sense, it should be known as the Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna adorned with twenty-four methods.

## Commentary on the Paccanīyānuloma-paṭṭhāna.
497:
Thus, in the four cycles starting with Dhammānuloma, there are 24 methods in each cycle, making 96 methods in total. Among these four cycles, excluding the Paccayanaya, this Great Treatise of the Samantapaṭṭhāna, adorned with these 24 methods through the sixfold methods of Tikas, Dukas, and so on in each Paṭṭhāna, should be understood. Some teachers, however, set forth what is called the Ārammaṇamātikā by the method starting with "Kusalārammaṇo dhammo akusalārammaṇo dhammo," and show the Ārammaṇapaṭṭhāna by the method starting with "Kusalārammaṇo dhammo kusalārammaṇassa dhammassa hetupaccayena paccayo," and also extract and show the Phassapaṭṭhāna by the power of Phassa and so on. Since the words of those teachers are found neither in the Pali nor in the Commentaries, they are not examined in this commentary. It should be understood that the explanation in this Paṭṭhāna has been made only according to the Pali as established in the Councils.

By this much sequence of words—

Wherein beings are greatly confused, falling into a state like a tangled ball of thread and so on, and cannot cross over the Saṃsāra, which is a forest of manifold sufferings.

The Teacher, who is skilled in the distinctions of conditions, who is revered in the world, explained in detail the seventh book of Abhidhamma called the Paṭṭhāna, based on the distinctions of phenomena such as wholesome (kusala), through various methods of counting, which is the range of the Buddha's knowledge, extremely subtle and profound.

The Buddha, who possessed well-established conclusion, has declared that book called the Paṭṭhāna. Without abandoning the tradition of the teachers who are disciples of the Vibhajjavādī Buddha, in this world of many dangers, I have composed this commentary with faith, without any obstacles, to clarify the meaning of that Paṭṭhāna.

This commentary, clarifying the meaning of the entire noble Paṭṭhāna, is now completed in about fourteen bhāṇavāras.

Just as this commentary has reached its conclusion, so may all the good intentions of the many people reach completion quickly.
498:
By this much—

The Lord, the God of gods, the Refuge of the world of beings, taught the Abhidhamma consisting of seven books to the devas in the deva world in the past.

This commentary on the whole of that Abhidhamma is now finished. It was completed by me for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma.

By the power of the merit gained from this work, may all beings, having known the Dhamma of the King of the True Dhamma which brings happiness, reach the supreme bliss of Nibbāna, which is free from sorrow and free from intense distress, through the pure and easy practice.

May the True Dhamma endure for a long time. May all beings be respectful towards the Dhamma. May the rain fall properly in due season.

Just as the good kings of old protected the multitude of beings, so may the King protect the subjects of this land righteously, like his own children.

## The Commentary on the Book of Paṭṭhāna is finished.
